MORASS

Pages 6-6

a marsh, fen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> low moor ground, which receives the waters from above without having any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to carry them off again. Somner derives the word from the Saxon merfe, "lake;" Salmatus from mare, "a collection of waters;" others from the German maraffe, "a muddy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>;" and others from marffe, of maricetum, à maricetis, i.e. rushes. See Draining, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, they have a peculiar kind of morasses called meller or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>-meller, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people dig their peat or turf for firing. See Moss.

MORAT

Pages 6-7
or MURLEN, a considerable town of Switzerland, Switzerland, capital of a bailiwick of the same name, belonging to the cantons of Bern and Friburg. It is seated on the lake Morat, on the road from Avenche to Bern, 10 miles west of Bern and 10 miles north-east of Friburg. The lake is about six miles long and two broad, and the country about it pleasant and well cultivated. The lakes of Morat and Neufchatel are parallel to each other, but the latter is more elevated, discharging itself by means of the river Broye into the lake of Neufchatel. According to M. de Luc, the former is 15 French feet above the level of Neufchatel lake; and both these lakes, as well as that of Biénnne, seem formerly to have extended considerably beyond their present limits, and from the position of the country appear to have been once united. Formerly the large fish named *filurus glanis*, or the saluth, frequented these lakes, but has not been caught in them for a long time past. The environs of this town and lake were carefully examined by Mr Cox, during his residence in Switzerland, who made several excursions across the lake to a ridge of hills situated betwixt it and Neufchatel. Here are many delightful prospects; particularly one from the top of Mount Vuilly, which, he says, is perhaps the only central spot from which the eye can at once comprehend the vast amphitheatre formed on one side by the Jura stretching from the environs of Geneva as far as Baffe, and, on the other, by that stupendous chain of snowy Alps which extend from the frontiers of Italy to the confines of Germany, and is lost at each extremity in the horizon. Morat is celebrated for the obstinate defence it made against Charles the Bold, duke of Burgundy, and for the battle which afterwards followed on the 22d of June 1476, where the duke was defeated, and his army almost entirely destroyed*. Not far from the town, and adjoining to the high road, there still remains a monument of this victory. It is a square building, filled with the bones of Burgundian soldiers who were slain at the siege and in the battle; the number of which appears to have been very considerable. There are several inscriptions in the Latin and German languages commemorating the victory. *MORATA, OLYMPIA FULVIA, an Italian lady, distinguished for her learning, was born at Ferrara, in 1436. Her father, after teaching the belles lettres in several cities of Italy, was made preceptor to the two young princes of Ferrara, the sons of Alphonso I. The uncommon abilities he discovered in his daughter determined him to give her all the advantages of education. Meanwhile the princes of Ferrara studying polite literature, it was judged expedient that she should have a companion in the same pursuit; and Morata being called, she was heard by the astonished courtiers to declaim in Latin, to speak Greek, and to explain the paradoxes of Cicero. Her father dying, she was obliged to return home to take upon her the management of family affairs, and the education of her brother and three sisters, both which she executed with the greatest diligence and success. In the mean time Andrew Grunthler, a young German physician, who had married her, and with him she went to Germany, taking her brother along with her, whom she instructed in the Latin and Greek tongues; and after staying a short time at Augsburg, went to Schweinfurt in Franconia, where her husband was born: but they had not been there long before that town was unhappily besieged and burnt; however, escaping the flames, they fled in the utmost distress to Hammelburg. This place they were also obliged to quit, and were reduced to the last extremities, when the elector Palatine invited Grunthler to be professor of physic at Heidelberg. He entered on his new office in 1554; but they no sooner began to taste the sweets of repose, than a disease, occasioned by the distresses and hardships they had suffered, seized upon Morata, who died in 1555, in the 29th year of her age; and her husband and brother did not long survive her. She composed several works, great part of which were burnt with the town of Schweinfurt; the remainder, which consist of orations, dialogues, letters, and translations, were collected and published under the title of *Olympiae Fulviae Moratae, formae doctissimae, et planè divinae, opera omnia que hactenus invenerit potuerint; quibus Caelli secundi curioris epiloce ac orationes acceperunt*.

MORAVIA

Pages 7-8

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, which rises in Bulgaria, runs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a> by Nilla, and falls into the Danube at Semendria, to the eastward of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>. Moravia, a marquisate of Germany, derives the name of *Mahern*, as it is called by the Germans, and of *Morava*, as it is called by the natives, from the river of that name, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Glatz, and passes through the middle of it. It is bounded to the south by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, to the north by Glatz and Silelia, to the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and to the east by Silelia and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; being about 120 miles in length and 120 in breadth. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is overrun with woods and mountains, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but much wholesome than in the low grounds, which are full of bogs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The mountains, in general, are barren; but the more <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> parts tolerably fertile, yielding corn, with plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, good saffron, and pasture. Nor is it altogether destitute of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and garden stuff. Moravia also abounds in horses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, sheep, and goats. In the woods and about the lakes there is plenty of wild fowl, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, venison, bees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, hares, foxes, wolves, beavers, &c. This country affords marble, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and vitriol, with mineral waters, and warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is imported. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, Morawa, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Morau, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, abound with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, crayfish, barbels, eels, perch, and many other sorts of fish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the inhabitants is a dialect of the Sclavonic, differing little from the Bohemian; but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and citizens speak German and French. Moravia was anciently inhabited by the Quadi, who were driven out by the Sclavi. Its kings, who were once powerful and independent, afterwards became dependent on, and tributary to, the German emperors and kings. At last, in the year 908, the Moravian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was parcelled out among the Germans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, and Hungarians. In 1086, that part of it properly called Moravia was declared a marquisate by the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> Henry IV. and united with Bohemia, to whose dukes and kings it hath ever since been subject. Though it is not very populous, it contains about 42 greater or walled <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 17 smaller or open towns, and 198 market towns, besides villages, &c. The states MORAVIA states of the country consist of the clergy, lords, knights, and burgesses; and the diets, when summoned by the regency, are held at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BRUNN">Brunn</a>. The marquisate is still governed by its own peculiar constitutions, under the direcTorum in publicis et cameralibus, and the supreme judicatory at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. It is divided into six circles, each of which has its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, and contributes to its sovereign about one third of what is exacted of Bohemia. Towards the expenses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> establishment of the whole Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> countries, its yearly quota is 1,856,492 florins. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> regiments of foot, one of cuirassiers, and one of dragoons, are usually quartered in it. Christianity was introduced into this country in the 9th century; and the inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome till the 15th, when they espoused the doctrine of John Huss, and threw off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>: but after the defeat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine, whom they had chosen king, as well as the Bohemians, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand II. re-established Popery; though there are still some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in Moravia. The bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLMUTZ">Olmutz</a>, who stands immediately under the pope, is at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> in this country. The supreme <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> jurisdiction, under the bishop, is vested in a confistory. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this country is inconsiderable. Of what they have, Brunn enjoys the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part. At <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGLAU">Iglau</a> and Trebix are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, &c. There are also some iron works and glasshouses in the country. The inhabitants of Moravia in general are open-hearted, not easy to be provoked or pacified, obedient to their masters, and true to their promises; but credulous of old prophecies, and much addicted to drinking, though neither such fots or bigots as they are represented by some geographers. The boors, indeed, upon the river Hank, are said to be a thievish, unpolished, brutal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. The sciences now begin to lift up their heads a little among the Moravians, the university of Olmutz having been put on a better footing; and a rising academy, with a learned <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, have been lately established there. MORAVIAN BRETHREN. See <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HERNHUTTERS">HERNHUTTERS</a>, and Unitas Fratrum.

MORAW

Pages 8-8
or MORAVA, a large river of Germany, which has its source on the confines of Bohemia and Silesia. It crosses all Moravia, where it waters Olmutz and Radisch, and receiving the Taya from the confines of Lower Hungary and Upper Austria, separates these two countries as far as the Danube, into which it falls.

MORBID

Pages 8-8

among physicians, signifies "diseased <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> corrupt;" a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied either to an unsound <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, or to those parts or humours that are affected by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>.

MORBUS COMITIALIS

Pages 8-8

a name given to the epilepsy; because <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> on any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the people were assembled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a> upon public business, any person suddenly seized with this disorder should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> was dissolved, and the business of the comitia, however important, was suspended. See Comitia.

MORDAUNT

Pages 8-8
CHARLES, earl of Peterborough, a celebrated commander both by sea and land, was the son of John Lord Mordaunt Viscount Avalon, and was born about the year 1638. In 1675 he succeeded his father in his honours and estate. While young he served under the admirals Torrington and Narborough in the Mediterranean against the Algerines; and in 1680 embarked for Africa with the earl of Plymouth, and distinguished himself at Tangier when it was besieged by the Moors. In the reign of James II. he voted against the repeal of the test act; and disliking the measures of the court, obtained leave to go to Holland to accept the command of a Dutch squadron in the West Indies. He afterwards accompanied the prince of Orange into this kingdom; and upon his advancement to the throne, was sworn of the privy-council, made one of the lords of the bedchamber to his majesty, also first commissioner of the treasury, and advanced to the dignity of earl of Monmouth. But in November 1692 he was dismissed from his post in the treasury. On the death of his uncle Henry earl of Peterborough in 1697, he succeeded to that title; and, upon the accession of Queen Anne, was invested with the commission of captain-general and governor of Jamaica. In 1725 he was sworn of the privy-council; and the same year declared general and commander in chief of the forces sent to Spain, and joint admiral of the fleet with Sir Cloudley Shovel, of which the year following he had the sole command. His taking Barcelona with a handful of men, and afterwards relieving it when greatly distressed by the enemy; his driving out of Spain the duke of Anjou, and the French army, which consisted of 25,000 men, though his own troops never amounted to 10,000; his gaining possession of Catalonia, the kingdoms of Valencia, Arragon, and the isle of Majorca, with part of Murcia and Castile, and thereby giving the earl of Galway an opportunity of advancing to Madrid without a blow; are astonishing instances of his bravery and conduct. For these important services his lordship was declared general in Spain by Charles III. afterwards emperor of Germany; and on his return to England he received the thanks of the house of lords. His lordship was afterwards employed in several embassies to foreign courts, installed knight of the garter, and made governor of Minorca. In the reign of George I. he was general of all the marine forces in Great Britain, in which post he was continued by King George II. He died in his passage to Lisbon, where he was going for the recovery of his health, in 1735. His lordship was distinguished by various shining qualities: for, to the greatest personal courage and resolution, he added all the arts and address of a general; a lively and penetrating genius; and a great extent of knowledge upon almost every subject of importance within the compass of ancient and modern literature; hence his familiar letters, inserted among those of his friend Mr Pope, are an ornament to that excellent collection.

MORE

Pages 8-10

SIR THOMAS, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England, the son of Sir John More, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, one of the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>, was born in the year 1480, in More in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">Milk</a>-street <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He was first sent to a school at St. Anthony's in Threadneedle Street; and afterward introduced into the family of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Moreton, who in 1497 sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. During his residence at the university he constantly attended the lectures of Linaere and Grocinus, on the Greek and Latin languages. Having in the space of about two years made considerable proficiency in academical learning, he came to New Inn in London, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; whence, after some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn, of which his father was a member. Notwithstanding his application to the law, however, being now about 20 years old, he was so bigotted to monkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, that he wore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> shirt next his skin, frequently fasted, and often slept on a bare plank. In the year 1503, being then a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he distinguished himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in opposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> for granting a subsidy and three fifteenths for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Henry VII.'s eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, Margaret, to the king of Scotland. The motion was rejected; and the king was so highly offended at this opposition from a beardless boy, that he revenged himself on Mr. More's father, by sending him, on a frivolous pretence, to the Tower, and obliging him to pay 100l. for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Being now called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he was appointed law reader at Furnival's inn, which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he held about three years; but about this time he also read a public lecture in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St. Lawrence, Old Jewry, upon St. Austin's treatise De civitate Dei, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. He had indeed formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of becoming a Franciscan friar, but was dissuaded from it; and, by the advice of Dr. Colet, married Jane, the eldest daughter of John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLT">Colt</a>, Esq., of Newhall in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. In 1508 he was appointed judge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London, was made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, and became very eminent at the bar. In 1516 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> in the retinue of Bishop Tonital, and Dr. Knight, who were sent by King Henry VIII. to renew the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the archduke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. On his return, Cardinal Wolsey would have engaged Mr. More in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and offered him a pension, which he refused. Nevertheless, it was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he accepted the place of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the requests, was created a knight, admitted of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and in 1520 made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the exchequer. About this time he built a house on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, at Chelsea, and married a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife. This wife, whose name was Middleton, and a widow, was old, ill tempered, and covetous; nevertheless Erasmus says, he was as fond of her as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she were a young maid. In the 14th year of Henry VIII. Sir Thomas More was made speaker of the house of commons; in which capacity he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to oppose the then powerful minister, Wolsey, in his demand of an oppressive subsidy; notwithstanding which, it was not long before he was made chancellor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, and was treated by the king with singular familiarity. The king having once dined with Sir Thomas at Chelsea, walked with him near an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> in the garden, with his arm round his neck. After he was gone, Mr. Roper, Sir Thomas's son-in-law, observed how happy he was to be so familiarly treated by the king: to which Sir Thomas replied, "I thank our lord, son Roper, I find his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> my very good lord indeed, and believe he doth as singularly favour me as any subject within this realm: howbeit, I must tell thee, I have no cause to be proud thereof; for if my head would win him a castle in France, it would not fail to go off." From this anecdote it appears, that Sir Thomas knew his grace to be a villain. In 1526 he was sent with Cardinal Wolsey and others, on a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> embassy to France, and in 1529 with Bishop Tonital to Cambrai. The king, it seems, was so well satisfied with his services on these occasions, that in the following year, Wolsey being disgraced, he made him chancellor; which seems the more extraordinary, when we are told that Sir Thomas had repeatedly declared his disapprobation of the king's divorce, on which the great defensor fidei was so positively bent. Having executed the office of chancellor about three years, with equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and integrity, he resigned the seals in 1533, probably to avoid the danger of his refusing to confirm the king's divorce. He now retired to his house at Chelsea; dismissed many of his servants; sent his children with their respective families to their own houses (for hitherto, he had, it seems, maintained all his children, with their families, in his own house, in the true style of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>; and spent his time in study and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>: but the capricious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> would not suffer him to enjoy his tranquillity. Though now reduced to a private station, and even to indigence, his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the legality of the king's marriage with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Boleyn was deemed of so much importance, that various means were tried to procure his approbation; but all persuasion proving ineffectual, he was, with some others, attainted in the house of lords of high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, for encouraging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Barton, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in her treasonable practices. His innocence in this affair appeared so clearly, that they were obliged to strike his name out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. He was then accused of other crimes, but with the same effect; till, refusing to take the oath enjoined by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of supremacy, he was committed to the Tower, and, after 15 months imprisonment, was tried at the bar of the King's Bench for high treason, in denying the king's supremacy. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> rested on the sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of Rich the solicitor general, whom Sir Thomas, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, sufficiently discredited; nevertheless the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> brought him in guilty, and he was condemned to suffer as a traitor. The merciful Harry, however, indulged him with simple decapitation; and he was accordingly beheaded on Tower hill, on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1535. His body, which was first interred in the Tower, was begged by his daughter Margaret, and deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of the church at Chelsea, where a monument, with an inscription written by himself, had been some time before erected. This monument with the inscription is still to be seen in that church. The same daughter, Margaret, also procured his head after it had remained 14 days upon London <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and placed it in a vault belonging to the Roper family, under a chapel adjoining to St. Dunstan's church in Canterbury. Sir Thomas More was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of some learning, and an upright judge; a very pious in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, yet cheerful, and even affectedly witty. witty (A). He wanted not sagacity, where religion was out of the question; but in that his faculties were so enveloped, as to render him a weak and credulous enthusiast. He left one son and three daughters; of whom Margaret, the eldest, was very remarkable for her knowledge of the Greek and Latin languages. She married a Mr Roper of Wellhall in Kent, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Sir Thomas More was published by Mr Hearne at Oxford in 1716. Mrs Roper died in 1544; and was buried in the vault of St Dunstan's in Canterbury, with her father's head in her arms. Sir Thomas was the author of various works, though his Utopia is the only performance that has survived in the esteem of the world; owing to the reft being chiefly of a polemic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: his answer to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> has only gained him the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of having the best knack of any man in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, at calling bad names in good Latin. His English works were collected and published by order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, in 1557; his Latin, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, in 1563, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, in 1566.

MOREA

Pages 10-10

formerly called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, to which it is joined by the isthmus of Corinth. Its form resembles a mulberry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and its name is derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of mulberry trees which it produces. It is about 180 miles in length, and 130 in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> fertile, except in the middle, where it is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and is watered by a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. It is divided into three provinces; Scarta, Belvedera, and Brizzio-di-Main. It was taken from the Turks by the Venetians in 1687; but they lost it again in 1715. The sanctae of the Morea resides at Modon. See GREECE and PELOPONNESUS.

MOREL

Pages 10-10

the name of several celebrated printers to the kings of France, who, like the Stephens, were also men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning. Frederic Morel, who was interpreter in the Greek and Latin tongues, as well as printer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, was heir to Valcofam, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> he had married.—He was born in Champagne, and he died in an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1583. His sons and grandsons trod in his steps; they distinguished themselves in literature, and maintained also the reputation which he had acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. The edition of St Gregory of Nyssa, by his son <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> Morel, is held in great estimation by the learned. Morel, Frederic, son of the preceding, and still more celebrated than his father, was professor and interpreter to the king, and printer in ordinary for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, Latin, and French languages. He was so devoted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, that when he was told his wife was at the point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he would not stir till he had finished the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> which he had begun. Before it was finished, he was informed that she was actually dead: I am sorry for it (replied he coldly), she was an excellent woman. This printer acquired great reputation from the works which he published, which were very numerous and beautifully executed. From the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> in the king's library, he published several treatises of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, Theodore, St Cyril; and he accompanied them with a translation. His edition of the works of Cæcumenius and Aretas, in 2 vols., folio, is much esteemed. In short, after distinguishing himself by his knowledge in the languages, he died <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 27, 1630, at the age of 78. His sons and grandsons followed the same profession. Morel, William, regius professor of Greek, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the king's printing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Paris, died 1564. He composed a Dictionnaire Græco-Latin François, which was published in quarto in 1622, and some other works which indicate very extensive learning. His editions of the Greek authors are exceedingly beautiful. This great scholar, who was of a different family from the preceding, had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> named John, who died in prison (where he had been confined for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>) at the age of 20, and whose body was dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, and burnt Feb. 27, 1559. They were of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Tilleul, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORTAIN">Mortain</a>, in Normandy.

MORELLA

Pages 8-8

a genus of insects of the coleoptera order. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORENA

Pages 10-11

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a district <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Mytia, in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was occupied by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEON">Cleon</a>, formerly at the head of a band of robbers, but afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Abrettanus, and enriched with possessions, first by Antony, and then by Cæsar. Moresque, Moresk, or Morish, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, carving, &c. done after the manner of the Moors; consisting of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> pieces and compartments promiscuously intermingled, not containing any perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or other animal, but a wild resemblance of birds, beasts, trees, &c. These are also called arabesques, and are particularly used in embroideries, damask <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, &c. Moresque Dancers, vulgarly called Morrice dancers, are those altogether in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Moors, as farabands, chacons, &c. and are usually performed with caltanets, tambours, &c. There are few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> places in England where the morrice dance is not known. It was probably introduced about, or a little before, the reign of Henry VIII. and is a dance of young men in their shifts, with bells at their feet, and ribbands of various colours tied round their arms and flung across their shoulders. MORGAGNA. See FATA. Morgagni, John Baptist, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine, first professor of anatomy in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, and member of several of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of learned men in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, was born in the year 1682, at Forli, a town in the district of La Romagna in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Morgagni. His parents, who were in easy circumstances, allowed him to follow that course in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> his genius dictated. He began his studies at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>; but soon after removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, where he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Doctor of Medicine, when he had but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> reached the 16th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Here his peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for anatomy found an able preceptor in Vallalva, who bestowed on him the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and such was the progress he made under this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, that at the age of 20 he himself taught anatomy with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation. Soon, however, the fame of his lectures, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his pupils, excited the jealousy of the public professors, and gave rise to injurious persecutions. But his abilities and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> gained him a complete triumph over his enemies; and all opposition to him was finally terminated from his being appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of Bologna to fill a medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, which soon became vacant. But the duties of this office, although important, neither occupied the whole of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, nor satisfied his anxious desire to afford instruction. He still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to labour in secret on his favourite subject, and soon after communicated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of these labours to the public in his *Adversaria Anatomica*, the first of which was published in the year 1706, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third in 1717, and the three others in 1719. The publication of this excellent work spread the fame of Morgagni far beyond the limits of the state of Bologna. Such was his reputation, that the wise republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> had no hesitation in making him an offer of the second chair of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of medicine in the university of Padua, then vacant by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of M. Molinetti; and, to ensure his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a>, they doubled the emoluments of that appointment. While he was in this department, he published his treatise, entitled *Nova Institutionum medicarum idea*, which first appeared at Padua in the year 1712. From this work his former reputation suffered no diminution. And soon after he rose, by different steps, to be first professor of anatomy in that celebrated university. Although Morgagni was thus finally settled at Padua, yet he gave evident proofs of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to Bologna, which he considered as his native country with respect to the sciences. He exerted his utmost efforts in establishing the academy of Bologna, of which he was one of the first associates; and he enriched their publications with several valuable and curious papers. Soon after this, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Societies of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> received him among their number. Not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the publication of his *Adversaria Anatomica*, he began, much upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, his *Epistle Anatomicae*, the first of which is dated at Padua in the beginning of April 1726. The works of Morgagni which have already been mentioned, are to be considered, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, as strictly anatomical: but he was not more eminent as an anatomist, than as a learned and successful physician. In the year 1765, when he was not far distant from the 80th year of his age, he published his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and valuable work *De causis et fedibus morborum per anatomen indagatis*. This last and most important of all his productions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> afford convincing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of his industry and abilities to latest posterity. Besides these works, he published, at different periods of his life, several miscellaneous pieces, which were afterwards collected into one volume, and printed under his own eye at Padua, in the year 1765. It does not appear that he had in view any future publications; but he intended to have favoured the world with a complete edition of all his works, which would probably have been augmented with many new observations. In this he was engaged when, on the fifth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1771, after he had nearly arrived at the 90th year of his age, death put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his long and glorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> in the learned world.

MORGES

Pages 11-11

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some trade, and situated on the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, five miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 42'. N. Lat. 46° 29'.

MORGO

Pages 11-11

anciently *Amorgos*, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, which produces wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and corm. It is well cultivated, and the inhabitants are affable, and generally of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The best parts belong to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. The greatest inconvenience in this island is the want of wood. It is 30 miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26° 15'. N. Lat. 36° 30'.

MORIAH

Pages 11-11

one of the eminences of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; on which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> went to offer his son, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> wanted to build the temple, which was afterwards executed by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of Aranah; originally narrow, so as scarce to contain the temple, but enlarged by means of ramparts; and surrounded with a triple wall, so as to add <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength to the temple, (Josephus). It may be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, to which it was joined by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> and gallery, (*Id.*).

MORILLES

Pages 11-11

a kind of mushroom, about the size of a walnut, pierced with holes like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>-comb, and said to be good for creating an appetite. It is often used in sauces and ragouts.

MORINA

Pages 11-11

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diandria clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, *Aggregate*. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORINDA

Pages 11-11

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, *Aggregate*. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORINORUM CASTELLUM

Pages 11-11

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, simply *Caffellum* (Antonine); situated on an eminence, with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on its top, in the territory of the Morini. Now *Mont Caffel*, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>.

MORISON

Pages 11-11

ROBERT, physician and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, was born at Aberdeen in 1620, bred at the university there, and taught <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in it; but having a strong inclination to botany, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in that science. The civil wars obliged him to leave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; which, however, he did not do till he had first signalized his zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and his courage, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the inhabitants of Aberdeen and the Presbyterian troops on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of Aberdeen, in which he received a dangerous wound on the head. As soon as he was cured of it, he went into France; and fixing at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he applied assiduously to botany and anatomy. He was introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, who gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>. He exercised the office till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and afterwards went over to England in 1665. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., to whom the duke of Orleans had presented him at Blois, sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of...

MORISONIA

Pages 12-12

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 25th order, Putanaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORLACHIA

Pages 12-14

a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. The inhabitants are called Morlacki <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Morlacchi; they inhabit the pleasant valleys of Koter, along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Kerka, Cettina, Narenta, and among the inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Dalmatia. The inhabitants are by some said to be of Walachian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, as is indicated by their name; Morlachia being a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of Meuro <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a>, that is, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Walachia; and the Walachians are said to be descendants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman colonies planted in these countries. This, however, is denied by the Abbé Fortis, who published a volume of travels into that country. He informs us, that the origin of the Morlacchi is involved in the darkness of barbarous ages, together with that of many other nations, resembling them so much in customs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, that they may be taken for one people, dispersed in the vast tracts from the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the Frozen ocean. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the name, the Abbé observes, that the Morlacchi generally call themselves, in their own language, Vlafii; a national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, of which no vestige is found in the records of Dalmatia till the 13th century. It signifies powerful men, or men of authority; and the denomination of Moro Vlafii, corruptly Morlacchi, as they are now called, may perhaps point out the original of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. This word may possibly signify the conquerors that came from the sea; moor, in all the dialects of the Slavonian language, signifying the sea. With regard to the character of these people, we are informed that they are much injured by their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> neighbours. The inhabitants of the sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Dalmatia tell many frightful stories of their avarice and cruelty: but these, in our author's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, are all either of an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any have happened in latter times, they ought rather to be ascribed to the corruption of a few individuals, than to the bad disposition of the nation in general; and though thievish tricks are frequent among them, he informs us, that a stranger may travel securely through their country, where he is faithfully escorted, and hospitably treated. As to the Morlacchi themselves, they are represented as open and sincere to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they would be taken for simpletons in any other country; and by means of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> they have been so often duped by the Italians, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of an Italian and the faith of a dog, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> among the Morlacchi. They are very hospitable to strangers; and their hospitality is equally conspicuous among the rich and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The rich prepares a roasted lamb or sheep, and the poor with equal cordiality offers whatever he has; nor is this generosity confined to strangers, but generally extends itself to all who are in want. When a Morlack is on a journey, and comes to lodge at a friend's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the family, or the new married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>, if there happen to be one, receives and kisses him when he alights from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or at the door of the house; but a foreigner is rarely favoured with these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> civilities; on the contrary, the women, if they are young, hide themselves, and keep out of his way. The Morlacchi in general have little notion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy, and readily consume in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> as much as would be sufficient for several months, whenever any occasion of merriment presents itself. A <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the holiday of the saint protector of the family, the arrival of relations or friends, or any other joyful incident, consumes of course all that there is to eat and to drink in the house. Yet the Morlack is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> economilist in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his wearing apparel; for rather than spoil his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, he takes it off, let it <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> ever so hard, and goes bareheaded in the storm. In the same manner he treats his shoes, if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is dirty and they are not very old. Nothing but an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> impossibility hinders a Morlack from being punctual; and if he cannot repay the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he borrowed at the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he carries a small present to his creditor, and requests a longer term. Friendship is lasting among the Morlacchi. They have even made it a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> point, and tie the sacred bond at the foot of the altar. The Slavonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> contains a particular benediction for the solemn union of two <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> or two female friends in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>. The male friends thus united are called Pobratimi, and the female Poljefreme, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> half-brothers and half-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>. From these consecrated friendships among the Morlacchi and other nations of the same origin, it should seem that the favored brothers arose; a denomination frequent enough among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between these and the Pobratimi of Morlachia consists not only in the want of the ritual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the union itself. For, among the Morlacchi, the sole view is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and advantage; but such a brotherhood among the Italians is generally commenced by bad men, to enable them the more to hurt and disturb <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. But as the friendships of the Morlacchi are strong and sacred, so their quarrels are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> unextinguishable. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from father to son; and the mothers fail not to put their children in mind of their duty to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> their father if he has had the misfortune to be killed, and to show them often the bloody shirt and arms of the dead. And so deeply is revenge rooted in the minds of this nation, that all the missionaries in the world would not be able to eradicate it. A Morlack is naturally inclined to do good to his fellow creatures, and is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for the smallest benefit; but implacable if injured or insulted. A Morlack who has killed another of a powerful family, is commonly obliged to leave himself by flight, and MORLACCHI and to keep out of the way for several years. If during that time he has been fortunate enough to escape the search of his pursuers, and has got a small sum of money, he endeavours to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> and peace; and, that he may treat about the conditions in person, he asks and obtains a safe conduct, which is faithfully maintained, though only verbally granted. Then he finds mediators; and, on the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the relations of the two hostile families are assembled, and the criminal is introduced, dragging himself along on his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet, the muklet, pittole, or cutlass, with which he committed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, hung about his neck; and while he continues in that humble posture, one or more of the relations recites a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on the dead, which sometimes rekindles the flames of revenge, and puts the poor prostrate in no small danger. The Morlacks, whether they happen to be of the Roman or of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, have very singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> about <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of their teachers daily augments this monstrous evil. They are as firmly persuaded of the reality of witches, fairies, enchantments, nocturnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a>, and fortresses, as if they had seen a thousand examples of them. Nor do they make the least doubt about the existence of vampires; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to them, as in Transylvania, the sucking the blood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>. Therefore, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> dies suspected of becoming a vampire, or vu-kodolak, as they call it, they cut his hams, and prick his whole body with pins; pretending, that after this operation he cannot walk about. There are even instances of Morlacchi, who, imagining that they may possibly thirst for children's blood after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, entreat their heirs, and sometimes oblige them to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, to treat them as vampires when they die. A most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> reigns in Morlachia, as it generally does in other parts, between the Latin and Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, which their respective priests fail not to foment, and tell a thousand little scandalous stories of each other. The churches of the Latins are poor, but not very dirty; those of the Greeks are equally poor, and shamefully ill kept. Our author has seen the curate of a Morlack village sitting on the ground in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, to hear the confession of women on their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> by his side: a strange posture indeed! but a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the innocent manners of those good people, who have the most profound veneration for their spiritual pastors, and a total dependence upon them; who, on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, frequently make use of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, and correct the bodies of their offending flock with the cudgel. Innocence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of pastoral ages, are still preserved among the Morlacchi, or at least many traces of them remain in the places farthest distant from our settlements. Pure cordiality of sentiment is not there restrained by other regards, and displays itself without any distinction of circumstances. A young handsome Morlack girl, who meets a man of her district on the road, kisses him affectionately, without the least imputation of impropriety; and M. Fortis has seen all the women and girls, all the young men and old, kissing one another as they came into the churchyard on a holiday; so that they looked as if they all belonged to one family. He often observed the same thing on the road, and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the maritime <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where the Morlacchi came to sell their Morlacchi commodities. The dress of the unmarried women is the most complex and whimsical, in respect to the ornaments of the head; for when married they are not allowed to wear anything else but a handkerchief, either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or coloured, tied about it. The girls use a scarlet cap, to which they commonly hang a veil falling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the shoulders, as a mark of their virginity. The better sort adorn their caps with strings of silver coins, among which are frequently seen very ancient and valuable ones; they have moreover <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> rings of very curious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and small silver chains with the figures of half moons fastened to the ends of them. But the poor are forced to content themselves with plain caps; or if they have any ornaments, they consist only of small exotic shells, round glass beads, or bits of tin. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> merit of these caps, which constitute the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> as well as vanity of the Morlack young ladies, is to attract and fix the eyes of all who are near them by the multitude of ornaments, and the noise they make on the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of their heads. Both old and young women wear about their necks <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> strings of round glass beads, of various size and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and many rings of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, tin, or silver, on their fingers. Their bracelets are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> covered with wrought tin or silver; and they embroider their stomachers, or adorn them with beads or shells. But the use of flays is unknown, nor do they put whalebone or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in the stomacher. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> woollen girdle surrounds their petticoat, which is commonly decked with shells, and of blue colour, and therefore called modrina. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> as well as petticoat, is of a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>; and both reach near to the ankle: the gown is bordered with scarlet, and called sadak. They use no modrina in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and only wear the sadak without sleeves over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> petticoat or shift. The girls always wear <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> stockings; and their shoes are like those of the men, called opante. The sole is of untressed ox hide, and the upper part of sheep's skin thongs knotted, which they call opante; and these they fasten above the ankles, something like the ancient cothurnus. The unmarried women, even of the richest families, are not permitted to wear any other sort of shoes; though after marriage, they may, if they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, lay aside the opante, and use the Turkish slippers. The girls keep their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> tressed under their caps, but when married they let it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> dishevelled on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; sometimes they tie it under the chin; and always have medals, beads, or bored coins, in the Tartar or American <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, twisted amongst it. Nothing is more common among the Morlacchi than marriages concluded between the old people of the respective families, especially when the parties live at a great distance, and neither see nor know each other; and the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of these alliances is the ambition of being related to a numerous and powerful family, famous for having produced valiant men. A denial in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> is very rare; nor does the father of the maid inquire much into the circumstances of the family that asks her. Sometimes a daughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> is given in marriage to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> or tenant, as was usual in patriarchal times; so little are the women regarded in this country. But on these occasions, the Morlacchi girls enjoy the privilege of refusal. For he MORLACCHI who acts by proxy, having obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, is obliged to go and bring the bridegroom; and, if on seeing each other, the young people are reciprocally content, the marriage is concluded, but not otherwise. In some parts it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the bride to go to see the house and family of the proposed husband, before she gives a definitive answer; and if the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> or persons are disagreeable to her, she is at liberty to annul the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>. The bride is conducted to a church, veiled, and surrounded by the friends of the bridegroom, or fratii, as they are called, on horseback; and the sacred ceremony is performed amidst the noise of muskets, pistols, barbaric shouts and acclamations, which continue till the return to her father's house or to that of her husband, if not far off. The first day's entertainment is sometimes made at the bride's house, but generally at the bridegroom's, whether the fratii hasten immediately after the nuptial benediction; and at the same time three or four men run on foot to tell the good news; the first who gets to the house has a kind of a towel embroidered at the ends, as a premium. The domachin, or head of the house, comes out to meet his daughter-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and a child is handed to her, before she lights, to care for it; and if there happen to be none in the house, the child is borrowed from one of the neighbours. When she lights, she kneels down, and kisses the threshold.—Then the mother in law, or in her place some other female relation, presents a corn sieve, full of different kinds of grain, nuts, almonds, and other small fruit, which the bride scatters upon the fratii, by handfuls, behind her back. The bride does not sit at the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> the first day, but has one apart for herself, the two diverti, and the itacheo. The bridegroom sits at table with the fratii; but in all that day, consecrated to the matrimonial union, he must neither unloosen nor cut any thing whatever. The knum carves his meat, and cuts his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. It is the domachin's business to give the toast; and the flari-fratii is the first who pledges him. Generally the bukkara, a very large wooden cup, goes round, first to the saint protector of the family; next to the prosperity of the holy faith; and sometimes to a name the most sublime and venerable. The most extravagant abundance reigns at these feasts; and each of the fratii contributes, by feeding a share of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The dinner begins with fruit and cheese; and the soup comes last, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> contrary to our custom. All sorts of domestic fowls, kid, lamb, and sometimes venison, are heaped in prodigal quantities upon their tables. These nuptial feasts, called sfarave by the ancient Huns, are by the Morlacchi called sfaravizze, from whence the Italian word sfaravizzo is undoubtedly derived. They continue three, six, eight, or more days, according to the ability or prodigal disposition of the family where they are held. The new married wife gets no inconsiderable profit in these days of joy; and it usually amounts to much more than all the portion she brings with her, which often consists of nothing but her own clothes and perhaps a cow; nay, it happens sometimes that the parents, instead of giving money with their daughter, get something from the bridegroom by way of price. The bride carries <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> every morning, to wash the hands of her guests as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the feasting lasts; and each of them throws a small piece of money into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASON">bason</a> after performing that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, which is a very rare one among them, excepting on such occasions. The Morlacchi pass their youth in the woods, attending their flocks and herds; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of quiet and leisure they often become dextrous in carving with a simple <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>: they make wooden cups, and whistles adorned with fanciful bas-reliefs, which are not void of merit, and at least show the genius of the people.

MORNAY

Pages 14-15

PHILIPPE DE, seigneur du Plessis <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLY">Marly</a>, was born at Buhy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bilhuy in Upper Normandy in France, in 1549, and was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. What was then thought a prodigy in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, he made a rapid progress in the belles lettres, in the learned languages, and in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. He was at first destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but the principles of Calvinism, which he had imbibed from his mother, effectually excluded him from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferments to which he was entitled by his intellect, abilities, and birth. After the horrible massacre of St Bartholomew, Philippe de Mornay made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Germany, England, and the Low Countries; and he was equally improved and delighted by his travels. Mornay afterwards joined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> of Navarre, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> leader of the Protestant party, and so well known since by the name of Henry IV. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> sent Mornay, who employed his whole abilities, both as a soldier and a writer, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Protestant cause, to conduct a negotiation with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of England; and left him wholly to his own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> in the management of that business. He was successful in almost every negotiation, because he conducted it like an able politician, and not with a spirit of intrigue. He tenderly loved Henry IV. and spoke to him on all occasions as to a friend. When he was wounded at Amiens, he wrote to him in these words: "Sire, You have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough acted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Alexander, it is now time you should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> that of Caesar. It is our duty to die for your majesty, &c. It is glorious for you, Sire, and I dare venture to tell you it is your duty, to live for us." This faithful subject did every thing in his power to raise Henry to the throne. But when he deserted the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, he reproached him in the bitterest manner, and retired from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Henry still loved him; and was extremely affronted with an insult which he received in 1597 from one Saint Phal, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> him with a cudgel, and left him for dead. Mornay demanded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> from the king, who gave him the following answer, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> as well of his spirit as of his goodness of heart. "Monseigneur Duplessis, I am exceedingly offended at the insult you have received; and I sympathize with you both as your sovereign and your friend. In the former capacity, I shall do justice to you and to myself; and had I sustained only the character of your friend, there are few perhaps who would have drawn their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> or sacrificed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> more cheerfully in your cause. Be satisfied, then, that I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> act the part of a king, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and a friend," &c. Mornay's knowledge, probity, and valour, made him the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the Protestant party, and procured him the contemptuous appellation of the Pope of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a>. He defended their doctrines both by speech and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. One of his books on the Inquiry of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">Mass</a>, having flattered up all the Catholic divines, he refused to MORAY to make any reply to their censures and criticisms except in a public conference. This was accordingly appointed to be held A.D. 1605, at Fontainebleau, where the court then was. The two champions were, Du Perron bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVREUX">Evreux</a>, and Moray. After a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many arguments and replies on both sides, the victory was adjudged to Du Perron. He had boasted that he would point out to the satisfaction of every one five hundred errors in his adversary's book, and he partly kept his word. The Calvinists did not fail to claim the victory on this occasion, and they still continue to do so. This conference, instead of putting an end to the differences, was productive of new quarrels among the controversialists, and of much profane <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> among the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIBERTINES">libertines</a>. A Huguenot minister, who was present at the conference, observed with great concern to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the same party, "The bishop of Evreux has already driven Moray from several strong holds." "No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> (replied the folder), provided he does not drive him from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>." This was an important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, of which Duplessis was governor. Hither he retired, his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> being constantly occupied in defending the Huguenots, and in making himself formidable to the Catholics. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. was making preparations against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, Duplessis wrote him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, dissuading him from such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. After employing the most plausible arguments, he concludes in the following manner: "To make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on the subject, is an indication of weakness in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>.
