Authority consists in the quiet submission of the people, and is established by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and justice of the governor. Force of arms ought never to be employed except in repelling a foreign enemy. The late king would have sent the new ministers of state to learn the first elements of politics, who like unskillful surgeons would apply violent remedies to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and advise a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to cut off an arm when his finger aches." These remonstrances produced no other effect than the loss of the government of Saumur, of which he was deprived by Louis XIII. in 1621. He died two years after, November 11, 1623, aged 74, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> de la Forêt-sur-Seure in Poitou. The Protestant cause never had an abler supporter, or one who did it more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> by his virtues and abilities. Censeur des courtisans, mais à la cœur aimé; Fier ennemi de Rome, et de Rome estimé.—Henriade. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of his works: 1. Un Traité de l'Encharisme, 1604, in folio. 2. Un Traité de la vérité de la <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> Chrétienne, 8vo. 3. A book entitled La Mystère d'Iniquité, 4to. 4. Un discours sur le droit pretendu par ceux de la maison de Guise, 8vo. 5. Curious and interesting <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> from the year 1572 to 1620, 4 vols., 4to, valuable. 6. Letters; which are written with great spirit and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> des Liques has given us his life in quarto; a book more interesting for the matter than the manner.

MORNE-GAROU

Pages 15-15

a very remarkable volcanic mountain on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Vincent's in the West Indies. It was visited by Mr James Anderson surgeon in the year 1784. See St Vincents.

MORNING

Pages 15-15

the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> rising. The astronomers reckon morning, mane, from the time of midnight to that of mid-day. Thus an eclipse is said to begin at 11 o'clock in the morning, &c. Morning <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>, is the planet Venus, when a little to the westward of the sun; that is, when she rises a little before. In this situation she is called by the Greeks Phosphorus; by the Latins Lucifer, &c.

MOROC

Pages 15-15
or MAROC, a beautiful bird of Abyssinia, described by Mr Bruce, who thinks its name is derived from mor "honey," though he says that he never heard it was further concerned in the honey than destroying bees. It seems to pursue those insects out of enmity or diversion as well as for food, leaving great numbers dead on the ground, besides those which it devours for food. The moroc resembles the cuckoo in size and shape, but differs in other respects. Its mouth is very wide, the opening reaching almost to its eyes; the inside of the mouth and throat yellow, the tongue sharp pointed, and capable of being drawn almost half its length out of the mouth beyond the point of its beak, and is very flexible. The head and neck are brown, without any mixture of other colours; there are likewise a number of very small and scarcely visible hairs at the root of the beak. This seems to be the bird mentioned by Sparman under the name of cuculus indicator, which (he says) has the singular property of discovering the nests of wild bees, and leading travellers by a certain cry to the place where the treasure is deposited. According to Sparman's account, it makes known these discoveries by the same cry to foxes as well as to the human species; but Jerome Lobo, who mentions the Abyssinian bird, takes no notice of the foxes, though he mentions its singing melodiously when it arrives at the place where the honey is deposited. Both these accounts are severely criticised by Mr Bruce, who says, that honey is so abundant on every hillock and every tree, that a bird possessing this faculty could be of no use to man or to any other animal in that country, and that having never heard of such a bird in Abyssinia, he considers the account of it as a fiction.

MOROCCO

Pages 15-28

an empire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, comprehending Situation a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, is bounded and bounded on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>; on the east by the river Muluya, which separates it from Algiers; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean; and on the south by Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUS">Sus</a>, which divides it from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Tafilet. Its greatest length is from the north-east to the south-west, amounting to above 590 miles; its breadth is not above 260 where broadest, and in the narrowest places it is not above half that breadth. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Morocco has been already Histv. given under the article MAURITANIA. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> upwards of 400 years. On the decline of that empire it fell under the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, who held it till about the year 600, when the Goths were driven out by the Vandals, the Vandals by the Greeks, and they in their turn by the Saracens, who conquered not only this empire, but we may say the whole continent of Africa; at least their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, one way or other, is to be found in all parts of it. The Saracen empire did not continue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> united under one head, and many princes set up for themselves in Africa as well as elsewhere, through whose divisions the Almoravides were at length raided to the sovereignty, as related under the article Algiers, No. 2. Yulef, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> monarch of that line, built the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Morocco, conquered the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and the Moorish dominions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; all which were lost by his grandson Abou Hali, who was defeated and killed by the Spaniards. On this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> passed to the Mohicans, or Almohades, with whom it had not continued above three generations, when Mohammed the son of Al Manfur lost the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Sierra Morena, in which 200,000 Moors were slain, and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which Alphonso X. retook a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many of the Moorish conquests immediately after. Mohammed died soon after this disgrace, and left several sons, between whom a civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> ensued, during which the viceroys of Fez, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, and Tremeten, found means to establish themselves as independent princes. At length one of the princes of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> blood of Tremeten having defeated the Almohades, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the kingdoms of Morocco and Fez, and entailed them on his own family. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, this family was expelled by the Merini, the Merini by the Oatazes, and these by the Sharifs of Hafsen, who have kept the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> ever since. Nothing can be conceived more unjust and despotic than the government of Morocco, and nothing more degenerate than the character of the people. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is allowed to have not only an uncontrollable power over the lives and fortunes of his subjects, but in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> over their consciences, in as much as he is the only person who, as the successor of the prophet, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to interpret the Koran; and appoints all the judges under him, of whom those of Morocco and Fez are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, whose business it is to explain and dispense all matters relating to their religion; and who, being his creatures and dependents, dare not steer otherwise than as he directs. Whenever therefore the laws are enacted by him, and proclaimed by his governors in all the provinces, as is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> done, that none may plead <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, they are everywhere received with an implicit and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> submission. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the subjects are bred up with a notion, that those who die in the execution of his command are entitled to an immediate admittance into paradise, and those who have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to die by his hand to a still greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in it. After this we need not wonder at finding so much cruelty, oppression, and tyranny on the one side, and so much submission, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, and misery on the other. This latter, however, extends no farther than the Moors; for as to the mountaineers, the subjection and tribute they pay to those tyrants was always involuntary; and as for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, their zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> is owing merely to the great sway and power which they have gained in the government, on various accounts. They were first introduced, or rather their importation increased, by the policy of Muley Ithmael, a late emperor, at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when there was a great decrease of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in the empire, occasioned in some degree by the enormous cruelties exercised by its former sovereigns, who have been known not unfrequently, through a flight difficult, to abandon a whole town or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. In the character of Muley Ithmael were found the most singular inconsistencies; for it is certain, that although a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, yet in other respects, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> to repair the mischief which he committed, Morocco, he left nothing undone for the encouragement of population.—He introduced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> colonies of negroes from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>; built <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> for them, many of which are still remaining; assigned them portions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and encouraged their increase by every possible means. He soon initiated them in the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; and had his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> been followed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by this time would have been populous, and probably flourishing. As the negroes are of a more lively, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and enterprising disposition than the Moors, they might soon have been taught the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>; and their singular ingenuity might have been directed to other useful purposes. It is true, Muley Ithmael, when he adopted this plan, had more objects in view than that of merely peopling his dominions. He <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> plainly that his own subjects were of too capricious a disposition to form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> calculated for his tyrannical purposes. They had uniformly manifested an inclination to change their sovereigns, though more from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of variety than to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the government, or restrain the abuses of tyranny. Muley Ithmael had discernment enough to see, that by forming an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of slaves, whose sole dependence should rest upon their master, he could easily train them in such a manner as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in the strictest conformity to his wishes. He soon learnt that the great object with the negroes was plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of plunder; in these he liberally indulged them, and the plan fully answered his expectations. Though, however, Muley Ithmael had no great merit in introducing subjects for the purposes of tyranny, yet the good effects of this new colonization were very generally experienced. By intermarrying among themselves, and intermixing among the Moors (for the Moors <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> keep negro women as concubines, though they seldom marry them), a new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people started up, who became as useful subjects as the native inhabitants, and brought the empire into a much more flourishing state than it had ever been in since their great revolution. Sidi Mahomet, his grandson and successor, had different views, and was actuated by different motives. From his inordinate avarice, he ceased to act towards his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> troops in the generous manner which had distinguished his predecessor Muley Ithmael; and they soon showed themselves discontented with his conduct. They offered to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his eldest son Muley <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, on the throne; but this prince, not unmindful of the duty which he owed his father and sovereign, declined their offer. They next applied to Muley Yazid, who at first accepted of the affiance they tendered, but in a short time relinquished the plan. Sidi Mahomet, disgusted with this conduct of the negroes, determined to curb their growing power, by disbarring a considerable part of these troops, and banishing them to distant parts of the empire. A most flagrant <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of despotism, which renders despotism the emperors more formidable to their subjects, is their of the making themselves their sole heirs, and, in virtue of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, seizing upon all their effects, and making only such provision for their families as they think proper; and often, on some frivolous pretence, leaving them destitute of any, according to the liking or dislike they bear to the deceased; so that, upon the whole, they are the only makers, judges, and interpreters, and in many instances likewise the executioners, of their own laws, which have no other limits than their own arbitrary will. The titles which the emperors of Morocco assume, are those of Most glorious, mighty, and noble emperor of Africa; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Fez and Morocco, Tafilet, Suz, Dorha, and all the Algarbe, and its territories in Africa; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> Sharif (or, as others write it, Xarif), that is, successor, or vicegerent, of the great Prophet Mohammed, &c. The judges or magistrates who act immediately under the emperor are either spiritual or temporal, or rather <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>. The mufti and the cadis are judges of all religious and civil affairs; and the baihaws, governors, alcaldes, and other military officers, of those that concern the flate or the army: all of them the most obsequious creatures and slaves of their prince, and no less the rapacious tyrants of his subjects, and from whom neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> nor favour can be obtained but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> dint of money and extortionate bribery, from the highest to the lowest. Neither can it indeed be otherwise in such an arbitrary government, where the highest posts must not only be bought of the prince at a most extravagant price, and kept only by an exorbitant tribute, which is yearly paid to him, but where no one is sure to continue longer than he can bribe some of the courtiers to insinuate to the monarch that he pays to the utmost of his power and much beyond what was expected from him. There are instances of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> elevating at once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldier to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a baihaw, or making him a confidential friend; the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he would perhaps imprison him, or reduce him again to the station of a private soldier. Yet such is the disposition of these people, that they have an unbounded thirst for rank and power with all their uncertainties; and what is more extraordinary, when they have obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> station, they seldom fail to afford their sovereign a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> for ill treating them, by abusing in some way or other their trust. From what has been said, it may be reasonably concluded that the revenue arising to the emperor from the last mentioned source, that of bribery, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTORTION">extortion</a>, and confiscation, must be very considerable, though there is no possibility to make any other conjecture of its real amount than that it must be an immense one. Another considerable branch is the piratical trade, which brings the greater income into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, as he is not at any expense either for fitting out of corsair vessels, or maintaining their men; and yet has the tenth of all the cargo and of all the captives; besides which, he appropriates to himself all the rest of them, by paying the captors 50 crowns per head, by which means he engrosses all the slaves to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and advantage. This article is indeed a very considerable addition to his revenue, not only as he sells their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> at a very high rate, but likewise as he has the profit of all their labour, without allowing them any other maintenance than a little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, or any other assistance when sick, than what medicines a Spanish convent, which he tolerates there, gives them gratis; and which, nevertheless, is forced to pay him an annual present for that toleration, besides furnishing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> with medicines, and the slaves with lodging and diet when they are not able to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Another branch of his revenue consists in the tenth part of all cattle, corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and other products of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is exacted of the Arabs and Berbes, as well as of the natives; and these are levied, or rather farmed, by the baihaws, go- vemors, alcaldes, &c., with all possible severity. The Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> likewise pay an income or capita- tion, the former of six crowns per head on all males from 15 years and upwards, besides other arbitrary imposts, fines, &c. That on the Christians, for the liberty of trading in his dominions, rises and falls according to their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> they drive; but which, whatever it may bring yearly into his coffers, is yet detrimental to trade in general, seeing it discourages great numbers from settling there, notwithstanding the artful invitations which the emperors and their ministers make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to invite them to it; for, besides those arbitrary exactions, there is still another great hardship attending them, viz. that they cannot leave the country without forfeiting all their debts and effects to the crown. The duties on all imports and exports is another branch of his income, the amount of which, it is said, does not exceed 165,000l. per annum. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of the empire of Morocco is in general sufficiently temperate, healthy, and not too hot as its situation might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to suppose. The chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which form Atlas, on the eastern side, defends it from the east winds, that would scorch up the earth were they frequent. The summit of these mountains is always covered with snow; and their abundant descending streams spread verdure through the neighbourhood, make the winter more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and temper the heats of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the west side, which extends along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> from north to south, also refreshes the land with regular breezes, that seldom vary according to their seasons. At a distance from the sea, within land, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is so great, that the rivulets become dry in summer; but as in hot countries dews are plentiful, the nights are there always cool. The rains are tolerably regular in winter; and are even abundant, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is not loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> as in northern latitudes. Those rains which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by intervals are favourable to the earth, and increase its fecundity. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> the country is covered with verdure, and enamelled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. Barley is cut in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, but the wheat <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. All fruits are early in this climate; and in forward years the vintage is over in the beginning of September. Though in general there is more uniformity and less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in hot than in northern climates, the first are nevertheless exposed to the intemperance of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>: too heavy rains often impede the harvest; and drought has still greater inconveniences, for it endures the propagation of locusts. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of Morocco is exceedingly fertile. It is soil, and most so in the inland provinces. On the western coast it is in general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and stony, and is better adapted to the vine and olive than the culture of wheat. They annually burn, before the September rains, the stubble, which is left rather long; and this and the dung of cattle, every day turned to pasture, form the sole manure the land receives. The soil requires but little labour, and the ploughing is so light that the furrows are scarcely six inches deep; for which reason, in some provinces, wooden ploughshares are used for cheapness. The empire of Morocco might supply itself with all produce necessaries, as well from the abundance and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of its products, as from the few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> wants of the Moors occasioned by climate or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Its wealth consists in the fruitfulness of its soil: its corn, fruits, flocks, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, and wax, would not only supply its necessities, but yield a superfluous, which might become an object of immense trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> with other nations. Such numerous exports might return an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, were its government fixed and secure, and did subjects enjoy the fruits of their labour and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in safety. The increase of corn in Morocco is often as sixty to one, and thirty is held to be but an indifferent harvest. The Moors, naturally indolent, take little care of the culture of their fruits. Oranges, lemons, and thick skinned fruits, the trees of which require little nurture, grow in the open fields; and there are very large plantations of them found, which they take the trouble to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in order to increase their product. Their vines, which yield excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, are planted as far as the 33rd degree, as in the southern provinces of France, and are equally vigorous. But at Morocco, where they yield a large and delicious grape, they are supported by vine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> five and six feet above ground; and as they are obliged to be watered, the little wine made there is seldom preferred. Figs are very good in some parts of the empire, but toward the south they are scarcely ripe before they are full of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>; the heats and night dews may, perhaps, contribute to this speedy decay. Melons, for the same reason, are rarely eatable; they have but a moment of maturity; which passes so rapidly that it is with difficulty seized. Water melons are everywhere reared, and in some provinces are excellent. Apricots, apples, and pears, are in tolerable plenty in the neighbourhood of Fez and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEQUINEZ">Mequinez</a>, where water is less scarce and the climate more temperate. But in the plain, which extends along the western coast, these delicate fruits are very indifferent, have less juice or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and the peaches there do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>. The tree called the prickly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, or the Barbary fig, is plentifully found in the empire of Morocco; and is planted round vineyards and gardens, because its thick and thorny leaves, which are wonderfully prolific, form impenetrable hedges. From these leaves a fruit is produced, covered with a thorny skin, that must be taken off with care. This fruit is mild, and full of very hard, small kernels. The olive is everywhere found along the coast, but particularly to the south. In the province of Suz, between the 25th and 30th degrees, the inhabitants have an almond harvest, which varies little because of the mildness of the climate; but the fruit is small, for which reason they take little care of the trees, and they degenerate with time. The palm tree is common in the southern provinces of Morocco; but dates ripen there with difficulty, and few are good except in the province of Suz and toward Tafilet. On the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALLEE">Sallee</a> and Mamora there are forests of oak, which produce acorns near two inches long. They taste like chestnuts, and are eaten raw and roasted. Salt abounds in the empire, and in some places on the coast requires only the trouble of gathering. Independent of the salt pits formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of the soft water, there are pits and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in the country whence great quantities are obtained. It is carried even as far as Tombut, whence it passes to the interior parts of Africa. The Moors cultivate their lands only in proportion to their wants; hence two-thirds of the empire at least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> waste. Here the doum, that is, the fan or wild palm tree, grows in abundance; and from which those people, when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> renders them industrious, find great advantage. The shepherds, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a> drivers, camel drivers, and travellers, gather the leaves, of which they make mats, fringes, baskets, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, sours or large wallets to carry corn, twine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, girths, and covers for their pack saddles. This plant, with which also they heat their ovens, produces a mild and resinous fruit that ripens in September and October. It is in form like the raisin, contains a kernel, and is astringent and very proper to temper and counteract the effects of the watery and laxative fruits, of which these people in summer make an immoderate use. Unacquainted with the sources of wealth of which their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were possessed, the Moors pretend there are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in the empire, which the emperors will not permit to be worked, lest their subjects should thus find means to shake off their yoke. It is not improbable but that the mountains of Atlas may contain unexplored <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>; but there is no good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that they have ever yielded gold and silver. There are known <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> mines in the south; but the working of them has been found so expensive, that the natives would rather use imported iron, notwithstanding the heavy duty it pays, by which its price is doubled. There are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> mines in the neighbourhood of Santa Cruz, which are not only sufficient for the small consumption of the empire, where copper is little used, but are also an object of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, and would become much more so were the duties less moderate. Neither the elephant nor the rhinoceros is to be found either in this or the other states of Barbary; but the deserts abound with lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, and monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>. The Barbary horses were formerly very valuable, and thought equal to the Arabian. Though the breed is now said to be decayed, yet some very fine ones are occasionally imported into England. Camels and dromedaries, asses, mules, and kumrabs (a most serviceable creature, begot by an ass upon a cow), are their beasts of burden. Their cows are but small, and barren of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. Their sheep yield but indifferent fleeces, but are very large, as are their goats. Bears, porcupines, foxes, apes, hares, rabbits, ferrets, weasels, moles, chameleons, and all kinds of reptiles, are found here. Partridges and quails, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, hawks, and all kinds of wild fowl, are frequent on the coast. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mountains form the chain which goes under the name of Mount Atlas, and runs the whole length of Barbary from east to west, passing through Morocco, and abutting upon that ocean which separates the eastern from the western continent, and is from this mountain called the Atlantic Ocean. See Atlas. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, besides the Malva or Muluya above mentioned, which rises in the deserts, and running from south to north divides Morocco from the kingdom of Algiers, are the Suz, Ommirabih, Rabbata, Larache, Darodt, Sebon, Gueron, and Tensift, which rise in Mount Atlas, and fall into the Atlantic ocean. The traffic of the empire by land is either with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> or Nigroland: to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> they send <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a>, consisting of several thousand camels, horses, and mules, twice every year, partly for traffic, and partly on a religious account; for numbers of pilgrims take that opportunity of paying their devotions to their great prophet. The goods they carry to the east are woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, Morocco manufactures, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, and ostrich feathers; and they bring back from thence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, muslins, and drugs. By their caravans to Negroland, they send salt, silk, and woollen manufactures, and bring back gold and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> in return, but chiefly negroes. The caravans always go strong enough to defend themselves against the wild Arabs in the deserts of Africa and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; though, notwithstanding all their vigilance, some of the druggists and baggage often fall into their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>: they are also forced to load one half of their camels with water, to prevent their perishing with drought and thirst in those inhospitable deserts. And there is still a more dangerous enemy, which is the sand itself: when the winds rise, the caravan is perfectly blinded with dust; and there have been instances both in Africa and Asia, where whole caravans, and even armies, have been buried alive in the sands. The natives have hardly any trading vessels, but are seldom without some corsairs. These, and European merchant ships, bring them whatever they want from abroad; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen cloth, flax, iron wrought and unwrought, arms, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, lead, and the like: for which they take in return, copper, wax, hides, Morocco leather, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> (which is very fine), gums, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, dates, almonds, and other fruits. The duties paid by the English in the ports of Morocco are but half those paid by other Europeans. It is a general observation, that no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is fond of trading with these states, not only on account of their capricious deportment, but the villany of their individuals, both natives and Jews, many of whom take all opportunities of cheating, and when detected are seldom punished. The land forces of the emperor of Morocco consist principally of black troops, and some few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; amounting altogether to an army of about 35,000 men upon the establishment, two thirds of which are cavalry. This establishment, however, upon occasion, admits of a considerable increase, as every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is supposed to be a folder, and when called upon is obliged to act in that capacity. About 6000 of the standing forces form the emperor's body <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and are always kept near his person; the remainder are quartered in the different towns of the empire, and are under the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the bashaws of the provinces. They are all clothed by the emperor, and receive a trifling pay; but their chief dependence is on plunder, which they have frequent opportunities of acquiring. The black troops are naturally of a very fiery disposition, capable of enduring great fatigue, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, thirst, and every difficulty to which a military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is exposed. They appear well calculated for skirmishing parties, or for the purpose of harassing an enemy; but were they obliged to undergo a regular attack, from their total want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> they would soon be routed. In all their manoeuvres they have no notion whatever of order and regularity, but have altogether more the appearance of a rabble than of an army. The emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> consists of about 15 small frigates, a few xebecs, and between 20 and 30 row-galleys. The whole is commanded by one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>; but as these vessels are principally used for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>, they seldom unite in a fleet. The number of the seamen in service is computed at 6000. The coins of this empire are a fluze, a bianquil, and Morocco ducat. The fluze is a small copper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, 20 whereof make a bianquil, of the value of twopence <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The bianquil is of silver, and the ducat of gold, not unlike that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and worth about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings. Both these pieces are liable to be clipped and filed by the Jews, that the Moors always carry scales in their pockets to weigh them; and when they are found to be much diminished in their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, they are recoined by the Jews, who are masters of the mint, by which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a considerable profit; as they do also by exchanging the light pieces for those that are full weight. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">Merchants</a>' accounts are kept in ounces, 10 of which make a ducat; but in payments to the government, it is said they reckon 17 one-half for a ducat. With respect to religion, the inhabitants of Morocco are Mohammedans, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Ali; and have a and mufti or high-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who is also the supreme civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> in all causes ecclesiastical and civil. They have a great veneration for their hermits, and for idiots and madmen; as well as for those who by their tricks have got the reputation of wizzards: all whom they look upon as inspired persons, and not only honour as saints while they live, but build tombs and chapels over them when dead; which places are not only religiously visited by their devotees far and near, but are esteemed inviolable sanctuaries for all sorts of criminals except in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. Notwithstanding the natives are zealous Mohammedans, they allow foreigners the free and open profession of their religion, and their very slaves have their priests and chapels in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city; though it must be owned that the Christian slaves are here treated with the utmost cruelty. Here, as in all other Mohammedan countries, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a> and their comments upon it are their only written laws; and though in some instances their cadis and other civil magistrates are controlled by the arbitrary determinations of their princes, bashaws, generals, and military officers, yet the latter have generally a very great deference and regard for their laws. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>, theft, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, are commonly punished with death: and their punishments for other crimes, particularly those against the state, are very cruel; as impaling, dragging the prisoner through the streets at a mule's heels till all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is torn off, throwing him from a high tower upon iron hooks. The inhabitants of the empire of Morocco, known by the name of Moors, are a mixture of Arabian and of the semi-African nations formed into tribes; with the origin of whom we are but imperfectly acquainted. These tribes, each strangers to the other, and ever divided by traditional hatred or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, seldom mingle. It seems probable that most of the casts who occupy the provinces of Morocco have been repulsed from the eastern to the western Africa, during those different revolutions by which this part of the world has been agitated; that they have followed the standard of their chiefs, whose names they have preserved; and that by these they, as well as the countries they inhabit, are distinguished. At present these tribes are called cafles or cabiles, from the Arabic word kabilea; and they are so numerous, that it is impossible to have a knowledge of them all. The native subjects of the empire of Morocco may be divided into two principal classes; the Brebes and the Moors. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the name, and the origin of the people, of the first class, are equally unknown. Like the Moors, at the time of the invasion by the Arabs, they may have adopted the Mahometan religion, which is consonant to their manners and principal usages; but they are an ignorant people, and observe none of the precepts of that religion, but the aversion it enjoins against other modes of worship. Confined to the mountains, the Brebes preserve great animosity against the Moors, whom they confound with the Arabs, and consider as usurpers.—They thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> in their retreats a ferocity of mind, and a strength of body, which makes them more fit for war and every kind of labour than the Moors of the plains in general are. The independence they boast of gives even a greater degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> to their countenance. The prejudices of their religion make them submit to the authority of the emperors of Morocco; but they throw off the yoke at their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and retire into the mountains, where it is difficult to attack or overcome them. The Brebes have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of their own, and never marry but among each other. They have tribes or castes among them who are exceedingly powerful both by their number and courage. The Moors of the plains may be distinguished into those who lead a pastoral life, and those who inhabit the cities. The former live in tents; and that they may allow their ground a year's rest, they annually change the place of their encampments, and go in search of fresh pasturage; but they cannot take this step without acquainting their governor. Like the ancient Arabs, they are entirely devoted to a pastoral life; their encampments, which they call douchars, are composed of several tents, and form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>; or they are ranged in two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and their flocks, when they return from pasture, occupy the centre. The tents of the Moors, viewed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, are of a conical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; they are from 8 to 10 feet high, and from 20 to 25 feet long; like those of high antiquity, they resemble a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> reversed. They are made of cloth composed of goats and camels <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and the leaves of the wild palm, by which they are rendered impervious to water; but at a distance their black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> gives them a very disagreeable look. The Moors, when encamped, live in the greatest simplicity, and exhibit a faithful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the inhabitants of the earth in the first ages of the world. The nature of their education, the temperature of the climate, and the rigour of the government, diminish the wants of the people, who find in their plains, in the milk and wool of their flocks, every thing necessary for food and clothing. Polygamy is allowed among them; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> so far from being injurious to a people who have few wants, that it is a great convenience in the economy of those <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, because the women are intrusted with the whole care of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> management. In their half-closed tents, they are employed in milking the cows for daily use; and when the milk abounds, in making <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, in picking their corn, their barley, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, which they do daily in a mill composed of two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> about 18 inches in diameter, the uppermost having a handle, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on an axis fixed in the under one: they make bread likewise every day, which they bake between two earthen plates, and often upon the ground after it has been heated by fire. Their ordinary food is the coofcoofoo; which is a paste made with their meal in the form of small grains like Italian paste. This coofcoofoo is dressed in the vapour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> soup, in a hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> perforated with many small holes in the bottom, and the dish is enclosed in a kettle where meat is boiled; the coofcoofoo, which is in the hollow dish, grows gradually soft by the vapour of the broth, with which it is from time to time moistened. This simple food is very nourishing, and even agreeable when one has got the better of the prejudices which every nation entertains for its own customs. The common people eat it with milk or butter indifferently; but those of higher rank, such as the governors of provinces and lieutenants, who live in the centre of the encampments, add to it some succulent broth, made with a mixture of mutton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, pigeons, or hedgehogs, and then pour on it a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fresh butter. The women in their tents spin wool, and weave it into cloth on looms suspended the whole length of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. Each piece is about five ells long, and one and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; it is neither dressed nor dyed, and it has no seam; they wash it when it is dirty; and as it is the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the Moors, they wear it night and day. It is called haick, and is the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the ancient draperies. The Moors of the plain wear nothing but their dress, &c., woollen stuff; they have neither shirts nor drawers. Linen among these people is a luxury known only to those of the court or the city. The whole wardrobe of a country Moor in easy circumstances consists in a haick for winter, another for summer, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, a hood, and a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of slippers. The common people both in the country and in towns wear a kind of tunic of woollen cloth, white, gray, or striped, which reaches to the middle of the leg, with great sleeves and a hood; it resembles the habit of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHUSIANS">Carthusians</a>. The women's dress in the country is likewise confined to a haick, which covers the neck and the shoulders, and is fastened with a silver clasp. The ornaments they are fond of are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> rings, which are either in the form of rings or crescents, made of silver, bracelets, and rings for the small of the leg; they wear these trinkets at their most ordinary occupations; lest out of vanity than because they are unacquainted with the use of caskets or cabinets for keeping them. They also wear necklaces made of coloured glass beads or cloves strung on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> of silk. The Moors consider their wives less in the light of companions than in that of slaves destined to labour. Except in the benefits of tillage, they are employed in every fertile operation; nay, in some of the poorer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> a woman is often seen yoked in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> along with a mule, an ass, or some other animal. When the Moors remove their douchars, all the men seat themselves in a circle on the ground; and with their elbows resting on their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the time in conversation, while the women strike the tents, fold them up into bundles, and place them on the backs of their camels or oxen. The old women are then each loaded with a parcel, and the young carry the children on their shoulders. shoulders suspended in a cloth girt round their bodies. In the more southern parts the women are likewise employed in the care of the horses; the husband, who in these climates is always a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a>, issues his orders, and seems only made to be obeyed. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> ceremonies of the Moors that live in tents pretty much resemble those of the same people that live in the cities. In the douchars they are generally most brilliant and gay; the strangers that pass along are invited, and made to contribute to the feast; but this is done more from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> than from any mercenary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>. The tribes of the plain generally avoid mixing by marriage with one another; the prejudices that divide these people are commonly perpetuated; or, if they are partially healed, they never fail to revive upon trifling occasions, such as a strayed camel, or the preference of a pasture or well. Marriages have sometimes taken place among them, that, to far from cementing their differences, have occasioned the most tragical scenes. Husbands have been known to murder their wives, and women their husbands, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> national quarrels. Parents are not encumbered with their children, however numerous they may be, for they are very early employed in domestic affairs; they tend the flocks, they gather wood, and they assist in ploughing and reaping. In the evening, when they return from the field, all the children of the douchar assemble in a common tent, where the iman, who himself can hardly spell, makes them read a few sentences from the Koran written on boards, and instructs them in their religion by the light of a fire made of straw, of bushes, and cow dung dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. As the heat is very great in the inland parts of the country, children of both sexes go quite naked till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of nine or ten. The douchars dispersed over the plains are always in the neighbourhood of some rivulet or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and they are a kind of inns for the reception of travellers. There is generally a tent erected for their use, if they have not brought one along with them, where they are accommodated with poultry, milk, and eggs, and with whatever is necessary for their horses. Instead of wood for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, they have the cow dung, which, when mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, makes a very brisk fire. A guard is always set on the tents of travellers, especially if they are Europeans, because the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of their wealth might tempt the avidity of the Moors, who are naturally inclined to thieving. With respect to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, a very judicious policy is established, which is adapted to the character of the Moors, and to their manner of life. The douchars are responsible for robberies committed in their neighbourhood and in sight of their tents; they are not only obliged to make restitution, but it gives the sovereign a pretence for exacting a contribution proportioned to the abilities of the douchar. In order to temper the rigour of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, they are made responsible only for such robberies as are committed during the day; those that happen after sunset are not imputed to them, as they could neither see nor prevent them; on this account, people here travel only from sunrise to sunsetting. To facilitate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of necessaries, there is in the fields every day, except Friday, which is a day of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, a public market in the different quarters of Morocco, each province. The Moors of the neighbourhood assemble to sell and buy cattle, corn, pulse, dried fruits, carpets, haicks, and in short all the productions of the country. This market, which is called Soc, resembles our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. The bustle of the people who go and come, gives a better idea of the manner of life of the Moors than can be had in the cities. The alcaldes, who command in the neighbourhood, always attend these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> with soldiers to keep the peace; as it frequently happens that the grudges which these tribes harbour against one another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out upon such occasions into open violence. The Moors who inhabit the cities differ from the others only in having a little more urbanity and a more easy deportment. Though they have the same origin with those of the plains, they affect to decline all intercourse with them. Some writers, without any foundation, have given the name of Arabs to the inhabitants of the towns, and that of Moors to those of the plains. But the greater part of the cities of this empire are more ancient than the invasion of the Arabs, who themselves lived in tents. The houses in most of the towns in this empire appear at a little distance like vaulted tombs in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard; and the entrance into the best of them has but furniture, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> appearance. The rooms are generally on the ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, and whitened on the outside. As the roofs are quite flat, they serve as verandas, where the Moorish women commonly sit for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and in some places it is possible to pass nearly over the whole town without having occasion to descend into the street. As the best apartments are all backwards, a stable, or perhaps something worse, is the place to which visitors are first introduced. Upon entering the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the stranger is either detained in this place, or in the street, till all the women are despatched out of the way; he is then allowed to enter a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> court, into which four narrow and long rooms open by means of large folding doors, which, as they have no windows, serve likewise to introduce light into the apartments. The court has generally in its centre a fountain; and if it is the house of a Moor of property, it is floored with blue and white chequered tiling. None of the chambers have fire places; and their victuals are always dressed in the court-yard in an earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a> heated with charcoal. When the visitor enters the room, where he is received by the master of the house, he finds him sitting <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-legged and barefooted on a mattress, covered with fine white linen, and placed on the floor or else on a common mat. This, with a narrow piece of carpeting, is in general the only furniture he will meet with in Moorish houses, though they are not destitute of other ornaments. The wardrobe of the inhabitants of cities is but little different from that of those who live in tents.—Like the men, the latter, they have a haick, and a hood more or less fine, and have also a hood of coarse European cloth of dark blue for the winter. What farther distinguishes them from the country Moors is, that they wear a flint and linen drawers, and an upper garment of cotton in summer, and of cloth in winter, which they call a caftan. The white or blue hood, the purpose of which seems to be to guard against bad weather, and which is called bernus, The Moorish women who live in cities are, as in other nations, more addicted to show and finery in dress than those of the country; but as they generally leave the house only one day in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, they seldom dress themselves. Not allowed to receive <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> visitors, they remain in their houses employed in their families, and so totally in delirium that they often wear only a shift, and another coarser shift over the first, tied round their waist, with their hair plaited, and sometimes with, though often without, a cap. When dressed, they wear an ample and fine linen shift, the bosom embroidered in gold; a rich caftan of cloth, stuff, or velvet, worked in gold; and one or two folds of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, streaked with gold and silk, round the head, and tied behind so as that the fringes, intermingled with their tresses, descend as low as the waist; to which some add a ribbon of about two inches broad, worked in gold or pearls, that encircles the forehead in form of a diadem. Their caftan is bound round their waist by a crimson velvet girdle, embroidered in gold, with a buckle of gold or silver, or else a girdle of tamboured stuff, manufactured at Fez. The women have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> slippers, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of wearing a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> of fine cloth somewhat large, which is tied below the knee and at the ankle, over which it falls in folds. This stocking is less calculated to show what we call a handsome leg, than to make it appear thick; for to be fat is one of the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> among the Moorish women. To obtain this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, they take infinite pains, feed when they become thin on a diet somewhat like forced meat balls, a certain quantity of which is given them daily; and in fine, the same care is taken among the Moors to fatten young women as is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to fatten fowls. The Negroes, who constitute a large proportion of the emperor's subjects, are better formed than the Moors; and as they are more lively, daring, and active, they are intrusted with an important share in the executive part of government. They constitute in fact the most considerable part of the emperor's army, and are generally appointed to the command of provinces and towns. This circumstance naturally creates a jealousy between them and the Moors, the latter considering the negroes as usurpers of a power which they have no right to assume. Besides those negroes which form the emperor's army, there are a great many others in the country, who either are or have been slaves to private Moors: every Moor of consequence, indeed, has his proportion of them in his service. To the disgrace of Europe, the Moors treat their slaves with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, employing them in looking after their gardens, and in the domestic duties of their houses. They allow them to marry among themselves; and after a certain number of years, spontaneously present them with the invaluable boon of liberty. They soon are initiated in the Mahometan persuasion, though they sometimes intermix with it a few of their original superstitious customs. In every other respect they copy the dress and manners of the Moors. Among the inhabitants of Morocco there is another class, of whom we must not omit to make mention. These are the Renegadoes, or foreigners, who have renounced their religion for the faith of Mahomet. Of these there are a great number who have been originally Jews: they are held in little estimation by the Moors; and would be held in abhorrence by the Jews, if they durst freely express their aversion. The families of these apostates are called Toonadis: not having at any time married with the Moors, they still preserve their ancient characteristics, and are known almost at sight to be the progeny of those who formerly embraced the Mahometan religion. The Christian renegadoes are but few; and generally are fugitive peculators of Spain, or men fallen from power, who because of their misfortunes, or in despair, quit one unfortunate situation for another much more deplorable. The Jews were formerly very numerous in this empire. After being proscribed in Spain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, multitudes of them passed over to Morocco, and spread themselves through the towns and over the country. By the relations they themselves give, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the places assigned them to dwell in, it would appear there were more than 30,000 families, of whom at present there is scarcely a residue of one-twelfth; the remainder either having changed their religion, sunk under their sufferings, or fled from the vexations they endured, and the arbitrary taxes and tolls imposed upon them. The Jews possess neither lands nor gardens, nor can they enjoy their fruits in tranquility: they must wear only black; and are obliged, when they pass near mosques, or through streets in which there are sanctuaries, to walk barefoot. The lowest among the Moors imagines he has a right to ill-treat a Jew; nor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> the latter defend himself, because the Koran and the judge are always in favour of the Mahometan.—Notwithstanding this state of oppression, the Jews have many advantages over the Moors: they better understand the spirit of trade; they act as agents and brokers, and profit by their own cunning and the ignorance of the Moors. The Moors, who derive their language and religion from the Arabs, seem not in any manner to have participated of their knowledge. United and confounded, as they are of Morocco have been with the Moors of Spain, the latter of whom cultivated the arts and gave birth to Averroes, and many other great men, the Moors of this empire have preserved no traces of the genius of their ancestors. They have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> sciences. Education consists merely in learning to read and write; and as the revenues of the learned are derived from these talents, the priests and talbes among them are the sole depositaries of thus much knowledge: the children of the Moors are taught in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> to read and repeat some sixty lefsons, selected from the Koran, which for the sake of economy are written upon small boards. The Moors who formerly inhabited Spain gave great application to physic and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>; and they have left <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> behind them which still remain monuments of their genius. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Moors are infinitely degenerate; they have not the least inclination to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of science; they know the properties of some simples; but as they do not proceed upon principle, and are ignorant of the causes and effects of diseases, they generally make a wrong application of their remedies. Their most useful physicians are their talbes, their fa- kirs, and their saints, in whom they place a superstitious confidence. Notwithstanding the Moors have occupied themselves little in the study of astronomy, they have been eager after astrology. This imaginary science, which made so rapid a progress at Rome in spite of the edicts of the emperors, may be conceived to make still greater advances among a people wholly fluid and ignorant, and ever agitated by the dread of present evils, or the hope of a more happy futurity. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">Magic</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of astrology, has here also found its followers, and is particularly studied by the talbes in the southern parts, who successfully use it in imposing upon Moorish credulity with strange <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> and ambiguous forebodings and prophecies. The Moorish manufactures are—The haick, which, as was before observed, is a long garment composed of white wool and cotton, or cotton and silk woven together, and is used by the Moors for the purpose of covering their under dress when they go abroad, which they do by totally wrapping themselves in it in a careless but easy manner; silk handkerchiefs of a particular kind, prepared only at Fez; silks checkered with cotton; carpeting, little inferior to that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; beautiful matting, made of the palmetto or wild palm tree; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> of a coarse kind; cordovan, commonly called Morocco leather; gunpowder of an inferior nature; and long-barrelled muskets, made of Billcay iron. The Moors are unacquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of casting cannon; and therefore those few which are now in the country are obtained from Europeans. The manufacture of glass is likewise unknown to them; as indeed they make great use of earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and have few or no windows to their houses, this commodity may be of less importance to them than many others. They make butter, by putting the milk into a goat skin, with its outward coat turned inwards, and shaking it till the butter collects on the sides, when it is taken out for use. From this operation it proves always full of hairs, and has an insipid flavour. Their cheese consists merely of curds hardened and dried, and has uniformly a disagreeable taste. The bread in some of the principal towns, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANGIER">Tangier</a> and Sallee, is remarkably good, but in many other places it is coarse, black, and heavy. Their looms, forges, ploughs, carpenters tools, &c., are much upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> with the improved instruments of the same kind which are used at this time in some parts of Europe, only still more clumsily finished. In their work, they attend more to strength than neatness or convenience; and, like all other ignorant people, they have no idea that what they do is capable of improvement. It is probable, indeed, that the Moors have undergone no very material change since the revolution in their arts and sciences, which took place soon after their expulsion from Spain. Previous to that period, it is well known they were an enlightened people, at a time when the greater part of Europe was involved in ignorance and barbarism; but owing to the weakness and tyranny of their princes, they gradually sunk into the very opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, and may now be considered as but a few degrees removed from a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> state. Their mosques or places of public worship are usually large square buildings, composed of the same materials as the houses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> consists of broad and lofty piazzas, opening into a square court, in a manner in some degree similar to the Royal Exchange of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. In the centre of the court is a large fountain, and a small stream surrounds the piazzas, where the Moors perform the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of ablution. The court and piazzas are floored with blue and white chequered tiling; and the latter are covered with matting, upon which the Moors kneel while repeating their prayers. In the most conspicuous part of the mosque fronting the east, stands a kind of pulpit, where the talbe or priest occasionally preaches. The Moors always enter this place of worship barefooted, leaving their slippers at the door. On the top of the mosque, is a square steeple with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, whither at stated hours the talbe ascends, hoists a white flag, and calls the people to prayers, for they have no bells. From this high situation the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> is heard at a considerable distance; and the talbes have a monotonous mode of enunciation, the voice sinking at the end of every short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, which in some measure resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. The moment the flag is displayed, every person forsook his employment, and goes to prayers. If they are near a mosque, they perform their devotions within it, otherwise immediately on the spot where they happen to be, and always with their faces towards the east, in honour of their prophet Mahomet, who it is well known was buried at Medina. Their Sabbath is on our Friday, and commences from six o'clock the preceding evening. On this day they use a blue flag instead of the white one. As it has been prophesied that they are to be conquered by the Christians on the Sabbath day, the gates of all the towns and of the emperor's palaces are shut when at divine service on that day, in order to avoid being surprised during that period. Their talbes are not distinguished by any particular dress. The Moors have three solemn devotional periods in the course of the year. The first, which is named Aid de Gabier, is held in commemoration of the birth of Mahomet. It continues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days; during which period, every person who can afford the expense kills a sheep as a sacrifice, and divides it among his friends. The second is the Ramadam. This is held at the season when Mahomet disappeared in his flight from Mecca to Medina. Every man is obliged at that period to fast (that is, to abstain from animal food from sunrise to sunset each day) for thirty days; at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which time a feast takes place, and continues a week. The third is named Llajbore, and is a day set apart by Mahomet for every person to compute the value of his property, in order for the payment of zakat, that is, one-tenth of their income to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and other pious uses. Although this feast only lasts a single day, yet it is celebrated with far greater magnificence than either of the others. The Moors compute time by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> months, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> the days of the week by the first, second, third, &c., beginning from our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>. They use a common reed for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, and begin their manuscripts from right to left. The Moors of the empire of Morocco, as well as those to the northern limits of Africa, speak Arabic; but this language is corrupted in proportion as we recede farther from Asia, where it first took birth; the intermixture intermixture which has happened among the African nations, and the frequent transmigrations of the Moors, during a succession of ages, have occasioned them to lose the purity of the Arabic language; its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> has been vitiated, the use of many words lost, and other foreign words have been introduced without thereby rendering it more copious; the pronunciation of the Africans, however, is softer to the ear and less guttural than that of the Egyptians. The language, when written, is in effect much the same at Morocco as at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, except that there are letters and expressions among the Moors which differ from those of the Oriental Arabs, who, however, understand the Moors in conversation, notwithstanding their vitiated manner of pronouncing. They mutually read each others writings with some difficulty. The Moors are naturally of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and pensive disposition, fervid in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> of friendship, but very insincere in their attachments. They have no curiosity, no ambition of knowledge; an indolent habit, united to the want of mental cultivation, renders them perhaps even more callous than other unenlightened people to every delicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; and they require more than ordinary excitement to render them sensible of pleasure or of pain. This languor of sentiment is, however, unaccompanied with the smallest spark of courage or fortitude. When in adversity, they manifest the most abject submission to their superiors; and in prosperity their tyranny and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> are inadmissible. Personal cleanliness has been considered as one of those circumstances which serve to mark and determine the civilization of a people. It was in vain that Mahomet enjoined the frequency of ablution as a religious duty to the Moors. Their dress, which should be white, is but seldom washed; and their whole appearance evinces that they perform this branch of their religious ceremonies in but a slovenly manner. With this degree of negligence as to their persons, we may be justly surprized to find united a most scrupulous nicety in their habitations and apartments. They enter their chambers barefooted, and cannot bear the slightest degree of contamination near the place where they are seated. This delicacy again is much confined to the inside of their houses. The streets receive the whole of their rubbish and filth; and by these means the ground is so raised in most parts of the city of Morocco, that the new buildings always stand considerably higher than the old. With respect to the hours for eating, the people of this country are remarkably regular.
