The apartments are in general exceedingly small, excepting one single room called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> chamber, in which the ancient czars used to give audience to foreign ambassadors, and which has been repeatedly described by several English travellers who visited Moscow before the imperial residence was transferred to Peterburgh. The room is large and vaulted, and has in the centre an enormous pillar of stone which supports the ceiling. In this palace Peter the Great came into the world, in the year 1672. In that part called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> are deposited the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, jewels, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> robes, used at the coronation of the sovereigns, besides several curiosities relative to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the country. Of the great number of churches contained in this city, two in particular, namely, that of St Michael and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSUMPTION">Assumption</a> of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, are remarkable; the one for being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the sovereigns of Russia were formerly interred, and the other where they are crowned. These edifices, which are situated in the Kremlin, are both in the same style of architecture; and their exterior form, though modelled according to the ancient style of the country, is not absolutely elegant. In the cathedral of St Michael, which contains the tombs of the Russian sovereigns, the bodies are not, as with us, deposited in vaults, or beneath the pavement, but are entombed in raised sepulchres, mostly of brick, in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, and about two feet in height. When Mr Coxe visited the cathedral, the most ancient were covered with pallis of red cloth, others of red velvet, and that of Peter II. with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> tissue, bordered with silver fringe and ermine. Each <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> has at its lower extremity a small silver plate, upon which is engraved the name of the deceased sovereign, and the era of his death. The cathedral of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, which has long been appropriated to the coronation of the Russian sovereigns, is the most splendid and magnificent in Moscow. The screen is in many parts covered with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> silver and gold richly worked. From the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> hangs an enormous chandelier of maffy silver, weighing 2940 pounds: it was made in England, and was a present from Moroloff, prime minister and favourite of Alexey Michaelovitch. The sacred utensils and episcopal vestments are extraordinarily rich, but the taste of the workmanship is in general rude, and by no means equal to the materials. Many of the paintings which cover the inside walls are of a colossal size: some are very ancient, and were executed so early as in the latter end of the 15th century. It contains, amongst the rest a head of the Virgin, supposed to have been delineated by St Luke, and greatly celebrated in this country for its sanctity and the power of working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> is almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; its head is ornamented with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and body are gilded, which gives it a most grotesque appearance. It is placed in the screen, and enclosed within a large silver covering, which is only taken off on great festivals, or for the curiosity of strangers. In this cathedral are deposited the remains of the Russian patriarchs. The place in the Khitaigorod, where the public archives are deposited, is a strong brick building, containing several vaulted apartments with iron doors. These archives, consisting of a numerous collection of state papers, were crowded into boxes and thrown aside like common lumber, until the empress Catharine ordered them to be revised and arranged. In conformity to this mandate, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a> has divided them in chronological order with such perfect regularity, that any single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCUMENT">document</a> may be inspected with little trouble. They are enclosed in separate cabinets with glass doors: those relative to Russia are all classified according to the several provinces which they concern; and over each cabinet is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the name of the province to which it is appropriated. In the same manner the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> relative to foreign kingdoms are placed in separate divisions under the respective titles of Poland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, England, France, Germany, &c. The university of Moscow, all situated in the Khitaigorod, was founded, at the instance of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Shuvaloff, by the empress <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, for 600 students; who are clothed, boarded, and instructed, at the expense of the crown. Besides this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, there are two gymnasia or seminaries for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of youth, endowed also by Elizabeth; in which are taught, by twenty-three professors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, classics, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, the Greek, Latin, Russian, German, French, Italian, and Tartar languages; history, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, architecture, fortification, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, music, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Moscow is the centre of the inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Russia, and particularly connects the trade between Europe and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The only <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> to this city is formed by the Moskva, which falling into the Oka near Columna, communicates by means of that river with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>. But as the Moskva is only navigable in spring upon the melting of the snows, the principal merchandise is conveyed to and from Moscow upon sledges in winter. The whole of the retail trade is carried on in the Khitaigorod; where, according to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> common in Russia, as well as in most kingdoms of the East, all the shops are collected together in one spot. The place is like a kind of fair, consisting of many rows of low brick buildings; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between them resembling alleys. These shops or booths occupy a considerable space; they do not, as with us, make part of the houses inhabited by the tradesmen, but are quite detached from their dwellings, which for the most part are at some distance in another quarter of the town. The tradesman comes to his shop in the morning; remains there all day, and returns home to his family in the afternoon. Every trade has its separate department; and they who sell the same goods have booths adjoining to each other. Furs and skins form the most considerable article of commerce in Moscow; and the shops which vend these commodities occupy several streets. Amongst the curiosities of Moscow, the market for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of houses is not the least remarkable. It is held in a large open space in one of the suburbs; and exhibits a great variety of ready made houses, thickly strewed upon the ground. The purchaser who wants a dwelling, repairs to this spot, mentions the number of rooms he requires, examines the different timbers, which are regularly numbered, and bargains for that which suits him. The house is sometimes paid for on the spot, and taken away by the purchaser; or sometimes the vender contracts to transport and erect it upon the place where it is designed to stand. It may appear incredible to assert, that a dwelling may be thus bought. MOSCOW bought, removed, raised and inhabited, within the space of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; but we shall conceive it practicable by considering that these ready made houses are in general merely collections of trunks of trees tenoned and mortised at each extremity into one another, so that nothing more is required than the labour of transporting and adjusting them. But this summary mode of building is not always peculiar to the meaner hovels; as wooden structures of very large dimensions and handsome appearance are occasionally formed in Russia with an expedition almost inconceivable to the inhabitants of other countries. A remarkable instance of this despatch was displayed the last time the empress came to Moscow. Her majesty proposed to reside in the mansion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Galitzin, which is esteemed the completest edifice in this city; but as it was not sufficiently spacious for her reception, a temporary addition of wood, larger than the original house, and containing a magnificent suite of apartments, was begun and finished within the space of six weeks. This <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>-like fabric was so handsome and commodious, that the materials which were taken down at her majesty's departure, were to be re-constructed as a kind of imperial villa upon an eminence near the city. Mr Coxe mentions an admirable <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> in this city for preventing riots, or for stopping the concourse of people in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of fires, which are very frequent and violent in those parts, where the houses are mostly of wood, and the streets are laid with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. At the entrance of each street there is a chevaux-de-frise gate, one end whereof turns upon a pivot, and the other rolls upon a wheel; near it is a canteen box in which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is occasionally stationed. In times of riot or fire the sentinel shuts the gate, and all passage is immediately stopped. Among the public institutions of Moscow, the most remarkable is the Foundling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, endowed in 1764 by the empress Catharine, and supported by voluntary contributions and legacies, and other charitable gifts. In order to encourage donations, her majesty granted to all benefactors some valuable privileges, and a certain degree of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in proportion to the extent of their liberality. Among the principal contributors must be mentioned a private merchant named Dimidoff, a person of great wealth, who has expended in favour of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> above 100,000l. The hospital, which is situated in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> part of the town upon a gentle ascent near the river Moskva, is an immense pile of building of a quadrangular shape, part of which was only finished when Mr Coxe (whose account we are transcribing) was at Moscow. It contained, at that time, three thousand foundlings; and, when the whole is completed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> receive eight thousand. The children are brought to the porter's lodge, and admitted without any recommendation. The rooms are lofty and large; the dormitories, which are separate from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> rooms, are very airy, and the beds are not crowded: each foundling, even each infant, has a separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. The children remain two years in the nursery, when they are admitted into the lowest class; the boys and girls continue together until they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which time they are separated. They all learn to read, write, and cast accounts. The boys are taught to knit; they occasionally card <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and work in the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. The girls learn to knit, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> work; they spin and weave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; they are employed in cookery, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>, and house work of all sorts. At the age of fourteen the foundlings enter into the first class; when they have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of choosing any particular branch of trade; and for this purpose there are different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of manufactures established in the hospital, of which the principal are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stockings, ribbands, lace, gloves, buttons, and cabinet work. A separate room is appropriated to each trade. Some boys and girls are instructed in the French and German languages, and a few boys in the Latin tongue; others learn music, drawing, and dancing.

MOSEHEIM

Pages 52-52

John Laurence, an illustrious German divine, was born in 1695, of a noble family, which might seem to open to his ambition a fair path to civil promotion; but his zeal for the interests of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, his thirst after knowledge, and particularly his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for sacred literature, induced him to consecrate his talents to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> loaded him with literary honours; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> invited him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> called him thence to Helmstadt, where he filled the academical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; was honoured with the character of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> counsellor to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and presided over the seminaries of learning in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wolfenbuttel and the principality of Blackenburgh. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was formed of giving an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of lustre to the universities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>, by filling it with men of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in letters, Dr Mohein was deemed worthy to appear at the head of it, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; and here he died, in 1755, universally lamented. In depth of judgement, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of learning, in purity of taste, in the powers of eloquence, and in a laborious application to all the various branches of erudition and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, he had certainly very few superiors. His Latin translation of Cudworth's Intellectual System, enriched with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> Mosquito annotations, discovered a profound acquaintance with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> learning and philosophy. His illustrations of the Scriptures, his labours in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Christianity, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon religion and philosophy, appear in many volumes of sacred and profane literature; and the Ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, from the birth of Christ to the beginning of the 18th century, is unquestionably the best that is extant. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, written in Latin, has been translated into English, and accompanied with notes and chronological tables by Archibald Maclean, D.D. and from this translator's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition, 1758, in 5 vols. 8vo, this short account is taken.

MOSELLE

Pages 50-50

a river of Germany, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOSGES">Vosges</a> in Lorraine, and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COBLENZ">Coblenz</a>. MOSELLE is also the name of a department of France, which includes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lorraine.

MOSES

Pages 50-52

the son of Amram and Jochebed, was born in the year 1571 before Christ. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, perceiving that the Hebrews were become a formidable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, issued forth an edict commanding all the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> children to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. To avoid this cruel edict, Jochebed, the mother of Moses, having concealed her son for three months, at length made an ark <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of bulrushes, daubed it with pitch, laid the child in it, and exposed him on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Thermuthis the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who happened to be walking by the river's side, perceived the floating cradle, commanded it to be brought to her, and struck with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the child, determined to preserve his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In three years afterwards the princess adopted him for her own son, called his name Moses, and caused him be diligently instructed in all the learning of the Egyptians. But his father and mother, to whom he was restored by a fortunate accident, were at still greater pains to teach him the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of his fathers. Many things are related by historians concerning the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of Moses's life, which are not to be found in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. According to Josephus and Eusebius, he made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on the Ethiopians, and completely defeated them. They add, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> Saba, in which the enemy had been forced to take refuge, was betrayed into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by the king's daughter, who became deeply enamoured of him, when she beheld from the top of the walls his valorous exploits at the head of the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. But as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this expedition is more than doubtful, we shall therefore confine ourselves to the narrative of sacred writ, which commences at the fortieth year of Moses's life. He then left the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Pharaoh, and went to visit his countrymen the Hebrews, who groaned under the ill usage and opprobrium of their unfeeling masters. Having perceived an Egyptian smiting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, he slew the Egyptian, and buried him in the sand. But he was obliged, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, to fly into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Midian, where he married Zipporah, daughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> Jethro, by whom he had two sons, Gerhohm and Eliezer. Here he lived 40 years; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his employment was to tend the flocks of his father-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Having one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> led his flock towards Mount Horeb, God appeared to him in the midst of a bush which burned with fire but was not consumed, and commanded him to go and deliver his brethren from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>. Moses at first refused to go; but was at length prevailed on by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. racles which the Almighty wrought for his conviction. Upon his return to Egypt, he, together with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>, went to the court of Pharaoh, and told him that God commanded him to let the Hebrews go to offer sacrifices in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. But the impious monarch disregarded this command, and caused the labour of the Israelites to be doubled. The messengers of the Almighty again returned to the king, and wrought a miracle in his sight, that they might move his heart, and induce him to let the people depart. Aaron having <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his miraculous rod, it was immediately converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>; but the same thing being performed by the magicians, the king's heart was hardened more and more; and his obstinacy at last drew down the judgements of the Almighty on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which was afflicted with ten dreadful plagues. The first was the changing of the waters of the Nile and of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> into blood, so that the Egyptians died of thirst. In consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, the land was covered with innumerable swarms of frogs, which entered even into Pharaoh's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. By the third plague, the dust was converted into <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>, which cruelly tormented both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beast. The fourth plague was a multitude of destructive flies which spread throughout Egypt, and infected the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The fifth was a sudden pestilence, which destroyed all the cattle of the Egyptians, without injuring those of the Israelites. The sixth produced numberless ulcers and fiery boils upon man and upon beast. The seventh was a dreadful storm of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, accompanied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which destroyed every thing that was in the field, whether man or beast, and spared only the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel dwelt. By the eighth plague swarms of locusts were brought into the country, which devoured every green <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, the fruit of the trees and the produce of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. By the ninth plague thick darkness covered all the land of Egypt, except the dwellings of the children of Israel. The tenth and last plague was the death of the firstborn in Egypt, who were all in one night cut off by the destroying angel, from the firstborn of the king to the firstborn of the slaves and of the cattle. This dreadful calamity moved the heart of the hardened Pharaoh, and he at length consented to allow the people of Israel to depart from his kingdom. Profane authors who have spoken of Moses, seem to have been in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> acquainted with these mighty wonders. That he performed miracles, must have been allowed by many, by whom he was considered as a famous magician; and he could scarcely appear in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to men who did not acknowledge him for the messenger of the Almighty. Both Diodorus and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> mention the distressed state to which Egypt was reduced by these terrible calamities. The Hebrews, amounting to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 650,000 men, without reckoning women and children, left Egypt on the 15th day of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Nisan, which, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this deliverance, was thenceforth reckoned the first month of their year. Scarcely had they reached the shore of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> when Pharaoh with a powerful army set out in pursuit of them. On this occasion Moses stretched forth his rod upon the sea; and the waters thereof being divided, remained suspended on both sides till the Hebrews passed through dry-footed.—The Egyptians determined to follow the same course; but God caused a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to blow, which brought back the waters to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and the whole army of Pharaoh perished in the waves. After the miraculous passage of the Red sea, the army proceeded towards Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>, and arrived at Marah, where the waters were bitter; but Moses, by calling a tree into them, rendered them fit for drinking. Their tenth encampment was at Rephidim; where Moses drew <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the rock in Horeb, by smiting it with his rod. Here likewise Amalek attacked Israel. While Joshua fought against the Amalekites, Moses stood on the top of a hill, and lifted up his hands; in consequence of which the Israelites prevailed, and cut their enemies in pieces. They at length arrived at the foot of Mount Sinai on the third day of the ninth month after their departure from Egypt. Moses having ascended several times into the mount, received the law from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of God himself in the midst of thunders and lightnings, and concluded the famous covenant betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> and the children of Israel. When he descended from Sinai, he found that the people had fallen into the idolatrous worship of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> calf. The messenger of God, shocked at such ingratitude, broke in pieces the tables of the law which he carried in his hands, and put 23,000 of the transgressors to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. He afterwards reascended into the mountain, and there obtained new tables of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on which the law was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>. When Moses descended, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> shone so that the Israelites dared not to come nigh unto him, and he was obliged to cover it with a veil. The Israelites were here employed in constructing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> according to a pattern shown them by God. It was erected and consecrated at the foot of the Mount Sinai on the first day of the first month of the second year after their departure from Egypt; and it served the Israelites instead of a temple till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, who built a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the God of his fathers after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> shown him by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. Moses having dedicated the tabernacle, he consecrated Aaron and his sons to be its ministers, and appointed the Levites to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He likewise gave various commandments concerning the worship of God and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Jews. This was a theocracy in the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the word. God himself governed them immediately by means of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Moses, whom he had chosen to be the interpreter of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the people; and he required all the honours belonging to their king to be paid unto himself. He dwelt in his tabernacle, which was situated in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, like a monarch in his palace. He gave answers to those who consulted him, and himself denounced punishments against the transgressors of his laws. This properly was the time of the theocracy, taken in its full extent; for God was not only considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> who was the object of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship, but as the sovereign to whom the honours of supreme majesty were paid. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> was nearly the same under Joshua; who, being filled with the spirit of Moses, undertook nothing without consulting God. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, both of the leader and of the people, was regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Almighty, who rewarded their fidelity and obedience by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of miracles, victories, and successes. After Moses had regulated every thing regarding the civil administration, tion, and the marching of the troops, he led the Israelites to the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, to the foot of Mount Nebo. Here the Lord commanded him to ascend into the mountain; whence he showed him the promised land, whereto he was not permitted to enter. He immediately after yielded up the ghost, without sickness or pain, in the 120th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and 1451 years before <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. Moses is incontestably the author of the first five books of the Old Testament, which go by the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>; and which are acknowledged to be inspired, by the Jews and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of every persuasion. Some, however, have denied that Moses was the author of these books; and have founded their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on this, that he always speaks of himself in the third person. But this manner of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> is by no means peculiar to Moses; it occurs also in several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians; such as Xenophon, Caesar, Josephus, &c., who possessed more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> or good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> historians, whose egotism is altogether disgusting, have not like them left to posterity a spectacle of ridiculous vanity and self-conceit. After all, it is proper to observe, that profane authors have related many falsehoods and absurdities concerning Moses, and concerning the origin and the religion of the Jews, with which they were but little acquainted. Plutarch, in his book concerning Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, says that Judah and Hieroofolmus were brothers, and descended from Typhon; and that the former gave his name to the country and its inhabitants, and the latter to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city. Others say that they came from Mount Ida in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>. Strabo is the only author who speaks anything like reason and truth concerning them; though he too says that they were descended from the Egyptians, and considers Moses their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> as an Egyptian priest. He acknowledges, however, that they were a people strictly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and sincerely religious. Other authors by whom they are mentioned, seem not to have had the smallest acquaintance either with their laws or their worship. They frequently confound them with the Christians, as is the case with Juvenal, Tacitus, and Quintilian.

MOSKITO

Pages 52-52
or Mosquito Country, is situated in North America, between 85 and 88 degrees of west longitude, and between 13 and 15 degrees of north latitude; having the north sea on the north and east, Nicaragua on the south, and Honduras on the west; and indeed the Spaniards esteem it a part of the principality of Honduras, though they have no colonies in the Mosquito country. When the Spaniards first invaded this part of Mexico, they massacred the greatest part of the natives, which gave those that escaped into the inaccessible part of the country an insuperable aversion to them; and they have always appeared ready to join any Europeans that come upon their coasts against the Spaniards, and particularly the English, who frequently come hither; and the Mosquito men being excellent marksmen, the English employ them in striking the manati fish, &c., and many of the Mosquito Indians come to Jamaica, and sail with the English in their voyages. These people are so situated between morasses and inaccessible mountains, and a coast full of rocks and shoals, that no attempts against them by the Spaniards, whom they mortally hate, could ever succeed. Nevertheless, they are a mild inoffensive people, of great morality and virtue, and will never trust a man who has once deceived them. They have so great a veneration towards the English, that they have spontaneously put themselves and their lands under the protection and dominion of the crown of England. This was first done when the duke of Albermarle was governor of Jamaica, and the king of the Moskitos received a commission from his grace, under the seal of that island; and since this time they have been steady in their alliance with the English. But in the year 1786, this country was ceded to Spain, and consequently became a Spanish province.

MOSQUE

Pages 52-53

a temple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship among the Mahometans. All mosques are <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buildings, generally constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> gate there is a square <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> paved with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble; and low galleries round it, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is supported by marble pillars. In these galleries the Turks wash themselves before they go into the mosque. In each mosque there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lamps; and between these hang many crystal rings, ostriches eggs, and other curiosities, which, when the lamps are lighted, make a fine show. As it is not lawful to enter the mosque with stockings or shoes on, the pavements are covered with pieces of stuff sewed together, each being wide enough to hold a row of men kneeling, sitting, or prostrate. The women are not not allowed to enter the mosque, but stay in the porches without. About every mosque there are six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers, called minarets, each of which has three little open galleries, one above another; these towers, as well as the mosques, are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and adorned with gilding and other ornaments; and from thence, instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, the people are called to prayers by certain officers appointed for that purpose. Most of the mosques have a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> belonging to them, in which travellers of what <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> ever, are entertained three days. Each mosque has also a place called tarbe, which is the burying-place of its founders; within which is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, covered with green velvet or satin; at the ends of which are two tapers, and round it several leeks for those who read the Koran and pray for the souls of the deceased.

MOSTRA

Pages 55-55

in the Italian music, a mark at the end of a line <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> space, to show that the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the next line is in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this note be accompanied with a sharp or flat, it is proper to place these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> along with the mostra.

MOTACILLA

Pages 55-55

the Wagtail and Warbler; a genus of birds of the order of palaeres. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MOTE

Pages 55-55

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> books, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convention; as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> mote, burgh mote, twain mote, &c. Mote was also used for a fortres or castle; as mota de <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, &c. Mote also denoted a standing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to keep fish in; and sometimes a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ditch encompassing a castle or dwelling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Mote-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">Bell</a>, or Mot-Bell, the bell so called, which was used by the English Saxons to call people together to the court. See Folkmote. MOTH. See Phalena, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MOTHER

Pages 55-70

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation, denoting a woman who hath born a child. Mother-of-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a>. See Mytilus, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">MOTION</a> is now generally considered as incapable Motion, of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, being a simple idea <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> notion received by the senses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, however, thought differently. Some of them defined it to be a passage out of one state into another; which conveys no idea to him who Motion. who is ignorant of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of motion.—The Peripatetic definition has been mentioned elsewhere and shown to be wholly unintelligible, as well as their celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of motion into four classes, belonging to the three categories, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, and where; (see Several definitions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, No 188, 189, 190.) The Cartesians, too, among the moderns, pretend to define motion, by calling it a passage or removal of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, out of the neighbourhood of those parts to which it is immediately contiguous, into the neighbourhood of others. Borelli defines motion to be the successive passage of a body from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place. Others say that it is the application of a body to different parts of infinite and immoveable space; and a late writer * of uncommon acuteness has given as a definition of motion—change of place. We have elsewhere offered our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of every possible attempt to define motion: but as the author of the last quoted definition has endeavoured to obviate such objections as ours, candour requires that he be heard for himself. "It is said (he observes) by some, that change implies motion, and therefore cannot be a part of its definition, being the very thing defined. To this I answer, We are speaking of the sensible idea of motion, as it appears to our sight; now changes do appear to our view, and to all our senses, which give us no idea of motion. Changes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, flavour, smell, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, softness, pain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; in these, and many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, changes do not produce ideas like that produced by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> rolling or a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> falling. We may perhaps ultimately trace them to motion, but to insensible motions; to motions which arise only in reflection, and constitute no part of the actual idea of change. We can therefore conceive of change, without conceiving at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of motion.—Change is a generic idea, including many <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; motion, as a sensible idea, is a species of that genus. Change is therefore a necessary part of the definition of motion; it marks the genus of the thing defined. Motion is a change; but as there are many species of change, which of those species is motion? The answer is, It is a change of place. This marks the species; and distinguishes it from change of colour, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>." This is the ablest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of an attempt to define motion that we have ever seen; and at first view the definition itself appears to be perfect. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of definers, "confiders a definition as a speech declaring what a thing is. Everything essential to the thing defined, and nothing more, must be contained in the definition. Now the essence of a thing consists of these two parts: first, what is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to it with other things of the same kind; and secondly, what distinguishes it from other things of the same kind. The first is called the genus of the thing; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, its specific <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. The definition, therefore, consists of these two parts." In obedience to this rule, the definition under consideration seems to consist of the genus, signified by the word change; and of the specific difference, denoted by the words of place. But does the speech change of place really declare what motion is? We cannot admit that it does; as, in our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, a change of place is the effect of motion, and not motion itself. Suppose a lover of dialectic undertaking to define the stroke by which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his neighbour wounded with a bludgeon; what should we think of his art were he to call it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTUSION">contusion</a> on the head? He might say that contusion is a general term, as contusions may be produced on the arms, on the legs, and on various parts of the body; and as there are many species of contusion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were asked which of those species was the stroke to be defined, he might answer, "a contusion on the head." Here would be apparently the genus and specific difference; the former denoted by contusion, and the latter by the words on the head. But would this be a definition of a stroke? No, surely: a contusion on the head may be the effect of a stroke; but it can no more be the stroke itself, than a blow can be a bludgeon, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> wound the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. Equally evident it is, that a change of place cannot be motion; because every body must have been actually moved before we can discern, or even conceive, a change of its place. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of changing the place would perhaps come nearer to a definition of motion; but so far would it be from "a speech declaring what motion is," that we are confident a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had never by any of his senses perceived a body in actual motion, would acquire no ideas whatever from the words "act of changing place." He might have experienced changes in heat, cold, smell, and sound; but he could not possibly combine the ideas of such changes with the signification of the word place, were he even capable of understanding that word, which to us appears to be more than doubtful. (See Metaphysics, No 42, 43.) The distinctions of motion into different kinds have been no less various, and no less insignificant, than the several definitions of it. The moderns who reject the two into Peripatetic division of motion into four classes, yet consider it themselves as either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> or relative. Thus we are told, that "absolute motion is the change of absolute place, and that its celerity must be measured by the quantity of absolute space which the moving body runs through in a given time." Relative motion, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is a mutation of the relative or vulgar place of the moving body, and has its celerity estimated by the quantity of relative space run through." Now it is obvious, that this distinction conveys no ideas without a farther explanation of the terms by which it is expressed; but that explanation is impossible to be given. Thus, before we can understand what absolute motion is, we must understand what is meant by absolute place. But absolute place is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>; for all place is relative, and consists in the positions of different bodies with regard to one another. Were a globe in the regions of empty space to be put in motion by Almighty Power, and all the rest of the corporeal world to be soon afterwards annihilated, the motion would undoubtedly continue unchanged; and yet, according to this distinction, it would be at first relative, and afterwards absolute. That the beginning of such a motion would be perceptible, and the remainder of it imperceptible, is readily granted; but on this account to consider it as of two kinds, is as absurd as to suppose the motion of the minute hand of a clock to be the Carrefiers and of Newton affected by our looking at it. Leaving therefore these unintelligible distinctions, reflecting we now come to consider a question full of a very abstruse nature, but much agitated among philosophers, viz. viz. What is the original source of motion in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>? Is it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to matter? or are we to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> it to the immediate and continual agency of some immaterial being? The former has been strenuously argued by the Cartesians, and the latter by the Newtonians. The arguments of the former, founded upon the chimerical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of vortices and the original <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of matter, were evidently inconclusive; and the hypothesis of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, who asserted that it was naturally incapable of motion, appeared more probable. To account for the quantity of motion in the universe, therefore, it became necessary to have recourse either to the Deity, or to some subordinate spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>; and this became the more necessary, as the doctrine of an absolute <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> in the celestial spaces, that is, throughout the incomparably greatest part of the creation, was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> maxims of the system. As it was absolutely denied that matter existed in these spaces, and it was plain that the celestial bodies affected one another at immense distances, the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> and repulsion were naturally called in as the sources of motion by their impulse upon inert and sluggish matter. These being admitted, a speculation ensued concerning their nature. Spiritual, it was confessed, they were; but whether they were to be accounted the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the divine Spirit himself, or that of some subordinate and inferior spirit, was a matter of no little dispute. Sir Isaac Newton, towards the latter part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, began to relax somewhat of the rigidity of his former doctrine; and allowed that a very subtle medium, which he called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>, might be the cause of attraction and repulsion, and thus of the whole phenomena of nature. Since his time the multitude of discoveries in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, the similarity of that fluid to fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, with the vast influence it has on every part of the creation with which we are acquainted, have rendered it very probable that the ether mentioned by Sir Isaac is no other than the element of fire, "the most subtle and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> of all bodies, which seems to pervade and expand itself throughout the whole universe." Electrical experiments show that this mighty agent is everywhere present, ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> forth into action if not restrained and governed with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. Being always restless and in motion, it actuates and enlivens the whole visible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; is equally fitted to produce and to destroy; distinguishes the various stages of nature, and keeps up the perpetual round of generations and corruptions, pregnant with forms which it constantly sends forth and reforms. So quick in its motions, so subtle and penetrating in its nature, so extensive in its effects, it feareth no other than the vegetative <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> or vital spirit of the world. "The animal spirit in man is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> both of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and motion. To suppose sense in the corporeal world would be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and unwarranted; but locomotive faculties are evident in all its parts. The Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Stoics, held the world to be an animal; though some of them have chosen to consider it as a vegetable. However, the phenomena do plainly show, that there is a spirit that moves, and a mind or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> that presides. This providence, Plutarch <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, was thought to be in regard to the world what the soul is in regard to man. The order and course of things, and the experiments we daily make, show that there is a mind which governs and activates this mundane system as the proper and real agent and cause; and that the inferior instrumental cause is pure ether, fire, or the substance of light, which is applied and determined by an infinite mind in the macrocosm or universe, with unlimited power, and according to stated rules, as it is in the microcosm with limited power and skill by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind. We have no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> either from experiment or reason of any other agent or efficient cause than the mind or spirit. When, therefore, we speak of corporeal agents, or corporeal causes, this is to be understood in a different, subordinate, and improper sense; and such an agent we know light or elementary fire to be." That this elementary fire, absorbed and fixed in all experimental bodies, may be the cause of the universal principle of gravity, is made sufficiently evident by numberless experiments. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a> having calcined in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> glass some regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, found that the immediate cause of the operation, sent up a thick <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, and thereby lost a considerable part of its own substance. It is vain to allege that any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matter floating in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, or that the air itself, may have been hurried into the mass by the action of the fire, and that by this additional matter the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> was increased; for it is known experimentally, that if a quantity of metal be even hermetically secured within a vessel of glass to keep off the air and all foreign matter, and the vessel be placed for some time in a strong fire, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> exhibit the same effect. "I have seen the operation performed (says Mr Jones) on two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a> filings, hermetically sealed up in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> flask, which in two hours gained 55 grains, that is nearly one seventh. Had it remained longer in the fire, it might probably have gained something more; as, in one of Mr Boyle's experiments, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> filings were found to have gained a fourth. Of accounting for these effects there are but two possible ways: 1. If the quantity of matter be the same, or, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of calcination, be somewhat less, after being exposed to the action of the fire, while the gravity of the whole is become greater; then does it follow, that gravity is not according to the quantity of matter, and of course is not one of its properties. 2. If there be an increase of the mass, it can be imputed to nothing but the matter of light or fire entangled in its passage through the substance, and so fixed in its pores, or combined with its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> parts, as to gravitate together with it. Yet it is certain, from the phenomenon of light darting from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, that this elementary fire does not gravitate till it is fixed in metal, or some other solid substance.—Here then we have a fluid which gravitates, if it gravitate at all, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> and not in others. So that which way ever the experiment be interpreted, we are forced to conclude that elementary or solar fire may be the cause of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>." That it is likewise in many cases the cause of repulsion, is known to every one who has seen it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and convert <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> into elastic vapour. But there is a fact recorded by Mr Jones, which seems to evince that the same fluid, which as it issues from the sun exhibits itself in the form of light and heat, is in other circumstances converted into a very fine air, or cold aether, which rushes very forcibly towards the body of that luminary. "As a sequel to what has been observed (says he) concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> of solid substances with the particles of fire, give me leave to subjoin an experiment of M. de Stair. He tells us, that upon heating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> in a glass, whence the air was exhausted by the rays of the sun collected in a burning glass, the vessel in which the said red lead was contained burst in pieces with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> noise. Now, as all explosions in general must be ascribed either to an admission of the air into a rarefied space, or to what is called the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of it; and as air was not admitted upon this occasion, it must have been <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> within the vessel; and certainly so, because Dr Hales has made it appear that this substance, like crude tartar and many others, will yield a considerable quantity of air in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. What went into the metal therefore as fire, came out of it again as air; which in a manner forces upon us conclusions of ineffinable value in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and such as may carry us very far into the most sublime part of it." One of the conclusions which the ingenious author thinks thus forced upon us, is, that the motion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> round the sun, as well as round their own axes, is to be attributed to the continual agency of this fluid, under its two forms of elementary fire and pure air. As fire and light, we know that it rushes with inconceivable rapidity from the body of the sun, and penetrates every corporeal substance, exerting itself sometimes with such force as nothing with which we are acquainted is able to resist. If it be indeed a fact, that this elementary fire, or principle of light and heat, afterwards cools, and becomes pure air, there cannot be a doubt, but that under such a form it will return with great force; though surely in a somewhat different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, towards the sun, forming a vortex, in which the planets are included, and by which they must of course be carried round the centre. Mr Jones does not suppose that the air into which the principle of light and heat is converted, is of so gross a nature as our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. He rather considers it as cold aether, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as he represents light to be ather heated: but he maintains, that this aether, in its aerial form, though not fit for human respiration, is a better pabulum of fire than the air which we breathe. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> is exceedingly plausible; and the author supports it by many experiments. He has not, indeed, convinced us that the solar light is converted or convertible into pure air; but he has, by just reasoning from undoubted facts, proved that the whole expanse of heaven, as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a> wander, is filled not only with light, which is indeed obvious to the senses, but also with a fluid, which, whatever it may be called, supplies the place of the air in feeding the fire of these ignited bodies. That the motion of the heavenly bodies should result from the perpetual agency of such a medium, appears to us a much more rational hypothesis, than that which makes them act upon each other at immense distances through empty space. But the hypothesis is by no means to complete a solution of the phenomena as some of its fond admirers pretend to think it. This fluid, whether called aether, heat, light, or air, is still material; and the question returns upon him who imagines that it is sufficient to account for gravitation, repulsion, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a>, &c. "What moves the fluid itself, or makes the parts of which it is composed cohere together?" However widely it may be extended, it is incapable of positive infinity; and therefore may be divided into parts separated from each other; so that it must be held together by a foreign force, as well as a ball of lead, or a piece of wax. As matter is not essentially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, the motion of this aether, under both its forms, must likewise be considered as an effect, for which we do not think that any propelling power in the body of the sun can be admitted as a sufficient cause. For how comes the sun to possess that power, and what makes the fluid return to the sun? We have no notion of power, in the proper sense of the word, but as intelligence and volition; and, by the pious and excellent author of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the First Principles of Natural Philosophy, we are certain that the sun was never supposed to be intelligent. Bishop Berkeley, who admits of light or aether as it is there, the instrumental cause of all corporeal motion, gets rid of this difficulty, by supposing, with the ancients, that some supernatural agent is animated. According to the Pythagoreans and Platonists (says his Lordship*), *Siris, there is a life infused throughout all things; the νοῦς No 277, νέος, νεύς τριπλοκτον, an intellectual and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> fire, an inward principle, animal spirit, or natural life, producing and forming within, as art doth without; regulating, moderating, and reconciling the various motions, qualities, and parts of this mundane system. By virtue of this life, the great masses are held together in their ordinary courses, as well as the minutest particles governed in their natural motions, according to the several laws of attraction, gravity, electricity, magnetism, and the rest. It is this gives instincts, teaches the spider her web, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">bee</a> her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. This it is that directs the roots of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to draw forth juices from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and the leaves and cortical vessels to separate and attract such particles of air and elementary fire as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> their respective natures." This life or animal spirit seems to be the same thing which Cudworth calls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLASTIC_NATURE"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTIC">plastic</a> nature, and which has been considered elsewhere. (See Metaphysics, No 200, and Plastic Nature). We shall therefore dismiss it at present, with just admitting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the bishop's position, "that if nature be supposed the life of the world, animated by one soul, compacted into one frame, and directed or governed in all its parts by one supreme and distinct intelligence, this system cannot be accused of atheism, though perhaps it may of mistake or impropriety." A theory of motion somewhat similar to that of Berkeley, though in several respects different from it, was not many years ago stated with great clearness, and supported with much ingenuity, in An Essay on the Powers and Mechanism of Nature, intended to improve, and more firmly establish, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> superstructure of the Newtonian system. Mr Young, the author of the essay, admits with most other philosophers of the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that body is composed of atoms which are impenetrable to each other, and may be denominated solid. These atoms, however, he does not consider as primary and simple elements, incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> into principles; Motion principles; but thinks that they are formed by certain motions of the parts of a substance immaterial and essentially active. As this notion is uncommon, and the offspring of a vigorous mind, we shall consider it more attentively under the article Plastic Nature. It is mentioned at present as a necessary introduction to the author's theory of motion, of which he attributes both the origin and the continuance to the agency of this elementary substance pervading the most solid atoms of the densest bodies. Of every body and every atom he holds the constituent principles to be essentially active; but those principles act in such a manner as to counterbalance each other; so that the atom or body considered as a whole is inert, unless in so far as it resists the compulsion or separation of its parts. No body or atom can of itself begin to move, or continue in motion for a single instant; but being pervious to the active substance, and coalescing with it, that substance, when it enters any body, it carries it along with it, till meeting some other body in the way, either the whole of the active substance lodged in the former body passes into the obstacle, in which case the impelling body instantly ceases to move; or else part of that substance passes into the obstacle, and part remains in the impelling body; and in this case both bodies are moved with a velocity in proportion to the quantity of matter which each contains, combined with the quantity of active substance by which they are respectively penetrated. In order to pave the way for his proof of the existence of one uniform active substance, he observes, that change being an essentially constituent part of motion, and change implying action, it follows that all motion implies action, and depends on an active cause. Every motion (he continues) has a beginning, a middle, and an end. The beginning is a change from rest to motion; the middle is a continuance in motion; the end is a change from motion to rest. He then proceeds to show, that the beginning of motion is by an action begun; the continuance of motion by an action <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>; and the end of motion by a cessation of action. "The first of these positions is admitted by everybody. That the continuance of motion is by an action continued, will be proved, if it shall be shown that the continuance of a motion is nothing different from its beginning, in regard to any point of time assumed in the continued motion. Now the beginning of motion (he says) consists in the beginning of change of place. But if any given portions of time and of space are assumed, a body beginning to move in the commencement of that time, and in the first portion of the space assumed, then and there begins that particular motion; and whether before the body began to move in that space it was moving in other spaces and times, has no relation to the motion in question; for this being in a space and time altogether distinct, is a distinct motion from any which might have preceded it immediately, as much as from a motion which preceded it a thousand years before. It is therefore a new motion begun; and so it may be said of every assumable point in the continued motion. The term continued serves only to connect any two distinct motions, the end of one with the beginning of the other; but does not destroy their distinctness." He then proceeds to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, which he does very successfully, the arguments by which the more rigid Newtonians endeavour to prove that a body in motion will continue to be moved by its own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INERTIA">inertia</a>, till kept by some opposite force. Having done this, he establishes the contrary conclusion by the following syllogisms: "I. Whatever requires an active force to stop its motion, is disposed to move. Every body in motion requires an active force to stop its motion; Therefore every body in motion is disposed to move. II. Whatever is disposed to motion is possessed of action. But a body in motion is disposed to continue in motion; Therefore a body in motion is possessed of action. Thus it appears, that the middle part of any motion is action equally with the beginning. The last part of motion is its termination. It is admitted that all motion is terminated by an action contrary to the direction of the motion. It is admitted, too, that the moving body acts at the time its motion is destroyed. Thus the beginning and the end of any uniform motion are confessed to be actions; but all the intermediate continuation which connects the beginning with the end is denied to be action. What can be more unaccountable than this denial? Is it not more consonant to reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, to ascribe to the whole continued motion one uninterrupted action? Such a conclusion true philosophy, we think, requires us to make. "To move or act, is an attribute which cannot be conceived to exist without a substance. The action of a body in motion is indeed the attribute of the body, and the body relatively to its own motion is truly a substance, having the attribute or quality of motion. But the body being a name figuring a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of certain ideas, which ideas are found to arise from action (see Plastic Nature), that action which is productive of those ideas whose combination we denominate body, is of the nature of an attribute so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it is considered as constituted of action.—To this attribute we must necessarily assign its substance. The actions which constitute body must be actions of something, or there must be something which acts. What then is this active something from whose agency we get the idea of body, or whose actions constitute body? Is it not sufficient that it is something active? A name might be surely given it, but a name would not render the idea more clear. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> may be found in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; it is colour to the eye, flavour to the palate, odour to the nose, sound to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, and feeling to the touch; for all our sensations are but so many ways in which this active something is manifested to us. A substratum of solidity philosophers have imagined to exist, and have in vain sought to find. Our active substance is the substratum so long sought for, and with so little success. We give it a quality by which it may be perceived; it acts. One modification of action produces matter, another generates motion. These modifications of action are modes of the active substance, whose presence is action; matter and motion constitute..." constitute the whole of nature. There is therefore throughout nature an active substance, the constituent essence of matter, and immediate natural agent in all effects. By an argument which we do not think very conclusive, our author determines this active substance to be unintelligent. "In our sensations individually, not discovering (says he) the traces, not seeing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of intelligence, but finding only action present and necessary, our inferences go no farther than our observations warrant us to do; and we conclude in all these things an action only, and that action unintelligent." Having given our opinion of real agency elsewhere (see Metaphysics, No. 118.), we shall not here stop to examine this reasoning.—We may however ask, Whether all our sensations individually be not excited for a certain end? If they be, according to our author's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of arguing in another place, the exciting agent should be an intelligent being. By this we are far from meaning to deny the reality of a secondary or instrumental cause of sensation which is destitute of intelligence. We are strongly inclined to think that there is such a cause, though our persuasion results not from this argument of our author's. In our opinion, he reasons better when he says, "that a subordinate agent constructed as the matter of creation, invested with perpetual laws, and producing agreeably to those laws all the forms of being, through the varieties of which inferior intelligences can, by progressive steps, arrive ultimately at the supreme contriver, is more agreeable to our ideas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and tends to impress us with more exalted sentiments, than viewing the Deity directly in all the individual impressions we receive, divided in the infinity of particular events, and unlawful, by his continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> in operations to our view insignificant and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>." This active substance, or secondary cause, our author concludes to be neither matter nor mind. "Matter (says he) is a being, as a whole quietest and inactive, but constituted of active parts, which resist separation, or cohere, giving what is usually denominated solidity to the mass. Mind is a substance which thinks. A being which should answer to neither of these definitions, would be neither matter nor mind; but an immaterial, and, if I may so say, an immental substance." Such is the active substance of Mr Young, which, considered as the cause of motion, seems not to differ greatly from the plastic nature, hyloarchical principle, or vis gentrix, of others.
