is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lanugo, which is produced on the surface of animal or vegetable matters in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>; and which viewed through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> appears like a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, out of which arise herbs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. See MUCOR, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MOULDING

Pages 72-72

any thing <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in a mould, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that seems to have been so, though in reality it were cut with a chisel or the axe.

MOULDINGS

Pages 72-72

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, projections beyond the naked wall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, wainscot, &c., the assemblage of which forms cornices, door <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and other decorations of Architecture. See that article. MOULINET is used, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>, which, being crossed with two levers, is usually applied to cranes, capstans, and other sorts of engines of the like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, to draw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, heave up <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, &c. MOULINET is also a kind of turnstile, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wooden <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, which turns horizontally upon a stake fixed in the ground; usually placed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> to keep out horses, and to oblige passengers to go and come one by one. These moulinets are often let near the outworks of

MOULDS

Pages 72-72

among tallow chandlers, are of two kinds: the first for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> dipped candles, being the vessel wherein the melted tallow is disposed, and the wick dipped. This is of wood, of a triangular form, and supported on one of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; so that it has an opening of near a foot across; the other, used in the fabric of mould candles, is of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tin.—Here each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> has its several mould. See CANDLE.

MOULINS

Pages 72-73

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIER">Allier</a>, and containing about 16,000 inhabitants. The houses of the Chartreux, and that of the Visitation, are magnificent. It has a considerable trade in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and is seated on the river Allier, in a pleasant fertile plain, almost in the middle of France, 30 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, and 55 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Clermont. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 25'. N. Lat. 46° 34'.

MOULTING

Pages 73-73
or MOLTING, the falling off or change of hair, feathers, skins, horns, or other parts of animals, happening in some annually, in others only at certain stages of life. The generality of animals moult in the spring. The moulting of a hawk is called mewing. The moulting of a deer is the quitting of his horns in February or March. The moulting of a serpent is the putting off his skin. See EXUVIA.

MOULTON

Pages 73-73

South, on the same stream, 182 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. This, as well as the former, was anciently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> demesne. It sent members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the reign of Edward I., consists of a mayor, 18 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses, a recorder, town clerk, and 2 serjeants at mace. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are ferges, balloons, and felts; and a considerable market for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>.

MOUND

Pages 73-73

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> globe with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> upon it, such as our kings are usually drawn with, holding it in their left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as they do the sceptre in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>.

MOUNT

Pages 73-73

an elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, called also mountain. See MOUNTAIN. Mount Edgecumbe, a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> peak, at the entrance of Cook's Strait, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, on the west side. Its height is supposed not to be much inferior to that of the Peak of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNT_SORREL">Mount <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORREL">Sorrel</a>, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, so named from a high mount <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fold rock adjoining to the town, of a dusky <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> or forel-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, extremely hard. Of rough <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> hewn out of this rock the town is built. It has a market on Mondays. It was noted formerly for its castle, and is seated on the river Stour, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It is 20 miles south-east by south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, and 105 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west by north of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 9'. N. Lat. 52° 45'. Mounts of Piety, certain funds or establishments in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> out on some small security. There were also mounts of piety in England, raised by contribution for the benefit of people ruined by the extortions of the Jews.

MOUNTAIN

Pages 73-76

a considerable eminence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, elevated above the surrounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> full of inequalities, cavities more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less exposed, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> uncovered. For the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, see MOUNTAIN, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">Attraction</a> of Mountains. This is a late discovery, and a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of universal gravity. According to the Newtonian system, an attractive power is not only exerted between those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which constitute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, but likewise between all comparatively smaller bodies, and even between the smallest particles of which they are composed. Agreeably to this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, a heavy body, which ought to gravitate or tend toward the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> perpendicular to its surface, supposing the said surface to be perfectly even and spherical, ought likewise, though in a less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, to be attracted and tend towards a mountain placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface; so that a plumb line, for instance, of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> hanging in the neighbourhood of such a mountain, ought to be drawn from a perpendicular situation, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the attractive power of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of matter of which it is composed acting in a direction different from that exerted by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of matter in the earth, and with a proportionably inferior degree of force. Though Sir Isaac Newton had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago hinted at an experiment of this kind, and had remarked, that "a mountain of an hemispherical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, three miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, would not, by its attraction, draw the plumb line two minutes out of the perpendicular (E)," yet no attempt to ascertain this matter by actual experiment was made till about the year 1738; when the French academicians, particularly Messrs Bouguer and Condamine, who were sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a degree under the equator, attempted to discover the attractive power of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIMBORAZO">Chimborazo</a>, a mountain in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Quito. According to their observations, which were however made under circumstances by no means favourable to an accurate solution of so nice and difficult a problem, the mountain Chimborazo exerted an attraction equal to eight seconds. Though this experiment was not perhaps sufficient to prove satisfactorily even the reality of an attraction, much less the precise quantity of it; yet it does not appear that any steps have been since taken to repeat it. Through the munificence of his Britannic majesty, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> were enabled to undertake the execution of this delicate and important experiment; the astronomer royal was chosen to conduct it. After various inquiries, the mountain Schehallien, situated nearly in the centre of Scotland, was pitched upon as the most proper for the purpose that could be found in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. The observations were made by taking the meridian zenith distances of different fixed stars, near the zenith, by means of a zenith <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a> of ten feet radius; first on the south, and afterwards on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the hill, the greatest length of which extended in an east and west direction. It is evident, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the mass of matter in the hill exerted any sensible attraction, it would cause the plumb-line of the sector, through which an observer viewed a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> in the meridian, to deviate from its perpendicular situation, and would attract it contrariwise to the (e) By a very easy calculation it is found that such a mountain would attract the plumb line 1' 18" from the perpendicular. Mountains, the two stations, thereby doubling the effect. On the fourth side the plummet would be drawn to the northward, by the attractive power of the hill placed to the northward of it; and on the north side, a contrary and equal deflection of the plumb line would take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in consequence of the attraction of the hill now to the southward of it. The apparent zenith distances of the stars would be affected contrariwise; those being increased at the one station which were diminished at the other: and the correspondent quantities of the deflection of the plumb line would give the observer the sum of the contrary attractions of the hill, acting on the plummet at the two stations; the half of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of course indicate the attractive power of the hill. The various operations requisite for this experiment lasted about four months; and from them it appears that the sum of the two contrary attractions of the mountain Schehallien, in the two temporary observations which were successively fixed half way up the hill (where the effect of its attraction would be greatest), was equal to $11''6$.—From a rough computation, founded on the known <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, and on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> that the density of the hill is equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> density of the earth, it appears that the attraction of the hill should amount to about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of this quantity. From thence it was inferred that the density of the hill is only about half the mean density of the earth. It does not appear, however, that the mountain Schehallien has ever been a volcano, or is hollow; as it is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and dense, and seemingly composed of an entire rock. The inferences drawn from these experiments may be reduced to the following: 1. It appears, that the mountain Schehallien exerts a sensible attraction; therefore, from the rules of philosophizing, we are to conclude, that every mountain, and indeed every particle of the earth, is endowed with the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, in proportion to its quantity of matter. 2. The law of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of this force, in the inverse ratio of the squares of the distances, as laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Sir Isaac Newton, is also confirmed by this experiment. For if the force of attraction of the hill had been only to that of the earth, as the matter in the hill to that of the earth, and had not been greatly increased by the near approach to its centre, the attraction thereof must have been wholly insensible. But now, by only supposing the mean density of the earth to be double to that of the hill, which seems very probable from other considerations, the attraction of the hill will be reconciled to the general law of the variation of attraction in the inverse duplicate ratio of the distances, as deduced by Sir Isaac Newton from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the heavenly bodies with the force of gravity at the surface of the earth; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> will be preserved. 3. We may now, therefore, be allowed to admit this law, and to acknowledge, that the mean density of the earth is at least double of that at the surface; and consequently that the density of the internal parts of the earth is much greater than near the surface. Hence also, the whole quantity of matter in the earth will be at least as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> again, as if it had been all composed of matter of the same density with that at the surface; or will be about four or five times as great as Mountains, if it were all composed of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.—This conclusion, Mr Maskelyne adds, is totally contrary to the hypothesis of some naturalists, who suppose the earth to be only a great hollow shell of matter; supporting itself from the property of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, with an immense vacuity in the midst of it. But, were that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the attraction of mountains, and even smaller inequalities in the earth's surface, would be very great, contrary to experiment, and would affect the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the degrees of the meridian much more than we find they do; and the variation of gravity, in different latitudes, in going from the equator to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, as found by pendulums, would not be near so regular as it has been found by experiment to be. 4. As mountains are by these experiments found capable of producing sensible deflections of the plumb <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of astronomical instruments; it becomes a matter of great importance, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> of degrees in the meridian, either to choose places where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> attraction of the elevated parts may be small; or where, by their situation, they may compensate or counteract the effects of each other." For measuring the heights of mountains, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">Barometer</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a> Mountains. See Aetna, Hecla, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>; see also Volcano, Geology Index. Marble Mountains. Of these there are great numbers in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, from which, though immense quantities have been carried off for the multitude of great works erected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians: yet in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Mr Bruce, who passed by them in his journey to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, there is still a sufficient supply to build Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, Corinth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and half a dozen more of such cities. The first mountain of this kind mentioned by Mr Bruce is one opposite to Terfowey, consisting partly of green marble, partly of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> blush upon a gray ground, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> spots. Here he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a monstrous obelisk of marble very nearly square, broken at the end, and nearly 30 feet long and 19 feet in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Throughout the plain there were scattered small pieces of jasper, with green, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and red spots, called in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> diafro sanguineus; and all the mountains upon that side seemed to consist of the same materials. From Mr Bruce's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of these mountains, it would appear that they are composed of serpentine, and not of calcareous marble. Written Mountain, Mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>, or Jbel-al-Mokateb, a supposed mountain, or chain of mountains, in the wilderness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>; on which, for a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of space, the marble of which the mountain consists is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, reaching from the ground sometimes to the height of 12 or 14 feet. These were mentioned by a Greek author in the third century, and some of them have been copied by Pococke and other late travellers; but, after all, there is still a very great uncertainty even of the existence of such mountain or mountains. The vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these inscriptions, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> place in which they are found, and the length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> requisite for executing the talk, have induced a notion by no means unnatural, that they are the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the Israelites during their forty years wandering in the wilderness. Others are of opinion that they contain nothing of any importance, Mountains importance, but consist merely of the names of travelers and the dates of their journeys. M. Niebuhr, who visited this country during his travels in the east, made every attempt in his power, though without success, to obtain a sight of this celebrated mountain. On applying to some Greeks at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, they all declared that they knew nothing of the writer mountain; they, however, directed him to an Arabian sheik, who had passed all his lifetime in travelling between Suez and Mount Sinai; but he knew no more of it than the former. Understanding, however, that a considerable reward would be given to any person who would conduct them thither, this Arab directed them to another; who pretended not only to know that mountain, but all others upon which there were any inscriptions throughout the desert. On inquiring particularly, however, our travellers found that he was not to be depended upon; so that they were obliged to have recourse to a fourth sheik, who by his conversation convinced them that he had seen mountains with inscriptions in unknown characters upon them. It does not appear, however, that this person was very capable, more than the rest, of leading them to the place they so much wished for; though he conducted them to some rocks upon which there were inscriptions in unknown characters. They are most numerous in a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between two mountains named Om-er-ridfein; and, says M. Niebuhr, "the pretended Jibel-el-Mokatteb may possibly be in its neighbourhood." Some of these inscriptions were copied by our author; but he does not look upon them to be of any consequence. "They seem (says he) to have been executed at idle hours by travellers, who were satisfied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the unpolished rock with any pointed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, adding to their names and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of their journeys some rude figures, which bespeak the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a people but little skilled in the arts. When such inscriptions are executed with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of transmitting to posterity the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of such events as might afford instructive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>, greater care is generally taken in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the inscriptions are engraven with more regularity." When M. Niebuhr arrived at last at the mountain to which the sheik had promised to conduct him, he did not find any inscriptions; but on climbing up to the top, he found out an Egyptian cemetery, the stones of which were covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> stones are from five to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet in length, some standing on end and others lying flat; and "the more carefully they are examined (says he), the more certainly do they appear to be sepulchral stones, having epitaphs inscribed on them. In the middle of these stones is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, of which only the walls now remain; and within it are likewise a great many of the sepulchral stones. At one end of the building seems to have been a small chamber, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> still remains. It is supported upon square pillars; and these, as well as the walls of the chamber, are covered with hieroglyphic inscriptions. Through the whole building are various busts executed in the manner of the ancient Egyptians. The sepulchral stones and the busts are of hard and fine grained sandstone." M. Niebuhr is of opinion that this cemetery was not the work of the Egyptians themselves, but of some colony which came from Egypt, and had adopted the manners and customs of the people. He supposes that it might have been built by the Arabs, who had conquered Egypt under the shepherd kings, and adopted the Egyptian manners during their residence there. As it must have belonged to an opulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, however, he owns that there is a great difficulty in accounting for the existence of such a city in the midst of a desert. The translator of Volney's travels ascribes these inscriptions to the pilgrims who visit Mount Sinai. But to this, as well as to every other conjecture, there is this objection, that whether the inscriptions be well executed or not, whether they contain matters of importance or not, they ought to have been written in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which somebody could understand; but from the copies that have been taken of them by Dr. Pococke and others, it does not appear that they could be explained either by him or any other person. When Dr. Clayton, bishop of Clogher, visited this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world about the year 1723, he expressed the greatest desire to have the matter concerning this written mountain or mountains ascertained, and even made an offer of 500l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> to any literary person who would undertake the journey and endeavour to decipher the inscriptions; but no such person has appeared, and the existence of the mountains is testified only by the superior of a convent at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, who gave that mentioned in the beginning of this article. Until that part of the world, therefore, become more accessible to travellers, there is but little hope that we can come to any certainty in the matter. M. Niebuhr plainly, from his own accounts, had not influence enough with the Arabs to show him almost anything, as they refused to conduct him even to the summit of Mount Sinai. White Mountains. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_HAMPSHIRE">New <a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. Mountains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>, a chain of mountains in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, extending between Abyssinia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONOMOTAPA">Monomotapa</a>, and so called from their great height. Mountains of the Lions, also in Africa, divide <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIGRITIA">Nigritia</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and extend as far as Ethiopia. They were styled by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> the mountains of God, on account of their being greatly subject to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. Mountain of Forty Days; a mountain of Judea, situated in the plain of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a> to the north of that city. According to the abbé Mariti's description, the summit of it is covered neither with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, turf, nor earth; it consists of a solid mass of white marble, the surface of which is become <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> by the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. "The path by which you ascend to it (says our author) fills one with terror, as it rises with a winding course between two abysses, which the eye <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> scarcely behold. This path is at first pretty broad, but it at length becomes so confined, that one can with difficulty place both feet upon it at the same time. When we had ascended a little higher, we found an Arab stretched out on the path, who made us pay a certain toll for our passage. Here the traveller requires courage. One of the parapets of the path being broken, we clung to the part which remained until we had reached a small grotto, situated very commodiously, as it gave us an opportunity of recovering our breath. When we had refreshed ourselves a little, we pursued our course, which became still more dangerous. Suspended almost from the rock, and having before our eyes all the horror of the..." MOU <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">Mourning</a> the precipice, we could advance only by dragging one foot after the other; so that had the smallest fragment given way under us, we should have been hurried to the bottom of this frightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>. "This mountain is one of the highest in the province, and one of its most sacred places. It takes its name from the rigorous fast which Christ observed here after having triumphed over the vanities of the world and the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of this miracle, a chapel was formerly constructed on the summit of the mountain. It may be seen from the plain, but we could not approach it, as the path was almost entirely destroyed. It, however, may be accessible on the other side of the mountain, which we did not visit. A great many scattered grottos are seen here; in one of which, according to Quarelinus, were deposited the bodies of several anchorites, which are still entire. I have heard the same thing asserted in the country, but I could never meet with any person who had seen them. Here we enjoyed the most beautiful prospect imaginable. This part of the mountain of Forty Days overlooks the mountains of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, the country of Gilead, the country of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a>, the plains of Moab, the plain of Jericho, the river Jordan, and the whole extent of the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. It was here that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> said to the Son of God, 'All these kingdoms will I give thee, if thou wilt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down and worship me.'"

MOURNING

Pages 76-77

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was expressed various ways. Amongst the Jews, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of their relations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> intimate friends, grief or mourning was signified by weeping, tearing their clothes, smiting their breasts, or tearing them with their nails, pulling or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and beards, walking softly, i.e. barefoot, lying upon the ground, fasting, or eating upon the ground. They kept themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> shut up in their houses, covered their faces, and abstained from all <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, even <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and saying their usual prayers. They neither dressed themselves, nor made their beds, nor shaved themselves, nor cut their nails, nor went into the bath, nor saluted any body: so that suchlike seems to have been an indication of sorrow; and dirtiness, of distress. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of mourning among the Jews was generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days: though this was lengthened or shortened according to circumstances; but 30 days were thought sufficient upon the severest occasions. The different periods of the time of mourning required different degrees of grief, and different tokens of it. The Greeks, on the death of friends, showed their sorrow by excluding themselves from all gaiety, entertainments, games, public solemnities, the enjoyment of wine, and the delights of music. They sat in gloomy and solitary places, stripped themselves of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> ornaments, put on a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> stuff by way of mourning; tore their hair, shaved their heads, rolled themselves in the dust and mire, sprinkled ashes on their heads, smote their breasts with their palms, tore their faces, and frequently cried out with a lamentable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and dawling tone, reiterating the interjection εἰ, εἰ, εἰ; hence funeral lamentations were called Ἐλέος. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they appeared in public during the time of mourning, they had a veil thrown over their faces and heads. During the funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, certain persons called ἐπιφορεῖς ἑρμῶν marched before, and sung melancholy strains called ἐπιφορεῖς ἑρμῶν, ἀνά and ἀνά. These vocal mourners sang thrice during the procession round the pile and round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>. Flutes were also used to heighten the solemnity. At the funerals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, their fellow soldiers who attended, as a testimony of their affliction, held their shields, their spears, and the rest of their armour, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>. The tokens of private grief among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were the same as those already observed as customary among the Greeks. Black or dark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> were the colours of the mourning habits worn by the men; they were also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to the women. The mourning of the emperors at first was black. In the time of Augustus, the women wore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> veils, and the rest of their dress black. From the time of Domitian they wore nothing but white habits, without any ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, jewels, or pearls. The men let their hair and beards grow, and wore no wreaths of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on their heads while the days of mourning <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. The longest time of mourning was ten months: this was Numa's establishment, and took in his whole year. For a widow to marry during this time was infamous. Mourning was not used for children who died under three years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. From this age to ten they mourned as many months as the child was years old. A remarkable victory, or other happy event, occasioned the shortening of the time of mourning: The birth of a child, or the attainment of any remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> in the family, certain feasts in honour of the gods, or the consecration of a temple, had the same effect. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cannae, the commonwealth decreed that mourning should not be worn for more than 30 days, that the lois might be forgotten as soon as possible. When public magistrates died, or persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, also when any remarkable calamity happened, all public meetings were interrupted, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, shops, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and all places of concourse were shut up, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> put on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of sorrow; the senators laid aside the laelative, and the consuls sat in a lower seat than ordinary. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> also, and was observed upon the death of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after he had been sentenced to death by their judges. Praeface, or mourning women, (by the Greeks called ἑρμῶν ἐπιφορεῖς), went about the streets; this was customary <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> among the Jews as well as the Greeks and Romans, (Jerem. ix. 17.) **MOUSE.** See Mus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Mouse-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">Ear</a>.** See Hieracium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. **Mouse-Tail.** See Myosurus, Mammalia Index. **<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DOR">Dor</a>-Mouse.** See Myoxus, Mammalia Index. **Shrew-Mouse.** See Sorex, **MOUSELLE,** the name of an East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> tree, with white tubular flowers, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in great plenty. They are of a sweet agreeable smell, and the Gentoos are very fond of wearing them, stringing and hanging them about their necks and arms. The fruit is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> cherry, of the shape and size of our white heart cherry, but the footstalk is not quite so long. This fruit has a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in it, containing a bitter oily kernel. The Indians rub this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> stung by a scorpion or bitten by a centipede, which it soon cures. The crows are very fond of the fruit. **MOUSUL,** or Mosul, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> city of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a beglerbegate, stands on the west <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tigris, in the latitude, according to Mr Ives's observation, of 36° 30' <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is surrounded with stone walls, but has many of its streets lying waste. Tavernier speaks of it as a ruined <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with only two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> and a sorry castle; yet, he says, that it is much frequented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and that its basha commands 3000 men. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of boats over the Tigris; and the city is a thoroughfare from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, which makes it a place of trade, and which is more augmented by a constant traffic from this place to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on this side the river is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and barren; but on the opposite side it is exceedingly fruitful, yielding good crops of corn and fruit in abundance. Mr Ives says it was the best built city he had seen in Turkey; but had nothing in it to attract the notice of an European. It was besieged for near six months by Nadir Shah without success. Breaches were frequently made in the walls, and assaults continued for three days successively; but the assailants were constantly repulsed, and the breaches made in the daytime repaired during the night. The besieged had unanimously resolved to die rather than to submit. The Turks declared, that should the place be forced to surrender, they were determined to put to death all their wives and daughters first, that they might not fall into the vile <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the abhorred Persians. The place was therefore defended with uncommon bravery; even the women and children exerted themselves with the greatest alacrity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> behaved in such a manner as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the esteem and admiration of the other inhabitants; and some of their churches being demolished, they were afterwards repaired at the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In this city there are a great many mosques, the largest and most stately of which is ornamented on the top with green tiles. At the doors of these houses there are usually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> in gilt letters, declaring the awfulness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, as being the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God. One of them has a minaret which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> like those of Bagdad. Some of the most bigotted Turks say, that Mahomet saluted this minaret as he passed; on which it bent its head in reverence to the prophet, and ever after continued in that situation. The manufacture of this city is muslin (muslin), which is made very strong and pretty fine. In the year 1757 this city and the country adjacent were visited by a dreadful famine, owing to the preceding hard winter, and innumerable multitudes of locusts, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> were destroyed. When Mr Ives was there in 1758, the country was comparatively depopulated. Almost all the brute <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> had been destroyed for the subsistence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. During the famine, the people had eaten dogs, and every kind of animal which is held in abhorrence at any other time, not sparing even their own children; and the dead bodies lay in the streets for want of people to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> them. Their fruit trees were also destroyed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>; so that when our author was there scarcely any fruit could be had. The neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> afford silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and they would yield much quicksilver if the Turks had either the skill or inclination to work them to advantage. Lanza says, that some time ago an Englishman who travelled through this country got two or three bottles of it, which he presented to the basha as a specimen of what might be done in that way; but no farther attempt was made. Here also are some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> mines, which supply as much of that metal as furnishes them with bullets and some necessary utensils. **MOUTAN,** or peony shrub of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>: also called hoo-ouang, or "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of flowers," and peleankin, "an hundred ounces of gold," in allusion to the excessive price given formerly by some of the virtuous for certain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this plant. The moutan seems to claim pre-eminence, not only on account of the splendour and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its flowers, and of the sweet odour which they diffuse around, but also on account of the multitude of leaves which compose them, and of the beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> spots with which they are interlaced. This plant, which is of a thrifty <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, shoots forth a number of branches, which form a top almost as large as those of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees. **MOUTH,** in Anatomy, a part of the face, consisting of the lips, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, the insides of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, the palate, the salivary glands, the os hyoides, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UVULA">uvula</a>, and the tonsils; which see under the article ANATOMY. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> observes, that the mouth in the several species of animals is nicely adapted to the uses of such a part, and well sized and shaped for the formation of speech, the gathering and receiving of food, the catching of prey, &c. In some creatures it is wide and large, in others little and narrow; in some it is formed with a deep incisure into the head, for the better catching and holding of prey, and more easy commination of hard, large, and troublesome food; and in others with a shorter incisure, for the gathering and holding of herbaceous food. In birds it is neatly shaped for piercing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; hard and horny, to supply the want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; hooked, in the rapacious kind, to catch and hold their prey; long and slender in those that have their food to grope for in moorish places; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and long in those that search for it in the mud. Nor is the mouth less remarkable in insects; in some it is forcipated, to catch, hold, and tear the prey; in others aculeated, to pierce and wound animals, and suck their blood; in others, strongly rigid, with jaws and teeth, to gnaw and scrape.

MOVEMENT

Pages 70-70
motion, a term frequently used in the same sense with automaton. The most usual movements for keeping time are watches and clocks: the first are such as show the parts of time, and are portable in the pocket; the second, such as publish it by sounds, and are fixed as furniture. See Horology. Movement, in its popular use among us, signifies all the inner works of a watch, clock, or other engine, which move, and by that motion carry on the design of the instrument. The movement of a clock or watch is the inside, or that part which measures the time, strikes, &c. exclusive of the frame, case, dial plate, &c. The parts common to both of these movements are, the main-spring, with its appurtenances; lying in the spring box, and in the middle thereof lapping about the spring-arbor, to which one end of it is fastened. A-top of the spring-arbor is the endless screw and its wheel; but in spring clocks, this is a ratchet-wheel with its click, that stops it. That which the main-spring draws, and round which the chain or string is wrapped, is called the fusey; this is ordinarily taper; in large works, going with weights, it is cylindrical, and called the barrel. The small teeth at the bottom of the fusey or barrel, which stop it in winding up, is called the ratchet; and that which stops it when wound up, and is for that end driven up by the spring, the guard-wheel. The wheels are various: the parts of a wheel are, the hoop or rim, the teeth, the cross, and the collet or piece of brass soldered on the arbor or spindle wherein the wheel is riveted. The little wheels playing in the teeth of the larger are called pinions; and their teeth, which are 4, 5, 6, 8, &c. are called leaves; the ends of the spindle are called pivots; and the guttered wheel, with iron spikes at bottom, wherein the line of ordinary clocks runs, the pulley. We need not say anything of the hand, screws, wedges, stops, &c. See WHEEL, Fusey, &c. Perpetual Movement. See Perpetual Motion.

MOWEE

Pages 77-78

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook, is 162 miles in circumference. A low isthmus divides it into two circular peninsulas, of which the eastern is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the size of the western. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in both rise to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, and may be seen at the distance of more than 30 leagues. The northern shores, like those of Owhyhee, afford no soundings, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> presents the same appearance of verdure and fertility. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants is computed at about 65,000. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 175° 56' N. Lat. 20° 53'.

MOXA

Pages 78-78
or MUGWORT of China, is a soft lanuginous substance, prepared in Japan from the young leaves of a species of Artemisia, by beating them together when thoroughly dried, and rubbing them betwixt the hands till only the fine fibres are left. The down on the leaves of mullein, cotton, hemp, &c., answers the same purpose. In the Eastern countries it is used by burning it on the skin: a little cone of the moxa is laid upon the part, previously moistened, and set on fire at the top; it burns down with a temperate glowing heat, and produces a dark coloured spot, the ulceration of which is promoted by applying a little garlic; the ulcer is left to discharge, or is soon healed, according to the intention in using the moxa. MOYRA. See MOIRA.

MUCILAGE

Pages 78-78

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, is in general any viscid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> glutinous liquor. Mucilage also imports the liquor which principally serves to moisten the ligaments and cartilages of the articulations, and is supplied by the mucilaginous glands.

MUCK

Pages 78-78
or RUNNING A MUCK, is a practice that has prevailed time immemorial in Batavia. To run a muck, in the original sense of the word, is to get intoxicated with opium, and then rush into the streets with a drawn weapon, and kill any one that comes in the way, till the party is himself either killed or taken prisoner. If the officer take one of these amocks or mohawks (as they have been called by an easy corruption) alive, he has a considerable reward; and the unhappy wretch is always broken alive on the wheel; but such is the fury of their desperation, that three out of four are necessarily destroyed in attempting to secure them. MUD-IGUANA. See Muræna, Ichthyology Index.

MUCOR

Pages 78-78

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of the order of fungi, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MUCUS

Pages 78-78

a mucilaginous liquor secreted by certain glands, and serving to lubricate many of the internal cavities of the body. In its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state it is generally limpid and colourless; but, from certain causes, assumes a thick consistence and a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> like pus. For the distinguishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> between pus and mucus, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No 2769.

MUFFLE

Pages 78-78

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, a vessel employed in some metallurgic operations. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> it represents an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vault, the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is closed by a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, and the lower part or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of which is a rectangular plane. It is a little oven that is placed horizontally in allay and enamelling furnaces, so that its open side corresponds with the door of the fireplace of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. Under this arched oven small cupsels or crucibles are placed; and the substances contained are thus exposed to intense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> without contact of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, finoke, or ashes.

MUFTI

Pages 78-78

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> order, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of the Mahommedan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The authority of the mufti is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> in the Ottoman empire; for even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would preferve any appearance of religion, cannot, without hearing his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, put any person to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, or to much as inflict any corporal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. In all actions, especially criminal ones, his opinion is required, by giving him a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is stated under signed names; which he subscribes with the words, He shall, or shall not, be punished. Such outward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> is paid to the mufti, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior himself rises up to him, and advances <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> steps to meet him when he comes into his presence. He alone has the honour of kissing the sultan's left shoulder, whilst the prime vizier kisses only the hem of his garment. When the grand signior addresses any writing to the mufti, he gives him the following titles: To the Efad, the wisest of the wise, instructed in all knowledge, the most excellent of excellent, abstaining from things unlawful, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of virtue and of true science, heir of the prophetic doctrines, resolver of the problems of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, revealer of the orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the treasures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to the doubtful allegories, strengthened with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">Legislator</a> of mankind, may the Most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> God perpetuate thy virtues! The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of the mufti is solely in the grand signior, who prefers him with a vest of rich fables, &c. If he is convicted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> or any great crime, he is put into a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> kept for that purpose in the Seven Towers at Constantinople, and pounded to death.

MUGGLETONIANS

Pages 78-78

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which arose in England about the year 1657; so denominated from their leader Lodowick Muggleton, a journeyman taylor, who, with his associate Reeves, set up for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> prophets, pretending, as it is said, to have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> power of saving and damning whom they pleased; and giving out that they were the two last witnesses of God that should appear before the end of the world.

MUGIL

Pages 78-78

the mullet, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MUID

Pages 78-78

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the French, for things dry. The muid is no real vessel used as a measure, but an estimation of several other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>; as the septier, mine, minot, bushel, &c. Muid, is also one of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> casks, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> regular vessels used in France, to put wine and other liquors in. The muid of wine is divided into two demi-muids, four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-muids, and eight half-quarter muids, containing 36 septiers.

MULATTO

Pages 78-79

a name given in the Indies to those who are begotten by a negro <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> woman, or by an Indian or white man on a negro woman. MULBERRY. See Morus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Mulberry-Cider, a name given by the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and some other parts of England, to a sort of cider rendered very palatable by an admixture of mulberry juice in the making; they choose for this purpose the ripest and blackest mulberries, and pressing out their juice, and mixing it with a full-bodied cider at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> and pressing, give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> so much of it as adds a perceptible flavour. It is very worthy the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of people who live in other countries, where strong and good cider is made, that this renders it a sort of wine much more agreeable than any other English liquor, and might be brought into general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage of the dealer. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of this liquor resembles that of the brightest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine, and the flavour of the mulberry never goes off. Phil. Transf. No 133.

MULCT

Pages 79-79

a fine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> laid upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has committed some fault <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> misdemeanor.

MULE

Pages 79-79

a mongrel kind of quadruped, usually <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> between an ass and a mare, and sometimes between a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and a she-ass; but the signification of the word is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> extended to every kind of animal produced by a mixture of two different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Mules, among gardeners, denote a sort of vegetable monsters produced by putting the farina fecundans of one species of plant into the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-UTRICLE">utricle</a> of another. The carnation and sweet-william being somewhat alike in their parts, particularly their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, the farina of the one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> impregnate the other, and the seed so enlivened will produce a plant differing from either. An instance of this we first had in Mr. Fairchild's garden at Hoxton; where a plant is seen neither sweet-william nor carnation, but resembling both equally: this was raised from the seed of a carnation that had been impregnated by the farina of the sweet-william. These couplings being not unlike those of the mare with the ass, which produce the mule, the same name is given them; and they are, like the others, incapable of multiplying their species. This furnishes a hint for altering the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of any fruit, by impregnating one tree with the farina of another of the same class; e.g., a codlin with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-main, which will occasion the codlin so impregnated to last a longer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> than usual, and to be of a sharper taste.

MULHAUSEN

Pages 79-79

a considerable town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a republic in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Swiss. It is populous, well built, and adorned with handsome public structures; seated in a pleasant fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> formed by the river Ill, 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Bâle, and 20 east of Belfort. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 24'. N. Lat. 47° 48'.

MULL

Pages 79-79

one of the Western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Scotland, about article 25 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and as much in breadth. It is in general rocky and barren, not producing a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of corn for the inhabitants; but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle are annually exported, which with the fishings and a considerable quantity of kelp are the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. It is deeply indented with bays and creeks, forming in several parts good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> harbours. There are no villages except Tobermorey, near the northern point of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, where a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> station has been erected. The island was originally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the dominions of the Lords of the Isles; but in after-times it became a part of the possessions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of Macleans, who still retain a considerable part. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyll is also a considerable proprietor. The ruins of several ancient castles are seen on this island. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Mull, in 1795, amounted to about 8000 persons. Mull of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTYRE">Cantyre</a>. See CANTYRE. Mull of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>. See GALLOWAY. MULLEIN. See VERBASCUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MULLER

Pages 79-79
or Mullar, denotes a stone flat and even at bottom, but round atop; used for grinding of matters on a marble.—The apothecaries use mullers to prepare many of their tinctuous powders; and painters for their colours, either dry or in oil. Muller is an instrument used by the glass grinders; being a piece of wood, to one end whereof is cemented the glass to be ground, whether convex in a basin, or concave in a sphere or bowl.—The muller is ordinarily about six inches long, turned round; the cement they use is composed of ashes and pitch. See GRINDING.

MULLERAS

Pages 79-79

a town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and margraviate of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, seated 38 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, upon a canal which joins the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a> and the Spree. This canal is 15 miles in length, 10 yards in breadth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet in depth. It was eight years in making; and since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a> have carried on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 50'. N. Lat. 52° 21'. MULLET. See MUGIL, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Mullet, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mollet, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> in form of the rowel of a spur, which it originally represented.

MULLIER

Pages 79-79

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the lawful issue born in wedlock, though begotten before. The Mullier is preferred to an older <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> born out of matrimony; as for instance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has a son by a woman before <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, which issue is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a>, and afterwards marries the mother of the bastard, and they have another son, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son is Mullier and lawful, and shall be heir of the father; but the other can be heir to no person*. By the civil law, where a man has issue by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULLINGAR">Mullingar</a>, a woman, if after that he marries her, the issue is Mullier.

MULLINGAR

Pages 79-80

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WESTMEATH">Westmeath</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, 38 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. MUM Dublin. N. Lat. 53° 32'. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 50'. Within a few miles of it are the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and also those of a castle. It is situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>. It holds a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> fair, and is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of good trade. In 1227, the priory of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, formerly known by the name of The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of God of Mullingar, was founded here by Ralph de Petey bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a>, for regular canons of the order of St Augustin. A Dominican friary was also founded here in 1237 by the family of Nugent; some ruins of which still remain. In 1622, the friars of Multifarnham began to erect a house there for friars of the order of St Francis, but it was never completed.

MULLUS

Pages 80-80

the Surnullet, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MULTICATUS FLOS

Pages 80-80

a luxuriant flower, whose petals are multiplied so as to exclude a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the whole of the flaminia.

MULTIPLE

Pages 80-80

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> which comprehends some other several times; thus 6 is a multiple of 2, and 12 is a multiple of 6, 4, and 3; comprehending the first twice, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> thrice, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">Action</a> of MULTIPLEPOINDING, in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. See Law, No clxxviii. 24.

MULTIPLICAND

Pages 80-80

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to be multiplied by another. See Arithmetic.

MULTIPLICATION

Pages 80-80

in general, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of increasing the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of any thing. Multiplication, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, is a rule by which any given number may be speedily increased, according to any proposed number of times. See Arithmetic. Multiplication, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>. See Algebra.

MULTIPLICATOR

Pages 80-80
or Multiplier, in Arithmetic, the number by which any other is multiplied, or the number of times it is supposed to be taken.

MULTIPLYING GLASS

Pages 80-80

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, a glass wherewith objects appear increased in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. See Optics.

MULTURE

Pages 80-80

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a certain stipulated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> given as payment to the proprietor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tackman of a mill for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> the corn: and all corn ground on farms thirled to the mill is obliged to pay multure whether the corn be ground at that mill or elsewhere.

MULVIA

Pages 80-80

a river of Barbary in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, and divides the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> from that of Algiers, and then falls into the Mediterranean, to the westward of Marsalquivier.

MUM

Pages 80-80

a kind of malt liquor much drunk in Germany, and chiefly brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> for making it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a> mum, as recorded in the townhouse of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, is as follows: Take 63 gallons of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> that has been boiled till one third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is consumed, and brew it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> bushels of wheaten malt, one bushel of oat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and one bushel of ground beans. When it is tinned, the hoghead must not be filled too full at first: as soon as it begins to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, put into it three pounds of the inner rind of fir, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of the tops of fir and beech, three handfuls of carduus benedictus, a handful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two of the flower of rofa folis: add burnet, betony, marjoram, avens, pennyroyal, and wild thyme, of each a handful and a half; of elder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, two handfuls or more; seeds of cardamom bruised, 35 ounces; barberries bruised, one ounce: when the liquor has worked a while, put the herbs and seeds into the vessel; and, after they are added, let it work over as little as possible; then fill it up: lastly, when it is stopped, put into the hoghead ten new-laid eggs unbroken; stop it up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it at two years end. The English brewers, instead of the inner rind of fir, use cardamom, ginger, and allspices; and also add eleocharis, madder, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> sanders.

MUMMIUS

Pages 80-80

L. a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> sent against the Achaeans, whom he conquered B. C. 127. He destroyed Corinth, Thebes, and Chalcis, by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Achaeicus from his victory. He did not enrich himself with the spoils of the enemy, but returned home without any increase of fortune. He was so little acquainted with the value of the paintings and works of the most celebrated artists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> which were found in the plunder of Corinth, that he said to those who conveyed them to Rome, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they lost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> injured them, they should make others in their stead.

MUMMY

Pages 80-81

a body embalmed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dried, in the manner used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians; or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> with which it is embalmed. There are two kinds of bodies denominated mummies. The first are only carcases dried by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and by that means kept from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>: these are frequently found in the sands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>. Some imagine, that these are the bodies of deceased people buried there on purpose to keep them entire without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a>; others think they are the carcases of travellers who have been overwhelmed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of sand raised by the hurricanes frequent in those deserts.
