The Egyptians, and indeed all the ancients without exception, deemed the mysteries of religion too sacred and solemn to be communicated to the herd of mankind, naked and unrevealed; a mode by which they imagined those sacred and sublime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> would have been defiled and degraded. "Procul, & procul est profani—Odi profanum vulgus et arceo." Egypt was the land of graven images; allegory and mythology were the veil which concealed religion from the eyes of the vulgar; fable was the groundwork of that impenetrable covering. In the earliest and most unpolished stage of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> we cannot suppose fable to have existed among men. Fables are always tales of other times, but at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> other times did not reach far enough backward to afford those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the imagination sufficient time to arrive at maturity. Fable requires a considerable space of time to acquire credibility, and to rise into reputation. Accordingly, we find that both the Chinese and Egyptians, the two most ancient nations whose annals have reached our times, were altogether unacquainted with fabulous details in the most early and least improved periods of their respective monarchies. It has been shown almost to a demonstration, by a variety of learned men, that both the one and the other people, during some centuries after the general deluge, retained and practised the primitive Noahic religion, in which fable and fancy could find no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; all was genuine unpolished truth. As soon as the authentic tradition concerning the origin of the universe was either in a good measure lost, or at least adulterated by the inventions of men, fable and fiction began to prevail. The Egyptian Thoth or Thothy, or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> Trismegistus, and Moë Fabulous the Phoenician, undertook to account for the formation and arrangement of the universe, upon principles purely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>. Here fable began to usurp logical doctrine, the place of genuine historical truth. Accordingly, tails, we find that all the historians of antiquity, who have undertaken to give a general detail of the affairs of the world, have ultered in their narrations with a fabulous cosmogony. Here imagination ranged unconfined over the boundless extent of the primary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>. To be convinced of the truth of this assertion, we need only look into Sanchoniathon's Cosmogony, Euseb. Prep. Evang. l. i. sub init. and Diodorus Sic. l. i. From this we suppose it will follow, that the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of fables owed their birth to the erroneous opinions of the formation of the universe. Having now endeavoured to point out the origin of mythology, or fabulous traditions, we shall proceed to lay before our readers a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> detail of the mythology of the most respectable nations of antiquity, following the natural order of their situation. The Chinese, if any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> be due to their own annals, or to the missionaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, who mythology pretend to have copied from them, were the first of the nations. Their fabulous records reach upwards many myriads of years before the Mosaic era of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. The events during that period of time, if any had been recorded, must have been fabulous as the period itself. These, however, are buried in eternal oblivion. The missionaries, who are the only sources of our information with relation to the earliest periods of the Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, represent those people as having retained the religion of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> many centuries after the foundation of their empire. Upon this supposition, their cosmogony must have been found and genuine, without the least tincture of those fabulous ingredients which have both disguised and disgraced the cosmogonies of most other nations. According to the most authentic accounts, Fo-hi laid the foundation of that empire about four thousand years ago. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, according to the Chinese, was conceived in a miraculous manner. His mother, say they, one day as she was walking in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> place, was surrounded by a rainbow; and, being impregnated by this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>, was in due time delivered of that celebrated legislator. This personage, like the Athenian Cecrops, was half a man and half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>. His intellectual powers were truly hyperbolic. In one day he discovered 50 different species of poisonous herbs. He taught his countrymen the whole art of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> in the space of a very few years. He instructed them how to sow five different sorts of grain. He invented boats, and nets for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, the art of fabricating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, the management of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, the manufacturing of silk, &c. In a word, that wonderful personage was inspired by Heaven with knowledge, which qualified him for composing that incomparable body of laws which are even at this day the wonder of the world. Our readers will admit, that this whole detail is fabulous and chimerical. The most learned part of them will readily observe, that the Chinese, in ascribing the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of all the useful arts to their Foht, are perfectly agreed with almost all the other nations of antiquity. The Indians ascribe every invention to <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-BUDHA">Budha</a>, or Vishnu, or Foe; the Persians to Zerdusht or Zarathustra; the Chaldeans to their man of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, whom they call Gannes; the Egyptians to Thoth or Thothot; the Phoenicians to Melicerta; the Greeks to the family of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a>; and the Scandinavians to Odin, &c. About 551 years before the Christian era, appeared the famous Chinese philosopher <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUCIUS">Confucius</a> or Confucius. Concerning the birth of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of philosophers, the Chinese have propagated the following legendary tale. His mother, walking in a solitary place, was impregnated by the vivifying influence of the heavens. The babe, thus produced, spoke and reasoned as soon as it was born. Confucius, however, wrought no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, performed no romantic exploits, but lived an austere ascetic life, taught and inculcated the doctrines of pure morality, and died, remarkable only for superior wisdom, religious, moral, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>. About the year of Christ 601, flourished the sectary Lao-tseun. His mother carried him 30 years in her womb, and was at last delivered of him under a plum-tree. This philosopher was the Epicurus of the Chinese. His disciples, who were denominated Fao-ffe, i.e. heavenly doctors, were the first who corrupted the religion of the Chinese. They were addicted to magic, and introduced the worship of good and bad demons. Their doctrine was embraced by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> succession of emperors. One of these princes, called Yiu-ti, had been deprived by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a favourite mistress, whom he loved with the most extravagant passion. The emperor, by the magical skill of one of these doctors, obtained an interview with his deceased mistress, a circumstance which riveted the whole order in the affections and esteem of the deluded prince. Here our readers will observe the exact counterpart of the fable of Eurydice, so famous in the mythology of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. That such a system of religious principles must have abounded with mythological adventures is highly probable; but as the missionaries, to whom we are chiefly indebted for our information relation to the religion of the Chinese, have not taken the pains to record them, we find it impossible to gratify the curiosity of our readers on that head. The worship of the idol Fo, or Foe, was transplanted from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> about the 56th year of the Christian era, upon the following occasion. One of the doctors of the Fao-ffe had promised a prince of the family of Tchou, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MING">Ming</a>-ti, to make him enter into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the spirits. At this solicitation an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> was despatched into India, in order to inquire where the true religion was to be found. There had been a tradition, lay the missionaries, ever since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Confucius, that the true religion was to be found in the west. The ambassador kept short in India; and finding that the god Foe was in high reputation in that country, he collected several images of that deity painted on chintz, and with it 42 chapters of the canonical books of the Hindoos, which, together with the images, he laid on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> elephant, and transported into his native country. At the same time he imported from the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> the doctrine of the transmigration of souls, which is firmly believed in China to this day. The doctrine and worship of Foe, thus introduced, made a most rapid progress all over China, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, &c. The priests of Foe are called among the Siamese, Talopogos; by the Tartars, Lamas; by the Chinese, Ha-chong; and by the people of Japan, Bonzos. By this last appellation they are generally known in Europe. An infinitude of fables was invented and propagated by the disciples of Foe, concerning the life and adventures of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. If the earlier ages of the Chinese history are barren of mythological incidents, the later periods, after the introduction of the worship of Foe, furnish an inexhaustible store of miracles, monsters, fables, intrigues, exploits, and adventures, of the most villainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. Indeed, most of them are so absurd, so ridiculous, and at the same time so impious and profane, that we are convinced our readers will easily dispense with a detail from which they could reap neither entertainment nor instruction. Such as may find themselves disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> into this abominable puddle, we must refer to the reverend fathers Du Halde, Complet, Amiot, Kircher, and other members of the propaganda, in whose writings they will find wherewithal to satisfy, and even to satiate, their appetite. The Hindoos, like the other nations of the east, for a long time retained the worship of the true God. At length, however, idolatry broke in, and, like an insatiable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, overwhelmed the country. First of all, the genuine history of the origin of the universe was either utterly lost, or disguised under a variety of fictions and allegories. We are told that Brimha, the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of the Hindoos, after three several efforts, at last succeeded in creating four persons, whom he appointed to rule over all the inferior creatures. Afterwards Brimha joined his efficient power with Bithon and Rulder; and by their united exertions they produced ten men, whose general appellation is Munies, that is, the inspired. The same being, according to another mythology, produced four other persons, as imaginary as the former; one from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, one from his back, one from his lip, and one from his heart. These children were denominated Bangs; the import of which word we cannot pretend to determine. According to another tradition, Brimha produced the Bramins from his mouth, to pray, to read, to instruct; the Chiltern from his arms, to draw the bow, to fight, to govern; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BICE">Bice</a> from his belly or thighs, to nourish, to provide the necessaries of life by agriculture and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; the Soder from his feet, for subjection, subjection, to serve, to labour, to travel. The reader will see at once, in these allegorical persons, the four calls or fests into which the Hindoo nations have, time immemorial, been divided. These are some of their most celebrated mythological traditions with relation to the origin of the universe. The Hindoos have likewise some mythological opinions which seem to relate to the general deluge. They tell us, that defining the preservation of herds and of brahmans, of genii and of virtuous men, of vedas of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and of precious things, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of the universe assumes many bodily shapes; but though he pervades, like the air, a variety of beings, yet he is himself unvaried, since he has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in him subject to change. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the last kalpa, there was a general destruction, occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> of Brahma, whence his creatures in different worlds were drowned in a vast ocean. Brahma being inclined to slumber after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of so many ages, the strong demon Hyagriva came near him, and stole the vedas which had flowed from his lips. When Hirni, the preserver of the universe, discovered this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of the prince of Dainavas, he took the shape of a minute fish called Sap-hari. After various transformations, and an enormous increase of size in each of them, the Lord of the universe loving the righteous man (A), who had still adhered to him under all these various shapes, and intending to preserve him from the sea of destruction caused by the depravity of the age, thus told him how he was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>: "In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days from the present time, O thou tamer of enemies! the three worlds will be plunged in an ocean of death; but in the midst of the destroying waves a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessel sent by me for thy use shall stand before thee." The remaining part of the mythology so nearly resembles the Mosaic history of Noah and the general deluge, that the former may be a strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of the truth of the latter. To dry up the waters of the deluge, the power of the Deity descends in the form of a boar, the symbol of strength, to draw up and support on his tusks the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which had been sunk beneath the ocean. Again, the same power is represented as a tortoise sustaining the globe, which had been convulsed by the violent assaults of demons, while the gods charmed the sea with the mountain Mandar, and forced it to disgorge the sacred things and animals, together with the water of life which it had swallowed. All these stories, we think, relate to the same event, shadowed by a moral, a metaphysical, and an astronomical allegory; and all three seem connected with the hieroglyphical sculptures of the old Egyptians. The Hindoos divide the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the world into four yugas or jugs, or jogs, each consisting of a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years. In each of those periods, the age and stature of the human race have been gradually diminished; and in each of them mankind has gradually declined in virtue and piety, as well as in age and stature. The present period they call the Colla, i.e., the corrupt jug, which they say is to last 400,000 years, of which near 5000 years are already past. In the last part of the preceding jug, which they call the dura paar, the age of man was contracted into 1000 years, as in the present it is confined to 300. From this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> diminution of the length of the human life, our readers will probably infer, that the two last jogs bear a pretty near resemblance to the Mosaic history of the age of the antediluvian and postdiluvian patriarchs; and that the two first are imaginary periods <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the creation of the world, like those of the Chinese, Chaldeans, and Egyptians. According to the mythology of the Hindoos, the world system of the world is subject to various dilutions, arising from revolutions. At the conclusion of the Colla jogs, say they, a grand revolution will take place, and when the solar system will be consumed by fire, and all the elements reduced to their original constituent atoms. Upon the back of these revolutions, Brimha, the supreme deity of the Hindoos, is sometimes represented as a new born infant, with his toe in his mouth, floating on a camala or water flower, sometimes only on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of that plant, on the surface of the vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>. At other times he is figured as coming forth of a winding shell; and again as blowing up the mundane foam with a pipe at his mouth. Some of these emblematical figures and attitudes, our learned readers will probably observe, nearly resemble those of the ancient Egyptians. But the vulgar religion of the ancient Hindoos was of a very different complexion, and opens a large field of mythological adventures. We have observed above, that the Fo or Foe of the Chinese was imported from India; and now we shall give a brief detail of the mythological origin of that divinity. We have no certain Birth, &c., account of the birth-place of this imaginary deity—of the god Fo. His followers relate, that he was born in one of the kingdoms of India near the line, and that his father was one of that country. His mother brought him into the world by the left side, and expired soon after her delivery. At the time of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, she dreamed that she had swallowed a white elephant; a circumstance which is supposed to have given birth to the veneration which the kings of India have always shown for a white animal of that species. As soon as he was born, he had strength enough to stand erect without assistance. He walked abroad at seven, and, pointing with one hand to the heavens, and with the other to the earth, he cried out, "In the heavens, and on the earth, there is no one but me who deserves to be honoured." At the age of 30, he felt himself all on a sudden filled with the divinity; and now he was metamorphosed into Fo or Pagod, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the Hindoos. He had no sooner declared himself a divinity, than he thought of propagating his doctrine, and proving his divine mission by miracles. The number of his disciples was immense; and they soon spread his dogmas over all India, and even to the higher extremities of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> doctrines which Fo and his disciples propagated, was the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a> or transmigration of souls. This doctrine, some imagine, has been given (A) He was Sovereign of the world. His name was Manu, or Satgavrata; his patronymic name was Vaijvata, or Child of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>. given rise to the multitude of idols reverenced in every country where the worship of Fo is established. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">Quadrupeds</a>, birds, reptiles, and the vilest animals, had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> erected for them; because, say they, the soul of the god, in his numerous transmigrations, may have at one time or other inhabited their bodies. Both the doctrine of transmigration and of the worship of animals seems, however, to have been imported from Egypt into India. If the intercourse between these two countries was begun at so early a period as some very late writers have endeavoured to prove, such a supposition is by no means improbable. The doctrine of the transmigration of souls was early established among the Egyptians. It was, indeed, the only idea they formed of the soul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>. The worship of animals among them seems to have been still more ancient. If such an intercourse did actually exist, we may naturally suppose that colonies of Egyptian priests found their way into India, as they did afterwards into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. That colonies of Egyptians did actually penetrate into that country, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there, many centuries before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a>, is a fact that cannot be called in question, for reasons which the bounds prescribed us in this article will not allow us to enumerate. We shall only observe, that from the hieroglyphical representations of the Egyptian deities seem to have originated those monstrous idols which from time immemorial have been worshipped in India, China, Japan, Siam, and even in the remotest parts of Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. Fo is often called Budha, or Buddha, and sometimes Viflhou; perhaps, indeed, he may be distinguished by many other names, according to the variety of dialects of the different nations among which his worship was established. An infinite number of fables was propagated by his disciples concerning him after his death. They pretended that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> was still alive; that he had been already born 8000 times, and that he had successively appeared under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of an ape, a lion, a dragon, an elephant, a boar, &c. These were called the incarnations of Viflhou. At length he was confounded with the supreme God; and all the titles, attributes, operations, perfections, and enigms of the Most High were ascribed to him. Sometimes he is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMIDA">Amida</a>, and represented with the head of a dog, and worshipped as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of mankind. He sometimes appears as a princely personage, issuing from the mouth of a fish. At other times, he wears a lunette on his head, in which are seen cities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, towers, trees, in short, all that the world contains. These transformations are evidently the children of allegorical or hieroglyphical emblems, and form an exact counterpart to the symbolical worship of the Egyptians. The enormous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of mythological traditions which have in a manner deluged the vast continent of India, would fill many volumes: We have selected the preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as a specimen only, by which our readers may be qualified to judge of the rest. If they find themselves disposed to indulge their curiosity at greater length, we must remit them to Thévenot's and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>'s Travels, to Mons. Anquetil in his Zond Avesta, Hallé's Introduction to his Translation of the Code of Gentoo Laws, Col. Dow's History of Hindostan, Grose's Voyage to the East Indies, Asiatic Researches, vol. i. and ii. The mythology of the Persians is, if possible, still more extravagant than that of the Hindoos. It supposes the world to have been repeatedly destroyed, and repeopled by creatures of different formation, who were successively annihilated or banished for their disobedience to the supreme Being. The monstrous griffin Sinergh tells the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Calherman that he had already lived to see the earth seven times filled with creatures and seven times a perfect void: that before the creation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, this globe was inhabited by a race of beings called Peri and Dives, whose characters formed a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>. The Peri are described as beautiful and benevolent; the Dives as deformed, malevolent, and mischievous, differing from infernal demons only in this, that they are not as yet confined to the pit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. They are for ever ranging over the world, to scatter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> and misery among the sons of men. The Peri nearly resemble the fairies of Europe; and perhaps the Dives gave birth to the giants and magicians of the middle ages. The Peri and Dives wage incessant wars; and when the Dives make any of the Peri prisoners, they shut them up in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cages, and hang them on the highest trees, to expose them to public view, and to the fury of every chilling blast. When the Peri are in danger of being overpowered by their foes, they solicit the assistance of some mortal hero; which produces a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of mythological adventures, highly ornamental to the strains of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARDS">bards</a>, and which, at the same time, furnishes an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of the most diversified machinery. One of the most celebrated adventurers in the mythology of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> is Tahmuras, one of their most ancient monarchs. This prince performs a variety of exploits, while he endeavours to recover the fairy Merjan. He attacks the Dive Demnuth in his own cave; where, having vanquished the giant or demon, he finds vast piles of hoarded wealth: there he carries off with the fair captive. The battles, labours, and adventures of Rostan, another Persian worthy, who lived many ages after the former, are celebrated by the Persian bards with the same extravagance of hyperbole with which the labours of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> have been sung by the poets of Greece and Rome. The adventures of the Persian heroes breathe all the wildness of achievement recorded of the knights' birthplace of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>. The doctrine of enchantments, chivalry, transformations, &c., exhibited in both, is a characteristic symptom of one common original. Persia is the genuine clastic ground of eastern mythology, and the source of the ideas of chivalry and romance; from which they were propagated to the regions of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>, and indeed to the remotest corners of Europe towards the west. Perhaps our readers may be of our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, when we offer it as a conjecture, that the tales of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of the Peri and Dives originated from a vague tradition concerning good and bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>; nor is it, in our opinion, improbable, that the fable of the wars between the gods and giants, so famous in the mythology of Greece and Italy, was imported into the former of these countries from the same quarter. For a more particular account of the Persian mythology, our readers may consult Dr. Hyde. The mythology of the Chaldeans, like that of the other nations of the east, commences at a period myriads of years prior to the era of the Mosaic creation. Their cosmogony, exhibited by Berosus, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Belus, and deeply versed in the antiquities of his country, is a piece of mythology of the most extravagant nature. It has been copied by Eusebius (Chron. lib. i. p. 5); it is likewise to be found in Syncellus, copied from Alexander Polyhistor. According to this historian, there were at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> written records preserved with the greatest care, comprehending a period of fifteen myriads of years. Those writings likewise contained a history of the heavens and the sea, of the earth, and of the origin of mankind. "In the beginning (says Berosus, copying from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OANNES">Oannes</a>, of whom we shall give a brief account below) there was nothing but darkness and an abyss of water, wherein reposed most hideous beings produced from a twofold principle. Men appeared with two wings; some with two and some with four faces. They had one body, but two heads; the one of a man, the other of a woman. Other human figures were to be seen, furnished with the legs and horns of goats. Some had the feet of horses behind, but before were fashioned like men, resembling hippocentaurs." The remaining part of this mythology is much of the same complexion; indeed so extravagant, that we imagine our readers will readily enough dispense with our translating the sequel. "Of all these (says the author) were preferred delineations in the temple of Belus at Babylon. The person who was supposed to preside over them was called Omorea. This word, in the Chaldean language, is Thalath, which the Greeks call Θαλάττης, but it more properly imports the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. Matters being in this situation, their god (says Eusebius), the god (says Syncellus) came and cut the woman asunder; and out of one half of her he formed the earth, and out of the other he made the heavens; and, at the same time, he destroyed the monsters of the abyss." This whole mythology is an allegorical history copied from hieroglyphical representations, the real purport of which could not be deciphered by the author. Such, in general, were the consequences of the hieroglyphical style of writing. Oannes, the great civilizer and legislator of the Chaldeans, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>, who copied from Berosus, was an amphibious animal of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> appearance. He was endowed with reason and a very uncommon acuteness of parts. His whole body resembled a fish. Under the head of a fish he had also another head, and feet below similar to those of a man, which were subjoined to the tail of the fish. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and language were articulate and perfectly intelligible, and there was a figure of him still extant in the days of Berosus. He made his appearance in the Erythrean or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Sea, where it borders upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>. This monstrous being conversed with men by day; but at night he plunged into the sea, and remained concealed in the water till next morning. He taught the Babylonians the use of letters, and the knowledge of all the arts and sciences. He instructed them in the method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> houses, constructing temples, and all other edifices. He taught them to compile laws and religious ceremonies, and explained to them the principles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. In a word he communicated to them every thing necessary, useful, and ornamental; and so universal were his instructions, that not one single article had ever been added to them since the time they were first communicated. Helladius is of opinion that this strange personage, whoever he was, came to be represented under the figure of a fish, not because he was actually believed to be such, but because he was clothed with the skin of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. By this account our readers will see that the Babylonian Oannes is the exact counterpart of the Fohi of the Chinese, and the Thoth or the Mercury Trismegistas of the Egyptians. It is likewise apparent, that the idea of the monster compounded of the man and the fish has originated from some hieroglyphic of that form grafted upon the appearance of man. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> mythologists have been of opinion, that Oannes was actually Noah the great preacher of righteousness; who, as some think, settled in Shinar or Chaldea after the deluge, and who, in consequence of his connexion with that event, might be properly represented under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the Man of the Sea. The nativity of Venus, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and The nativ- love, is another piece of mythology famous among the Babylonians and Assyrians. An <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, say they, of beauty and a prodigious size, drops from heaven into the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. Some doves settled upon this egg, after that the fishes had rolled it to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. In a short time this egg produced Venus, who was afterwards called Dea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, the Syrian goddess. In consequence of this tradition (says Hyginus), pigeons and fishes became sacred to this goddess among the Syrians, who always abstained from eating the one or the other. Of this imaginary being we have a very exact and entertaining history in the treatise De Dea Syria, generally ascribed to Lucian. In this mythological tradition our readers will probably discover an allusion to the celebrated Mundane egg; and at the same time the story of the fishes will lead them to anticipate the connexion between the sea and the moon. This same deity was the Atargatis of Acalon, described by Diodorus the Sicilian; the one half of her body a woman and the other a fish. This was no doubt a hieroglyphic figure of the moon, importing the influence of that planet upon the sea and the sex. The oriental name of this deity evidently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> to the moon; for it is compounded of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> words (א), which import "the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the half of heaven." The fable of Semiramis is nearly connected with the preceding one. Diodorus Siculus has preserved this mythological history of this deity, which he and all the writers of antiquity have confounded with the Babylonian princess of the same name. That historian informs us, that the word Semiramis, in the Syrian dialect, signifies "a wild pigeon;" but we apprehend that this term was a name or epithet of the moon. (B) Adar or Haidar, "magnificus;" and God, "exercitum turmi." moon, as it is compounded of two words (c) of an import naturally applicable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> planet. It was a general practice among the Orientals to denominate their sacred animals from that deity to which they were consecrated. Hence the moon being called Semi-rumitis, and the pigeon being sacred to her divinity, the latter was called by the name of the former. As the bounds prescribed this article render it impossible for us to do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to this interesting piece of mythology, we must beg leave to refer our readers for further information to Diod. Sic. lib. ii. Hyginus Poet. Alfron. Fab. 197. Pharmutus de Nat. Deor. Ovid. Metam. lib. iv. Athen. in Apol. Izettes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>. ix. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 275. Seld. de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIS">Dis</a> Syr. Syr. ii. p. 183. We should now proceed to the mythology of the Arabians, the far greatest part of which is however, buried in the abyss of ages; though, when we reflect on the genius and character of that people, we must be convinced that they too, as well as the other nations of the east, abounded in fabulous relations and romantic compositions. The natives of that country have always been enthusiastically addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, of which fable is the essence. Wherever the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> have erected their throne, fables and miracles have always appeared in their train. In the Koran we meet with frequent allusions to well-known traditional fables. These had been transmitted from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation by the bards and rhaptoïdits for the entertainment of the vulgar. In Arabia, from the earliest ages, it has always been one of the favourite entertainments of the common people, to assemble in the serene evenings around their tents, or on the platforms with which their houses are generally covered, or in large halls erected for the purpose, in order to amuse themselves with traditional narrations of the most distinguished actions of their most remote <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. Oriental imagery always embellished their romantic details. The flow of fancy, the love of the marvellous, the propensity towards the hyperbolic and the vast, which constitute the essence of oriental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, must ever have drawn the relation aside into the devious regions of fiction and fairy land. The religion of Mahomet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the original fabric of idolatry and mythology together. The Arabian fables current in modern times are borrowed or imitated from Persian compositions; Persia being still the grand nursery of romance in the east. In Egypt we find idolatry, theology, and mythology, almost inseparably blended together. The inhabitants of this region, too, as well as of others in the vicinity of the centre of population, adhered for several centuries to the worship of the true God. At last, however, conscious of their own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>, imperfection, and total unfitness to approach an infinitely perfect Being, distant, as they imagined, and invisible, they began to call about for some beings more exalted, and more perfect than themselves, by whose mediation they might prefer their prayers to the supreme Majesty of heaven. The luminaries of heaven, which they imagined were animated bodies, naturally presented themselves. These were splendid and glorious beings. They were thought to partake of the divine nature: they were revered as the satrapes, prefects, and representatives of the supreme Lord of the universe. They were visible, they were beneficent; they dwelt nearer to the gods, they were near at hand and always accessible. These were, of course, employed as mediators and intercessors between the supreme Divinity and his humble subjects of this lower world. Thus employed, they might claim a subordinate share of worship, which was accordingly assigned them. In process of time, however, that worship, which was originally addressed to the supreme Creator by the mediation of the heavenly bodies, was in a great measure forgotten, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of mankind ultimately terminated on those illustrious creatures. To this circumstance, we think, we may ascribe Origin of the origin of that species of idolatry called Zabibim, Zabibim, or the worship of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> of heaven, which overspread the world early and almost universally. In Egypt this mode of worship was adopted in all its most absurd and most enthusiastic forms; and at the same time the most heterogeneous mythology appeared in its train. The mythology of the ancient Egyptians was so various and multiform, so complicated and so mysterious, that it would require many volumes even to give a superficial account of its origin and progress, not only in its mother country, but even in many other parts of the eastern and western world. Besides, the idolatry and mythology of that wonderful country are so closely connected and so inseparably blended together, that it is impossible to describe the latter without at the same time developing the former. We hope, therefore, our readers will not be disappointed, if, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this nature, we touch only upon some of the leading or most interesting articles of this complicated subject. The Egyptians confounded the revolutions of the Reign of heavenly bodies with the reigns of their most early gods and monarchs. Hence the incredible number of years included in the reign of their eight superior gods, who, according to them, filled the Egyptian throne successively in the most early periods of time. To these, according to their system, succeeded twelve demigods, who likewise reigned an amazing number of years. These imaginary reigns were no other than the periodical revolutions of the heavenly bodies preserved in their almanacks, which might be carried back, and actually were carried back, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Hence the fabulous antiquity of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The imaginary exploits and adventures of these gods and demigods furnished an inexhaustible fund of mythological romances. To the demigods succeeded the kings of the cynic cycle, personages equally chimerical with the former. The import of this epithet has greatly perplexed critics and etymologists. We apprehend it is an oriental word importing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. This appellation intimated, that the monarchs of that cycle, admitting that they actually existed, were more powerful and more highly revered than their successors. After the princes of the cynic cycle comes another race, denominated Nekyes, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> likewise implying royal, splendid, glorious. These cycles (c) Shem or Sem, "a sign," and ramah, "high." cycles figure high in the mythological annals of the Egyptians, and have furnished materials for a variety of learned and ingenious disquisitions. The wars and adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, Oris, Typhon, and other allegorical personages who figure in the Egyptian rubric; the wanderings of Isis, the sister and wife of Osiris; the transformation of the gods into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds of animals; their birth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, peregrinations, and exploits;—compose a body of mythological fictions so various, so complicated, so ridiculous, and often so apparently absurd, that all attempts to develop and explain them have hitherto proved unsuccessful. All, or the greatest part, of those extravagant fables, are the offspring of hieroglyphical or allegorical emblems devised by the priests and sages of that nation, with a view to conceal the mysteries of their religion from that class of men whom they stigmatized with the name of the uninitiated rabble. The worship of brute animals and of certain vegetables, universal among the Egyptians, was another exuberant source of mythological adventures. The Egyptian priests, many of whom were likewise profound philosophers, observed, or pretended to observe, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between the qualities of certain animals and vegetables, and those of some of their subordinate deities. Such animals and vegetables they adopted, and consecrated to the deities to whom they were supposed to bear this analogical resemblance; and in process of time they considered them as the visible emblems of those deities to which they were consecrated. By these the vulgar addressed their archetypes: in the same manner, as in other countries, pictures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> were employed for the very same purpose. The mob, in process of time, forgetting the emblematical character of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> and vegetables, addressed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> immediately to them; and of course these became the ultimate objects of vulgar adoration. After that these objects, animate or inanimate, were consecrated as the visible symbols of the deities, it soon became fashionable to make use of their figures to represent those deities to which they were consecrated. This practice was the natural consequence of the hieroglyphical style which universally prevailed among the ancient Egyptians. Hence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a> was represented under the figure of a ram, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a> under that of a cow, Osiris of a bull, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> of a goat, Thoth or Mercury of an ibis, Bubalis or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> of a cat, &c. It was likewise a common practice among those deluded people to dignify these objects, by giving them the names of those deities which they represented. By this mode of dignifying these sacred emblems, the veneration of the rabble was considerably enhanced, and the ardour of their devotion inflamed in proportion. From these two sources, we think, are derived the fabulous transformations of the gods, so generally celebrated in the Egyptian mythology, and from it imported into Greece and Italy. In consequence of this practice, their mythological system was rendered at once enormous and unintelligible. Their Thoth, or Mercury Trismegistus, was, in our opinion, the inventor of this unhappy system. This personage, according to the Egyptians, was the original author of letters, geometry, astronomy, music, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; in a word, of all the elegant and useful arts, and of all the branches of science and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He it was who first discovered the analogy between the divine affections, influences, appearances, operations, and the corresponding properties, qualities, and instincts of certain animals, and the propriety of dedicating particular kinds of vegetables to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of particular deities. The priests, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> it was to expound the mysteries of that allegorical hieroglyphical religion, (see Mysteries), gradually lost all knowledge of the primary import of the symbolical characters. To supply this defect, and at the same time to veil their own ignorance, the sacerdotal instructors had recourse to fable and fiction. They heaped fable upon fable, till their religion became an accumulated chaos of mythological absurdities. Two of the most learned and most acute of the ancient philosophers have attempted a rational explication of the latent import of the Egyptian mythology; but both have failed in the attempt; nor have the moderns, who have laboured in the same department, performed their part with much better success. Instead, therefore, of prosecuting this inexplicable subject, which would swell this article beyond all proportion, we must beg leave to refer those who are desirous of further information to the following authors, where they will find enough to gratify their curiosity, if not to inform their judgment: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, lib. ii. Diodorus Siculus, lib. i. Plut. Isis et <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OPHIR">Ophir</a>; Jamblichus de Myth. Egypt. Horapollo Hieroglyp. Egypt. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MACROBI">Macrobi</a>. Sat. cap. 23. among the ancients; and among the moderns, Kircher's Oedip. Voss. de Orig. et Prog. Idol. Mr Bryant's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">Analysis</a> of Anc. Mythol. Monf. Gebelin Monde Prim.; and above all, to the learned Jabloniski's Panth. Egyptianorum. The elements of Phoenician mythology have been preserved by Eusebius, Prep. Evang. sub. init. In mythology, the large extracts which that learned father hath copied from Philo Biblius's translation of Sanchoniathon's History of Phenicia, we are furnished with several articles of mythology. Some of these throw considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the sacred history; and all of them are strictly connected with the mythology of the Greeks and Romans. There we have preserved a brief but entertaining detail of the fabulous adventures of Uranus, Cronus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAGON">Dagon</a>, Tytho or Mercury, probably the same with the Egyptian hero of that name. Here we find Muth or Pluto, Æphcectus or Vulcan, ÆCulapius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a>, Poseidon or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, &c. Astarte, or Venus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URANIA">Urania</a>, makes a conspicuous figure in the catalogue of Phoenician worthies; Pallas or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> is planted on the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>; in a word, all the branches of the family of the Titans, who in after ages figured in the rubric of the Greeks, are brought upon the stage, and their exploits and adventures briefly detailed. By comparing this fragment with the mythology of Grecian the Atlantide and that of the Cretans preserved by Diodorus the Sicilian, lib. v. we think there is good reason to conclude, that the family of the Titans, the several branches of which seem to have been both the authors and objects of a great part of the Grecian idolatry, originally emigrated from Phenicia. This conjecture will receive additional strength, when it is considered, that almost all their names recorded in the fabulous records of Greece, may be easily traced up to a Phoenician Phoenician original. We agree with Herodotus, that a considerable part of the idolatry of Greece may have been borrowed from the Egyptians; at the same time, we imagine it highly probable, that the idolatry of the Egyptians and Phoenicians was, in its original <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, nearly the same. Both systems were Sabism, or the worship of the host of heaven. The Pelagia, according to Herodotus, learned the names of the gods from the Egyptians; but in this conjecture he is certainly warped by his partiality for that people. Had those names been imported from Egypt, they would no doubt have bewrayed their Egyptian original; whereas, every etymologist will be convinced that every one is of Phoenician <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. The adventures of Jupiter, Juno, Mercury, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, Diana, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, Minerva or Pallas, Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, Proserpine, Pluto, Neptune, and the other deities and coadjutors of the ambitious family of the Titans, furnish by far the greatest part of the mythology of Greece. They left Phoenicia, we think, about the age of Moses; they settled in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, a large and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; from this region they made their way into Greece, which, according to the most authentic accounts, was at that time inhabited by a race of savages. The arts and inventions which they communicated to the natives; the mysteries of religion which they inculcated; the laws, customs, policy, and good order, which they established; in short, the blessings of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and civilization, which they everywhere diffused, in process of time inspired the unpolished inhabitants with a kind of divine admiration. Those ambitious mortals improved this admiration into divine homage and adoration. The greater part of that worship, which had been formerly addressed to the luminaries of heaven, was now transferred to those illustrious personages. They claimed and obtained divine honours from the deluded rabble of enthusiastic Greeks. Hence sprung an inexhaustible fund of the most inconsistent and irreconcilable fictions. The foibles and frailties of the deified mortals were transmitted to posterity, incorporated as it were with the pompous attributes of supreme divinity. Hence the heterogeneous mixture of the mighty and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> which chequers the characters of the heroes of the Iliad and Odyssey. The Greeks adopted the oriental fables; the import of which they did not understand. These they accommodated to heroes and illustrious personages, who had figured in their own country in the earliest periods. The labours of Hercules originated in Egypt, and evidently relate to the annual progress of the sun in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, though the vain-glorious Greeks accommodated them to a hero of their own, the reputed son of Jupiter and Alcmene. The expedition of Osiris they borrowed from the Egyptians, and transferred to their Bacchus, the son of Jupiter and Semele the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>. The transformation and wanderings of Io are evidently transcribed from the Egyptian romance of the travels of Isis in quest of the body of Osiris, or of the Phoenician Atharte, drawn from Sanchoniathon. Io or Iola is in reality the Egyptian name of the moon, and Atharte was the name of the same planet among the Phoenicians. Both these fables are allegorical representations of the anomalies of the lunar planet, or perhaps of the progress of the worship of that planet in different parts of the world. The fable of the conflagration occasioned by Phaeton is clearly of oriental extraction, and alludes to an excessive drought which in the early periods of time scorched Ethiopia and the adjacent countries. The fabulous adventures of Perseus are said to have happened in the same regions, and are allegorical representations of the influence of the solar luminary; for the original Perseus was the sun. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> of Proserpine and the wanderings of Ceres: the Eleusinian mysteries; the orgia or sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of Bacchus; the rites and worship of the Cabiri—were imported from Egypt and Phoenicia; but strangely garbled and disguised by the hierophants of Greece. The gynantomachia, or war between the gods and the giants, and all the fabulous events and varieties of that war, form an exact counterpart to the battles of the Peri and Dives, celebrated in the romantic annals of Persia. A considerable part of the mythology of the Greeks sprang from their ignorance of the oriental languages, ignorant of oriental languages spoken by people whom, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of their heart, they stigmatized with the epithet of barbarian. This aversion to every foreign dialect was highly detrimental to their progress in the sciences. The same neglect or aversion has, we imagine, proved an irreparable injury to the republic of letters in all succeeding ages. The poets or trolling bards laid hold on those oriental legends, which they sophistically with their own additions and improvements, in order to accommodate them to the popular taste. These wonderful tales figured in their rhapsodical compositions, and were greedily swallowed down by the credulous vulgar. Those fictions, as they rolled down, were constantly augmented with fresh materials, till in process of time their original import was either forgotten or buried in impenetrable darkness. A multitude of these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> has collected in his Theogonia, or Generation of the Gods, which unhappily became the religious creed of the illiterate part of the Greeks. Indeed, fable was so closely interwoven with the religion of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> volatile people, that it seems to have contaminated not only their religious and moral, but even their political tenets. The far-famed oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a> was copied from that of Ammon at Thebes in Egypt: the oracle of Apollo at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> was an emanation from the same source: the celebrated Apollo Pythius of the Greeks was no other than Ob or Aub of the Egyptians, who denominated the basilisk or royal snake On Cai, because it was held sacred to the sun. Ob or Aub is still retained in the Coptic dialect, and is one of the many names or epithets of that luminary. In short, the groundwork of the Grecian mythology is to be traced in the east. Only a small part of it was fabricated in the country; and what was imported pure and genuine was miserably sophificated by the hands through which it passed, in order to give it a Grecian air, and to accommodate its style to the Grecian taste. To enlarge upon this topic would be altogether superfluous, as our learned readers must be well acquainted with it already, and the unlearned may without much trouble Roman or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> furnish themselves with books upon that subject. The Roman mythology was borrowed from the Greek-Greeks. Greeks. That people had addicted themselves for many centuries to the arts of war and civil polity. Science and philosophy were either neglected or unknown. At last they conquered Greece, the native land of science, and then "Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit arte et intulit agresti Latio." This being the case, their mythology was, upon the whole, a transcript from that of Greece. They had indeed gleaned a few fables from the Pelasgi and Hetrucans, which, however, are of so little consequence, that they are scarce worth the trouble of transcribing. The mythology of the Celtic nations is in a good measure lost. There may possibly still remain some vestiges of the Druidical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> in the remotest parts of the Highlands and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Scotland; and perhaps in the uncivilized places of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. These we presume, would afford our readers but little entertainment, and still less instruction. Instead therefore of giving a detail of those uninteresting articles, we shall beg leave to refer our readers to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>'s Poems, and Col. Valency's Collections of Irish Antiquities, for satisfaction on that subject. The mythology of the northern nations, i.e. of the Norwegians, Danes, Swedes, Icelanders, &c., are uncommonly curious and entertaining. The Edda and Voluspa contain a complete collection of fables which have not the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with those of the Greeks and Romans. They are wholly of an oriental complexion, and seem almost congenial with the tales of the Persians above described. The Edda was compiled in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> in the 13th century. It is a kind of system of the Scandinavian mythology: and has been reckoned, and we believe justly, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the Voluspa, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> of the northern nations. Odin or Othin, or Woden or Wadon, was the supreme divinity of those people. His exploits and adventures furnish the far greatest part of their mythological creed. That hero is supposed to have emigrated from the east; but from what country or at what period is not certainly known. His achievements are magnified beyond all credibility. He is represented as the god of battles, and as slaying thousands at a blow. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is called Valhalla: it is situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Midgard, where, according to the fable, the souls of heroes who had bravely fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> enjoy supreme felicity. They spend the day in mimic hunting matches, or imaginary combats. At night they assemble in the palace of Valhalla, where they feast on the most delicious viands, dished and served up by the Valkyries, virgins adorned with celestial charms, and flushed with the bloom of everlasting youth. They solace themselves with drinking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAD">mead</a> out of the skulls of enemies whom they killed in their days of nature. Mead, it seems, was the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a> of the Scandinavian heroes. Sleipner, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> of Odin, is celebrated along with his master. Hela, the hell of the Scandinavians, affords a variety of fables equally shocking and heterogeneous. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOKE">Loke</a>, the evil genius or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> of the northern people, nearly resembles the Typhon of the Egyptians. Signa or Sinna is the comfort of Loke; from this name the English word sin is derived. The giants Weymar, Ferhanter, Belupher, and Hellunda, perform a variety of exploits, and are exhibited in the most frightful attitudes. One would be tempted to imagine, that they perform the exact counterpart of the giants of the Greek and Roman mythologies. Instead of glancing at these ridiculous and uninteresting fables, which is all that the limits prescribed us would permit, we shall take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to lay before our readers a brief account of the contents of the Voluspa, which is indeed the text of the Scandinavian mythology. "The world Voluspa imports, 'the prophecy of Vola' or Fola." This was perhaps a general name for the prophetic ladies of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, as Sibyl was appropriated to women endowed with the like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> in the south. Certain it is, that the ancients generally connected madness with the prophetic faculty. Of this we have two celebrated examples: the one in Lycophron's Alexandra, and the other in the Sibyl of the Roman poet. The word vola signifies "mad or foolish;" whence the English words fool, foolish, folly. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPA">Spa</a>, the latter part of the composition, signifies "to prophecy," and is still current among the common people in Scotland, in the word Spae, which has nearly the same signification. The Voluspa consists of between 200 and 300 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. The prophetess having implored silence on all intelligent beings, declares that she is about to reveal the works of the Father of nature, the actions and operations of the gods, which no mortal ever knew before herself. She then begins with a description of the chaos; and then proceeds to the formation of the world, the creation of the different species of its inhabitants, giants, men, and dwarfs. She then explains the employments of the fairies or deities, whom the northern people call norries; the functions of the deities, their most memorable adventures, their disputes with Loke, and the vengeance that ensued. She at last concludes with a long and indeed animated description of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> state of the universe, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> by a general conflagration. In this catastrophe, Odin and all the rabble of the Pagan divinities, are to be confounded in the general ruin, no more to appear on the stage of the universe. Out of the ruins of the former world, according to the Voluspa, a new one shall <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up, arrayed in all the bloom of celestial beauty. Such is the doctrine exhibited in the fabulous Voluspa. So congenial are some of the details therein delivered, especially those relating to the final dissolution of the present system, and the succession of a new heaven and a new earth, that we find ourselves strongly inclined to suspect, that the original fabricator of the work was a semi-pagan writer, much of the same complexion with the authors of the Sibylline oracles, and of some other apocryphal pieces which appeared in the world during the first ages of Christianity. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the only mythological countries must be <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. The other parts of that large continent were originally inhabited by savages, most of them as remote from religion as from civilization. The two vast empires of Mexico and Peru had existed about 400 years only before the Spanish invasion. In neither of them was the use of letters understood; and of course the ancient opinions of the natives relating to the origin of the universe, the changes which succeeded, and every other monument of antiquity, were obliterated and lost. Clavigero has indeed enumerated a vast canaille of fanguary gods worshipped by the Mexicans; Mexicans; but produces nothing either entertaining or interesting with respect to their mythology. The information to be derived from any other quarter is little to be depended upon. It passes through the hands of bigotted millionaries or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, who were so deeply tinctured with fanaticism, that they viewed every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, every sentiment, every custom, every religious opinion and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of those half-civilized people, through a false medium. They often imagined they discovered resemblances and analogies between the rites of those savages and the dogmas of Christianity, which nowhere existed but in their own heated imagination. The only remarkable piece of mythology in the annals of the Peruvians, is the pretended extraction of Manco Capac the first Inca of Peru, and of Mama Ocalla his consort. These two illustrious personages appeared first on the banks of the lake Titicaca. They were persons of a majestic stature, and clothed in decent garments. They declared themselves to be the children of the Sun, sent by their beneficent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, who beheld with pity the miseries of the human race, to instruct and to reclaim them. Thus we find these two legislators availed themselves of a pretence which had often been employed in more civilized regions to the very same purpose. The idolatry of Peru was gentle and benevolent, that of Mexico gloomy and fanatical. Hence we may see, that every mode of superstition, where a divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> is not concerned, borrows its complexion from the characters of its professors. In the course of this article, our readers will observe, that we have not much enlarged upon the mythology of the Greeks and Romans; that subject we imagine to be so universally known by the learned, and so little valued by the vulgar, that a minute discussion of it would be altogether superfluous. Besides, we hope it will be remembered, that the narrowness of the limits prescribed us would scarce admit of a more copious detail. We would flatter ourselves, that in the course of our disquisition, we have thrown out a few reflections and observations, which may perhaps prove more acceptable to both descriptions of readers.

It was made of garlic, onions, eggs, cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and reckoned very wholesome.

MYUS

Pages 215-215

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the twelve <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>; situated on the Meander, at the distance of 30 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was incorporated with the Milesians, on account of the paucity of inhabitants, from its being formerly overwhelmed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>: for which reason the Ionians configned its suffrage and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies to the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> allotted this town to Themistocles, in order to furnish his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with meat: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a> was to support him in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and Lampacus in wine. The town now lies in ruins.

MYXINE

the Hag; a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes intestina. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. N. N, A liquid consonant, and the 13th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the Greek, Latin, English, &c. alphabets. The n is a nasal consonant: its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is that of a d, puffed through the nose; so that when the nose is stopped by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, it is usual to pronounce d for n. M. Abbé de Dangeau observes, that in the French, the n is frequently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> nasal vowel, without any thing of the consonant in it. He calls it the Slavonic vowel. The Hebrews call their n <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a>, which signifies child, as being supposed the offspring of m; partly on account of the resemblance of sound, and partly on that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. Thus from the m, by omitting the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, is formed n; and thus from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> N, by omitting the first column, is formed the Greek minuscule ν. Hence for biennies, &c. the Latins frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> binnus, &c. and the same people convert the Greek ν, at the end of a word, into an m, as Φαρμακευς, pharmacum, &c. See M. N before p, b, and m, the Latins change into m, and frequently into l and r; as in in-ludo, illudo; in-rigo, irrigo, &c.: in which they agree with the Hebrews, who, in lieu of nun, frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>; and the Greeks do the same; as when for Manlius, they write Μανλιος, &c. The Greeks also, before κ, γ, χ, ν changed the ν into γ: in which they were followed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>: who, for Angulus, wrote Angulus; for ancops, ageps, &c. The Latins retrench the n, from Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> ending NAB Naarda ing in or; as Λων, Leo; Δρακον, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a>; on the contrary, the Greeks add it to the Latin ones ending in o; as Kater, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, Cato, Nero. N, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was a numeral letter, signifying 900; according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in Baronius, N, quoque nongentos numero designat habendos. And when a line was struck over it, N, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> thousand. Among the ancient lawyers, N. L. stood for non liquet, i.e. the cause is not clear enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon. N, or N°, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, &c. is used as an abbreviation of numero, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

NAARDA

Pages 216-216

Naarda, Neerda, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nehardea, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town situated on the confines of Mesopotamia and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>; populous, and with a rich and extensive territory, not easily to be attacked by an enemy, being surrounded on all sides by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and strong walls (Jos. p. 48). In the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> the Jews had a celebrated school there.

NAAS

Pages 216-216

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>. It is the shire town of that county, and alternately with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHY">Athy</a> the assizes town. It is distant above 15 miles south-west from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, in N. Lat. 53° 10' W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 50'. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of vicount to the family of Burke. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was anciently the residence of the kings of Leinster: the name signifies "the place of elders," for here the states of that province assembled during the 6th, 7th, and 8th centuries, after the Naasleghen of Carmen had been anathematized by the Christian clergy. On the arrival of the English it was fortified; many castles were erected, the ruins of which are partly visible; and parliaments were held there. At the foot of the mount <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rath are the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> founded in 1484, for eremites of the order of St Augustin. In the 12th century the baron of Naas founded a priory dedicated to St John the Baptist, for Augustinian regular canons. In the centre of this town the family of Eustace erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> for Dominican friars, dedicated to St Eustachius; and it appears that their possessions in Naas were granted them in the year 1355. This place was a strong hold during the civil wars.

NABATENE

Pages 216-216
or REGIO NABATEORUM, according to Jerome, comprised all the country lying between the Euphrates and the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red sea, and thus contained Arabia Deserta, with a part of the Petraea; so called from Nabaioth, the first born of Ishmael. According to Diodorus, it was situated between Syria and Egypt. The people Nabataei (1 Maccabees, Diodorus Siculus): inhabiting a desert and barren country: they lived by plundering their neighbours according to Diodorus. Nabatheus the epithet.

NABIS

Pages 216-216
tyrant of Sparta, reigned about 204 B.C.; and is reported to have exceeded all other tyrants so far, that, upon comparison, he left the epithets of gracious and merciful to Dionysius and Phalaris.
