He is said to have contrived an instrument of torture in the form of a statue of a beautiful woman, whose rich drapery concealed a number of iron spikes in her bosom and arms. When any one therefore opposed his demands, he would say, "If I have not talents enough to prevail with you, perhaps my woman Apega may persuade you." The statue then appeared; which Nabis taking by the hand, led up to the person, who, being embraced by it, was thus tortured into compliance. To render his tyranny less unpopular, Nabis made an alliance with Flamininus the Roman general, and pursued with the most inveterate enmity the war which he had undertaken against the Achaeans. He besieged Gythium, and defeated Philopoemen in a naval battle. His triumph was short, the general of the Achaeans soon repaired his losses, and Nabis was defeated in an engagement, and killed as he attempted to save his life by flight, about 194 years before the Christian era.

NABLOUS

Pages 216-216

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, anciently celebrated under the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, likewise called Nablous, is situated near to Sichem on the ruins of the Neapolis of the Greeks, and is the residence of a sheik, who is subordinate to the pasha of Damascus, from whom he farms the tribute of the province.

NABLUM

Pages 216-216

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Nebel, was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music among the Jews. It had strings like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, and was played upon by both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Its form was that of a Greek Λ. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and Vulgate, it is called nobulum, psalterion, lyra; and sometimes cithara.

NABO

Pages 216-216
or NERO, in mythology, a deity of the Babylonians, who possessed the next rank to Bel. It is mentioned by Isaiah, chap. xlvi. Vollius apprehends that Nabo was the moon, and Bel the sun; but Grotius supposes that Nabo was some celebrated prophet of the country; which opinion is confirmed by the etymology of the name, signifying, according to Jerome, "one that presides over prophecy."

NABOB

Pages 216-216

properly NAVAB, the plural of Naib, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>. As used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, it is the same as NAZIM. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> also given to the wives and daughters of princes, as well as to the princes themselves.

NABONASSAR

Pages 216-216

first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Chaldeans <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Babylonians; memorable for the Jewish era which bears his name, which is generally fixed in 3257, beginning on Wednesday, February 26th, in the 3967th of the Julian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, 747 years before Christ. The Babylonians revolting from the Medes, who had overthrown the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, did, under Nabonassar, found a dominion, which was much increased under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>. It is probable, that this Nabonassar is that Baladan in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of Kings, ix. 12. father of Merodach, who sent ambassadors to Hezekiah. See 2 Chron. xxxii.

NABOPOLASSAR

Pages 216-216
king of Babylon: he joined with Ashyages the Mede, to destroy the empire of Assyria; which having accomplished, they founded the two empires of the Medes under Ashyages, and the Chaldeans under Nabopolassar, 627 B.C.

NABUCHADNEZZAR

Pages 216-216
or NABUCHODONOSOR II., king of Assyria, son of Nabopolassar, and styled the Great, was associated by his father in the empire, 607 B.C. and the following year he took Jehoiakim king of Judah prisoner, and proposed to carry him and his subjects in captivity into Babylon; but upon his submission, and promising to hold his kingdom under Nabuchodonosor, he was permitted to remain at Jerusalem. In 603 B.C. Jehoiakim attempted to shake off the Assyrian yoke, but without success; and this revolt brought on the general captivity. Nabuchadnezzar having subdued the Ethiopians, Arabians, Idumæans, Philistines, Syrians, Persians, Medes, Assyrians,

NADIR

Pages 216-217

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, that point of the heavens which is diametrically opposite to the zenith <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> point directly over our heads.

NAENIA

Pages 217-217

the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of funerals at Rome. Her temple was without the gates of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The songs which were sung at funerals were also called nenia. They were generally filled with the praises of the deceased; but sometimes they were so unmeaning and improper, that the word became proverbial to signify nonsense.

NAERDEN

Pages 217-217

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, seated at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The foundations of it were laid by William of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, in 1350. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1572, and by the French in 1672; but it was retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> the next year. It stands at the south end of the Zuider Zee, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 3' N. Lat. 51° 22'.

NAEVUS

Pages 217-217

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> on the skin, generally called a mother's mark; also the tumour known by the name of a wen. All preternatural tumours on the skin, in the form of a wart <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tubercle, are called excrescences; by the Greeks they are called acrothymia; and when they are born with a person, they are called naevi materni, or marks from the mother. See TUMOURS, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">SURGERY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NAGERA

Pages 217-217
or NAGARA, a town of Spain, in Old Castile, and the territory of Rioja, with the title of a duchy and fortress; famous for a battle fought in its neighbourhood in 1369. It is situated in a fertile country, on a brook called Noferilla. W. Long. 2° 20'. N. Lat. 42° 45'.

NAGRACUT

Pages 217-217

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, with a rich temple to which the Indians go in pilgrimage. It is seated on the river Ravi. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78° 10'. N. Lat. 33° 12'.

NAHUM

Pages 217-217
or the Prophecy of Nahum, a canonical book of the Old Testament. Nahum, the seventh of the 12 lesser prophets, was a native of Elkoshai, a little village of Galilee. The subject of his prophecy is the destruction of Nineveh, which he describes in the most lively and pathetic manner; his style is bold and figurative, and cannot be exceeded by the most perfect masters of oratory. This prophecy was verified at the siege of that city by Assyrians, in the year of the world 3378, 622 years before Christ.

NAIADES

Pages 217-217

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, certain inferior deities who presided over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and fountains. The Naiades generally inhabited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and resorted to the woods <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> meadows near the stream over which they presided. They are represented as young and beautiful virgins, often leaning upon an urn, from which flows a stream of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIGLE">Aigle</a> was the fairest of the Naiades, according to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. Their name seems to be derived from naio, "to flow." They were held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and often sacrifices of goats and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a> were offered to them, with libations of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Sometimes they received only offerings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, fruit, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>.

NAIAS

Pages 217-217

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NAIL

Pages 217-218

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length, containing the 16th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a yard. Nailing of Cannon. When circumstances make it necessary to abandon cannon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> when the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> are seized, and it is not however possible to take them away, it is proper to nail them up, in order to render them useless; which is done by driving a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> nail or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> spike into the vent of a piece of artillery, to render it unserviceable. There are various contrivances to force the nail out, as also foundry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> invented for that purpose, but they have never been found of general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; so that the best method is to drill a new vent. One Gaper Vimercatus was the first who invented the nailing of cannon. He was a native of Bremen, and made use of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> first in nailing up the artillery of Sigismund Malatesta.

NAILS

Pages 217-217

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c., small spikes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, &c., which being driven into wood, serve to bind several pieces together, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to fasten something upon them. Nails were made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hebrews for cancelling bonds: and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed by striking them through the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. This seems to be alluded to in Scripture, where God is said by our crucified Saviour to have "blotted out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-writing of ordinances that was against us, and to have taken it out of the way, nailing it to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>," Col. ii. 14. For the cause and ceremony of driving the annual nail, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAVUS">clavus</a> annalis, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, see ANNALIS Clavus.

NAIN

Pages 218-218
or NAIM, situated at the bottom of Mount Hermon on the north side, was anciently a city of the tribe of Issachar, in the province of Galilee. It was near the gates of this city that our Saviour restored to life the only son of a widow, and where he inspired Mary Magdalen to come and mourn for her sins at his feet. These circumstances alone make this place worthy of notice; for at present Nain is only a hamlet inhabited by Christians, Mahometans, and Hebrews, where there is not a single monument to attract the curiosity of the traveller.

NAINT

Pages 217-217

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> fishes, when borne in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> posture, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>.

NAIRES

Pages 218-218

NAHERS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> NAYERS, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name which is given by the Malabarians to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, who form a very numerous class or tribe, out of which the sovereigns of Malabar choose their body <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>.

NAIRN

Pages 218-218

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, comprehending the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Murray. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Murray frith, on the west and south by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, and on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a>. The length is about 18 miles, and the breadth about 14. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate and salubrious, and the winters are remarkably mild. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is rough and mountainous; yet there are some fruitful valleys, which produce good crops of oats and barley; but in general the country is much better adapted for pasture. Here are also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> woods of fir, and other trees, that afford shelter to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, of which there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty. The most remarkable straths <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> valleys in this county are Strathnairn, on the river of that name, in the north-west part of theshire; and on the south-east side, Strathnairn, on both sides of Findhorn river. Nairn is well watered with streams, rivulets, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> abounding with fish. In the southern part there is a small lake, called Moy. The greater part of theshire is peopled by the Frasers, a warlike Highland clan, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Lovat, lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> on the scaffold for having been concerned in the rebellion of 1745. Here are a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages; but no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> except Nairn, supposed to be the Tucris of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, situated at the mouth of the river which bears the same name; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, which gave the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of lord to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, forfeited in the rebellion of 1715. The harbour, which opened in the Murray frith, is now choked up with sand; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the town is too inconsiderable to deserve notice. About four miles from Nairn stands the castle of Calder, on the river of that name, belonging to a branch of the family of Campbell; and six miles to the north-west of Nairn, stands Fort George, built by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Arderfer, a small illusmus upon the Murray frith. The following is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the parishes of this county, according to the Statistical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland. | Parishes | Population in 1755 | Population in 1790-1792 | |----------|------------------|------------------------| | Ardclach | 1163 | 1186 | | Auldearn | 1951 | 1406 | | Calder | 882 | 1062 | | Nairn | 1098 | 2400 | | | 5694 | 6054 | | Increase | | 360 | Population in 1801, including part of some other Parishes. | Ardclach | - | 1256 | | Auldearn | - | 1401 | | Calder | - | 1179 | | Croy (Nairn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>) | - | 562 | | Moy do. | - | 34 | | Nairn town | - | 2215 | | Urquhart (do.) | - | 1610 |

NAISSANT

Pages 218-218

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is applied to any animal issuing out of the midst of some ordinary, and showing only his head, shoulders, fore feet, and legs, with the tip of his tail; the rest of his body being hid in the shield, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon it; in which it differs from effuant, which denotes a living creature arising out of the bottom of any ordinary or charge.

NAISSUS

Pages 218-219

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Dardania, a district of Moesia Superior, said to be the birthplace of Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, which seems probable from his often residing at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Naissant, the NAKED seeds, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, those that are not enclosed in any pod <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>.

NAKIB

Pages 219-219

in the oriental dignities, the name of an officer who is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to the cadilliker, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as he may be called, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior. His office is to carry the standard of Mahomet.

NAKOUS

Pages 219-219

an Egyptian musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, made like two plates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and of all sizes, from two inches to a foot in diameter; they hold them by strings fastened to their middles, and strike them together so as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They are used in the Coptic churches and in the Mahometan processions.

NAME

Pages 219-220

denotes a word whereby men have agreed to express some idea; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> which serves to denote or signify a thing or subject spoken of. See Word. This the grammarians usually call a noun, nomen, though their noun is not of quite so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> as our name. See Noun. Seneca, lib. ii. de Beneficiis, observes, that there are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of things which have no name; and which, therefore, we are forced to call by other borrowed names. Ingens est (says he) rerum copia sine nomine, quas cum propriis appellativibus signare non possumus, alieuis accommodatis utimur: which may show why, in the course of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, we frequently give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> senses to the same word. Names are distinguished into proper and appellative. Proper Names, are those which represent some individual thing or person, so as to distinguish it from all other things of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; as, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, which represents a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Appellative or General Names, are those which signify <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; or which are common to several individuals of the same species; as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, animal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, oak, &c. Proper names are either called Christian, as being given at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>; or surnames: The first imposed for distinction of persons, answering to the Roman praenomen; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, for the distinction of families, answering to the nomen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and the patronymicum of the Greeks. Originally every person had but one name; as among the Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, &c.; among the Egyptians, Buhris; among the Chaldees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINUS">Ninus</a>; the Medes, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a>; the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>; the Romans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>; the Gauls, Divitiacus; the Germans, Ariovitus; the Britons, Caffilelan; the English, Hengil, &c. And thus of other nations, except the savages of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, whom Pliny and Marcellinus represent as anonymi, "nameless." The Jews gave the name at the circumcision, viz. eight days after the birth: the Romans, to females the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to males the ninth; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they held a feast, called nomina. Since Christianity has obtained, most nations have followed the Jews, baptizing and giving the name on the eighth day after the birth; except our English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, who, till of late, baptized and gave the name names on the birth day. The first imposition of names was founded on different views, among different people; the most common was to mark the good wishes of the parents, or to entitle the children to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> a happy name seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. Hence, Victor, Cæsar, Faustus, Statius, Probus, &c. Accordingly, we find such names, by Cicero called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONA">bona</a> nomina, and by Tacitus suafa nomina, were first enrolled and ranged in the Roman mutters; first called to serve at the sacrifices, in the foundation of colonies, &c.—And, on the contrary, Livy calls Atrius Unber, abominandi omnis nomen; and Plautus, on occasion of a person named Lyco, i.e. "greedy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>," says: Vosmet nunc facite conjecturam ceterum Quid id sit hominis, cui Lyco nomen fiet. Hence, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> recommends it to men to be careful in giving happy names; and the Pythagoreans taught expressly, that the minds, actions, and successes of men, were according to their names, genius, and fate. Thus Panormitan, ex bono nomine critur bona praesumpio; and the common proverb, Bonum nomen bonum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>; and hence the foundation of the onomantia. See ONOMANTIA. It is an observation deserving <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, says the abbe Barthelemy, that the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of names found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> are marks of distinction. They were given in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the qualities most esteemed in the heroic ages. From the word polemos, which signifies <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, have been formed Tlepolemus and Archepolemus, the names of two heroes mentioned in the Iliad. The former name signifies able to support, and the latter, able to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, the labours of war. By adding to the word mache, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, certain prepositions and different parts of speech, which modify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> in a manner always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, are composed the names Amphimachus, Antimachus, Promachus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>. Proceeding in the same way, with the word honora, "strength or intrepidity," they formed the names Agapenor, "he who esteems valour;" Agenor, "he who directs it." From these, "swift," are derived, Alcaethes, Pantheus, Perithoas, &c. From nous, "mind or intelligence," come Alynoes, Arfinoes, Autenoes, &c. From medes, "counsel," Agamedes, Eumedes, Lycomedes, Thrasymedes; and from elios, "<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>," Amphicles, Agacles, Iphicles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, Cloebulus; with many others. Hence Camden takes it for granted, that the names, in all nations and languages, are significative, and not simple sounds for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> distinction's sake. This holds not only among the Jews, Greeks, Latins, &c., but even the Turks; among whom, Abdala signifies God's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, Soliman, peaceable; Mahomet, glorified, &c. And the savages of Hispaniola, and throughout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who, in their languages, name their children, Glittering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, Bright, Fine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, &c.; and they of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, by the names of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. To suppose names given without any meaning, however by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of languages their signification may be lost, that learned author thinks is to reproach our ancestors; and that contrary to the sense of of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers. Porphyry notes, that the barbarous names, as he calls them, were very emphatical, and very concise; and accordingly it was esteemed a duty to be ἐπιστολοῦνται, or sui nominis honores; as Severus, Probus, and Aurelius, are called sui nominis imperatores. It was the usual way of giving names, to wish the children might discharge their names. Thus when Gunthram <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France named Clotharius at the font, he said, Crescat puer, et hujus sit nominis executor. The ancient Britons, Camden says, generally took their names from colours, because they painted themselves; which names are now lost, or remain hid among the Welsh. When they were subdued by the Romans, they took Roman names, some of which still remain corrupted; though the greatest part became extinct upon the admission of the English Saxons, who introduced the German names, as Crida, Penda, Oswald, Edward, &c.—The Danes, too, brought with them their names; as Sweyn, Harold, Knute, &c. The Normans, at the Conquest, brought in other German names, as originally using the German tongue; such as Robert, William, Richard, Henry, Hugh, &c. after the same manner as the Greek names Apollonius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>, Symmachus, &c. were introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire. After the Conquest, our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, which had ever been averse to foreign names, as deeming them unlucky, began to take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> names; as Matthew, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Sampson, &c. The various names anciently or at present obtaining among us, from what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> or people forever borrowed, are explained by Camden in his Remains. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when names began to be multiplied, and surnames introduced, &c. see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">Surname</a>. Of late years it has obtained among us to give surnames for Christian names; which some dislike, on account of the confusion it may introduce. Camden relates it as an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the practice first began in the reign of Edward VI. by such as would be godfathers, when they were more than half fathers. Upon which some were persuaded to change their names at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>; which, it seems, is usual in other countries.—Thus, two sons of Henry II. of France, christened Alexander and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, changed them at confirmation into Henry and Francis. In monasteries, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assume new names at their admittance, to show they are about to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and have renounced the world, their family, and even their name: v. g. fuller <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of the Incarnation, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Henry of the Holy Sacrament, &c. The popes also changed their names at their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> to the pontificate; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> first introduced by Pope Sergius, whose name till then, as Platin informs us, was Swine's-shoot. But Onuphrius refers it to John XII. or XIII. and at the same time adds a different reason for it from that of Platin, viz. that it was done in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul, who were first called Simon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, those deified by the Heathen confections had new names given them; as Romulus was called Quirinus; Melicertes, Portunus or Portumnus, &c. New names were also given in adoptions, and sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>: thus L. Aemilius, adopted by Scipio, took the name of Scipio Africanus; and thus Augustus, who was at first called C. Octavius Thurinus, being adopted by the testament of Julius Caesar into his name and family, took the name of Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus. Names were also changed at enfranchisements into new cities. Thus Lucumo, at his first being made free of Rome, took the name Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, &c.; and slaves when made free, usually assumed their masters names. Those called to the equestrian order, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had base names, were always new named, nomine ingenuorum veterumque Romanorum. And among the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, it was the practice to change the names of the catechumens: Thus the renegade <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCIANUS">Lucianus</a>, till his baptism, was called Lucius. Toward the middle of the 15th century, it was the fancy of the wits and learned men of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, particularly in Italy, to change their baptismal names for classical ones. As Sannazzarius, for instance, who altered his own plain name Jacopo to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIUS">Actius</a> Synecus. Numbers did the same, and among the rest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">Platina</a> the historian at Rome, who, not without a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>, took the name of Gallinachus instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>. Pope Paul II. who reigned about that time, unluckily chanced to be culpacious, illiterate, and heavy of comprehension. He had no idea that persons could wish to alter their names unless they had some bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and actually scrupled not to employ imprisonment and other violent methods to discover the fancied mystery. Platina was most cruelly tortured on this frivolous account: he had nothing to confess: so the pope, after endeavouring in vain to convict him of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, sedition, &c. released him after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> imprisonment.

NAMPTWICH

Pages 220-220
or NANTWICH, a town of Cheshire in England, situated on the river Weaver, 14 miles S. E. from Chester, and 162 miles from London. It lies in the Vale Royal, and is one of the largest and best built towns in the county, the streets being very regular, and adorned with many gentlemen's houses. The inhabitants trade in corn, cattle, cheese, fine white salt, and shoes. It is governed by a constable, &c. who are guardians of the salt springs. It is divided into two equal parts by the Weaver, which is navigable to Winsford bridge. The Chester canal, terminates in a large basin near this place. In this town were several religious foundations, now no more. The church is a handsome pile of building in the form of a cross, with an octangular tower in the middle.

NAMUR

Pages 220-221

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Sambre and Meuse; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Brabant, on the east and south by the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, and on the west by Hainault. It is pretty fertile; has several forests, marble quarries, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and pit coal; and is about 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Namur is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town. Namur, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and very strong town of the Netherlands, capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Namur, with a strong castle, several forts, and a bishop's see. The most considerable forts are, Fort William, Fort Meuse, Fort Conquetel, and Fort Esprinor. The castle is built in the middle of the town, on a craggy rock. It was besieged by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William in 1695, who took it in the fight of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 100,000 French, though there were 16,000 men in the garrison. It was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> in 1713, but taken by the French in 1746; and restored by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle. It was again taken by the French in 1792, who evacuated it the following year, and retook it in 1794. It is situated between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, at the confluence of the rivers Maese and Sambre, in E. Long. 4° 57'. N. Lat. 50° 25'.

NAN-KING

Pages 221-222

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Kiang-nan, is said to have been formerly one of the most beautiful and flourishing cities in the Nan-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> world. When the Chinese speak of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, they say, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> two horsemen should go out by the same gate, and ride round it on full speed, taking different directions, they would not meet before night. This account is evidently exaggerated; but it is certain, that Nan-king surpasses in extent all the other cities of China. We are assured that its walls are five leagues and a half in circumference. This city is situated at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YANG_TSE_KIANG">Yang-tse-kiang</a>: it is of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which are within its circumference having prevented its being built on a regular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. It was formerly the imperial city; for this reason it was called Nan-King, which signifies, "the Southern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>;" but since the six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> tribunals have been transferred from hence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEKING">Peking</a>, it is called Kiang-ning in all the public acts. Nan-king has lost much of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> splendour: it had formerly a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, no vestige of which is now to be seen; an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at present neglected, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, tombs of the emperors, and other superb monuments, of which nothing remains but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>. A third of the city is deserted, but the rest is well inhabited. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of it are extremely populous and full of business; particularly the manufacture of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cotton cloth, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities are imported into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> under the name of Nankin. The streets are not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> as those of Peking; they are, however, very beautiful, well paved, and bordered with rich shops. In this city resides one of those great mandarins called Tjong-gou, who takes cognizance of all important affairs, not only of both the governments of the province, but also of those of the province of Kiang-fu. The Tartars have a numerous garrison here, commanded by a general of their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and they occupy a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the city, separated from the rest by a plain wall. The palaces of the mandarins, whether Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tartars, are in this city neither larger nor better built than those in the capital cities of other provinces. Here are no public edifices corresponding to the reputation of so celebrated a city, excepting its gates, which are very beautiful, and some temples, among which is the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> tower. It is 200 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and divided into <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stories by plain boards within, and without by cornices and small projections covered with green varnished tiles. There is an ascent of 40 steps to the first story; between each of the others there are 21. The breadth and depth of the river Yang-tse-kiang formerly rendered the port of Nan-king very commodious; but at present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> barks, or rather Chinese junks, never enter it; whether it be that it is flut up by sand banks, or that the entrance of it has been forbidden, in order that navigators may insensibly lose all knowledge of it. In the months of April and May a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent fish are caught in this river near the city, which are sent to court; they are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, and transported in that manner by barks kept entirely on purpose. Although this city is more than 200 leagues from Peking, these boats make such expedition, that they arrive there in eight or nine days. This city, though the capital of the province, has under its particular jurisdiction only eight cities of the third class. The number of its inhabitants is said to be 1,000,000, without comprehending the garrison of 40,000 men. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 119. 25. N. Lat. 32. 46.

NAN-TCHANG-FOU

Pages 221-221

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Kiang-fu, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> has no trade but that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, which is made in the neighbourhood of Jao-tehou. It is the residence of a viceroy, and comprehends in its district eight cities; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of which are of the third class, and only one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. So much of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is cultivated, that the pastures left are scarcely sufficient for the flocks.

NANCI

Pages 221-221

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEURTHE">Meurthe</a>, situated on the river Meuse, in the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. It is divided into the Old and New <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>. The first, though irregularly built, is very populous, and contains the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; the streets of the New Town are as straight as a line, adorned with handsome buildings, and a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a magnificent structure, and in that of the Cordeliers are the tombs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dukes. The two towns are separated by a canal; and the new town was very well fortified, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France demolished the fortifications. It has been taken and retaken several times; particularly by the French, to whom it was ceded in 1736, to enjoy it after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Stanislaus. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 17'. N. Lat. 48° 41'.

NANCOWRY

Pages 221-221
or SOWRY, one of the Nicobar s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands, lying at the entrance of the bay of Bengal. See NICOBAR.

NANI

Pages 221-221

JOHN BAPTIST, was born in 1616. His father was procurator of St Mark, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to Rome. He was educated with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and made considerable improvement. Urban VIII. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> value of merit, soon perceived that of young Nani. He was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of senators in 1641, and was shortly after nominated ambassador in France, where he signalized himself by his compliant manners. He procured considerable succours for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of Candia against the Turks; and became, after his return to Venice, superintendent of the war office and of finances. He was afterwards ambassador to the empire; where he rendered those services to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which, as a zealous and intelligent citizen, he was well qualified to discharge. He was again sent into France in 1660 to solicit fresh succours for Candia; and on his return was appointed procurator of St Mark. He died November 5, 1768, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 63, much regretted by his countrymen. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had appointed him to write the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Republic; which he executed to the satisfaction of the Venetians, although the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was less admired by foreigners, who were not proper judges of the accuracy with which he stated the facts, of the purity of his diction, nor of the simplicity of his style; although it must be acknowledged that his narrative is much interrupted by too frequent parentheses. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> his history of Venice he has given an universal history of his times, especially with respect to the affairs of the French in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. This history, which is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from 1613 to 1671, was printed at Venice in 2 vols 4to, in the years 1662 and 1679.

NANSIIO

Pages 222-222

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, a little to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the island of Santorino, 16 miles in circumference; but has no harbour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are nothing but bare rocks, and there are not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> the fields. There is a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of partridges, whose eggs they destroy every year to preserve the corn, and yet vast numbers of them are always produced. The ruins of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> are yet to be seen, and consist chiefly of marble columns. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. 20. N. Lat. 36. 15.

NANTES

Pages 222-222

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, rich, and very considerable town of France, in the department of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, with a bishop's see, an university, and a mint. It is one of the most considerable places in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; contains the richest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and was formerly the residence of the dukes of Bretagne, where they built a very strong castle on the side of the river, and which is strongly fortified. There are several parishes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> contains the tombs of the ancient dukes. There are several fine bridges over the river Loire, which is navigable. The suburbs are so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people that come from all parts to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> here, that they exceed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The Spaniards trade here in wine, fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, oranges, and lemons; and they carry back cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, corn, and hardware. The Dutch send fustian, and all sorts of spices; and in return have wine and brandy. The Swedes bring <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; and the English, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, tin, &c. It was in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> that Henry IV. promulgated the famous edict in 1598, called the Edict of Nantes, and which was revoked in 1685. Nantes was anciently, like almost every considerable city in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, very strongly fortified. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREUX">Dreux</a>, one of the dukes of Bretagne, surrounded it with walls, which have only been demolished within these few years. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> is an object of curiosity. It is near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in length, being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> across all the little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Loire, from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south. The territory of Nantes lies on both sides the Loire, and feeds a great number of cattle. Large vessels can come no higher than Port Launay, which is 12 miles from Nantes. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 45. N. Lat. 47. 13. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANTWICH">NANTWICH</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMPTWICH">NAMPTWICH</a>.

NAPAEA

Pages 222-222

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyadelphia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Columniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NAPHTHA

Pages 222-222

an inflammable substance of the bituminous kind. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>.

NAPHTHALI

Pages 222-222
or NEPHTHALI (Josh. xix.), one of the tribes of Israel; having Zabulon on the north, Asher on the west, the Jordan on the east, and on the north Antilibanus.

NAPIER

Pages 222-224

JOHN, baron of Merchiston in Scotland, inventor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a>, was the eldest son of Sir Archibald Napier of Merchiston, and born in the year 1550. Having given early discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> parts, his father was careful to have them cultivated by a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. After going through the ordinary courses of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at the university of Napier, St Andrew's, he made the tour of France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Germany. Upon his return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, his literature and other fine accomplishments soon rendered him conspicuous, and might have raised him to the highest offices in the state; but declining all civil employments, and the duties of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he retired from the world to pursue literary researches, in which he made an uncommon progress, so as to have favoured mankind with sundry useful discoveries. He applied himself chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> did not neglect that of the Holy Scriptures. In both these he hath discovered the most extensive knowledge and profound penetration. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> upon the book of the Apocalypse, indicates the most acute <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, and an uncommon strength of judgement; though time hath discovered, that his calculations concerning particular events hath proceeded upon fallacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATA">data</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has been printed abroad in several languages; particularly in French at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a> in the year 1593, 8vo, announced in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> as revised by himself. Nothing, says <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, could be more agreeable to the Rochellers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a> of France at this time, than the author's annunciation of the pope as antichrist, which in this book he has endeavoured to set forth with much zeal and erudition.—But what has principally rendered his name famous, was his great and fortunate discovery of logarithms in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>, by which the ease and expedition in calculation have so wonderfully assisted the science of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and the arts of practical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. That he had begun about the year 1593 the train of inquiry which led him to that great achievement in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Crugerus from Kepler in the year 1624; wherein, mentioning the Canon Mirificus, he writeth thus: "Nihil autem supra Neperianum rationem eft puto: etfi Scotus quidem literis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> Tycholem, anno 1564, scriptis jam fepem fecit Canonis illius mirifici;" which allusion agrees with the idle story mentioned by Wood in his Athenae Oxoni, and explains it in a way perfectly consonant to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of Napier as the inventor. When Napier had communicated to Mr Henry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIGGS">Briggs</a>, mathematical professor in Gresham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, his wonderful canon for the logarithms, that learned professor set himself to apply the rules in his Imitatio Neperiana; and in a letter to Archbishop Usher in the year 1615, he writes thus: "Napier, baron of Merchiston, hath set my head and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> at work with his new and admirable logarithms. I hope to see him this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it please God; for I never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a book which pleased me better, and made me more wonder." The following passage from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Lilly the astrologer is quoted by Lord Buchan, as giving a picturesque view of the meeting betwixt Briggs and the inventor of the logarithms at Merchiston near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. "I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> acquaint you (says Lilly) with one memorable story related unto me by John Marr, an excellent mathematician and geometrician, whom I conceive you remember. He was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. When Merchiston first published his logarithms, Mr Briggs, then reader of the astronomy lectures at Gresham college in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was so much surprised with admiration of them, that he could have no quietness in himself until he had seen that noble person..." Napier whose only <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> they were: he acquaints John Marr therewith, who went into Scotland before Mr Briggs, purposely to be there when these two so learned persons should meet. Mr Briggs appoints a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> when to meet at Edinburgh; but failing thereof, Merchiston was fearful he would not come. It happened one day as John Marr and the baron Napier were speaking of Mr Briggs; 'Ah, John (said Merchiston), Mr Briggs will not come.' At the very instant one knocks at the gate; John Marr halts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and it proved to be Mr Briggs to his great contentment. He brings Mr Briggs up to the baron's chamber, where almost one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> was spent, each beholding the other with admiration before one word was spoken. At last Mr Briggs began; 'Sir, I have undertaken this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> journey purposely to see your person, and to know by what engine of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> or ingenuity you came first to think of this most excellent help into astronomy, viz. the logarithms; but, Sir, being by you found out, I wonder nobody else found it out before, when now being known it appears so easy.' He was nobly entertained by Baron Napier; and every summer after that, during the laird's being alive, this venerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, Mr Briggs, went purposely to Scotland to visit him. There is a passage in the life of Tycho Brahe by Gassendi, which may mislead an attentive reader to suppose that Napier's method had been explored by the Writings of Napier of Merchiston. It is in Gassendi's Observations on a Letter from Tycho to Herwart of the last day of August 1599, "Dixit Herwartus nihil morari se enim multiplicationem, ac divisionem vice additiones solum, subtractiones 93 ulipare (quod ut fieri posset, docuit postmodum suae logarithmorum Canone Nipperus)." But Herwart here alludes to this work afterwards published in the year 1610, which solves triangles by prosthapheresis; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> totally different from that of the logarithms. Kepler dedicated his Ephemerides, to Napier, which were published in the year 1617; and it appears from many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his letter about this time, that he held Napier to be the greatest man of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in the particular department to which he applied his abilities. "And indeed (says our noble biographer), if we consider that Napier's discovery was not like those of Kepler or of Newton, connected with any analogies or coincidences which might have led him to it, but the fruit of unassisted reason and science, we shall be vindicating in placing him in one of the highest niches in the temple of Fame. Kepler had made many unsuccessful attempts to discover his canon for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIODIC">periodic</a> motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon it at last, as he himself candidly owns, on the 15th of May 1618; and Newton applied the palpable tendency of heavy bodies to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to the system of the universe in general; but Napier fought out his admirable rules by a slow scientific progress, arising from the gradual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVOLUTION">evolution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>." The last literary exertion of this eminent person was the publication of his Rhabdology and Promptuary in the year 1617, which he dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SETON">Seton</a>; and soon after died at Merchiston on the 3d of April O.S. of the same year, in the 68th year of his age and 23d of his happy invention.—The particular titles of his works published are: 1. A plain discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> of St John. 2. Mirifici ipsius canonis constructione et logarithmorum, ad naturales ipsorum numeros habitudines. 3. Appendix de alia atque praestantia logarithmorum specie constituenda, in qua faciliter unitas logarithmus est. 4. Rhabdologiae seu numerationis per virgulas libri duo. 5. Propositiones quaedam eminentissime, ad triangula sphaerica mira faciliate resolvenda. To which may be added, 6. His Letter to Anthony <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> (the original of which is in the archbishop's library at Lambeth), entitled, "Secret inventions, profitable and necessary in these days for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and withstanding strangers enemies to God's truth and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>?" which the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Buchan has caused to be printed in the Appendix to his Account of Napier's Writings. This letter is dated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 2, 1596, about which time it appears the author had set himself to explore his logarithmic canon. This eminent person was twice married. By his first wife, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir James Stirling of Keir, he had only one son named Archibald, who succeeded to the estate. By his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife, a daughter of Sir James Chilholm of Cromlix, he had a numerous issue.—Archibald Napier, the only son of the first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, was a person of fine parts and learning. Having more a turn to public business than his father had, he was raised to be a privy counsellor by James VI. under whose reign he also held the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>-depute, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>-clerk, and senator of the college of justice. By Charles I. he was raised to the peerage by the title of Lord Napier. Napier's Rods, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">Bones</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> invented by Baron Napier, whereby the multiplication and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> numbers is much facilitated. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">Construction</a> of Napier's Rods: Suppose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of multiplication to be made upon a plate of metal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, or pasteboard, and then conceive the several columns (ranging downwards from the digits on the head) to be cut asunder; and these are what we call Napier's rods of multiplication. But then there must be a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of each; for as many times as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is in the multiplicand, so many rods of that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> (i.e., with that figure on the top of it) must we have; though six rods of each species will be sufficient for any example in common affairs: there must be also as many rods of o's. But before we explain the way of using these rods, there is another thing to be known, viz. that the figures on every rod are written in an order different from that in the table. Thus the little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> space or division in which the several products of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> are written, is divided into two parts by a line across from the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the lower on the left; and if the product is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIGIT">digit</a>, it is set in the lower division; if it has two places, the first is set in the lower, and the second in the upper division; but the spaces on the top are not divided; also there is a rod of digits, not divided, which is called the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> rod, and of this we need but one single rod. See the figure of all the different rods, and the index, separate from one another, in Plate CCCXLIX. fig. 1. Multiplication by Napier's Rods. First lay down the index rod; then on the right of it set a rod, whose Napier. top is the figure in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the multiplicand; next to this again, let the rod whose top is the next figure of the multiplicand; and so on in order to the first figure. Then is your multiplicand tabulated for all the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> digits; for in the same line of squares standing against every figure of the index rod, you have the product of that figure; and therefore you have no more to do but to transfer the products and sum them. But in taking out these products from the rods, the order in which the figures stand obliges you to a very easy and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> addition; thus, begin to take out the figure in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, or units place, of the square of the first rod on the right; add the figure in the upper part of this rod to that in the lower part of the next, and so on; which may be done as fast as you can look on them. To make this practice as clear as possible, take the following example. Example: To multiply 4768 by 385. Having set the rods together for the number 4768 (fig. 2) against 5 in the index, I find this number, by adding according to the rule, \[ \begin{<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>}{c} - \\ - \\ - \\ \end{array} \] Against 8, this number \[ \begin{array}{c} - \\ - \\ - \\ \end{array} \] Against 3, this number \[ \begin{array}{c} - \\ - \\ - \\ \end{array} \] Total product \[ \begin{array}{c} 1835680 \\ \end{array} \] To make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the rods yet more regular and easy, they are kept in a flat square box, whose breadth is that of ten rods, and the length that of one rod, as thick as to hold six (or as many as you please) the capacity of the box being divided into ten cells, for the different species of rods. When the rods are put up in the box (each species in its own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> distinguished by the first figure of the rod set before it on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the box near the top), as much of every rod stands without the box as shows the first figure of that rod: also upon one of the flat sides without and near the edge, upon the left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the index rod is fixed; and along the foot there is a small ledge; so that the rods when applied are laid upon this side, and supported by the ledge, which makes the practice very easy; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the multiplicand should have more than nine places, that upper face of the box may be made broader. Some make the rods with four different faces, and figures on each for different purposes. Division by Napier's Rods. First tabulate your divisor; then you have it multiplied by all the digits, out of which you may choose such convenient divisors as will be next less to the figures in the dividend, and write the index answering to the quotient, and so continually till the work is done. Thus 2179788, divided by 6123, gives in the quotient 356. Having tabulated the divisor 6123, you see that 6123, cannot be had in 2179; therefore take five places, and on the rods find a number that is equal or next less to 21797, which is 18369; that is, 3 times the divisor; wherefore set 3 in the quotient, and subtract 18369 from the figures above, and there will remain 3428; to which add 8, the next figure of the dividend, and seek again on the rods for it, or the next less, which you will find to be five times; therefore set 5 in the quotient, and subtract 32615 from 34288, and there will remain 3673; to which add 8, the last figure in the dividend, and finding it to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> six times the divisor, set six in the quotient.

NAPLES

Pages 224-235

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, comprehending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> countries of Samnium, Campania, Apulia, and Magna Graecia. It is bounded on all sides by the Mediterranean and Adriatic, except on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east, where it terminates on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> state. Its greatest length from south-east to north-west is about 280 English miles; and its breadth from north-east to south-west, from 96 to 120. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> falls under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> ROME and ITALY; the present state of it, as well as of the rest of Italy, is owing to the conquests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. When that monarch put an end to the kingdom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, he obliged the dukes of Friuli, Spoleto, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEVENTO">Benevento</a>, to acknowledge him as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Italy; but allowed them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the same power and authority which they had enjoyed before his conquest. Of these three dukedoms Benevento was by far the most powerful and extensive, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">Extent</a> of it comprehended almost all the present kingdom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">Duchy</a> Naples; that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of farther <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> beyond the river of Benevento's Savuto and Peto, a few <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> cities in Hither Calabria, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Acripoli, and the promontory in its neighbourhood called Capo di Licio; and lastly, the dukedoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAETA">Gaeta</a>, Naples, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a>, which were very inconsiderable, and extended along the shore only about 100 miles, and were interrupted by the Gaffaldate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>. This flourishing and extensive dukedom was at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> governed by Arechis, who had married one of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Benevento's daughters, the last king of the Lombards, and had submitted, and taken the oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>. However, a few years after, Charles renounced his allegiance to the Franks, declared himself an independent sovereign, and was acknowledged as such by all the inhabitants of his dukedom. To strengthen himself against Pepin king of Italy, who resided at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, he enlarged and fortified the city of Benevento, and likewise built Salerno on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, surrounding it with a very strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wall. He engaged in several wars with the Greeks, whom he sometimes obliged to give him hostages; but having invaded the territories of the pope, whom Pepin could not afflit, Charlemagne was prevailed on to return to Italy. Arechis, unable to oppose such a formidable enemy, sent his eldest son, Romuald, to Rome, with an offer of submission: but, at the instigation of the pope, Charles refused the offer, and detained his son prisoner; after which he ravaged the country, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Capua. Other deputies, however, proved more successful; and, in the year 787, a peace was concluded on these conditions: That Arechis and the Beneventans should renew their allegiance to the Franks; that he should pay a yearly tribute to Pepin; deliver up all his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; and give Charles had no sooner left Italy, than Arechis forgot all his engagements, and began to negotiate with Irene, empress of Constantinople, and her son Constantine, for expelling the Franks out of Italy. For himself, he desired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of patriciate, and the dukedom of Naples with all its dependencies; and, in return, promised to acknowledge the Greek emperor as his sovereign, and to live after the manner of the Greeks. He required, however, to be supported by a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and that his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Adalgisus, son-to Desiderius the last king of the Lombards, should be sent over into Italy, to raise a party among his countrymen. These conditions were readily accepted, on condition that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Romuald should be sent as an hostage; ambassadors were sent to Naples with the ensigns of the Patrician order, namely the mantle of cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, the comb, and the sandals; but before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> could be performed, Prince Romuald died, and soon after him his father; whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was supposed to have been hastened by that of his son. After the death of Arechis, the Beneventans sent a most submissive embassy to Charlemagne, entreating him to send them Grimoald, the late king's son, and only lawful heir to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; threatening at the same time to revolt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their prince was denied them. Charles readily granted their request, and allowed Grimoald to depart, after he had agreed to the following conditions, viz.
