The castle of Saint Elmo commands Naples in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and is in reality calculated rather to annoy and awe the citizens than to defend them from foreign invaders. The city is indeed far from being secure against a bombardment; for the sea is so deep, that a large vessel may come up to the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> in defiance of the blockhouse and batteries, &c. Pictures, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and antiquities, are not so common in Naples as might be expected in so great and ancient a city, many of the most valuable pieces having been sent to Spain by the viceroys. The bay is one of the finest in the world, being almost of a round figure, about 30 miles in diameter, and three parts of it sheltered with a noble circuit of woods and mountains. The city stands in the bow of this bay, in a pleasant situation, perhaps, as is in the world. Mr Keyfley says, they reckon about 18,000 donne libere, or courtezans, in the city; and Dr Moore computes the number of lazzaroni or blackguards at above 30,000. The greater part of these wretches have no dwelling houses, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> every night under porticos, piazzas, or any kind of shelter they can find. Those of them who have wives and children, live in the suburbs of Naples near Pausilippe, in huts, or in caverns or chambers dug out of that mountain. They are generally represented as a lazy, licentious, and turbulent set of people, as indeed by far the greater part of the rabble are, who prefer begging or robbing, or running errands, to any fixed and permanent employment. Yet there are in Naples some flourishing manufactures, particularly of silk flockings, soap, snuff-boxes of tortoise shells and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> of Mount Vesuvius, tables, and ornamental furniture of marble. The city is supplied with a vast quantity of water, by means of a very costly aqueduct, from the foot of Mount Vesuvius. Mr Addison says, it is incredible how great a multitude of retainers to the law there are in Naples, who find continual employment from the fiery temper of the inhabitants. There are five piazzas or squares in the city, appropriated to the nobility, viz. those called Capuana, Nido, Montagna, Porto, and Porta Nova. Of all the palaces, that of the king is not only the most magnificent, but also in the best style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, though Gothic, is a very grand splendid edifice. It is here that the head and blood of St Janarius, the tutelary saint of Naples, are kept, the latter in two glass or crystal vials. The pretended liquefaction of the dried blood, as soon as brought near the head of the saint, is a thing well known; Mr Addison says, it is one of the most bungling tricks he ever <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>. The harbour is spacious, and kept in good repair. It is fortified with a mole, which runs about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> into the sea, and at the extremity has a high lanthorn to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> ships safely into the harbour. Luxury here is restrained by severe sumptuary laws, and the women are more closely confined than in any other city of Italy. Here is an university and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> of arts, the one called Gli Ardenti, and the other Gli Ottici. The nunnery for ladies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is said to be the largest in the whole world, containing no less than 350 nuns, besides servants. The Mount of Piety, or the office for advancing money to the poor, on pledges, at a low interest, or without any, has an income of upwards of 50,000 ducats. The arsenal is said to contain arms for 50,000 men. The walls of the city consist of hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> stones, called piperno. Instead of ice vast quantities of snow are used for cooling their liquors, not so much as water being drank without it; so that, it is said, a scarcity of it would as soon occasion a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> as a dearth of corn or provisions. Certain persons, who <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> the monopoly of it from the government, supply the city all the year round from a mountain about 18 miles off, at so much the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. In the beginning of 1799, it was taken by a body of French troops under General Championet. The streets of this city were lighted for the first time on the 16th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, 1826. Naples stands 110 miles south-east from Rome, 164 north-east from Palermo in Sicily, 217 south-east from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and 300 from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. Long. 14. 20. N. Lat. 40. 55.

NARBO

Pages 235-235

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Volcae Tectosages, called also Narbo Martius, from the Legio Martia, the colony led thither 59 years before the consulate of Caesar, (Velleius); increased with a colony of the Decumanii <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenth legion by Caesar. An ancient trading town on the Atax, which discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> through the Lacus Rubres, or Rubrensis. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">Capital</a> of Gallia Narbonensis; surnamed Colonia Julia Paterna, from Julius Caesar, the father of Augustus by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a>. Now called <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>.

NARBONNE

Pages 235-236

is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of Aude, with an archbishop's see, and is particularly famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. It is seated on a canal cut from the river Aude, which being but three miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, vessels come up it laden with merchandise, which renders Narcissus renders it a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some trade. But though it pretends to the most remote antiquity under the Celtic kings, in ages anterior even to the Roman conquests, which under these latter masters gave its name to all Gallia Narbonensis, and was a colony of the first consideration, it is now dwindled to a wretched solitary town, containing scarce 8000 inhabitants, of whom three fourths are priests and women. The streets and buildings are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and ruinous; it has indeed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the Mediterranean, from which Narbonne is only about three leagues distant, by means of a small river which intersects the place; but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is very limited, and chiefly consists in grain which they export to Cete and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>. No marks of Roman magnificence remain, except several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> in different parts of the city. It is divided into the city and the town, which are joined together by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, with houses on each side, in which the richest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> live. There are several churches and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>; the metropolitan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has a handsome steeple. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 6. N. Lat. 43. 11.

NARCISSUS

Pages 236-236

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the son of the river Cephalus and Liriope the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Oceanus, was a youth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Tireias foretold that he should live till he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself. He despised all the nymphs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and made <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECHO">Echo</a> languish till she became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, by refusing to return her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>: but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> coming weary and fatigued from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, he stopped on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of a fountain to quench his thirst: when, seeing his own form in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, he became so in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with the shadowy image, that he languished till he died. On which the gods, being moved at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, changed him into the flower which bears his name. Narcissus, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 6th order, Spatulacea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NARCOTICS

Pages 236-236

in Medicine, soporiferous drugs, which bring on a stupification. Among narcotics the most eminent are those usually prepared for medicinal uses from the poppy, especially opium; as also all those prepared from mandragora, hyoscyamus, stramonium and datura. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NARDO

Pages 236-236

a pretty populous town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Terra d'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OTRANTO">Otranto</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> and a bishop's see. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 27. N. Lat. 43. 28. In this little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> are 8000 inhabitants. The steeple of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is built in a very uncommon but showy style of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. Luco Giordano and Solimene have adorned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with some agreeable paintings. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Balzo estate. The Aquavivas were the next possessors: they are thought to have come from the Marca di <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>. In 1401, in consideration of their relationship to Pope Boniface IX. Laudillaus erected their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATRI">Atri</a> into a dukedom, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> till then seldom granted to any but princes of the blood <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>. Claudius Aquaviva, a famous general of the Jesuits, who died in 1615, was of this family.

NARDUS

Pages 236-236

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tritandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAMINA">Gramina</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This plant was highly valued by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, both as an article of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and medicine. The unguentum nardinum, was used at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> and feasts as a favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>. Its value is evident from that passage of Scripture, where our Saviour's head was anointed with a box of it, with which Judas found fault. From a passage in Horace it appears that this ointment was so valuable among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, that as much as could be contained in a small box of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was considered as a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessel of wine, and a proper quota for a guest to contribute at an entertainment, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>: Nardo <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VINA">vina</a> mererebe, Nardi parvus onyx eliciet cadum.

NAREA

Pages 236-236

the most southerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> still governed by its own princes, who have the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Beneros. Its territory was formerly more extensive than at present, the Galla having almost quite surrounded it, especially on the south-east and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the west is the most unknown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; the kingdom itself stands like a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the middle of a plain, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and mountainous country. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, rising in the fourth and fifth degrees of north latitude, spread themselves over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> part of the country, and fill it with marshes all the way from south by east to north <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> north-west. These marshes are bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, of which those nearest the marshes are overgrown with coffee trees, the largest, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the only ones, which grow in this country. The kingdom of Narea Proper is interspersed with small, wholesome, but very fertile valleys. The mountainous country of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a> adjoins immediately to Narea, and is said to be governed by a separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; but the Galla having settled themselves in all the flat ground to the very edge of the marshes, have in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with Abyssinia for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> past. The Nareans who inhabit the mountainous country have the lightest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of any people in Abyssinia; but those who inhabit the borders of the marshes are perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and have the features and woolly heads of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>; but the mountaineers of Narea, and much more those of Caffa, are fair complexioned, more so than even the Neapolitans or Sicilians. It is said that snow has been seen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on some of the mountains of Caffa; but Mr Bruce imagines this to be a mistake, and thinks that it must have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>. Narea abounds with cattle, grain, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, both in the high and low country. The medium of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which they sell by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of trade are coarse cotton cloths, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, beads, and incense, which are carried from this country to the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>, and the parts of the African continent towards the Atlantic. The people are exceedingly brave; and though they have been driven out of the low country by multitudes of Galla, they now bid them defiance, and drive them from their frontiers whenever they come too near. The Narean prisoners taken in these skirmishes are sold to the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> at Gondar; and at Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the women are more esteemed than those of any other part of the world. Both sexes have a cheerful kind disposition, and attach themselves inviolably to their masters, if properly treated. The people of Narea and Caffa speak a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> peculiar to themselves.

NARRATION

Pages 236-244

NARRATION, in oratory, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a recital <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rehearsal of a fact as it happened, or as it is supposed to have happened. See ORATORY, No. 26. Concerning NARRATION and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">DESCRIPTION</a> we have the following rules and observations in the Elements of Criticism. 1. The first rule is, That in history the reflections ought to be chaste and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>; for while the mind is intent upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, it is little disposed to the operation of the imagination. STRADA's Belgic History is full of poetical images, which being discordant with the subject, are unpleasant; and they have a still worse effect by giving an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of fiction to a genuine history. Such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> ought to be scattered with a sparing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, even in epic poetry; and at no rate are they proper till the reader be warmed, and by an enlivened imagination be prepared to relish them; in that state of mind, they are agreeable; but while we are sedate and attentive to an historical chain of facts, we reject with disdain every fiction. 2. VIDA, following Horace, recommends a modest commencement of an epic poem; giving for a reason that the writer ought to husband his fire. Besides bold thoughts and figures are never relished till the mind be heated and thoroughly engaged, which is not the reader's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> at the commencement. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> introduces not a single simile in the first book of the Iliad, nor in the first book of the Odyssey. On the other hand, Shakespeare begins one of his plays with a sentiment too bold for the most heated imagination: <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>. Hung be the heav'ns with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, yield <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to night! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">Comets</a>, importing change of times and states, Brandish your crystal tresses in the sky; And with them scourge the bad revolving stars, That have consented unto Henry's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>! Henry the Fifth, too famous to live <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>! England ne'er lost a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of so much worth. First <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> Henry VI. The passage with which Strada begins his history, is too poetical for a subject of that kind; and at any rate too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> for the beginning of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> performance. 3. A third rule or observation is, That where the subject is intended for entertainment solely, not for instruction, a thing ought to be described as it appears, not as it is in reality. In running; for example, the impulse upon the ground is proportioned in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the celerity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; though in appearance it is otherwise, for a person in swift motion seems to skim the ground, and scarcely to touch it. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">VIRGIL</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, describes quick running according to appearance; and raises an image far more lively than by adhering scrupulously to truth: Hos super adventit Volscæa de gente Camilla, Agmen agens equitum, et florentes ære catervas, Bellatrix: non illa colo calathivæ Minervæ Feminææ affluitæ manus; fed prælia virgo Dura pati cursuque pedum, prævertere ventos. Illa vel intactæ legetis per summa volaret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAMINA">Gramina</a>, nec teneras curfu leefifet arilias: Vel mare per medium, fluctu suspensa tumenti, Ferret iter, celestes nec tingeret æquore plantas. Æneid, vii. 803. In narration as well as in description, objects ought to be painted so accurately as to form in the mind of the reader distinct and lively images. Every useless circumstance ought indeed to be suppressed, because every such circumstance loads the narration; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a circumstance be necessary, however slight, it cannot be described too minutely. The force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> consists in raising complete images, which have the effect to transport the reader as by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> into the very <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and to convert him as it were into a spectator, beholding every thing that passes. The narrative in an epic poem ought to rival a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in the liveliness and accuracy of its representations: no circumstance must be omitted that tends to make a complete image; because an imperfect image, as well as any other imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and uninteresting. We shall illustrate this rule by several examples, giving the first place to a beautiful passage from Virgil: Qualis populea merens Philomela sub umbra; Amìsìs queritur fœtus, quos durus arator Observans nido implantes detraxit. Georg., lib. iv. 511. The poplar, ploughman, and unsledged young, though not essential in the description, tend to make a complete image, and upon that account are an embellishment. Again: Hic viridem Æneas frondenti ex ilice metam Constituit, signum nautis. Æneid. v. 129. Horace addressing to Fortune: Te pauper ambit follicita prece Ruris <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONUS">colonus</a>: te dominam sequoris, Quicumque Bithynæ lacessit Carpathium pelagus carinæ. Carm. lib. i. ode 35. — Illum ex moenibus hosticis Matrona bellantis tyranni Prospiciens, et adula virgo, Subspiret: Eheu, ne rudi agminum Sponfus lacessat regius aperum Tactu leonem, quem cruenta Per medias rapit ira caedes. Carm. lib. iii. ode 2. Shakespeare says, "You may as well go about to turn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> by fanning in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s feather." The peacock's feather, not to mention the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the object, completes the image: an accurate image cannot be formed of that fanciful operation, without conceiving a particular feather; and one is at a loss when this is neglected in the description. Again, "The rogues flighted me into the river with as little remorse, as they would have drown'd a bitch's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> puppies, fifteen i' th' litter." Old Lady. You would not be a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. No, not for all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> under heaven. Old Lady. 'Tis strange: a threepence bow'd would hire me, old as I am, to queen it. Henry VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. ii. sc. 5. In the following passage, the action, with all its materi- Narration al circumstances, is represented so much to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, that it would scarce appear more distinct to a real spectator; and it is the manner of description that contributes greatly to the sublimity of the passage— He spoke; and, to confirm his words, out flew Millions of flaming swords, drawn from the thighs Of mighty cherubim; the sudden blaze Far round illumining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>: highly they rag'd Against the Highest, and fierce with grasped arms, Clash'd on their founding shields the din of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, Hurling defiance toward the vault of heav'n. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, book i. The following passage from Shakespeare falls not much short of that now mentioned in particularity of description: 'O you hard hearts! you cruel men of Rome! Knew you not Pompey? Many a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and oft Have you climb'd up to walls and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, To towers and windows, yea, to chimney tops, Your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> in your arms; and there have sat The live-long day with patient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> To see great Pompey <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the streets of Rome; And when you <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his chariot but appear, Have you not made an universal shout, That Tyber trembled underneath his banks, To hear the replication of your sounds, Made in his concave shore? Julius Cæsar, act i. sc. i. The following passage is scarcely inferior to either of those mentioned: "Far before the rest, the son of Offian comes: bright in the smiles of youth, fair as the first beams of the sun. His long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> waves on his back: his dark brow is half beneath his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> hangs loose on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>'s side; and his spear glitters as he moves. I fled from his terrible eye, king of high Temora." Fingal. The Henriade of Voltaire errs greatly against the foregoing rule: every incident is touched in a summary way, without ever descending to circumstances. This manner is good in a general history, the purpose of which is to record important transactions: but in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> it is cold and uninteresting; because it is impracticable to form distinct images of persons or things represented in a manner so superficial. It is observed above, that every useless circumstance ought to be suppressed. The crowding such circumstances is, on the one hand, not less to be avoided, than the conceitens for which Voltaire is blamed, on the other. In the Æneid, Barce, the nurse of Sichæus, whom we never hear of before nor after, is introduced for a purpose not more important than to call <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> to her sister Dido: and that it might not be thought unjust in Dido, even in this trivial circumstance, to prefer her husband's nurse before her own, the poet takes care to inform his reader, that Dido's nurse was dead. To this may be opposed a beautiful passage in the same book, where, after Dido's last speech, the poet, without detaining his readers by describing the manner of her death, hastens to the lamentation of her attendants: Dixerat: atque illam media inter talia ferro Collapsam alpiciunt comites, enfemque cruroe Spurnantem, sparviasque manus. It clamor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTA">alta</a> Atria; concussam baccatur <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANA">sana</a> per urbem; Lamentis gemituque, et femineo ululatu Tecta fremunt, relonat magnis plangoribus aether. Lib. iv. 663. As an appendix to the foregoing rule, may be added the following observation, That to make a sudden and strong <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, some single circumstance, happily selected, has more power than the most laboured description. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, mentioning to his lady some voices he heard while he was murdering the King, says, There's one did laugh in's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and one cry'd <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>! They wak'd each other; and I stood and heard them: But they did say their prayers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> them Again to sleep. Lady. There are two lodg'd together. Macbeth. One cry'd, God blest us! and, Amen! the other; As they had seen me with these hangman's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, Listening their fear. I could not say, Amen, When they did say, God blest us. Lady. Consider it not so deeply. Macbeth. But wherefore could not I pronounce Amen! I had most need of blessing, and Amen Stuck in my throat. Lady. These deeds must not be thought After these ways; so, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make us mad. Macbeth. Methought, I heard a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> cry, Sleep no more! Macbeth doth murder sleep, &c. Act ii. sc. 2. Describing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry: I saw young Harry, with his beaver on, His cuisses on his thighs, gallantly arm'd, Rise from the ground like feather'd <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>; And vaulted with such ease into his seat, As if an angel dropt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, To turn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> a fiery Pegasus, And witch the world with noble <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a>. First part Henry IV. act iii. sc. 3. King Henry. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a>, if thou think'st on Heaven's bliss, Hold up thy hand, make signal of thy hope. He dies, and makes no sign! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> part Henry VI. act iii. sc. 3. The same author, speaking ludicrously of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> debilitated with diseases, says, "Half of them dare not shake the snow from off their caftocks, lest they shake themselves to pieces." "I have seen the walls of Bactriana, but they were defoliate. The flames had resounded in the halls: and the voice of the people is heard no more. The stream of Clutha was removed from its place by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the walls. The thistle shook there its lonely head: the moths whirled to the wind. The fox looked out from the windows: and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> grass of the wall waved round..." round his head. Defolate is the dwelling of Morna: silence is in the houle of her fathers." To draw a character is the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> stroke of description. In this Tacitus excels: his portraits are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and lively, not a feature wanting or misplaced. Shakespeare, however, exceeds Tacitus in liveliness; some characteristic circumstance being generally invented or laid hold of, which paints more to the life than many words. The following instances will explain our meaning, and at the same time prove our observation to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>. "Why should a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, whose blood is warm within, Sit like his grandfathers cut in alabaster? Sleep when he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAKES">wakes</a>, and creep into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>, By being peevish? I tell thee what, Anthonio, (I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> thee, and it is my love that speaks), There are a fort of men, whose villages Do cream and mantle like a standing pond; And do a wilful stillness entertain, With purpose to be dreary in an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> Of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, gravity, profound conceit; As who should say, I am Sir Oracle, And when I ope my lips, let no dog bark! O my Anthonio! I do know of those, That therefore only are reputed wise, For saying nothing." Merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, act i. sc. 1. Again: "Gratiano speaks an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of nothing, more than any man in all Venice: his reasons are two grains of wheat hid in two bushels of chaff; you shall seek all day ere you find them; and when you have them, they are not worth the search." Ibid. In the following passage a character is completed by a single stroke: Shallow. O the mad days that I have spent; and to see how many of mine old acquaintance are dead. Silence. We shall all follow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>. Shallow. Certain, 'tis certain, very sure, very sure; Death (as the Psalmist saith) is certain to all: all shall die. How good a yoke of bullocks at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a> fair? Slender. Truly cousin, I was not there. Shallow. Death is certain. Is old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> of your town living yet? Silence. Dead, Sir. Shallow. Dead! fee, fee: he drew a good bow: and dead. He <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> a fine shot. How a score of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a> now? Silence. Thereafter as they be. A score of good ewes may be worth ten pounds. Shallow. And is old Double dead? Second part Henry IV. act iii. sc. 2. Describing a jealous husband: "Neither press, coffer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, well, vault, but he hath an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of such places, and goes to them by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. There is no hiding you in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>." Merry Wives of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, act iv. sc. 3. Congreve has an inimitable stroke of this kind in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of Love for Love: Ben <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGEND">Legend</a>. Well, father, and how do all at home? how does <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Dick, and brother Val. Vol. XIV. Part II. NARRATION Interea magno misceri murmure pontum, Emifamque hyemem fenit Neptunus, et imis Stagna refusa vadis; graviter commotus, et alto Prospiciens, summa placidum caput extulit unda. *Eneid*, i. 128. Again: When first young Maro, in his boundless mind, A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> t'outlast immortal Rome deg'n'd. *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Criticism*, 30. The following examples are of absurdities. "Alii pulvis è torrente catenis disceptri sectique, dimidiato corpore pugnabant sibi superflites, ac peremptae partes ulteriores." *Strada, Dec.* ii. 2. Il pover huomo, che non fen' era accorto, Andava combattendo, ed era morto. *Berni.* He fled, but <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, left his life behind. *Iliad*, xi. 443. Full through his neck the weighty falchion sped: Along the pavement roll'd the muttering head. *Odyssey*, xxii. 365. The last article is of raving like one mad. Cleopatra speaking to the asp, Welcome, thou kind deceiver; Thou best of thieves; who, with an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>, Dost open life, and unperceived by us Ev'n steal us from ourselves; discharging so Death's dreadful office, better than himself; Touching our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> so gently into slumber, That Death stands by, deceiv'd by his own image, And thinks himself but sleep. *Dryden, All for Love*, act v. Having discussed what observations occurred upon the thoughts or things expressed, we proceed to what more peculiarly concerns the language or verbal drefs. As words are intimately connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> they represent, the emotions raised by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> ought to be concordant. An elevated subject requires an elevated style; what is familiar, ought to be familiarly expressed; a subject that is serious and important, ought to be clothed in plain nervous language; a description, on the other hand, addressed to the imagination, is susceptible of the highest ornaments thatounding words, and figurative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> can bestow upon it. We shall give a few examples of the foregoing rules. A poet of any genius is not apt to dress a high subject in low words; and yet blemishes of that kind are found even in classical works. Horace, observing that men are satisfied with themselves, but seldom with their condition, introduces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> indulging to each his own choice: Jam faciam quod vultis; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERIS">eris</a> tu, qui modo miles, Mercator; tu, consultus modo, rufticus: hinc vos, Vos hinc, mutatis difcedite partibus. eia, Quid? statis? nolint, atqui licet effe beatis. Quid caufa eff, merito quin illis Jupiter ambas Tratus buccas inflet, neque fe fore poft hac Tam facilem dicat, votis ut pribeat aurem? *Sat.*, i. 16. Jupiter in wrath puffing up both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, is a low and even ludicrous expression, far from suitable to the gravity and importance of the subject; every one must feel the discordance. The following couplet, sinking far below the subject, is no less ludicrous: Not one looks backward, onward still he goes, Yet ne'er looks forward farther than his nose. *Essay on Man*, ep. iv. 223. On the other hand, to raise the expression above the tone of the subject, is a fault than which none is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Take the following instances: Orcan le plus fidèle à servir ses desseins, Ne sous le ciel brûlant des plus noirs Africains. *Bajazet*, act iii. sc. 8. Les ombres par trois fois ont obscurci les cieux Depuis que le sommeil n'eft entré dans vos yeux; Et le jour a trois fois chaffé la nuit obscure Depuis que votre corps languit fans nourriture. *Phaedra*, act i. sc. 3. Affueris. Ce mortel, qui montra tant de zèle pour moi, Vit-il encore? *Aph.* —— Il voit l'autre qui vous éclaire. *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a>*, act ii. sc. 3. Oui, c'eft Agamemnon, c'eft ton roi qui teveille; Viens, reconnais la voix qui frappe ton oreille. *Iphigenie.* No jocund <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> drinks to-day, But the great cannon to the clouds hath tell; And the king's rowfe the heav'n shall bruit again, Repealing earthly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>*, act i. sc. 2. In the inner room I spy a winking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>, that weakly strikes The ambient air, scarce kindling into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. *Southerne, Fate of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>*, act iii. In the Funeral Orations of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are raised far above the tone of the subject; "L'Ocean etonné de fe voir traversé tant de fois, en des appareils fi <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, et pour des caufes fi différentes, &c." Pag. 6. "Grande reine, je satisfais à vos plus tendres desirs, quand je célèbre ce monarque; et fon cœur qui n'a jamais vécu que pour lui, s'éveille, tout poudre qu'il est, et devient tendre, même sous ce drap mortuaire, au nom d'un époux fi cher" Pag. 32. The following passage, intended, one would imagine, as a receipt to boil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is altogether <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> by the laboured elevation of the diction: A maffy cauldron of stupendous frame They brought, and plac'd it o'er the rising <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>: Then heap the lighted wood; the flame divides Beneath the vale, and climbs around the sides: In its wide womb they pox the rushing stream: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water bubbles to the brim. *Iliad*, xviii. 405. In a passage at the beginning of the 4th book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>, one feels a sudden bound upward without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, which accords not with the subject: "Calypso," My waking thought admits no balmy rest, Nor the sweet bliss of soft oblivion share: But watchful woe distracts my aching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, My heart the subject of corroding care: From haunts of men with wandering steps and flow I solitary steal, and soothe my pensive woe. Here every substantive is faithfully attended by some tumid epithet. We proceed to a second remark, not less important than the former. No person of reflection but must be sensible, that an incident makes a stronger impression on an eye witness, than when heard at second hand. Writers of genius, sensible that the eye is the best avenue to the heart, represent every thing as passing in our sight; and, from readers or hearers, transform us as it were into spectators: a skilful writer conceals himself, and presents his personages: in a word, every thing becomes dramatic as much as possible. Plutarch, de gloria Atheniensium, observes, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> makes his reader a spectator, and inspires him with the same passions as if he were an eye witness. In the fine arts, it is a rule to put the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> objects in the strongest point of view; and even to present them oftener than once, where it can be done. In history <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and in the best light: an equestrian statue is placed in a centre of streets, that it may be seen from many places at once. In no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is there greater opportunity for this rule than in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>: --- Sequitur pulcherrimus Astur, Astur equo fidens et verficoloribus armis. Eneid, x. 180 --- Full many a lady I've ey'd with beld regard, and many a time Th' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of their tongues hath into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> Brought my too diligent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>: for several virtues Have I lik'd several women: never any With so full <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, but some defect in her Did quarrel with the noblest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> she ow'd, And put it to the foil. But you, O you, So perfect, and so peerless, are created Of every creature's best. Tempest, act iii. sc. i. --- Orlando.—Whate'er you are That, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> inaccessible, Under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of melancholy boughs, Loafe and neglect the creeping hours of time; If ever you have look'd on better days; If ever been where bells have knoll'd to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; If ever sat at any good man's feast: If ever from your eyelids wip'd a tear, And known what 'tis to pity, and be pity'd; Let gentleness my strong enforcement be, In the which hope I blush, and hide my sword. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> sen. True is it that we have seen better days; And have with holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> been knoll'd to church; And sat at good men's feasts; and wip'd our eyes Of drops that sacred pity had engender'd: And therefore sit you down in gentleness, And take upon command what help we have, That to your wanting may be minist'<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. As you like it. With thee conversing I forget all time; All seasons and their change, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> alike. --- The language of Homer is suited to his subject, not less accurately than the actions and sentiments of his heroes are to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. Virgil, in that particular, falls short of perfection: his language is stately throughout; and though he descends at times to the simplest branches of cookery, roasting and boiling for example, yet he never relaxes a moment from the high tone.—In adjusting his language to his subject, no writer equals Swift. We can recollect but one exception, which at the same time is far from being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a>: The Journal of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Lady is composed in a style blending sprightliness with familiarity, perfectly suited to the subject: in one passage, however, the poet, deviating from that style, takes a tone above his subject. The passage we have in view begins l. 116. But let me now a while survey, &c. and ends at l. 135. It is proper to be observed upon this head, that writers of inferior rank are continually upon the stretch to enliven and enforce their subject by exaggeration and superlatives. This unluckily has an effect contrary to what is intended; the reader, disgusted with language that dwells above the subject, is led by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to think more meanly of the subject than it may possibly deserve. A man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, beside, will be no less careful to husband his strength in writing than in walking; a writer, too liberal of superlatives, exhausts his whole stock upon ordinary incidents, and reserves no share to express, with greater energy, matters of importance. Many writers of that kind abound so in epithets, as if poetry consisted entirely in high sounding words. Take the following instance: When black brow'd night her dusky mantle spread, And wrapt in solemn gloom the fable sky; When soothing sleep her opiate dews had shed, And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>'d in silken slumber every eye; --- Calypso, qui avoit été jusqu'à ce moment immobile et transportée de plaisir en écoutant les aventures de Télémaque, l'interrrompt pour lui faire prendre quelque repos. Il est temps, lui dit-elle, que vous alliez goûter la douceur du sommeil après tant de travaux. Vous n'avez rien à craindre ici; tout vous est favorable. Abandonnez vous dorénavant à la joie. Goutez la paix, et tous les autres dons des dieux dont vous allez être comblé. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMAIN">Demain</a>, quand l'Aurore avec ses doigts de rêves entr'ouvrira les portes dorées de l'Orient, et que les chevaux du soleil, sortant de l'onde amère, répandront les flammes du jour, pour chasser devant eux toutes les étoiles du ciel, nous reprendrons, mon cher Télémaque, l'histoire de vos malheurs." This obviously is copied from a similar passage in the Æneid, which ought not to have been copied, because he lies open to the same censure; but the force of authority is great: At <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a> gravi jamdudum saucia cura, Vulnus alti venis, et caeco carpitur igni. Multa viri virtus animo, multique recurvat Gentis honos: haerent infixo pectore vultus, Verbaque: nec placidam membri dat cura quietem. Postera Phœbea lustrabat lampade terras, Humentemque <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLO">polo</a> dimovet umbram; Cum fic unanimem alloquuitur malesca fororem. Lib. iv. 1. --- The language of Homer is suited to his subject, not less accurately than the actions and sentiments of his heroes are to their characters. Virgil, in that particular, falls short of perfection: his language is stately throughout; and though he descends at times to the simplest branches of cookery, roasting and boiling for example, yet he never relaxes a moment from the high tone.—In adjusting his language to his subject, no writer equals Swift. We can recollect but one exception, which at the same time is far from being gross: The Journal of a modern Lady is composed in a style blending sprightliness with familiarity, perfectly suited to the subject: in one passage, however, the poet, deviating from that style, takes a tone above his subject. The passage we have in view begins l. 116. But let me now a while survey, &c. and ends at l. 135. It is proper to be observed upon this head, that writers of inferior rank are continually upon the stretch to enliven and enforce their subject by exaggeration and superlatives. This unluckily has an effect contrary to what is intended; the reader, disgusted with language that dwells above the subject, is led by contrast to think more meanly of the subject than it may possibly deserve. A man of prudence, beside, will be no less careful to husband his strength in writing than in walking; a writer, too liberal of superlatives, exhausts his whole stock upon ordinary incidents, and reserves no share to express, with greater energy, matters of importance. Many writers of that kind abound so in epithets, as if poetry consisted entirely in high sounding words. Take the following instance: When black brow'd night her dusky mantle spread, And wrapt in solemn gloom the fable sky; When soothing sleep her opiate dews had shed, And seal'd in silken slumber every eye; Sweet is the breath of morn, her rising sweet, With <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> of earliest birds; pleasant the sun When first on this delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> he spreads His orient beams on herbs, tree, fruit, and flow'r Glist'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>; fragrant the fertile <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> After soft show'rs; and sweet the coming on Of grateful ev'n'ing mild, the silent night With this her solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, and this fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, And these the gems of heav'n, her starry train: But neither breath of morn, when she ascends With charm of earliest birds, nor rising sun On this delightful land, nor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, fruit, flow'r, Glist'ring with dew, nor fragrance after show'rs, Nor grateful ev'n'ing mild, nor silent night, With this her solemn bird, nor walk by moon, Or glittering <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> light, without thee is sweet. Paradise Lost, book iv. l. 634. "What <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> ye, that ye <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> this proverb, The fathers have eaten four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and the children's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion to use this proverb in Israel. If a man keep my judgements to deal truly, he is just; he shall surely live. But if he be a robber, a shedder of blood: if he have eaten upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and defiled his neighbour's wife: if he have oppressed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and needy, have spoiled by violence, have not restored the pledge, have lifted up his eyes to idols, have given forth upon usury, and have taken increase: shall he live? he shall not live: he shall surely die; and his blood shall be upon him. Now, lo, if he beget a son, that feeth all his father's fins, and considereth, and doth not such like; that hath not eaten upon the mountains, hath not lifted up his eyes to idols, nor defiled his neighbour's wife, hath not oppressed any, nor withheld the pledge, neither hath spoiled by violence, but hath given his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> to the hungry, and covered the naked with a garment: that hath not received usury nor increase, that hath executed my judgements, and walked in my statutes: he shall not die for the iniquity of his father; he shall surely live. The soul that finneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. Have I any pleasure that the wicked should die, saith the Lord God; and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> xvii. A concise comprehensive style is a great ornament in narration; and a superfluity of unnecessary words, not less than of circumstances, a great nuisance. A judicious selection of the striking circumstances, clothed in a nervous style, is delightful. In this style, Tacitus excels all writers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and modern. Instances are numberless: take the following specimen: "Crebra hinc praëlia, et fæpius in modum iatrocinii: per saltus, per paludes; ut cuique fors aut virtus: temere, proviso, ob iram, ob prædam, jussu, et aliquando ignaris ducibus." Annal. lib. xii. § 39. After Tacitus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a> in that respect justly merits the place of distinction. One cannot go wrong for examples in any part of the book. If a concise or nervous style be a beauty, tautology must be a blemish; and yet writers, fettered by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, are not sufficiently careful to avoid this slovenly practice: they may be pitied, but they cannot be justified. Take for a specimen the following instances, from the best poet, for verification at least, that England has to boast of: High on his helm celestial lightnings play, His heavy shield emits a living ray; Th' unwearied blaze incessant streams supplies, Like the red star that fires the autumnal skies. Iliad. 5. Strength and omnipotence invest thy throne. Ibid. 576. So silent fountains, from a rock's tall head, In fable streams soft trickling waters shed. Ibid. ix. 19. His clanging armour rung. Ibid. xii. 94. Fear on their cheek, and horror in their eye. Ibid. xv. 4. The blaze of armour flash'd against the day. Ibid. xvii. 736. As when the piercing blasts of Boreas blow. Ibid. xix. 380. And like the moon, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> resplendent shield Blaz'd with long rays, and gleam'd athwart the field. Ibid. xix. 402. "No—could our swiftness o'er the winds prevail, Or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the pinions of the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">gale</a>, All were in vain— The humid sweat from every pore defends. Ibid. xxiii. 829. We <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> this article with a curious inquiry. An object, however ugly to the sight, is far from being so when represented by colours or by words. What is the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>? With respect to painting, the cause is obvious: a good picture, whatever the subject be, is agreeable by the pleasure we take in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>; and this pleasure overbalancing the disagreeableness of the subject, makes the picture upon the whole agreeable. With respect to the description of an ugly object, the cause follows. To connect individuals in the social state, no particular contributes more than language, by the power it possesses of an expeditious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of thought, and a lively representation of transactions. But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> hath not been satisfied to recommend language by its utility merely: independent of utility, it is made susceptible of many beauties, which are directly felt, without any intervening reflection. And this unfolds the mystery; for the pleasure of language is so great, as in a lively description to overbalance the disagreeableness of the image raised by it. This, however, is no encouragement to choose a disagreeable subject; for the pleasure is incomparably greater where the subject and the description are both of them agreeable. The following description is upon the whole agreeable, though the subject described is in itself dismal: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> times the space that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> day and night To mortal men, he with his horrid crew. Lay Lay vanquished, rolling in the fiery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, Confounded though immortal! but his doom Reserved him to more wrath; for now the thought Both of loft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and lasting pain Torments him: round he throws his baleful eyes That witness'd huge affliction and dismay, Mix'd with obdurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and steadfast hate. At once as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> ken he views The dismal situation waste and wild: A dungeon horrible, on all sides round As one great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> flamed; yet from those flames No light, but rather darknefs visible Serv'd only to discover sights of woe, Regions of sorrow, doleful shades, where peace And rest can never dwell, hope never comes That comes to all; but torture without end Still urges, and a fiery deluge, fed With ever-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sulphur unconsum'd! Such place eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> had prepar'd For those rebellious. *Paradise Lost*, book i. 50. An unmanly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirits in time of danger is not an agreeable sight; and yet a fine description or representation of it will be relished: *K. Richard*. What must the king do now? must he submit? The king shall do it: must he be depos'd? The king shall be contented: must he lose The name of king? o' God's name let it go: I'll give my jewels for a set of beads; My gorgeous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, for a hermitage; My gay apparel, for an almsman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>; My figur'd goblets, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of wood; My sceptre, for a palmer's walking-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>; My subjects, for a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of carved saints; And my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, for a little grave; A little, little, grave,—an obscure grave. Or I'll be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a>'d in the king's highway; Some way of common <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a>, where subjects feet May hourly trample on their sovereign's head; For on my heart they tread now, whilst I live; And, bury'd once, why not upon my head? *Richard II.*, act iii. sc. 6. Objects that strike terror in a spectator, have in poetry and painting a fine effect. The picture, by raising a slight <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> of terror, agitates the mind; and in that condition every beauty makes a deep impression. May not contrast heighten the pleasure, by opposing our present security to the danger of encountering the object represented? The other shape, If shape it might be call'd that shape had none Distinguishable in member, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, or limb; Or substance might be call'd that shadow seem'd, For each seem'd either; black it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> as night, Fierce as ten furies, terrible as hell, And shook a dreadful dart. *Par. Lost*, book ii. 666. Now storming fury rose, And clamour such as heard in heaven till now Was never: arms on armour clashing bray'd Horrible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, and the madding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> Of brazen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> rage; dire was the noise Of conflict; overhead the dismal hiss Of fiery darts in flaming volleys flew, And flying vaulted either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLT">holt</a> with fire. So under fiery cope together rush'd Both battles main, with ruinous assault And unextinguishable rage: all heaven Refounded, and had earth been then, all earth Had to her centre hooke. *Ibid*, book vi. 207. *Ghoft.*—But that I am forbid To tell the secrets of my prison-house, I could a tale unfold, whose lightest word Would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a> up thy soul, freeze thy young blood, Make thy two eyes, like stars start from their spheres, Thy knotty and combined locks to part, And each particular hair to stand on end, Like quills upon the fretful porcupine: But this eternal blazon must not be To ears of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> and blood. *Hamlet*, act i. sc. 8. *Gratiano*. Poor Desdemona! I'm glad thy father's dead: Thy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> was mortal to him; and pure grief Shore his old thread in twain. Did he live now, This fight would make him do a desperate turn: Yea, curse his better angel from his side, And fall to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>. *Othello*, act v. sc. 8. Objects of horror must be excepted from the foregoing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>; for no description, however lively, is sufficient to overbalance the disgust raised even by the idea of such objects. Every thing horrible ought therefore to be avoided in a description. *Narses*, the eunuch who rivalled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELISARIUS">Belisarius</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> under the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, emerged from obscurity A.D. 538. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the palace, and the administration of the private revenue, he was suddenly exalted to the head of an army. He is ranked among the few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> who have refused that unhappy name from the contempt and hatred of mankind. A feeble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> body concealed the soul of a statesman and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>. His youth had been employed in the management of the loom and distaff, in the cares of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and the service of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>; but, while his hands were busy, he secretly exercised the faculties of a vigorous and discerning mind. A stranger to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, he studied in the palace to dissemble, to flatter, and to persuade; and as soon as he approached the person of the emperor, Justinian listened with surprise and pleasure to the manly counsels of his chamberlain and private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>. The talents of Narses were tried and improved in frequent embassies; he led an army into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, acquired a practical knowledge of the war and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and presumed to strive with the genius of Belisarius. Twelve years after his return, the eunuch was chosen to achieve the conquest which had been left imperfect by the first of the Roman generals. Instead of being dazzled by vanity or emulation, he seriously declared, that unless he were armed with an adequate force, he would never consent to risk his own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and that of his sovereign. Justinian granted to the favourite what he might have denied to the hero: the Gothic war was rekindled from its ashes, and the preparations were not unworthy of the ancient majesty of the empire. Narses defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, the Franks, and the Alamanni; Alamanni; the Italian cities opened their gates to the conqueror; he entered the capital in triumph; and having established the seat of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 15 years to govern Italy under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXARCH">Exarch</a>. His virtues, we are told, were stained with avarice; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> reign he accumulated a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver which surpassed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of a private fortune. His government was oppressive or unpopular; and the general discontent was expressed with freedom by the deputies of Rome. Before the throne of Justinian they boldly declared, that their Gothic servitude had been more tolerable than the despotism of a Greek eunuch; and that unless their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> were instantly removed, they would consult their own happiness in the choice of a master. Thus was his disgrace the effect of the people's dissatisfaction; and his death, though in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was unseasonable and premature, since his genius alone could have repaired the last and fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of his life. He died about the year 567, and, as some say, at the advanced age of 95; but this does not appear very probable. See Gibbon's Rom. Hist. vol. iv. 4to edit. p. 194, 208, &c.

NARVA

Pages 244-244

a strong town of the Russian empire, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, with a castle and a harbour. It was taken by the Muscovites from the Danes in 1558, by the Swedes in 1581, and they defeated the Muscovites near it in 1700; but it was retaken by the Russians in 1704 by storm, and the inhabitants sent to Afracan. It is situated on the river Narva, 95 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIBURG">Wiburg</a>, and 172 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29° c. N. Lat. 59° 8'.

NASSAU-SIEGEN

Pages 244-244

a small principality of Germany in the Westerwalde, is in general a mountainous woody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with some arable and pasture ground, and a good breed of cattle. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are chiefly those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, having an iron mine in the neighbourhood of Siegen. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> John the Younger, in 1626, embraced the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and endeavoured to introduce it into the country; but the principality, upon the extinction of the line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>-Siegen in 1743, falling to the line of Nassau-Dietz, and therein to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> of the United Provinces, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> were delivered from their apprehensions of Popish tyranny and bigotry. The prince, on account of these territories, has a seat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> at the diets of the empire and circle in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of princes. His assentment in the matricula for Nassau-Siegen is 773 florins monthly; and towards the maintenance of the chamber judicatory, 50 rixdollars, six kruitzers and a half, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. The revenue of this principality is estimated at 100,000 rixdollars. Nassau-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILLENBURG">Dillenburg</a>, a principality of Germany, situated near the former. It has not much arable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but plenty of wood, good quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, some silver and vitriol, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, with store of iron, for the working and smelting of which there are many forges and founderies in the country; and by these, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of their iron, the inhabitants chiefly subsist. Calvinism is the religion of the principality, which contains five <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and two boroughs, and belongs entirely to William V. prince of Orange, and hereditary stadtholder of the United Provinces, whose father succeeded to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it in 1739 on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Prince Christian, and to the rest in 1743 on the death of Prince William Hyacinth of Siegen. The prince, on account of this principality also and Dietz, has a seat and voice in the college of princes, at the diets of the empire and circle. His assentment in the matricula, for Nassau-Dillenburg, is 102 florins monthly; and to the chamber judicatory, 59 rixdollars six and a half kruitzers, each term. His revenue from this principality is computed at above 130,000 florins. Nassau-Hadamar, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Germany, which, till the year 1711, had princes of its own; but now belongs wholly to William V. prince of Orange. Nassau, prince of Orange. See MAURICE.

NATES

Pages 244-244

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> expressing those two fleshy exterior parts of the body, vulgarly called the buttocks. See ANATOMY. Nates Cerebri, are two circular protuberances of the brain, situated on the back side of the medulla oblongata, near the cerebellum.

NATION

Pages 244-250

a collective <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, used for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people inhabiting a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, confined within fixed limits, and under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. NATIONAL DEBT: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> owing by government. Our limits permit us to give but a very general sketch of this subject: However, as it is of considerable importance to every inhabitant of these kingdoms, we shall endeavour to give as clear and comprehensive a view of it as the bounds necessarily preferred us <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit. In order to this, it may not be improper to refer back to the times that have gone before us, that we may better discover the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of public revenues, the manner of their expenditure, and the causes of public debt. In that rude state of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> which precedes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and the improvements of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, when those expensive luxuries which commerce and manufactures can alone introduce, are altogether unknown; the person who possesses a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> revenue can spend <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enjoy that revenue in no other way than by maintaining nearly as many people as it can maintain. Among our feudal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> during which estates used to continue in the same family, sufficiently demonstrates the general disposition of nations' people to live within their income. Though the rustic hospitality constantly exercised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> landholders may not to us in the present times seem consistent with that order which we are apt to consider as inseparably connected with good economy, yet we must certainly allow them to have been at least so far frugal as not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> to have spent their whole income. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this money, perhaps, they spent in purchasing the few objects of vanity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> with which the circumstances of the times could furnish them; but some part of it they seem commonly to have hoarded. They could not well indeed do any thing else but hoard whatever money they saved. To trade was disgraceful to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>; and to lend money at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, which at that time was considered as usury and prohibited by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, would have been still more so. The same disposition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> and to hoard prevailed in the sovereign as well as in the subjects.
