Among nations to whom commerce and manufactures are little known, the sovereign is in a situation which naturally disposes him to the parsimony requisite for accumulation. In that situation the expense even of a sovereign cannot be directed by that vanity which delights in the gaudy finery of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the times affords but few of the trinkets in which that finery consists. Standing armies are not then necessary; so that the expense even of a sovereign, like that of any other great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, can be employed in scarce anything but bounty to his tenants and hospitality to his retainers. But bounty and hospitality very seldom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to extravagance; though vanity almost always does. All the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sovereigns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> accordingly had treasuries. Every Tartar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> in the present times is said to have one. In a commercial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with every sort of expensive luxury, the sovereign, in the same manner as almost all the great proprietors in his dominions, naturally spends a great part of his revenue in purchasing those luxuries. His own and the neighbouring countries supply him abundantly with all the costly trinkets which compose the splendid but insignificant pageantry of a court. His ordinary expense becomes equal to his ordinary revenue, and it is well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it does not frequently exceed it. The amassing of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> can no longer be expected; and when extraordinary exigencies require extraordinary expenses, he must necessarily call upon his subjects for an extraordinary aid. The late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> and his father are the only great princes of Europe who, since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Henry IV. of France in 1610, are supposed to have amassed any considerable treasure. The parsimony which leads to accumulation has become almost as rare in republican as in monarchical governments. The Italian republics, the United Provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, are all in debt. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> is the single republic in Europe which has amassed any considerable treasure. The other Swiss republics have not. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for some sort of pageantry, for splendid buildings at least and other public ornaments, frequently prevails as much in the apparently sober <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a little republic as in the dilapidated court of the greatest king. The want of parsimony in time of peace imposes the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of contracting debt in time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. When war comes, there is no money in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> but what is necessary for carrying on the ordinary expense of the peace establishment. In war an establishment of three or four times that expense becomes necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the state, and consequently a revenue three or four times greater than the peace revenue. Supposing that the sovereign should have what he scarce ever has, the immediate means of augmenting his revenue in proportion to the augmentation of his expense; yet still the produce of the taxes, from which this increase of revenue must be drawn, will not begin to come into the treasury till perhaps ten or twelve months after they are imposed. But the moment in which war begins, or rather the moment in which it appears likely to begin, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> must be augmented, the fleets must be fitted out, the garrisoned <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> must be put into a posture of defence; that army, that fleet, those garrisoned towns, must be furnished with arms, ammunition, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. An immediate and great expense must be incurred in that moment of immediate danger, which will not wait for the gradual and slow returns of the new taxes. In this exigency government can have no other resources but in borrowing. The same commercial state of society which, by the operation of moral causes brings government in this manner into the necessity of borrowing, produces in the subjects both an ability and an inclination to lend. If it commonly brings along with it the necessity of borrowing, it likewise brings along with it the facility of doing so. A country abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and manufacturers, necessarily abounds with a set of people through whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> not only their own capitals, but the capitals of all those who either lend them money or trust them with goods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> as frequently or more frequently than the revenue of a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who without trade or business lives upon his income, passes through his hands. The revenue of such a man can regularly pass through his hands only once in a year. But the whole amount of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of a merchant who deals in a trade of which the returns are very quick may sometimes pass through his hands two, three, or four times in a year. A country abounding with merchants and manufacturers, therefore, necessarily abounds with a set of people who have it at all times in their power to advance, if they choose to do so, a very large sum of money to government. Hence the ability in the subjects of a commercial state to lend. The progress of the enormous debts which at present oppresses, and will in the long-run probably ruin, Comment all the great nations of Europe, has been pretty uniform. In England, after the Revolution, when new connexions with Europe introduced a new system of foreign politics, the expenses of the nation, not only in settling the new establishment, but in maintaining long wars, as principals, on the continent, for the security of the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, reducing the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, settling the Spanish succession, supporting the house of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, maintaining the liberties of the Germanic body, and other purposes, increased to an unusual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; insomuch that it was not thought advisable to raise all the expenses of any one year by taxes to be levied within that year, lest the unaccustomed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of them should create murmurs among the people. It was therefore the policy of the times to anticipate the revenues of their posterity, by borrowing immense sums for the current <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the state, and to lay no more taxes upon the subject than would suffice to pay the annual interest of the sums so borrowed; by this means converting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> debt into a new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, transferable from one man to another at any time and in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. This system indeed seems to have had its original in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, A.D. 1344; which government then owed about 60,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; and being unable to pay it, formed the principal into an aggregate sum, called metaphorically a mount or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, the shares whereof were transferable like our stocks, with interest at per cent, the prices varying according to the exigencies of the state. This laid the foundation of what is called the national debt; for a few long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> created in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. will hardly deserve that name. Nations, like private men, have generally begun to borrow upon what may be called personal credit, without affixing or mortgaging any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the payment of the debt; and when this resource has failed them, they have gone on to borrow upon assignments or mortgages of particular funds. What is called the unfunded debt of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is contracted in the former of those two ways. It consists partly in a debt which bears, or is supposed to bear, no interest, and which resembles the debts that a private man contracts upon account; and partly in a debt which bears interest, and which resembles what a private man contracts upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> or promissory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. The debts which are due either for extraordinary services, or for services either not provided for or not paid at the time when they are performed; part of the extraordinary expenses of the army, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, and ordnance, the arrears of subsidies to foreign princes, those of seamen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, &c., usually constitute a debt of the first kind. Navy and exchequer bills, which are issued sometimes in payment of a part of such debts, and sometimes for other purposes, constitute a debt of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind; exchequer bills <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> interest from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which they are issued, and navy bills six months after they are issued. The Bank of England, either by voluntarily discounting those bills at their current value, or by agreeing with government for certain considerations to circulate exchequer bills, that is, to receive them at par, paying the interest which happens to be due upon them, keeps up their value, and facilitates their circulation, and thereby frequently enables government to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> a very large debt of this kind. During the great reconnoitre in King William's time, when the bank of England thought proper to put a stop to its usual transactions, exchequer bills and tallies are said to have sold from 25 to 60 per cent. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a>; owing partly, no doubt, to the supposed instability of the new government established by the Revolution, but partly too to the want of the support of the bank of England. When this resource is exhausted, and it becomes necessary, in order to raise money, to assign or mortgage some particular branch of the public revenue for the payment of the debt, government has upon different occasions done this in two different ways. Sometimes it has made this assignment or mortgage for a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of time only, a year or a few years, for example; and sometimes for perpetuity. In the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the fund was supposed sufficient to pay within the limited time both principal and interest of the money borrowed; in the other, it was supposed sufficient to pay the interest only, or a perpetual annuity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the interest; government being at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to redeem at any time this annuity upon paying back the principal sum borrowed. When money was raised in the one way, it was said to be raised by anticipation; when in the other, by perpetual funding, or, more shortly, by funding. In the reign of King William, when the debt began to be amassed, and during a great part of that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, before we had become so familiar as we are now with the practice of perpetual funding, the greater part of the new taxes were imposed but for a short period of time (for four, five, six, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years only), and a great part of the grants of every year consisted in loans upon anticipation of the produce of those taxes. The produce being frequently insufficient for paying within the limited term the principal and interest of the money borrowed, deficiencies arose to make good which it became necessary to prolong the term. On the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1697, the funded and unfunded debts amounted to £21,515,742l. 13s. 8½d.; at the same time, in 1714, they were £33,681,076l. 5s. 6½d. In 1755, before the breaking out of the war, they amounted to £29,289,673l.; and on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1763, at the conclusion of the peace, they had accumulated to £122,603,336l. 8s. 2½d. of funded debt, and of unfunded £3,027,589l. 2s. 2½d. more. In 1775, they were very nearly 130 millions; and the last American war added upwards of 120 millions more to that enormous sum: to pay the interest of which, and the charges of management, amounting annually to nearly eight millions and a half, the extraordinary revenues elsewhere enumerated * (excepting only the land-tax and annual malt-tax) are in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> mortgaged and made perpetual by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Perpetual we say; but still redeemable by the same authority that imposed them: which, if at any time can pay off the capital, will abolish those taxes which are raised to discharge the interest. By this means, then, the quantity of property in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is greatly increased in idea compared with former times; yet, if we coolly consider it, not at all increased in reality. We may boast of large fortunes, and quantities of money in the funds. But where does this money exist? It exists only in name, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in parliamentary security: and that is undoubtedly sufficient for the creditors of the public to rely on. But then what is the pledge which the public faith has pawned for the security of these debts? The land, the trade, and the personal industry of the subject; from which the money must arise that supplies the several taxes. In these, therefore, and these only, the property of the public creditors does really and intrinsically exist; and of course the land, the trade, and the personal industry of individuals, are diminished in their true value <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> so much as they are pledged to answer. If A's income amounts to 100l. per annum; and he is so far indebted to B, that he pays him 50l. per annum for his interest; one half of the value of A's property is transferred to B the creditor. The creditor's property exists in the demand which he has upon the debtor, and nowhere else; and the debtor is only a trustee to his creditor for one half of the value of his income. In short, the property of a creditor of the public consists in a certain portion of the national taxes; by how much therefore he is the richer, by so much the nation, which pays these taxes, is the poorer. The only advantage that can result to a nation from public debts, is the increase of circulation, by multiplying the cash of the kingdom, and creating a new species of currency, assignable at any time and in any quantity; always therefore ready to be employed in any beneficial undertaking, by means of this its transferable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and yet producing some profit even when National when it lies idle and unemployed. A certain proportion of debt seems to be highly useful to a trading people; but what that proportion is, it is not for us to determine. This much is indubitably certain, that the present magnitude of our national encumbrances very far exceeds all calculations of commercial benefit, and is productive of the greatest inconveniences. For, first, The enormous taxes that are raised upon the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for the payment of the interest of this debt, are a hurt both to trade and manufactures, by raising the price as well of the artificer's subsistence as of the raw material, and of course, in a much greater proportion, the price of the commodity itself. Nay, the very increase of paper circulation itself, when extended beyond what is requisite for commerce or foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tendency to increase the price of provisions as well as of all other merchandise. For as its effect is to multiply the cash of the kingdom, and this to such an extent that much must remain unemployed, that cash (which is the universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the respective values of all other commodities) must necessarily sink in its own value, and everything grow comparatively dearer. Secondly, If part of this debt be owing to foreigners, either they draw out of the kingdom annually a considerable quantity of specie for the interest; or else it is made an argument to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them unreasonable privileges in order to reduce them to reside here. Thirdly, If the whole be owing to subjects only, it is then charging the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and industrious subject, who pays his share of the taxes to maintain the indolent and idle creditor who receives them. Lastly, and principally, It weakens the internal strength of a state, by anticipating those resources which should be reserved to defend it in case of necessity. The interest we now pay for our debts would undoubtedly be sufficient to maintain the most vigorous war that any national motives could possibly require. If indeed our ancestors in King William's time had annually paid, so long as their exigencies lasted, a far less sum than we now annually raise upon their accounts, they would not in time of war have borne so great burdens as they have bequeathed to and settled upon their posterity in time of peace; and might have been eased the instant the exigence was over. On the whole, then, the national debt is undoubtedly a subject of vast importance, and as such it has been always considered; for much has been said and written upon it, and many schemes have been proposed at various times and by various persons for gradually removing it, it being considered by the most judicious as a most pernicious encumbrance to a commercial country. Some, we are aware, think it of vast utility; but this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is too eccentric, and in our estimation too feebly supported, to be convincing. The public debt is indubitably a great grievance; and every lover of his country must surely wish to see it removed: the period, however, when this blessing shall take place, if indeed it ever arrive, must at least be very distant. We refer such as will, for farther information on this interesting topic to those who have treated of it at full length, as Smith in his Wealth of Nations, and Sir John Sinclair in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Revenue. The writings of Dr Price likewise deserve considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, especially as one of his plans for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the debt has in fact been adopted, and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> established, by the legislature: His three plans may be found in a pamphlet by William Morgan, entitled, A Review of Dr Price's Writings on the Subject of the Finances of this Kingdom. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATAL">Natal</a> day, the day of a person's birth. The word nativity is chiefly used in speaking of the saints; as, the nativity of St John the Baptist, &c. But when we say the Nativity, it is understood of that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, or the feast of Christmas. Nativity, nativitas, in ancient law books, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> or servitude. Nativity, in Astrology, the theme or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the heavens, and particularly of the twelve houses, at the moment when a person was born; called also the horoscope. Casting the nativity, or by calculation seeking to know how long the queen should live, &c. was made felony, an. 23 Eliz. c. 2. Nativo habendo, in Law, a writ directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, for a lord who claimed inheritance in any villain, when a villain was run away from him, for the apprehending and restoring him to the lord. Nativix, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural History</a>, a name given by some old writers to the nerita. Natalia, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name of the Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, being the most westerly part of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Asia, and consisting of a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, which extends from the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> as far as the Archipelago, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Marmora, the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLIPOLI">Gallipoli</a> and of Constantinople, which separate it from Europe on the west. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Sea, and on the south by the Mediterranean. Natrix, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-snake, called also torquata, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> about its neck. See Ophiology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Natrum, or Natron, the nitre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, one of the fixed alkalis. See Soda, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. It is found in great abundance in many parts of Asia, where the natives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> it up from the surface of the ground, and call it <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The earliest account we have of it is in the Scriptures, where we find that the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> called nitre in those times would ferment with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and possessed a detergent quality, so that it was used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> and in washing. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> compares the flinging of fongs with a heavy heart, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> of vinegar and nitre; and Jeremiah says, that if the finer wash himself with nitre, his sin is not cleansed off. These are properties that perfectly agree with this salt, but not at all with our <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, which is the nitre of the moderns. Natter-Jack, a species of Rana, which see, Herpetology Index. Natural, in general, something that relates to nature. See Nature. Natural Children, are those born out of lawful wedlock. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">Bastard</a>. Natural Functions, are those actions whereby the aliment are changed and assimilated so as to become a part of the body. Natural, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is used where animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. are blazoned with the colours they naturally have, though different from the common colours. of heraldry; and this is to prevent their armories being accused of falsity, when blazoned with the names of colours unknown in heraldry. **Natural Note**, in Music, is used in opposition to flat and sharp notes, which are called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> notes. See Note, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">Scale</a>, &c. **Natural** is also used; or something coming immediately out of the hands of nature; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to factitious or artificial, which signifies something wrought by art. See Artificial. Bishop Wilkins observes, that there appears a world of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between natural and artificial things, when viewed with microscopes. The first ever appear adorned with all imaginable elegance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; the latter, though the most curious in their kind, infinitely rude and unshewn: the finest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> appears a rough <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and the most accurate engraving or embossment, as if done with a mattock or a trowel. **Natural Beauty**, or the beauty of natural objects, is that quality or those qualities in the works of nature, or more properly of God, which are calculated to excite pleasing sensations in the minds of all such persons of true taste as attentively observe them. It will not, we trust, be deemed improper or impertinent, therefore, to introduce a few observations on this subject, previous to our treating of natural history.—To many, it is hoped, it will appear to be a very proper introduction to that important article. "That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> to beauty, which, when cultivated and improved, we term taste, is universally diffused through the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> species; and it is most uniform with respect to those objects, which being out of our power, are not liable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from accident, caprice, or fashion. The verdant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, the shady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, the variegated landscape, the boundless ocean, and the starry firmament, are contemplated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> by every attentive beholder. But the emotions of different spectators, though similar in kind, differ widely in degree; and to relish with full delight the enchanting scenes of nature, the mind must be uncorrupted by avarice, sensuality, or ambition; quick in her sensibilities; elevated in her sentiments; and devout in her affections. He who possesses such exalted powers of perception and enjoyment, may almost say, with the poet, I care not, Fortune! what you me deny; You cannot rob me of free Nature's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; You cannot shut the windows of the sky, Through which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> shows her bright'ning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>; You cannot bar my confident feet to trace The woods and lawns, by living stream, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>: Let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> my nerves and finer fibres brace, And I their toys to the great children leave: Of fancy, reason, virtue, nought can me bereave. "Perhaps such ardent enthusiasm may not be compatible with the necessary toils and active offices which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> has assigned to the generality of men. But there are none to whom some portion of it may not prove advantageous; and if it were cherished by each individual, in that degree which is consistent with the indispensable duties of his station, the felicity of human life would be considerably augmented. From this source, the refined and vivid pleasures of the imagination are almost entirely derived; and the elegant arts owe their choicest beauties to a taste for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of nature. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> are express imitations of visible objects; and where would be the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, if divested of the imagery and embellishments which the borrow from rural scenes? Painters, statuaries, and poets, therefore, are always ambitious to acknowledge themselves the pupil of nature; and as their skill increases, they grow more and more delighted with every view of the animal and vegetable world. But the pleasure resulting from admiration is transient; and to cultivate taste, without regard to its influence on the passions and affections, 'is to rear a tree for its blossoms, which is capable of yielding the richest and most valuable fruit.' Physical and moral beauty bear so intimate a relation to each other, that they may be considered as different gradations in the scale of excellence; and the knowledge and relish of the former should be deemed only a step to the nobler and more permanent enjoyments of the latter. "Whoever has visited the Leasowes, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, must have felt the force and propriety of an inscription which meets the eye at the entrance into those delightful grounds. Would you then taste the tranquil <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>? Be sure your bosoms be serene: Devoid of hate, devoid of strife, Devoid of all that poisons life: And much it vails you, in their place, To graft the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. "Now such scenes contribute powerfully to inspire that serenity which is necessary to enjoy and to heighten their beauties. By a secret contagion, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> catches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> which she contemplates; and, the frame within assimilates itself to that which is without. For, Who can forbear to smile with Nature? Can The florid passions in the bosom roll, While every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">gale</a> is peace, and every grove Is <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>? "In this state of sweet composure, we become susceptible of virtuous impressions, from almost every surrounding object. The patient ox is viewed with generous complacency; the guileless sheep with pity; and the playful lamb raises emotions of tenderness and love. We rejoice with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, in his liberty and exemption from toil, while he ranges at large through enamelled pastures; and the frolics of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLT">colt</a> would afford unmixed delight, did we not recollect the bondage which he is soon to undergo. We are charmed with the song of birds, foamed with the buzz of insects, and pleased with the sportive motions of fishes, because these are expressions of enjoyment; and we exult in the felicity of the whole animated <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. Thus an equal and extensive benevolence is called forth into exertion; and having felt a common interest in the gratifications of inferior beings, we shall be no longer indifferent to their sufferings, or become wantonly instrumental in producing them. "It seems to be the intention of Providence, that the lower order of animals should be subservient to the comfort, convenience, and sustenance of man. But his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of dominion extends no farther; and if this right be exercised with mildness, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the subjects of his power will be no less benefi- For various species of living creatures are annually multiplied by human art, improved in their perceptive powers by human culture, and plentifully fed by human industry. The relation, therefore, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> between such animals and man; and he may supply his own wants by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their labour, the produce of their bodies, and even the sacrifice of their lives, whilst he co-operates with all-gracious Heaven in promoting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, the great end of existence. "But though it be true, that partial evil, with respect to different orders of sensitive beings, may be universal good; and that it is a wise and benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of nature, to make destruction itself, within certain limitations, the cause of an increase of life and enjoyment; yet a generous person will extend his compassionate regards to every individual that suffers for his sake: and whilst he sighs Even for the kid or lamb that parts its life Beneath the bloody <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, he will naturally be solicitous to mitigate pain, both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and degree, by the gentlest modes of inflicting it. "We are inclined to believe, however, that this sense of humanity would soon be obliterated, and that the heart would grow callous to every soft <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, were it not for the benignant influence of the smiling face of nature. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Lauzun, when imprisoned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in the castle of Pignerol, amused himself during a long period of time with catching flies, and delivering them to be devoured by a rapacious spider. Such an entertainment was equally singular and cruel; and inconsequent, we believe, with his former character, and his subsequent turn of mind. But his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> had no window, and received only a glimmering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from an aperture in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. In less unfavourable circumstances, may we not presume, that instead of sporting with misery, he would have released the agonizing flies, and bid them enjoy that freedom of which he himself was bereaved? "But the taste for natural beauty is subservient to higher purposes than those which have been enumerated; and the cultivation of it not only refines and humanizes, but dignifies and exalts the affections. It elevates them to the admiration and love of that Being who is the author of all that is fair, sublime, and good in the creation. Scepticism and irreligion are hardly compatible with the sensibility of heart which arises from a just and lively relish of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, harmony, and order subsisting in the world around us: and emotions of piety must <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up spontaneously in the bosom that is in unison with all animated nature. Actuated by this divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, man finds a fane in every grove; and, glowing with devout fervour, he joins his song to the universal chorus, or mutes the praise of the Almighty, in more expressive silence. Thus they "Whom Nature's works can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, with God himself Hold <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>: grow familiar, day by day, With his conceptions; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; And form to his the relish of their souls." On the whole then, it certainly appears, that the advantages resulting from a taste for natural beauties are great and important: it is equally certain, that as it is useful, so it is a continual source of real enjoyment; for a more rational pleasure cannot possibly occupy the attention or captivate the affections of mankind, than that which arises from a due consideration of the works of nature. Pleasure, we know, is a necessary ingredient in human life, in order to some measure to counterbalance the pains, the evils, and little necessities, which are at times perhaps unavoidable, and in order to render life tolerable. It is the part then of the moralist, and it has been frequently his business, to point out and recommend such pleasures as are highly gratifying, and are yet perfectly innocent. The Spectator, whose works will be admired as long as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in which they are written is understood, recommends strongly and elegantly the pleasure of a garden; and a later writer, of no common degree of merit, and of very considerable fame, has an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on Dr Knox, the same subject, from which we shall select a few observations, and to conclude the article. "Not he alone (says this elegant writer) is to be esteemed a benefactor to mankind, who makes an useful discovery; but he also who can point out and recommend an innocent pleasure. Of this kind are the pleasures arising from the observation of nature; and they are highly agreeable to every taste uncorrupted by vicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. Rural scenes of almost every kind are delightful to the mind of man. But the misfortune is, that the greater part are hurried on in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of life with too great rapidity to be able to give attention to that which solicits no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The darkest habitation in the dirtiest street of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, where money can be earned, has greater charms with many than the groves of Hagley. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of refined pleasure, the elegant Epicurus, fixed the seat of his enjoyment in a garden. He was of opinion, that a tranquil spot, furnished with the united sweets of art and nature, was the best adapted to delicate repose. And even the severer philosophers of antiquity were wont to discourse in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of a spreading tree, in some cultivated plantation. It is obvious, on intuition, that nature often intended solely to please the eye in her vegetable productions. She decorates the flowery that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> beneath our feet in all the perfections of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> beauty. She has clothed the garden with a constant succession of various hues. Even the leaves of the tree undergo a pleasing vicissitude. The fresh verdure which they exhibit in the spring, the various shades which they assume in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and russet tinge of autumn, and the nakedness of winter, afford a constant pleasure to a lively imagination. From the snowdrop to the moss rose, the flower garden displays an infinite variety of shape and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The taste of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIST">florist</a> has been ridiculed as trifling; yet surely without reason. Did nature bring forth the tulip and the lily, the rose and the honeyuckle, to be neglected by the haughty pretender to superior reason? To omit a single social duty for the cultivation of a polyanthus were ridiculous as well as criminal; but to pass by the beauties lavished before us, without observing them, is no less ingratitude than stupidity. A bad heart finds little amusement but in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the active world, where scope is given for the indulgence of malignancy." malignant passions; but an amiable disposition is commonly known by a taste for the beauties of the animal and the vegetable creation." In short, since the world was made for our use, since the beauties of nature are alike displayed before all men, and since they are unquestionably an inexhaustible fund of innocent amusement; that subject must be of vast importance which enables us to relish them properly.

NATURAL HISTORY

Pages 257-263

Objects and only the knowledge of the distinctive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of utility of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and he who knows the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and is most accurate in determining the different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, is accounted the best botanist. This however constitutes but a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the science; there is another distinct department, which may properly be termed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, which is both more interesting and more useful. This includes the knowledge of the structure, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the anatomy of plants; and the knowledge of the uses, or functions of their various parts, as of the leaves, the bark, the pith, the roots, the juices, &c.; which is called the physiology of plants. It includes also an acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> adapted to different vegetables, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of propagation, and the various uses to which their several parts or productions may be applied. Botany, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, which may be called practical botany, is sublative, and absolutely necessary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the philosophy of botany; for no one that is unacquainted with the classification of plants can either convey to others his own information, or himself receive the benefit of that of others, respecting either the structure and economy, or the habits and the uses of such plants, as may have been investigated. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> medical virtues are discovered in any vegetable production; without the accuracy of the practical botanist, to ascertain and describe the particular plant which affords it, the discovery is often lost; or perhaps, what is worse, the virtues are attributed to a different plant, and it is only by repeated failures, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> after much mischief, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> is detected. It is evident that the same may happen to the agriculturist, the dyer, or any other artizan, who has discovered in the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> the means of improving his art, but has not botanical knowledge sufficient to give an accurate character of the plant, to which he is indebted for his discovery. 3. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the mineral kingdom, almost half the students are of that class, who content themselves with collecting, and being able to arrange systematically the minerals they meet with. But in this department of natural history, as well as the other two, which we have considered, something more than arrangement is required. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who can analyze, and separate the component parts of mineral productions; who knows the art of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a>, and who knows a priori the probable site of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, or a mine, and can tell the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a stratum of coal, or of marble, that we may call a mineralogist. The natural history of the mineral kingdom includes <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">geology</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATA">data</a> upon which are founded the different theories of the formation of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It includes the knowledge of those facts, upon which the art of mining, and the art of separating and purifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, is founded; and its object is to teach likewise the properties of those metals, as well as of the earths, and other mineral productions, when separated and in their simple state. With respect to the utility of the study of natural history, we have unavoidably given many instances of it, in considering the object of the science. We need therefore add but few others. The grazier knows the advantage of attending to the objects and habits and distinctive marks of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals. It is natural history, though not often studied scientifically, that teaches him what variety of sheep to prefer; by what means to obtain a variety of cows, remarkable for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; how to choose the stock to the best adapted to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and what is the best food for them during winter. Much benefit is likely to accrue from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> lately paid to the cultivation of what are termed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> grasses. Instead of sowing his hay feeds indiscriminately, the grazier may select only such grasses as are, by observation, found to be most suited to his soil and cattle. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>'s knowledge of the proper succession of crops, the best times for sowing them, when to weed, and with what to manure, as well as how to destroy both weeds and insects, is the knowledge of a naturalist; and surely he, who is scientifically acquainted with the growth of plants, knowing what part the soil acts in vegetation, and what is the aliment most required by them, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> empirical farmer, who has no better reason for what he does, than that his father did the same before him. By studying the natural history of insects, we learn the habits of such as are noxious and injurious, and thence derive the means of destroying them. The mineralogist has often enriched individual proprietors of land, and benefited his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, by the discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; he is enabled to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the planners of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> by warning them of obstructions; and his knowledge has aided the physician in ascertaining the virtues of minerals, and of mineral waters. In the arts, a knowledge of natural history prevents that confusion, and those innumerable errors that must be committed, when the natural productions which are employed cannot be accurately discriminated from others. It is to the naturalist that we are many times indebted for the introduction of foreign animals and foreign plants into our own country. Wheat, oats, barley, and other vegetables, which are now become necessary to our existence, were not originally of British growth. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>, now so general and so useful, was first introduced into this country by Gerard, a noted botanist, and was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> cultivated in his garden as a rarity. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit tree, the farinaceous palms, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, have all been transported by naturalists of the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to regions where they never grew before. Besides the above, and many similar instances of advantage to be derived from studying the different branches of natural history, these two incalculable benefits necessarily arise to the student himself, from attending to the whole, or any part of the science; namely, a power of abrading the mind, and reasoning methodically; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of contemplating the Creator in his works*: Our limits do not permit us to enter further into the fertile topic of the utility and advantages of natural history. Its utility, in a moral and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> point of view, has been ably illustrated by Mr Ray, in his "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> of God;" by Mr Bingley, in the introduction Mode of preserving specimens. Art of preserving specimens. III. We have stated it to be one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects of natural history, to teach the mode of preserving specimens. This art, called by the French Taxidermie, is exceedingly curious, and would well deserve a much fuller consideration than we can here allot to it. We shall confine our attention on this subject entirely to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal kingdom</a>, and even here we must be very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>. The art of preparing and mounting the skins of animals appears to be pretty old; but it made no great progress before the 17th century, when Reaumur made some attempts to preserve the specimens from the attacks of insects. In the Journal de Physique for 1773, there is a memoir addressed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, by M. Kuckhan, on the methods of preparing birds, which is very curious, but is liable to many objections. In the same volume is a memoir by Mauduit, principally respecting the means of preserving animal specimens from the attacks of insects. His preservatives are of a poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and, of course, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is dangerous, while they do not appear to have been attended with the expected success. The arsenical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> of Becquer, much celebrated about the same time, is liable to similar objections. The latest, and probably the best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on this subject, is that published a few years ago by M. Nicolas; and from this the following observations are derived. The instruments employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of specimens are much the same as those used by anatomists in their ordinary dissections, consisting of small knives or scalpels, forceps or pincers of various forms, probes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, and pins or wires. The preservatives employed by M. Nicolas to protect the specimen from insects, are principally of two kinds: 1. Sulphur, which he applies to the skins by means of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUMIGATION">fumigation</a>, thus impregnating them with fulphurous acid; 2. A liquor for macerating the skins, another liquor for rubbing over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and a pomatum for anointing the inside of the skin. The first liquor is prepared by steeping a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> and a half of powdered oak bark, and four ounces of powdered <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, in twenty English pints of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, for two days, taking care to shake the mixture from time to time.—The pomatum is prepared of a pound of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> soap, half a pound of caustic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, four ounces of powdered alum, two English pints of water, four ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a>, and the same of camphire. The soap, cut into small pieces, is put into an earthen pipkin, over a moderate fire; the water poured over it; and when the whole is formed into a sort of soft paste, the alum and then the oil are added; the whole well stirred together, removed from the fire, and when it is nearly cold the camphire is added, being before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> rubbed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> with a little spirit of wine. The pomatum, thus prepared, must be kept in glass vessels, well stopp'd; and, when used, is to be lowered with water to the consistence of thin cream, and laid on the skins by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. The liquor employed for preserving the fur is prepared by infusing an ounce of white soap three very small, two ounces of camphire broken into very small pieces, the same of colocynth or bitter-apple grossly powdered, in two English pints of spirit of wine, for four or five days, shaking the vessel from time to time, after which the liquor is to be filtered through blotting-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. M. Nicolas has given directions for preparing and preserving specimens of all the various classes of animals. We shall, as far as our limits permit, briefly follow him through each. In skinning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, he proposes to make an incision along the middle of the back, from the haunches to the shoulders, except in those animals whose skin is very thick and hard, or is fet with spines, in which the opening must be made at the belly in the usual manner. In detaching the skin from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, we must occasionally employ the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and as we proceed, must insert tow between the skin and flesh, to prevent foiling the fur. When the whole body is detached, and the skin drawn down as far as the ankles, the nose, and the tip of the tail, the whole body is to be cut away except the head and extremities, which are left to give a better form and support to the specimen. All the fleshy and fatty parts, the brain, and the eyes, however, must be cut away, and nothing left but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, the spaces between which and the skin must be stuffed with tow cut fine, and a little soft clay must be put within the orbits, in order to fix the artificial eyes. Before stuffing, the skin is to be steeped for several days, from five to fifteen, according to the size of the animal, in the liquor first described, and after steeping, the inside is to be well anointed with the pomatum. When the legs and head are stuffed, the cavity of the skull filled with very dry moss, and the eyes fixed, wires are to be passed through the inside of the body, the extremities, and the head and tail, in the following manner. Three <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wires of a moderate size, well annealed, at least twice as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the animal, are to be twisted together for nearly half their length, and while one wire is left straight, the other two are to be bent at each end, so as to form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. When the skin is turned, ready for stuffing, these wires are to be placed within it in such a manner as that the straight wire shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the head and tail, and the crooking wires through the extremities, coming out at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of each foot; and in this way after the cavity is filled up with tow, and the open part neatly stitched, the specimen may be fixed on a board in its natural position. Nothing remains now but to impregnate the fur with the bitter liquor last described, which is done by means of a sponge, with which the whole outside is to be well washed, then covered with folds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. The art of preserving birds is perhaps the most curious part of the present subject, and is that to which the most attention has been given. M. Nicolas has explained at some length the mode recommended by M. Kuckhan in the Journal de Physique; that by Dr Letton, in the Naturalist's and Traveller's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">Companion</a>; that of Mauduit, inserted in the fifth number of the Encyclopédie Methodique; and that of Dufresne, adopted by M. Daudin, and inserted in his Traité d'Ornithologie; after which he details his own. He describes three methods of preparing birds, according as we can procure fresh-killed specimens, whole dried skins brought from abroad, or detached parts of feathers. Mode of preserving specimens. We shall here confine ourselves to the first of these, as being best adapted to the generality of our readers. When a fresh-killed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> is procured, it is to be placed upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, upon its back, with the tail turned towards the operator, who, after having separated with his fingers the feathers which cover the belly towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left, is to make with a scalpel, a longitudinal incision through the skin, from the point of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>-bone to about the middle of the belly. The edges of the skin are now to be raised with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of flat pincers, on each side, carefully separating the flesh as occasion may require, by the knife, and inserting a little cotton from time to time, to prevent foiling the feathers. In this way the skin is to be detached from the shoulders and neck, and as much as possible of the body laid bare, after which a pretty strong thread is to be passed through the nostrils, and tied under the lower mandible, leaving the ends of the thread when tied together, at least twice as long as the neck. Now, holding the bird by the thread, with the back turned towards him, the operator is to hold together the feathers on the two edges of the incision as well as those that cover the breast, and pushing the head of the bird inwards with his thumb so as to form the neck into an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, is to cut this off near the body, detach from it the gullet and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-pipe, and all the fleshy parts, both of the neck and head, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the skin as far back as possible towards the beak, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the neck-bones <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the head; he is to empty the skull with a little iron <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-picker, and clean it properly with cotton. He is now to wrap cotton or tow about the head and neck, and to separate the rest of the skin, leaving the pinions and bones of the wings, legs, and the tail, as directed for quadrupeds. After this has been done, the skin is to be turned out like a glove, with all its feathers turned inwards, all the natural openings of the bird, as well as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>-holes, &c. made in killing the bird, are to be stitched up with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> and fine thread; then the whole skin as well as the bones, are to be washed with a strong infusion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> with a little alum, by means of a pencil-brush, and the skin inclosed in a covered vessel that it may not dry too hastily. In ten or twelve hours time we may wash the skin and bones again with the astringent liquor. Twice washing in this manner will be sufficient for very small birds, but those of a middling size will require maceration in the first liquor employed for quadrupeds during two days, and four or five days for those of larger size. The skins being well impregnated with the astringent liquor, are to be smeared with the foamy pomatum, have artificial eyes fixed in the orbits by means of wax, and fluffed and mounted much in the same manner as quadrupeds, except that the wires employed for this purpose are rather differently bended. Great nicety is required in fixing the different parts of a bird in its natural position, and in arranging the feathers smoothly and evenly. M. Nicolas directs thin plates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, to be placed so as to secure the wings in the proper position till the whole is completely arranged. To preserve the feet and legs of birds, he anoints them with linseed oil mixed with camphire, and applied a little warm. The last operation consists in enveloping the bird with bandages of muslin or fine linen, pinned round the neck, breast, body, and rump, as well to secure the feathers in their places during drying, as to allow of their being drenched with the bitter liquor to preserve them from the attacks of insects. The different orders of insects require different modes of preparation. The following is a summary of our author's mode of preserving each kind. For the coleoptera and hemiptera.—One of these insects, as soon as caught, is to be carefully wrapped in very fine paper, with the ends of the paper curled round to prevent the animal from moving; and this roll of paper including the insect, is to be put into a little box of pasteboard till the insect-hunter returns home. Each insect is then to be held between the thumb and forefinger of the left hand, the wings to be raised by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>, and held open with the middle finger, while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> of the animal is slit open from the back, and the entrails abstracted by means of an iron wire, and the cavity as well as the edges of the wound are to be washed with the bitter spirituous liquor described in No. 36, by means of a very fine pencil. Then a small cotton plug impregnated with oil of petroleum is to be stuffed into the cavity, with the point of a wire, till the cavity is sufficiently full, when the wings are to be suffered to return to their natural situation, and the insect is ready for mounting. For mounting these insects, M. Nicolas employs little squares of card, through the middle and across which he passes a small iron wire well annealed, and about the size of a harpsicord string. A very fine needle is now to be passed through the animal, as near as possible to the corset; and after having covered the upright iron wire with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> coating of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water, he passes it through the hole made by the needle, and fixes the animal in such a manner that its feet may rest upon the card. For the lepidoptera.—He recommends them to be put, when caught, into a triangular piece of paper, and afterwards into a pasteboard box of the same form, opening with a hinge. For mounting these insects it is sufficient to perforate their bodies with a fine needle, armed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> thread impregnated with the bitter spirituous liquor, making the needle enter by the head and come out at the end of the belly, and then cutting the thread with scissors. The insect thus prepared is mounted by means of a card, as directed for the coleoptera, and a piece of wood about an inch long, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and a proper thickness, is placed below the wings on each side very near the body, and the wings are kept down by means of plates of lead. In the preparation of specimens of fishes, M. Nicolas prefers the method of Mauduit to that given by Dr Lettlow in the Naturalist's and Traveller's Companion; but as Mauduit's methods require much skill and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, he recommends the following, especially for the flat kinds of fish. He makes a longitudinal incision with scissors along the belly of the fish from the anus to the lower mandible, and then gradually and carefully separates the skin from the flesh with the assistance of the blade and flat handle of a scalpel, till he has laid bare one side of the animal. He then passes to the other side, proceeding in the same manner to detach the skin from that part, after which he separates the head from the body with a pair pair of scissors, and clears away the fleshy parts attached to the head. He now detaches the skin from the back as far as the anus, and then laying the fish on the table, he passes the flat handle of the scalpel below the skin that covers the tail and neighbouring parts, in order to separate it completely. This done, he pushes the tail inwards, and with the assistance of the scalpel and drawing the skin very gently, he detaches this as near as possible to the end of the tail, which he then separates with scissors, thus leaving the skin with nothing attached to it but the head and extremity of the tail. It only remains now to clear away the ears and eyes, and properly clean the head. The skin is now steeped for some days in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a> liquor, then laid on a table, and when the head is properly arranged, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the body of the fish made of soft clay, mixed with fine sand, is placed within the skin, which is made to fit neatly over it, is then bound with little bandages of linen, and suffered to dry. When the clay is quite dry and hard, and the skin has acquired so much firmness as to retain its proper form, it is to be gently beaten all over to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the clay, so that it may be withdrawn through the opening. When this is done, the whole inside of the skin and head is to be smeared by means of a pencil brush with the soap pomatum. After which it is to be entirely filled with cut tow, and the opening stitched up as neatly as possible. Then artificial eyes are to be placed in the orbits by means of soft wax, and the whole body is to be covered with a coat of white <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> prepared by dissolving four ounces of clear turpentine, three ounces of sandarac, and one ounce of mastic in teak, with eight ounces of oil of turpentine, and four ounces of spirit of wine, in a bottle placed in a water bath. In preparing specimens of reptiles,—after what has been said above, little direction will be required. The skin is to be stript backwards as far as the head, which is to be cut off and cleaned as in other specimens; after which the skin is to be macerated, anointed within with pomatum, stuffed and varnished as before. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSTACEA">crustacea</a>, including <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, lobsters, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>-fish, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-urchins, require but little preparation. In crabs the shell, and in lobsters the tail, is to be separated from the rest of the body; as much as possible of the meat is to be picked out from the body and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> claws; the whole interior is to be smeared with the soap pomatum, and after having united the parts, the whole is to be suffered to dry. The star-fish and urchins, if taken alive, should be killed by plunging them in spirit of wine, and afterwards drying them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or in an oven moderately heated. As to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> the only mode of preserving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>, or those with naked bodies, is to keep them in spirits; and of the testacea, or shell-fish, the only part thought worth preserving is the shell; for the preparation of which, see <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a>. The above is but an imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of M. Nicolas's "Methode de preparer et conserver les Animaux de toutes les classes," which is illustrated by plates, and is well deserving the attention of collectors of specimens. There is also an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on this subject by Dutrelle, under Taxidermie, in the Nouveau Dictionnaire d'Histoire Naturelle. It will be expected that in this introductory article on natural history, we should say something of its rise and progress. Much of our observations on this subject have been anticipated in preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> on the particular branches of natural history, so that little remains for us to do in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> than to give a general sketch of the early history of this branch of physics. We have reason to believe that the works of nature Jewish have formed the favourite study among the ingenious and writers inquisitive from the earliest ages of the world. From the continual allusions to the Creator's works, and the beautiful metaphors drawn from them, which abound in the inspired writings of the Jewish prophets and poets, especially those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, Isaiah, Daniel and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, we know that these sages were well acquainted with natural history, as far at least as observation extended. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, as we are told, was acquainted with all vegetables, "from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> of Lebanon to the hyssop that springeth out of the wall," and probably so wise a man was well acquainted with the other kingdoms of nature. Some writers have gone so far as to assert that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a> learned natural history from the writings of Solomon, though on what data they ground this assertion, we are at a loss to determine. The principal writers on natural history among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, whose writings have come down to us are Aristotle, Theophrastus and Pliny the elder. Of the first Aristotle, we may remark with Haller, that his writings on this subject exhibit a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> chain of physical and anatomical facts, which for the most part appear to have been the result of accurate observation. He relied less than any of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists on uncertain and fabulous report; he industriously collected and examined natural bodies, and appears to have himself dissected many animals, especially fishes, or at least to have been present at their dissection. There are even to be found in his writings, references by letters to figures which he employed to illustrate his observations. Theophrastus wrote chiefly on the natural history of plants and animals, on winds, and on fire. His works have been edited by Heineius, but, except in plants, they do not contain much that is worthy of our observation more than what is to be found in the writings of Aristotle. The natural history of Pliny is a valuable repository of ancient knowledge, which, notwithstanding all its errors and extravagances, we may venture to call after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> of his nephew, a comprehensive and learned work, little less various than nature herself. The author in the dedication of his work to Vespasian, sensible of the defects with which it abounds, apologizes for them, from the consideration that the path which he took had been in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> untrodden, and held forth to the traveller few inducements; while some parts of his subject had been so often handled, that readers were become cloyed with them: that it was an arduous task to give what is old an appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>; to add <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and authority to what is new; to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> a luster upon subjects that have been obscured by time; to render acceptable what is become trite and disgusting; to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to doubtful relations; and, in a word, to represent every thing according to nature, and with all its natural properties. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> must be acknowledged to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and noble, and when we consider that the work was composed in the midst of important engagements, engagements, and chiefly at broken periods stolen from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, we shall not wonder that it was imperfectly executed. The ancients had no idea of methodical or systematic distinctions. As they were acquainted with but few bodies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the moderns, and attended only to those which were useful to man; they distinguished them only by their usual properties, their native country, their habitations, and the useful purposes to which they might be applied. From the few productions which they described, they were not led to perceive the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of searching among them for distinctive marks or relations, which may prevent their being confounded with each other. They doubtedly believed that their descriptions were sufficient, and that the names which they imposed would descend with their customs to posterity, without being affected by the disorders and alterations that have changed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of countries and the seat of empires. But the revolutions that have defoliated the fairest regions of the globe, by inflating or displacing their inhabitants, or by confounding them with one another, and altering their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, have frequently almost extinguished the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> of science. After many ages of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and barbarity, we find in the few works of the ancient naturalists, which have escaped the ravages of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and the devastations of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, little more than uncertainty and obscurity, with respect to those species which they have described.
