Notwithstanding the labours of numerous commentators, we do not certainly know what species of plant is the cicuta employed by the Greeks for the execution of criminals, and which terminated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. We cannot be sure that the animals, which we find best characterized in the ancient writings, bore the names which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to them; nor are we more certain with respect to the ancient nomenclature of minerals. As long as studious men cultivated the sciences only through the medium of the writings of the ancients, and attempted nothing beyond the interpretation of these, natural history, like every other branch of physics, remained obscure and confused, and fiction or imagination took the place of facts; but when they perceived the advantage of studying nature herself, and interrogating her by observation, methods were erected, and distinctive characters for the species introduced. This fortunate revolution took place in the 16th century. Caesalpinus first attempted to reduce vegetables to classes, and distinguish them into tribes according to their form.—Gesner, besides the fine hints that he first gave of the constant relation between the structure of the seed and that of the other parts of plants, was the first who attempted any systematic and methodical arrangement of animals. In the 17th century, Morison, Ray, and Rivinus, improved on the hints of Caesalpinus respecting the classification of vegetables; and Aldrovandus, Rhedi, and Swammerdam upon those of Gesner. respecting animals; and in a short time this first impulse given to the art of arranging and distinguishing natural bodies by constant characters, was communicated to all those who were employed in the study of nature. Tournefort, profiting by all the attempts towards method and system in the classification of vegetables that had been made before him, advanced a considerable step in botany, by his beautiful method of distinguishing plants according to the form of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, which he published towards the end of the 17th century. The same year of the 18th century (1707) gave Linné birth to two men who have advanced the science of Buffon's natural history far beyond any of their predecessors. We need scarcely mention the names of Linné and Buffon. The Swedish naturalist extended his enlarged views through every branch of natural history; he arranged in his Systema Naturae and Systema Vegetabilium all the productions of nature, and distinguished them by characters that were precise and simple; he created a new language for expressing with brevity all these characters, and thus presented to the view, as in a compendious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, all the properties of bodies. Buffon, proceeding in a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, treated more copiously the most important parts of natural history, and of the animals that are most nearly allied to man, in a work which the fire of his genius and the brilliancy of his style have rendered a universal favourite. The rival of Aristotle and Pliny, whose genius he seems to have combined in the greatness of his views and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and altogether one of the first writers of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he inspired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for the study of nature in numbers, who without his works would never have engaged in such a study, and communicated to his countrymen that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> which has ever since survived him. After what has been given in the particular treatises on natural history in this Encyclopedia, both as to the progress of the science, and the principal works on each department of it, since the time of Linné and Buffon; it is unnecessary for us to trace its progress beyond that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The advances made within these few years are immense, our stock of information is prodigiously increased, and the modes of study greatly improved and facilitated. The labours of Cuvier, Geoffroy, Lacepede, Dumont, Dumeril, Lamarck, Duvernois, Sennin, Bloch, Spallanzani, Esper, Joffre, Wildenow, Werner, Patrin, St Fond, Brochant, Bronniart, Klaproth, Fourcroy, Vaquelin, Shaw, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LATHAM">Latham</a>, Bancroft, Cateby, Ellis, Smith, Withering, Woodville, Kirwan, Playfair, Thomson, Jameon, &c. with the affluence to be derived from the Annales de <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> National, the Naturalist's Miscellany, the Linnaean Transactions, and the splendid plates of Merian, Schreber, Curtis, Sowerby, Sotheby, &c. afford ample proofs of the industry and success with which this delightful field has been cultivated, and of the rich <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> that has been derived from the united efforts of so many men of genius and talents. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">Natural Philosophy</a>, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> defined to be that branch of knowledge which considers the powers and properties of natural bodies, and their mutual actions on one another. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a> is the mind of man; its inquiries and researches are into the intellectual world. Natural philosophy, on the other hand, is only concerned with the material part of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. The Moralist's business is to inquire into the nature of virtue, the causes and effects of vice; to propose remedies for it, and to point out the mode of attaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, which only can be the result of virtuous conduct. The Naturalist, on the contrary, has nothing to do with spirit; his business is solely about body or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and he ought to have a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and accurate knowledge of all material substances, together with their affections and properties; and if possible, he is to investigate the reasons of such and such appearances.—Indeed, the first and principal part of this science is, to collect all the manifest and sensible appearances of things, and reduce them into a body of natural history. Philosophy, it has often been said, and it is even now very generally thought, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> an inquiry into all the causes of things; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> informs us, that though we are acquainted with a good number of effects, we can trace but few of their causes; so that philosophy itself will really be found to be in general but a collection of facts. Still, however, it differs from natural history in its appropriated sense; the business of which is only to observe the appearances of natural bodies separately, and from these appearances to classify them with other bodies; natural philosophy goes farther, and recites the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of two or more bodies of the same or different kinds upon one another; and though it can neither investigate nor point out the causes of those effects, whatever they are, yet, from mathematical reasoning combined with experience, it can be demonstrated, that in such circumstances such effects must always take place. There are evidently two ways of making observations on the material world: the first is, when we view things nearly as they happen to occur, without any design or intervention of our own; in which way, indeed, no great improvements can be expected in the art, because chance having the direction, only exhibits occasional or temporary properties. The other method is, when, after a thorough acquaintance with bodies, we apply them to other bodies equally known, diligently attending to the result, and observing whether anything new arises. Such seems to be in general the nature of our article; nor is it our intention to be much more particular at present. We must therefore refer our readers reflectively to those parts of the subject, respecting which they wish for more satisfaction and minute details. The ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> definitions of the word philosophy, together with its origin, as well as the manner of philosophizing in former times as well as at present, with the gradual improvement of science, particularly natural, we shall introduce, we think, more properly under the words Philosophy and Physics. We need only add under the present article, what however is well known, that natural philosophy was till lately divided only into four parts, commonly called the four branches, viz. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>; 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a>; 3. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>; and 4. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>; and these again are subdivided into various parts. Modern discoveries have added, however, two more parts to the number, viz. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">Magnetism</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>. It is remarkable, that in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> these two latter branches are never taken notice of in lecturing on natural philosophy, the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> being still retained, without any mention of these two important articles. The reason may be, that they are only subject to experiment, and not yet reduced to mathematical reasoning; which is the method of teaching philosophy in one of those celebrated seminaries. Of these branches of this extensive science, it is not our intention to take even a general view in this place. We must therefore refer our readers to each particular article, where they will find them treated at considerable length.

NATURALISATION

Pages 263-263

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of naturalizing an alien, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> putting him into the condition of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> born subject, and entitling him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges thereof. But none can be naturalized unless they have received the sacrament within one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> before the bringing in of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, and taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> and supremacy in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. A person who is naturalized may have lands by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, as heir at law, as well as obtain them by purchase; but he is disabled from being a member of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> or parliament; or from holding offices, 7 Jac. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 2. 12 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">Will</a>. III. cap. 2. All children born out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s dominions, whose fathers were or are subjects of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their birth, are adjudged to be natural born subjects of this realm, except children of parents attainted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, or that are in the actual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> at enmity with us, 4 Geo. II. cap. 21. Every foreign seaman, who in time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> serves two years on board an English ship, is ipso facto naturalized, 13 Geo. II. cap. 3. And all foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Jews, upon their residing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years in any of the British colonies, without being absent above two months at a time, or serving two years in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity there, are upon taking the oaths naturalized to all intents and purposes, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been born in this kingdom; and therefore are admissible to all such privileges, and no other, as Protestants or Jews born in this kingdom are entitled to. See ALIEN and DEZINIZEN. In France before the Revolution, naturalization was the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>; in England it is only done by act of parliament. In the former of those places, before their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was overturned, Switz, Savoyards, and Scots, did not require naturalization, being reputed regniques, or natives.

NATURALS

Pages 263-263

among Physicians, whatever naturally belongs to an animal, in opposition to non-naturals. See NON-NATURALS.

NATURE

Pages 263-264

according to Mr Boyle, has eight different significations; it being used, 1. For the author of nature, whom the schoolmen call Natura Naturans, being the same with God. 2. By the nature of a thing, we sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> its essence; that is, the attributes which make it what it is, whether the thing be corporeal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not; as when we attempt to define the nature of a fluid, of a triangle, &c. 3. Sometimes we confound that which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has by nature with what accrues to him by birth; as when we say, that such a man is noble by nature. 4. Sometimes we take nature for an internal principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; as when we say, that a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> by nature falls to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Sometimes we understand by nature, the established course of things. 6. Sometimes we take nature for an aggregate of powers belonging to a body, especially a living one; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> physicians say, that nature is strong, weak, or spent; or that, in such or such diseases, nature left to herself <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> perform the cure. 7. Sometimes we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> nature for the universe, or whole system of the corporeal works of God; as when it is said of a phoenix, or chimera, that there is no such thing in nature. 8. Sometimes too, and that most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a>, we express by the word nature, a kind of semi-deity, or other strange kind of being. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, says the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, I were to propose a notion of nature, less ambiguous than these already mentioned, and with regard to which many axioms relating to that word may be conveniently understood, I should first distinguish between the universal and the particular nature of things. Universal nature I would define to be the aggregate of the bodies that make up the world in its present state, considered as a principle, by virtue whereof they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> and suffer, according to the laws of motion prescribed by the Author of all things. And this makes way for the other subordinate notion; since the particular nature of an individual consists in the general nature applied to a distinct portion of the universe; or, which is the same thing, it is a particular assemblage of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> properties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, motion, &c. Kingdoms of Nature. See Kingdoms. Conduct or Operations of Nature. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>.

NAUCOPY

Pages 371-371

the art of discovering the approach of ships <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> at a considerable distance. This pretended art was discovered by M. Bottineau, employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of France, from the year 1782 to 1784; the account of it is as follows: "This knowledge is not derived either from the undulation of the waves, or from the subtlety of sight, or from any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; but merely from observation of the horizon, which discovers signs indicating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> of ships or of land. "On the approximation of a ship toward the land, or towards another ship, there appears in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a> of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, visible to everyone without any painful <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. It is not by any kind of accident that this meteor appears under these circumstances; on the contrary, it is the necessary result of the approximation of one vessel towards another, or towards the land. The existence of the meteor, and the knowledge of its different modifications, are what constitute the certainty and the precision of my informations. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> I am asked, how it is possible that the approach of a ship towards land should give birth to any meteor whatsoever in the atmosphere, and what connexion there can be between two objects at such a distance from each other? I reply, that I am not obliged to give an account of the hows and the wherefores: that it is sufficient for me to have discovered the fact, without being obliged to account for its principle." The writer concludes, by defining to be called on for experimental proofs, and by promising in future a complete treatise of Naucopy, with maps, plates, &c.

NAULUM

Pages 368-368

in Roman antiquity, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> put into the mouth of a person deceased to enable him to pay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a> the ferryman for his passage. It was to be of the current <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the reigning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>; so that from this money the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> may be known. The sum for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> men was a farthing, but the rich in general were very liberal to Charon, as appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of coins often found in the neighbourhood of Rome on opening the graves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men. Charon was looked upon as a very morose and obstinate old fellow, who would not carry over any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> without his fare; and hence the proverbial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in Juvenal, Furor est <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> omnia perdere naulum. A similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the Greeks: The money put into the mouth of the deceased was by them called Δανάκης.

NAUMACHIA

Pages 368-371

in antiquity, a show <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spectacle among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, representing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fight. These mock sea fights are supposed to have originated at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, when the Romans first instructed their men in the knowledge of naval affairs. Afterwards they were intended to entertain the populace, as well as to improve the seamen. They were often, like other shows, exhibited at the expense of individuals, to increase their popularity. In these <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> they sometimes strove to excel each other in swiftness; and sometimes engaged in a warlike manner. The naumachiae of Claudius indeed was a most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> diversion. The combatants used to destroy each other to amuse a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> and a cruel mob. As they passed before him, they used this melancholy greeting, "Ave Imperator, morituri te salutant." The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> replied, "Ave victor!" This they understood as an answer of kindness, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of their lives; but they soon discovered that it proceeded from wanton cruelty, and barbarous insensibility. In the time of the emperor Domitian, such a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vessels engaged as would have nearly formed two regular fleets for a real fight, and the channel of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> was equal in magnitude to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> river. The emperor Heliogabalus is reported to have filled the channel where the vessels were to ride with wine instead of water. Tritons and sea monsters were frequently exhibited during the engagement. Suetonius and Dio Cassius inform us, that at one of these sea fights of Domitian a violent shower fell; the emperor, however, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the end of the engagement, often changing his clothes, nor would he suffer any one to depart; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> continued for several hours, many were seized with distempers, and some even died, Suet. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 4. Dio. lib. lxvii. Naumachiae were also places fitted up for these shows, a fort of circi or amphitheatres, with seats and porticoes, &c. There were several of them at Rome; three built by Augustus, one by Claudius, another by Domitian, and another by Nero: which served for the reverse of his medals. Claudius used the lake Fucinus as a naumachia.

NAUMBURG

Pages 371-371

a town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Saxe-Naumburg, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALA">Sala</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 20'. N. Lat. 51° 12'.

NAUPACTUS

Pages 371-371
or NAUPACTUM, in Ancient Geography, a city of Aetolia, at the mouth of the Evenus. The word is derived from ναῦς and πάγκωμα, because it was there that the Heraclidae built the first ship which carried them to Peloponnesus. It first belonged to the Locri Ozolae, and afterwards fell into the hands of the Athenians, who gave it to the Messenians, who had been driven from Peloponnesus by the Lacedemonians. It became the property of the Lacedemonians after the battle of Egolopotamos, and it was restored to the Locri. Philip of Macedon afterwards took it, and gave it to the Aetolians; from which circumstance it has generally been called one of the chief cities of their country. E. Long. 2° 29'. N. Lat. 38° 0'. There was on the shore a temple of Neptune, and near it a cave filled with offerings, and dedicated to Venus, where widows referred to request new husbands of the goddess. Paulan. lib. x. p. 898.

NAUPLIA

Pages 371-371

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. It was the naval station of the Argives. The fountain Canathos was in its neighbourhood.

NAUPLIUS

Pages 371-371

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a son of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> and Amyomone, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Euboea. He was the father of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALAMEDES">Palamedes</a>, who was so unjustly sacrificed to the artifice and resentment of Ulysses by the Greeks at the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Palamedes highly enraged Nauplius; and to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the injustice of the Grecian princes, he endeavoured to debauch their wives, and ruin their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. When the Greeks Nauportus returned from the Trojan war, Nauplius was pleased to see them distressed in a storm on the coasts of Euboea; and to make their disaster still more universal, he lighted fires on such places as were surrounded with the most dangerous rocks, that the fleet might be shipwrecked upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. This had the desired effect; but Nauplius was so disappointed when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Ulysses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a> escape from the general distress, that he threw himself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. According to some mythologists there were two persons of this name; one a native of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, who went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> with Jason. He was son of Neptune and Amyomone.—The other was king of Euboea, and lived about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Trojan war. He was, as some observe, son of Clytonas, one of the descendants of Nauplius the Argonaut. The Argonaut was remarkable for his knowledge of sea affairs and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. He built the town of Nauplia, and sold Auga <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Aleus to King Teuthras, to screen her from her father's resentment.

NAUPORTUS

Pages 371-371
or NAUPORTUM, in Ancient Geography, a town on a cognominal river, towards its source, in Panonia Superior. The reason of the name, according to Pliny, is, that the ship Argo, after coming up the Danube, the Save, and the Laubach, was thence carried on men's shoulders over the Alps into the Adriatic. The river Nauportus rises in the Alps, near Longaticum, at the distance of six miles from the town Nauportum; which was a colony of the Taurisci, a people on the confines of Noricum. Now Upper Laubach in Carinthia, on the river Laubach. E. Long. 14° 40'. N. Lat. 46° 28'.

NAUSEA

Pages 371-372
or sickness; a retching or propensity and endeavour to vomit, arising from something which irritates the stomach.

NAUTILUS

Pages 372-372

a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes testacea. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">CONCHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NAVAL

Pages 264-264

something relating to a ship; whence, Naval <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. See Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>. Naval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>, in antiquity, a fortification, consisting of a ditch and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> side, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a wall built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, and extended from one point of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to another. This was sometimes defended with towers, and beautified with gates, through which they issued forth to attack their enemies. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> hath left us a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Grecian fortifications of this fort, in the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, beginning at ver. 436. Iliad 9. Then, to secure the naval camp and towers, They rais'd embattled walls with lofty towers: From space to space were ample gates around, For passing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>; and a trench profound, Of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and deep in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> below Strong piles infix'd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> adverse to the foe. POPE'S Transl. Towards the sea, or within it, they fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pales of wood, like those in their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> harbours: before these vessels of burden were placed in such order, as that they might be instead of a wall, and give protection to those within; in which manner Nicias is reported by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> to have encamped himself: but this seems only to have been practised when the enemy was thought superior in strength, and raised great apprehensions of danger in them. When their fortifications were thought strong enough to defend them from the assaults of enemies, it was frequent to drag their ships to shore, which the Greeks called στρατόπεδον, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> salubducere. Around the ships the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> disposed their tents, as appears everywhere in Homer: but this seems only to have been practised in winter, when their enemy's fleet was laid up and could not assault them; or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> sieges, and when they lay in no danger from their enemies by sea; as in the Trojan war, where the defenders of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> never once attempted to encounter the Grecians in a sea-fight. The adjacent places were usually filled with inns and stews, well stocked with females, that prostituted themselves to the mariners, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and artificers of all sorts, who flocked thither in great numbers; this, however, appears to have happened only in times of peace. Naval <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a>, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Romans, a crown adorned with figures of prows of ships, conferred on persons who in sea engagements first boarded the enemy's vessel. See Crown. Naval Engagement. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACTICS">Tactics</a>, Naval. Naval Stores, comprehend all those particulars made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, not only in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, but in every other kind of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> for shipping, pitch, tar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, cordage, sail cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, ordnance, and fire arms of every sort, ship chandlery wares, &c. Naval Tactics, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations of fleets. See Tactics, Naval.

NAVAN

Pages 264-264

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>; situated about 25 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>. It consists of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> streets, which intersect each other at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>.—The tholfe, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> town <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was formerly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute, and walled in by Hugh de Lacy. An <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> for regular canons, dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, was erected here; but whether antecedent to the end of the 12th century is not certain: about that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, however, it was either founded or re-edified by Joceline de Angulo or Nangle. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> ground are the remains of many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tombs. A barrack for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is now built on the site of the abbey.

NAVARRE

Pages 264-266

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Navarre, erected soon after the invasion of the Moors; and is otherwise called Upper Navarre, to distinguish it from Lower Navarre belonging to the French. It is bounded on the south and east by Arragon, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Pyrenees, and on the west by Old Castile and Bilcay; extending from south to north about 80 miles, and from east to west about 75. It abounds in sheep and cattle; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> of all kinds, as boars, flags, and roebucks; and in wild fowl, horses, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; yielding also some grain, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and a variety of minerals, medicinal waters, and hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. Some of the ancient chiefs of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> were called Sobrarbadores, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, as it is supposed, which prevailed among some of those free nations, of choosing and swearing their Navarre, their princes under some particular tree. The name of the province is supposed to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of Nava Errea, signifying, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Vacones, its ancient inhabitants, "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of valleys." —For the particulars of its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, see the article Spain. Navarre, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, an officer of eminence in the 16th century, and particularly celebrated for his dexterity in the directing and springing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. He was a native of Bilcay, and of low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. According to Paul Jove, who affirms that he had an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> from his own mouth, he was first a sailor; but being disgusted with that employment, he fought his fortune in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, when poverty compelled him to become footman to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>. He afterwards enlisted himself a soldier in the Housline <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and having served there for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> again, and distinguished himself by his courage. The reputation of his valour having reached the ears of Gonzalo de Cordova, the general employed him in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and raised him to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. Having contributed greatly to the taking of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> by very opportunely springing a mine, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> rewarded him for this signal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> with the earldom of Alveto, situated in that kingdom, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of Navarre. Having the command of a naval expedition against the Moors in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, he was at first very successful, and took possession of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and some other places; but being afterwards shipwrecked on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Gerbes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heats and the Moorish cavalry destroyed a part of his army. Our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> was equally unfortunate in Italy: He was made prisoner at the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> in 1512, and languished in France for the space of two years. When finding that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Spain, who had been prejudiced against him by his courtiers, would do nothing towards his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>, he went into the service of Francis I, who gave him the command of 20 companies of infantry, consisting of Galcons, Biscayans, and the inhabitants of the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. He distinguished himself in several successful expeditions, until the year 1522, when having been sent to the relief of the Genoese, he was taken by the Imperialists. They conducted him to Naples, where he remained a prisoner for three years in the Castle del Ovo. From this confinement he was released by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, and afterwards fought at the siege of Naples under Lauric in 1528: but being again made prisoner at the unfortunate retreat from Averfa, he was conducted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time to the Castle del Ovo. Here the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, having, by order of the emperor, caused several persons of the Angevine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> to be beheaded, our hero would undoubtedly have suffered the same fate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the governor, seeing his distressed situation, and feeling for the misfortunes of so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, had not saved him the shame of this last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> by allowing him to die a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Others pretend that he was strangled in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, having arrived at a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Paul Jove and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Thomassin have written his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. This last informs us, that he was of a tall size, had a swarthy countenance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eyes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Sessa, in the last century, being desirous to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> and that of the marshal de Lautree, caused a monument to be erected to each of them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Saint-Marie-le-Neuve at Naples, where they had been interred without any funeral honours. Navarre, Martin, fumated Azpilcueta, because he was born in the kingdom which bears that name, successively professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, was consulted from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> as the oracle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. For a part of his knowledge he was indebted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAHORS">Cahors</a> and Toulouse, in which he had studied. His friend Barthelemy Carrewza, a Dominican, and archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, having been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> at Rome, Navarre set out at the age of 80 years to defend him. Pius V appointed him advisor to Cardinal Francis Alciat, vice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENITENTIARY">penitentiary</a>. Gregory XIII never passed his gate without sending for him; and sometimes would <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with him for an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> together on the street: he even deigned to visit him, accompanied by several cardinals. These honours did not render him more haughty. His character became so eminent, that even in his own time the greatest encomium that could be paid to a man of learning was to say that he was a Navarre: this name thus included the idea of erudition, as that of Rocei formerly marked an accomplished comedian. Azpilcueta was the oracle of the city of Rome, and of the whole Christian world. For the influence which he had acquired, he was indebted not only to his knowledge, but also to his probity and virtue. Faithful to the duties which the church prescribed, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and frugality preferred to him a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and at a very advanced age his genius was equal to the fervent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. His savings enabled him to give liberal assistance to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. His charities, indeed, were so great, that his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>, it is said, would stop as soon as the perceived a beggar. He died at Rome in 1586, at the age of 92. His works were collected and printed in 6 vols. folio at Lyons in 1597, and at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1602. They display more learning than judgment, and are now very seldom consulted. Navarre was uncle by the mother's side to St Francis of Sales. See Sales. Naucrari, among the Athenians, was the name given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> magistrates of the Δημοι, "boroughs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> townships," called Naucrariae; because each was obliged, besides two horsemen, to furnish out one ship for the public service. Naucrates, a Greek poet, who was employed by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> to write a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> upon Mausolus.—An orator who endeavoured to alienate the cities of Lycia from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Brutus. Naucratitis, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> on the left side of the Canopic mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. It was celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and no ship was permitted to land at any other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but was obliged to sail directly to the city, there to deposit its cargo. It gave birth to Athenaeus. Naucratites Nomos, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, (Pliny); a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the Delta, so called from that town Naucratitis; though <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> comprises it under the Nomos Sautes. Naucydes, a statuary who lived about four centuries before the Christian era. Nave, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the body of a church, where the people are disposed, reaching from the balustrade, or rail of the door, to the chief choir. Some derive NAV Navel. derive the word from the Greek ναῦς, "a temple;" and others from ναῦς, "a ship," by reason the vault or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a church bears some resemblance to a ship.

NAVEL

Pages 266-266

in Anatomy, the centre of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>; being that part where the umbilical vessels palled out of the placenta of the mother. See Navel-Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. NAVEL-WORT. See Cotyledon, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. NAVEW. See Brassica, Botany Index.

As the distance CD - 51 1.70757 is to the diff. of latitude CA - 18 1.25527 fo is the secant of ACB - 2 points 10.63438 to the cosine of BCD - 67° 32' 9.58208 CHAP. X. Of Current Sailing. The computations in the preceding chapters have been performed upon the assumption that the water has no motion. This may no doubt answer tolerably well in those places where the ebbsings and flowings are regular, as then the effect of the tide will be nearly counterbalanced. But in places where there is a constant current or setting of the sea towards the same point, an allowance for the change of the ship's place arising therefrom must be made: And the method of resolving these problems, in which the effect of a current, or heave of the sea, is taken into consideration, is called current sailing. In a calm, it is evident a ship will be carried in the direction and with the velocity of the current. Hence, if a ship sails in the direction of the current, her rate will be augmented by the rate of the current; but if sailing directly against it, the distance made good will be equal to the difference between the ship's rate as given by the log and that of the current. And the absolute motion of the ship will be a-head, if her rate exceeds that of the current; but if less, the ship will make sternway. If the ship's course be oblique to the current, the distance made good in a given time will be represented by the third side of a triangle, whereof the distance given by the log, and the drift of the current in the same time, are the other sides; and the true course will be the angle contained between the meridian and the line actually described by the ship. The first of these will measure 159 miles, and the second 6° 23'. By Calculation. In the triangle ACB, given AC = 144 miles, AB = 45 miles, and the angle CAB = 9 points, to find BAC and BC.
