On the edges of these wheels are teeth of an equal number in each wheel; and as the teeth of the wheels mutually fall into each other, the revolutions of both must be performed in the same time. By this contrivance also the cylinders will turn different ways; and the ropes on the two different cylinders will constantly one pair be wound up, and the other wound down, by the natural moving of the machine. DDD is the frame that supports the whole, which must be made very firm and secure. Let us now suppose, that there is a boat in the upper canal to be brought down, but none to go up for a balance. In this case, as one of the vehicles must be at the top to receive the boat, the other will be at the bottom to take in water. Let then any of the movements just described be set to work, and it is plain, that as the upper vehicle with its boat descends, the under vehicle will ascend with the water; the valve being in the mean time lifted up till a sufficient quantity of water has flowed out, to make the one nearly a counterbalance to the other; so that the vessel may slide down gently and without any violence. If it happens that a boat is to go up while none is to come down, one of the vehicles being at the foot of the plane under water, and in readiness to have the boat towed upon its horizontal part, one of the sluices at K or L is to be opened, and a quantity of water let into the cistern of the upper vehicle sufficient to counterbalance the boat with its contents which is to ascend. This being done, the machine is set to work, the valve of the under vehicle kept open till the water is all discharged; and then the boat will roll up to the top of the plane. From this description of the canal and machinery for raising and lowering the vessels, the reader can be at no loss to understand the principles on which it depends. It would be superfluous to adduce examples, or follow our author through his calculations relative to particular cases. We shall only observe, that the difference of time in which vessels may be raised or lowered by the machinery just described, in comparison with what can be done in the common way by dams and locks, must give a very favourable idea of the new method. According to Mr Leach's computations, a boat with its cargo weighing 10 tons might be raised by the walking machine in 12 or 14 minutes, by the under-shot wheel in 15 minutes, and by the overshot wheel in 30 minutes; and that through a space of no less than 30 fathoms measured on the inclined plane, or 114 feet perpendicular. NAVIGATORS ISLANDS. See OPOUN.

NAVY

Pages 372-372

the fleet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shipping of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or state. See MARINE. The management of the British navy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is intrusted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers and commissioners of the navy, who hold their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by patent. The principal officers of the navy are four, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, whose business it is to receive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> out of the exchequer, and to pay all the charges of the navy, by warrant from the principal officers; comptroller, who attends and controuls all payment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, is to know the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> of stores, to examine and audit all accounts, &c.; surveyor, who is to know the states of all stores, and see wants supplied; to estimate repairs, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> boatswains, &c. with what stores they receive, and at the end of each voyage to state and audit accounts; clerk of the acts, whose business it is to record all orders, contracts, bills, warrants, &c. The commissioners of the navy are five: The first executes that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the comptroller's duty which relates to the comptrolling the victualler's accounts; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, another part of the said comptroller's duty relating to the account of the storekeepers of the yard; the third has the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the navy at the port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>; the fourth has the same at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>; and the fifth at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>. There are also other commissioners at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> more or less according to the exigencies of public affairs; and since the increase of the royal navy, there have several clerks under them, with salaries allowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. The victualling of the royal navy hath formerly been undertaken by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>; but is now managed by commissioners, who hold their office on Tower-hill, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The navy office is where the whole business concerning the navy is managed by the principal officers and commissioners. The royal navy of Great Britain is now in a very flourishing state, having been diligently kept up in late reigns, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> strength of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. When it is complete, it is divided into three squadrons, distinguished by the colours of the flags carried by the respective admirals belonging to the same, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and blue; the principal commander of which bears the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of admiral; and each has under him a vice admiral and a rear admiral, who are likewise <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> officers. NAVY <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">Exercise</a>. See EXERCISE. NAVY <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">Discipline</a>, or Regulations. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">MARITIME</a> State.

NAWORTH CASTLE

Pages 372-372

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, 10 miles from Carlisle, near the Gelt. This castle is still entire and inhabited. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pile, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and built round a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> it stands over the river Ithing, at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, the banks fringed with wood. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; the rooms numerous, accessible by 16 staircases, with most frequent and sudden ascents and descents, &c. The great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> has a gallery at one end, adorned with four vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a> carved in wood, viz. a griffin and dolphin, with the scolops; an unicorn, and an ox with a coronet round his neck. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in wood of an armed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; two others, perhaps valets, in short jackets and caps. The top and upper end of the room is painted in squares, representing the Saxon kings and heroes. This castle was built by one of the Dacres about the reign of Henry III. In the garden walls were <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> with Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, which the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Carlisle gave to Sir Thomas Robinson, and were by him removed to his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at Rookby: On one of these stones is this inscription, pediment centum quinquaginta Britannorum; whence it appears that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, when in possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, sometimes indulged the national troops with the favour of garrisoning their own territories.

NAXIA

Pages 372-372
or NAXOS, a considerable island of the Archipelago, 25 miles in length, and 88 in circumference. The whole island is covered with orange, olive, lemon, cedar, citron, pomegranate, fig, and mulberry trees; and there are a great many springs and brooks. This island has no harbour; and yet they carry on a considerable trade in barley, wine, figs, cotton, silk, flax, cheese, salt, oxen, sheep, mules, and oil. They burn only oil of mastic, though olive oil is exceedingly cheap. It is inhabited both by Greeks and Latins, who live in great dread of the Turks; for when the meanest of their ships appear here, they always wear red caps like galley-slaves, and tremble before the lowest officer; but as soon as they are gone, they put on their caps of velvet. The ladies are so vain, that when they return out of the country, they have 40 women in their train, half on foot and half on asses, one of whom carries a napkin or two, another a petticoat, another a pair of stockings, and so on; which is a very ridiculous sight to strangers. There are four archbishops fees in this island, and a great many villages; but so thin of people, that the whole island does not contain above 8000 inhabitants. The highest mountain is Zia, which signifies "the mountain of Jupiter." There are but few antiquities, except some small remains of the temple of Bacchus. Some say they have mines of gold and silver; however, there is one of emery, which is so common here and so cheap, that the English often ballast their ships therewith.

NAXOS

Pages 372-372
or NAXIA, a considerable town, and capital of the isle of Naxos, over against the isle of Paros, with a castle and two archbishops fees, the one Greek and the other Latin. The greatest part of the inhabitants are Greeks. E. Long. 25° 51' N. Lat. 37° 8'.

NAXUS

Pages 373-373

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> Naxius. Another of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, built by the Chalcidians; situated on the south side of Mount Taurus, destroyed by Dionysius the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>: from its ruins Tauromenium, built by Timoleon, either arose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> was increased, (Plutarch).

NAYRES

Pages 373-373

the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of the Malabar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. We may with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> affirm that they are the oldest nobility in the world; for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers mention them, and quote the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> that permits the Nayre ladies to have many husbands; every one being allowed four. Their houses, which stand single, have as many doors as the lady has husbands. When one of them visits her, he walks round the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, striking with his sabre on his buckler; he then opens his door, and leaves a domestick with his arms in a kind of porch, who serves to inform others that the lady is engaged. It is said, that one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> the four doors are all opened, and all her husbands visit her, and dine together with her. Each husband gives a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> portion, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; and the wife only has the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the children. The Nayres, even the Samoim, and the other princes, have no other heirs than the children of their fathers. This law was established, that the Nayres, having no family, might be always ready to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> against the enemy. When the nephews are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> to bear arms, they follow their uncles. The name of father is unknown to a Nayre child. He speaks of the husbands of his mother and of his uncles, but never of his father.

NAZARETH

Pages 373-374

a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the tribe of Zebulun, in Lower Galilee, to the west of Tabor, and to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a>. Eusebius says, it is 15 miles from Legion towards the east. This city is much celebrated in the Scriptures, for having been the usual <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the residence of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ for the first 33 years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, Luke ii. 51. It was there our Saviour became incarnate, where he lived in obedience to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, and from whence he took the name of a Nazarean. After he had begun to execute his mission, he preached there sometimes in the synagogue, Id. iv. 16. But because his countrymen had no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in him, and were offended at the manner of his original, he did not many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> there, Matth. xiii. 54, 58; nor would he dwell therein; so he fixed his habitation at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPERNAUM">Capernaum</a> for the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life, Id. iv. 13. The city of Nazareth was situated upon an eminence; and on one side there was a precipice, from whence the Nazareans one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of throwing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> our Saviour, because he upbraided them with their incredulity, Luke iv. 29. St Epiphanius says, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Nazareth was only a village, and that to the reign of Constantine it was inhabited by Jews alone, exclusive of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Adamnanus, a writer of the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, says, that in his time there were two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> churches to be seen at Nazareth, one in the midst of the city, built upon two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, in the place where our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> had stood. Under the two arches now mentioned, was a very fine fountain, which furnished <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the whole city, and from whence water was drawn also by the help of a pulley for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> above. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> church of Nazareth was built in a place where the house stood wherein the angel Gabriel revealed to the virgin Mary the mystery of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s incarnation; and we are assured that the church of Incarnation, which is supported by two arches, is still in being to this Nazareth, this day. Mr Maundrell tells us, that there is a convent built over what is said to be the place of annunciation; for the chamber where she received the angel's salutation was about 500 years ago removed from Nazareth, and, according to the Roman legends, transported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> to Loreto, then a small village in the pope's dominions, now become a bishopric, &c. However, Calmet's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> (which is certainly the true one) upon the different translations of this famous house of Loreto, is, that they were no other than so many different buildings made upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the church of Nazareth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as in several places sepulchres have been built upon the model of that at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Mariti tells us, that in the eastern part of the city stands the church dedicated to the Blest Virgin: the zeal of the Cenobites raised it from the ruins of that which had been destroyed by the Saracens. It is a very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and consists of three naves; in the middle of which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> altar; to which there is an ascent by two magnificent stairs, much admired for their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> balustrades, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of an ingenious monk of the convent. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to the grotto <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> annunciation chapel below is by steps of beautiful marble, cut with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Two beautiful columns of oriental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> strike the eye of the observer in the entrance. They appear to have been constructed both to support and ornament the grotto. The altar of this subterranean chapel is extremely elegant; and the different kinds of marble with which it is ornamented, receive an additional lustre from the combined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of several silver lamps presented by Christian princes. On solemn festivals, the walls and the pilasters are ornamented with various pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, representing the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the virgin; a superb present from the House of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. In the western part of the city stands a Christian church, built, as it is said, on the site of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> synagogue where Jesus showed the Jews the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of the prophecies in his person. This place served a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time as a shelter for flocks, but at present it is in good repair. In the neighbourhood may be seen a fountain of excellent water, which is, however, esteemed by the people on another account. They conjecture that it was contiguous to the habitation of the virgin, and that it was used by her. At some distance is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of a round form, called Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. It is pretended that he came hither more than once with his disciples to eat. The inhabitants of Nazareth pay it a kind of worship, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> perfumes and incense around it. It is situated in 34° E. Long, and in 32° N. Lat.; and formerly held the third <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Jerusalem. At present it is part of the domains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a>. The ancient city, after the ravages of fanaticism, was reduced to a miserable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a>, containing only a few Arab huts.—Under the protection of Daher Omar, however, it recovered very considerably, and is now of far more importance.

NAZARITE

Pages 374-375
or Nazarean, or Nazarines, a term which may signify, 1. One that is of Nazareth, or any native of this city. 2. It was given to Jesus Christ and his disciples, and is commonly taken in a sense of derision and contempt in such authors as have written against christianity. 3. It has been taken for a sect of heretics called Nazareans. 4. For a Nazarite, a man that has laid himself under the obligation of a vow to observe the rules of Nazariteness, whether it be for Nazarite his whole life, as Samson and John the Baptist, or only for a time, as those mentioned in Numbers vi. 18, 19, 20. Amos ii. 11, 12. Lastly, The name Nazarite, in some passages of Scripture, denotes a man of particular distinction and great dignity in the court of some prince. But we must speak of these several sorts of Nazarites something more distinctly. The name of Nazarene belongs to Jesus Christ, not only because of his having lived the greatest part of his life at Nazareth, and because this city has always been considered as his country, but also because the prophets had foretold that he should be called a Nazarene, Matth. ii. 23. "And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene." We find no particular place in the prophets in which it is said that the Messiah should be called a Nazarene; and St Matthew only quotes the prophets in general. Perhaps he would intimate, that the consecration of the Nazarites, and the great purity of which they made profession, was a type and a sort of prophecy of those of our Saviour, or else that the name נזיר or Nazarite given to the patriarch Joseph, Gen. xlii. 26. Deut. xxxiii. 16. was a prophecy which was to be fulfilled in the person of Jesus Christ, of whom Joseph was a figure. Lastly, St Jerome was of opinion, that St Matthew here alludes to that passage of Isaiah xi. 1. and lx. 21. "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a branch (in Hebrew נזר) shall grow out of his roots." This branch or נזר, and this rod, are certainly intended to denote Jesus Christ, by the general consent of all the fathers and interpreters. When the word Nazarean is put for the heretics known by this name, it denotes Christians converted from Judaism, whose chief error consisted in defending the necessity or expediency of the works of the law, and who obstinately adhered to the practice of the Jewish ceremonies. The name of Nazarenes at first had nothing odious in it, and it was often given to the first Christians. The fathers frequently mention the gospel of the Nazarenes, which differs nothing from that of St Matthew, which was either in Hebrew or Syriac, for the use of the first converts, but was afterwards corrupted by the Ebionites. These Nazarenes preserved this first gospel in its primitive purity. Some of them were still in being in the time of St Jerome, who does not reproach them with any error. They were very zealous observers of the law of Moses, but held the traditions of the Pharisees in very great contempt. Nazarite, when put to signify those under the ancient law who made a vow of observing a more than ordinary degree of purity (Numb. ubi. cit.), denotes a man or woman who engage themselves by a vow to abstain from wine and all intoxicating liquors, to let their hair grow without cutting or shaving, not to enter into any house that was polluted by having a dead corpse in it, nor to be present at any funeral. And if by chance any one should have died in their presence, they began again the whole ceremony of their consecration and Nazariteness. This ceremony generally lasted eight days, sometimes a month, and sometimes their whole lives. When the time of their Nazariteness Nazarene ship was accomplished, the priest brought the person to the door of the temple, who there offered to the Lord a he lamb for a burnt-offering, a she lamb for an expiatory sacrifice, and a ram for a peace-offering. They offered likewise loaves and cakes, with wine necessary for the libations. After all this was sacrificed and offered to the Lord, the priest or some other shaved the head of the Nazarite at the door of the tabernacle, and burnt his hair, throwing it upon the fire of the altar. Then the priest put into the hand of the Nazarite the shoulder of the ram roasted, with a loaf and a cake, which the Nazarite returning into the hands of the priest, he offered them to the Lord, lifting them up in the presence of the Nazarite. And from this time he might again drink wine, his Nazaritehip being now accomplished. As to those that were perpetual Nazarites, as were Samson and John the Baptist, it appears that they were consecrated to their Nazaritehip by their parents, and continued all their lives in this state, without drinking wine or cutting their hair. Those that made a vow of Nazaritehip out of Palestine, and could not come to the temple when their vow was expired, contented themselves with observing the abstinence required by the law, and after that cutting their hair in the place where they were; as to the offerings and sacrifices prescribed by Moses, which were to be offered at the temple by themselves, or by others for them, they deferred this till they could have a convenient opportunity. Hence it was, that St Paul being at Corinth, and having made the vow of a Nazarite, he had his hair cut off at Cenchrea, and put off fulfilling the rest of his vow till he should arrive at Jerusalem. Acts xviii. 18. When a person found that he was not in a condition to make a vow of Nazaritehip, or had not leisure to perform the ceremonies belonging to it, he contented himself by contributing to the expense of the sacrifice and offerings of those that had made and fulfilled this vow; and by this means he became a partaker in the merit of such Nazaritehip. When St Paul came to Jerusalem, in the year of Christ 58, the apostle St James the Less, with the other brethren, said to him, Acts xxii. 23, 24, that to quiet the minds of the converted Jews, who had been informed that he everywhere preached up the entire abolition of the law of Moses, he ought to join himself to four of the faithful who had a vow of Nazaritehip upon them, and contribute to the charge of the ceremony at the shaving of their heads; by which the new converts would perceive that he continued to keep the law, and that what they had heard of him was not true. The Hebrew word Nazir, or Nazarite, which is made use of to express a man exalted to great dignity, as it is said of the patriarch Joseph, Gen. xlii. 26, and Deut. xxxiii. 16, "that he was separate from his brethren," as it is in our translation; or as the Vulgate and others understand the Hebrew, "that he was a Nazarite among his brethren," is variously understood. Some think that the Hebrew word נזיר, Nazir, in these places, signifies one who is crowned, chosen, separated, or distinguished; the word נזיר, Nazir signifies a crown. The Septuagint translates this word a chief, or him that is honoured. Calmet thinks that this was a term of dignity in the courts of eastern princes, and that at this day in the court of Persia the word Nazir signifies the superintendent general of the king's household, the Nazirian chief officer of the crown, the high steward of his family, treasurers, and revenues; and that in this sense Joseph was the Nazir of the court of Pharaoh. Le Clerc translates the Nazir, a prince, and calls Joseph "the prince of his brethren," in the two places already quoted. Mr Pool declares in favour of this last translation. See Joseph, Chardin, Chrysostom, St Jerome, &c. NAZIANZEN. See Gregory Nazianzen.

NAZIM

Pages 375-375

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, viceroy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governor of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in Hindoostan; the same as Subahdar, or Nabob.

NE EXEAT REGNO

Pages 385-385

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a writ to restrain a person from going out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s licence. F. N. B. 85. It may be directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, to make the party find surety that he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not depart the realm, and on refusal to commit him to prison: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it may be directed to the party himself; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he then goes, he may be fined. And this writ is granted on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> being commenced against a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, when the plaintiff fears the defendant will fly to some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and thereby avoid the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; which hath been sometimes practised: and when thus granted, the party must give bonds to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the rolls, in the penalty of £100, or some other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum, for yielding obedience to it; or satisfy the court, by answer, affidavit, or otherwise, that he hath no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of leaving the kingdom, and give security.

NEALED

Pages 375-375

among seamen, is used when the sounding is deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the shore; as also when the shore is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, clayey, oozy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foul and rocky ground.

NEALING

Pages 375-375
or rather Annealing, a term used for the preparing of several matters, by heating or baking them in the oven, or the like. Nealing of glass, is the baking of glass, to dry, harden, and give it the due consistence, after it has been blown, and fashioned into the proper works. This is usually performed in a kind of a tower called the leer, built over the melting furnace. See Glass. Nealing of glass is also used for the art of staining glass with metallic colours. "One fine use of silver (says Mr Boyle) was only discovered since the art of annealing upon glass came to be practised. For prepared silver, or even the crude metal, being burnt on a glass plate, will tinge it of a fine yellow or golden colour. And there are several mineral earths, and other coarse matters, of use in this art, which by means of fire impart transparent colours to glass, and sometimes very different ones from those of the bodies themselves. Nealing of steel, is the heating it in the fire to a blood-red heat, and then taking it out, and letting it cool gently of itself. This is done to make it softer, in order to engrave or punch upon it. See Tempering and Engraving. Nealing is also used for the art or act of burning or baking earthen or other ware in an oven. The miners at Mendip, when they meet with a rock they cannot cut through, anneal it by laying on wood and coal, and contriving the fire so that they quit the mine before the operation begins, it being dangerous to enter it again before it be quite cleared of the smoke. Nealing of tile is used in ancient statutes for the burning of tile. The word is formed of the Saxon onelan, accendere, to light, burn. NEAP or NEFT TIDES, are those tides which happen when the moon is in the middle of the second and fourth quarters. The neap tides are low tides, in respect of their opposites the spring tides. As the highest of the spring tides is three days after the full or change, so the lowest of the neap is four days before the full or change. On which occasion the seaman say that it is deep neap. NEAPED. When a ship wants water, so that she cannot get out of the harbour, off the ground, or out of the dock, the seaman say she is neaped, or benepaged.

NEAPOLIS

Pages 375-376

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the Nomos Panopolitanus, between Thebae to the south, and Panopolis to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, on the east side of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; otherwise called Caerene. A Neapolis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Neapolis of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>, situated near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> on the south side.—A third of Campania, an ancient town and a colony from Cumae. See Velius, Pliny, Strabo; accounted a Greek city, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stickler for Greek usages, (See Livy, Tacitus). Its hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> were in nothing inferior to those of Baiae, according to Strabo: at two miles distance from it stands the monument of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, held in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> veneration by learned posterity. The Younger Pliny relates, that Virgil's birth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> was more religiously observed by Silius Italicus than his own, especially at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, where he resorted to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> as to a temple. The city is washed by the river Sebethus. Virgil feigns the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Sebethis to preside over the stream. Now Naples, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of that name. See Naples. A fourth, Neapolis of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, near the Meander, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>).—A fifth, an inland town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a> and Arsinoe, (Ptolemy); and to be distinguished from the Canopis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Neapolis, on the east border of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, (id.) A sixth of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, (Strabo); which belonged first to the Ephesians, but afterwards to the Samians, who exchanged Marathusium, a more distant city, for a nearer.—A seventh, Neapolis of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> Adjecta, situated at the distance of 12 miles to the east of Philippi, (Antonine).—An eighth, Neapolis of Paphia, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>, situated between Ambla and Pappa, (Ptolemy).—A ninth of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, the ancient Sichem, which see; so called upon its restoration by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a>, Pliny, Josephus).—A tenth of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, situated on the south-west side of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 30 miles to the north of Metalla; now called Neapolis.—An eleventh, of the Regio Syrtica, called also Leptis.—A twelfth, of Zeugitana on the Mediterranean, to the east of Clypea, and south of the Promontorium Mercuri.

NEBEL

Pages 376-376
or NABLUM, a musical instrument among the Jews. See Nablum.

NEBIO

Pages 376-376
or NEBBIO, a ruined city of Italy, on the north side of the island of Corsica, with a bishop's see, whose bishop resides at San Fiorenzo, from which it is a mile distant.

NEBO

Pages 376-376

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Abarim, and their highest top, whither Moses was ordered to ascend to take a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, and there die. Situated in the land of Moab over against <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>; with a cognominal town at its foot (Niaah) belonging to the Reubenites, which afterwards returned to the Moabites; in Jerome's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> desolate; eight miles to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRON">Hebron</a>.

NEBULY

Pages 376-376
or NEBULEE, in Heraldry, is when a coat is charged with several little figures, in form of words running within one another, or when the outline of a bordure, ordinary, &c., is indented or waved.

NECESSITY

Pages 376-378

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a power superior to all other powers, and equally irresistible by gods and by men. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, as he is quoted by Cudworth, mentions an oracle which declared that "God himself could not shun his destined fate." And among the fragments of Philemon collected by Le Clerc, is the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>: Δούλοι Βασιλέως τοῦτον, ὁ βασιλεὺς δὲν, ὁ δὲν αὐτόν. "We are subject to kings, kings to the gods, and God to Necessity." Hence it is, that, in the Iliad, we find Jove himself, the fire of gods and men, regretting that he was restrained by Necessity from refusing his favourite son from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>. Nay to such a height was this impiety carried in the earliest ages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, that we find <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> teaching that the gods themselves were <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by Necessity, of Night and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">Chaos</a>. This power, though always represented as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> and unintelligent, was however worshipped as a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> nails, wedges, anchors, and melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, as emblems of the inflexible severity of her <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. "In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Corinth she had a temple, in which the goddess Violence likewise reigned, and into which no person was ever permitted to enter but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> who officiated in sacris." Learned men have exercised their ingenuity in vain attempts to trace this potentest notion to its origin. Some, who wished to interpret it in a pious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, have supposed that the gods who are subject to Necessity were only those who were the ministers of the supreme numen; and that by necessity itself was meant nothing more than divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>. But this is not consistent with Hesiod and Homer's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a> of the Gods, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with the epithets fava necesse, dura necesse, by which this power was perpetually distinguished. Others, and among them Moheim, have supposed that this monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> was invented by the Pagan priests, and diligently inculcated upon the minds of the people, in order to excuse the vilenesses of the objects of their worship. For, says he, who could be indignant at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s numberless adulteries, after it was known that in all his actions he was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of blind Necessity: In the thefts of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, the whoredoms of Venus, and the frequent squabbles of the other gods, there could be no moral turpitude, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were under the influence of a superior power. Numina cum videas duris obnoxia futis, Inviaque polys exonerare deos. Necesflty. This account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is at least as plausible as any other which is usually given; but the real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> undoubtedly was, that when men "did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind to do those things which are not convenient; when their foolish heart was darkened, and professing themselves to be wise, they became fools." See PARCE. Necessity, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, as it implies a defect of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, excuses from the guilt of crimes. See Crime. Compulsion and inevitable necessity are a constraint upon the will, whereby a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is urged to do that which his judgement disapproves; and which, it is to be presumed, his will (if left to itself) would reject. As punishments are therefore only inflicted for the abuse of that free will which God has given to man, it is highly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and equitable that a man should be excused for those acts which are done through unavoidable force and compulsion. 1. Of this nature, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, is the obligation of civil subjection, whereby the inferior is constrained by the superior to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> contrary to what his own reason and inclination would suggest: as when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> establishes iniquity by a law, and commands the subject to do an act contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> morality. How far this excuse will be admitted in furo conscientiae, or whether the inferior in this case is not bound to obey the divine rather than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> law, it is not our business to decide; though, among the casuists, it is believed the question will hardly bear a doubt. But, however that may be, obedience to the laws in being is undoubtedly a sufficient extenuation of civil guilt before the municipal tribunal. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> who burnt Latimer and Ridley, in the bigotted days of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, was not liable to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> for executing so horrid an office; being justified by the commands of that magistracy which endeavoured to restore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a>, under the holy auspices of its merciless filter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">Persecution</a>. As to persons in private relations, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> case where constraint of a superior is allowed as an excuse for criminal misconduct, is with regard to the matrimonial subjection of the wife to her husband: for neither a son nor a servant are excused for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of any crime, whether <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> or otherwise, by the command or coercion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; though in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the command or authority of the husband, either express or implied, will privilege the wife from punishment, even from capital offences. And therefore, if a woman commit theft, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGLARY">burglary</a>, or other civil offences against the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, by the coercion of her husband, or even in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, which the law construes a coercion, she is not guilty of any crime; being considered as acting by compulsion, and not of her own will. This doctrine is at least 1000 years old in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, being to be found among the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Ina the West Saxon. And it appears, that among the northern nations on the continent, this privilege extended to any woman transgressing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with a man, and to any servant that committed a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> offence with a freeman: the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> or freeman only was punished, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> or slave dismissed; procul dubio quod alterum liberatis, alterum necessitas impelleret. But (besides that, in our law, which is a stranger to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, no impunity is given to servants, who are as much free agents as their masters) even with regard to wives, this rule admits of an exception in crimes that are mala in se, and prohibited by the law of nature; as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, and the like: not only because these are of a deeper dye, but also, since in a state of nature no one is in subjection to another, it would be unreasonable to screen an offender from the punishment due to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> crimes, by the refinements and subdivisions of civil society. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> also (the highest crime which a member of society can, as such, be guilty of), no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> in coverture shall excuse the wife; no presumption of the husband's coercion shall extenuate her guilt; as well because of the odiousness and dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the crime itself, as because the husband, having broken through the most sacred tie of social <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> by rebellion against the state, has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to that obedience from a wife, which he himself as a subject has forgotten to pay. In inferior misdemeanours also, we may remark another exception, that a wife may be indicted and set in the pillory with her husband, for keeping a brothel: for this is an offence touching the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in which the wife has a principal share; and is also such an offence as the law presumes to be generally conducted by the intrigues of the female <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. And in all cases where the wife offends alone, without the company or coercion of her husband, she is responsible for her offence as much as any femme-folle. 2. Another <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of compulsion or necessity is what our law calls dura per minas; or threats and menaces, which induce a fear of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or other bodily harm, and which take away for that reason the guilt of many crimes and misdemeanors, at least before the human tribunal. But then that fear which compels a man to do an unwarrantable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> ought to be just and well-grounded; such, "qui cadere posse in virum constaret, non timentium et metuendorum," as Bracton expresses it, in the words of the civil law. Therefore, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> or rebellion, a man may be justified in doing many treasonable acts by compulsion of the enemy or rebels, which would admit of no excuse in the time of peace. This, however, seems only, or at least principally, to hold as to positive crimes, so created by the laws of society, and which therefore society may excuse; but, not as to natural offences, so declared by the law of God, wherein human magistrates are only the executioners of divine punishment. And therefore though a man be violently assaulted, and hath no other possible means of escaping death but by killing an innocent person, this fear and force shall not acquit him of murder; for he ought rather to die himself than escape by the murder of an innocent. But in such a case he is permitted to kill the assailant; for there the law of nature, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-<a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> its primary canon, have made him his own protector. 3. There is a third species of necessity, which may be distinguished from the actual compulsion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force or fear; being the result of reason and reflection, which act upon and constrain a man's will, and oblige him to do an action which without such obligation would be criminal. And that is, when a man has his choice of two evils set before him, and, being under a necessity of choosing one, he chooses the least pernicious. pernicious of the two. Here the will cannot be said freely to exert itself, being rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>; or, if active, it is rather in rejecting the greater evil than in choosing the less. Of this sort is that necessity, where a man by the commandment of the law is bound to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> another for any capital offence, or to disperse a riot, and resistance is made to his authority: it is here justifiable, and even necessary, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>, to wound, or perhaps to kill, the offenders, rather than permit the murderer to escape, or the riot to continue. For the preservation of the peace of the kingdom, and the apprehending of notorious malefactors, are of the utmost consequence to the public; and therefore excuse the felony, which the killing would otherwise amount to. 4. There is yet another case of necessity, which has occasioned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> speculation among the writers upon general law; viz. whether a man in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> want of food or clothing may justify stealing either, to relieve his present necessities. And this both Grotius and Puffendorf, together with many other of the foreign jurists, hold in the affirmative; maintaining by many ingenious, humane, and plausible reasons, that in such cases the community of goods, by a kind of tacit concession of society, is revived. And some even of our lawyers have held the same; though it seems to be an unwarranted doctrine, borrowed from the notions of some civilians; at least it is now antiquated, the law of England admitting no such excuse at present. And this its doctrine is agreeable not only to the sentiments of many of the wisest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, particularly Cicero, who holds, That siem cuique incommodum ferendum est, potius quam de alterius commodis detrahendum est; but also to the Jewish law, as certified by King <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> himself: "If a thief steal to satisfy his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> when he is hungry, he shall restore sevenfold, and shall give all the substance of his house:" which was the ordinary punishment for theft in that kingdom. And this is founded upon the highest reason: for men's properties would be under a strange insecurity, if liable to be invaded according to the wants of others; of which wants no man can possibly be an adequate judge but the party himself who pleads them. In England especially, there would be a peculiar impropriety in admitting so dubious an abuse: for by the laws such sufficient provision is made for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> by the power of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, that it is impossible that the most needy stranger should ever be reduced to the necessity of thieving to support nature. The case of a stranger is, by the way, the strongest instance put to Baron Puffendorf, and wherein he builds his principal arguments: which, however they may hold upon the continent, where the parsimonious industry of the natives orders every one to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> or starve, yet must lose all their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and efficacy in England, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> is reduced to a system, and interwoven in our very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. Therefore our laws ought by no means to be taxed with being unmerciful, for denying this privilege to the necessitous; especially when we consider, that the king, on the representation of his ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, hath a power to soften the law, and to extend mercy in cases of peculiar hardship. An advantage which is wanting in many states, particularly those which are democratical: and these have in its stead introduced and adopted, in the body of the law itself, a multitude of circumstances tending to alleviate its rigour. But the founders of our constitution thought it better to vest in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> the power of pardoning particular objects of compassion, than to countenance and establish theft by one general undistinguishing law.

NECHO

Pages 378-378
king of Egypt, began his reign 690 B.C., and was killed eight years after by Sabacon king of Ethiopia. Pianmiticus his son succeeded him, and was the father, as Herodotus informs us, of Necho II. who reigned in the 616 B.C. This Necho II. is celebrated in history for attempting, though in vain, to cut a canal from the Nile to the Arabian gulf. He carried his arms as far as the Euphrates, and conquered the city of Carchemish. This prince is not only known in Scripture under the name of Necho, but also in profane history. He no sooner succeeded to the crown than he raised great land armies, and fitted out vast fleets, as well upon the Mediterranean as upon the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red Sea: he gave battle to the Syrians near the city of Migdol; routed them, and made himself master of the city of Cadys. The learned, however, are not agreed about this city Cadys. Some will have it to be Cades in Arabia Petraea, others Jerusalem; and others say it is the city of Cedes, or Kedesh, in Galilee, in the tribe of Naphtali. The Scriptures acquaint us with the whole expedition of Necho in all its particulars, 2 King xxiii. 29. &c. and 2 Chr. xxxv. 20, 21, &c. In the year of the world 3394, this prince having drawn out his army into the field to make war with the Assyrians or Babylonians, and to take the city of Carchemish, otherwise called Circuism, upon the Euphrates, Josiah king of Judah, who was a tributary to the king of Babylon, marched to oppose his passage. Necho, who had no designs against him, sent to tell him, "What have I to do with you, king of Judah? It is not against you that I am come forth, but against another people, against whom the Lord has commanded me to make war. Leave off therefore to set yourself against me for fear the Lord should punish you for your resistance." But Josiah would not hearken to the remonstrances of Necho, but gave him battle at Megiddo, where he received the wound of which he died. The people of Jerusalem set up Jehoahaz for king of Judah, and Necho soon palled forwards, without making any longer stay in Judea. But at his return from his expedition, which was very successful, he halted at Riblah in Syria; and sending for Jehoahaz king of the Jews, he deposed him, loaded him with chains, and sent him into Egypt. Then coming to Jerusalem, he set up Eliakim, or Jehoiakim, in his place, and exacted the payment of 100 talents of silver and one talent of gold from the country. Jeremiah (xlvii. 2.) acquaints us, that the city of Carchemish was taken from Necho by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah; so that Necho did not enjoy his conquest above four years. Josephus adds, that the king of Babylon pursuing his victory, brought under his dominion all the country which is between the Euphrates and Egypt, excepting Judea. Thus Necho was again reduced within the limits of his own country.

NECROLIUM

Pages 379-379

a word used by some of the alchemical writers to express a remedy almost always capable of averting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and continuing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>.

NECROLOGY

Pages 379-379

necrologium, formed of νεκρός, "dead," and λόγος, "discourse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enumeration," a book anciently kept in churches and monasteries, wherein were registered the benefactors of the same, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their deaths, and the days of their commemoration; as also the deaths of the priors, abbots, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, canons, &c. This was otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> and obituary.

NECROMANCY

Pages 379-381

the art of revealing future events by a pretended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the dead. This superstitious and impious imposture appears to have had its origin at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and to have been thence propagated in every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> with the manners of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> has made us acquainted. The conquests of Sesostris might introduce it into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; the Israelites would naturally borrow it from the people among whom they sojourned 400 years; and it would easily find its way into Phoenicia, from the vicinity of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>. From the Egyptians and Phoenicians it was adopted, with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of paganism, by the Greeks; and it was imported into Rome with Grecian literature and Grecian manners. It was not however confined to the pagan nations of antiquity; it spread itself through all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> nations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and took such deep root as to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> retained even after those nations were converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Of its early antiquity we have complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in the writings of Moses, where it is severely condemned as an abomination to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; and though it appears to have been even then spread into Phoenicia, we might yet conclude its birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to have been Egypt, because, at their exodus, the Israelites were corrupted only by Egyptian superstitions, and because necromancy seems to be one of those whorehouses which the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> represents his countrymen as having brought with them from Egypt, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to practise till they were carried captives into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> from sacred we proceed to consult profane authors, we shall find them not only affirming Egypt to have been the birthplace of necromancy, but in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> accounting for the origin of so impious a delusion. From Diodorus the Sicilian we learn, that the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a> the ferryman of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, of Styx, Cocytus, the Elysian Fields, Tartarus, the judgement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHADAMANTHUS">Rhadamanthus</a>, &c. with the whole scenery of the infernal regions, were imported from Egypt into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians, and indeed all the people of the east, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of caves for burying places, which were well suited to the solemn sadnefs of the surviving friends, and proper receptacles for those who were never more to behold the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. In Egypt, many Necromancers of those subterraneous cavities, being dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rock, still remain, and command the admiration of travellers; and near to the pyramids in particular there are some apartments of a wonderful fabric, which though they extend in length 4400 feet, and are about 30 feet in depth, appear to have been, if not entirely dug, at least reduced to form by the chisel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pickaxe of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. From the practice of burying in such caverns sprung the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the infernal mansions were situated somewhere near the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which by the Egyptians was believed to be not very distant from its surface. In these dreary mansions, it was very easy for such adepts as the priests of Egypt to fabricate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a>, Tartarus, the Elysian Fields, and all those scenes which were displayed before the initiated (see <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">Mysteries</a>), and by them described to the million of the people. As it was in those dark abodes that necromancy was practised, it would be no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for such magicians as withstood Moses to impose so far upon the credulous vulgar, as to make them believe, that in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their invocations they actually <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the ghosts of their friends ascend out of the earth. It appears from the book of Exodus, that the Israelitish women were, even in the wilderness, well acquainted with the use of the mirror, which was therefore undoubtedly known to the Egyptians. But a mirror of a particular form and properly illuminated at the instant required, might easily be made to reflect, in a cavern from which all other light was carefully excluded, the image of the deceased, who was called upon by the necromancer; and we can readily conceive, that with respect to the question to be propounded, a person might be concealed, prepared to give such ambiguous answers as would satisfy the inquirer, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the oracle. The terrified imaginations of the spectators would aid the delusion, and make a very slight resemblance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for the ghost or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of their departed friend; or the necromancer might assign plausible reasons why a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a>, after having dwelt for some time in the infernal regions, should lose something of its resemblance to the body which it animated. Such juggling tricks, though performed by artists less accomplished than Jannes and Jambres, have gained credit among people much more enlightened than the Egyptians could possibly have been when the science of necromancy was invented by their priests. That the Israelites, notwithstanding the prohibition of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, continued to practise the rites of necromancy, is apparent from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>'s transaction with the witch of Endor (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">Magic</a>). From the same transaction, it is likewise apparent that the witches of Israel, and therefore in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the necromancers of Egypt, pretended to evocate the ghosts of the dead by a demon or familiar spirit, which they had at their command to employ upon every emergency. This demon was called Ob; and therefore Saul desires his servants to find him a woman who was mistress of an Ob (A). (A) The original, or radical, signification of this word occurs in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> xxxii. ver. 19.; where Elihu compares his belly to new bottles, which he calls oboth, the plural of ob. But as bottles were then made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, new bottles filled with wine and ready to burst, as Elihu describes them, would of course be of a form nearly globular. It is probable that those wretched impostors had in their pay some persons who occasionally acted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the demon, and when the execution of the plot required their agency, emitted, by means of a cavity dug for that purpose, a low hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> from below the ground. Hence we find Isaiah, in his denunciations against Ariel, saying, "Thou shalt be brought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and shalt speak out of the ground; and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be as of one that hath a familiar spirit (an ob) out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust." But though the Egyptian priests were undoubtedly the inventors of the whole mystery of necromancy, and though it was from them imported into Greece by the Selli or priests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a>, it does not appear that the Grecian necromancers pretended to be masters of obs or familiar spirits. Mopius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, Eumolpus, &c., who either travelled into Egypt in quest of knowledge, or were actually natives of that country, instructed the early Greeks in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> science: but whatever might be the practice of these apostles themselves, their disciples professed to do all the feats of magic by performing certain rites, by offering certain sacrifices, by muttering a certain form of words, by charms, spells, and exorcisms. By these they pretended to evoke the dead as certainly as the Egyptians and Jews did by their familiar spirits. By a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> display of critical learning this might be easily proved from the popular story of Orpheus and Eurydice, which certainly was founded on one of these necromantic deceptions exhibited in a cave near Dodona, where the priests had a hallowed or infernal mansion, in humble <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of those with which the first of them were well acquainted in Egypt. It is indeed evident, without the aid of criticism: no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of any letters is ignorant, that whatever superstitions of this kind prevailed among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were borrowed from the Greeks. But we all know that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> makes one of his shepherds, by means of certain herbs, poisons, and seerlike charms, raise up ghosts from the bottoms of their graves; and Lucan has fabricated a story of this kind, which may be considered as an exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the witch of Endor. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a> he makes young Pompey travel by night to a Thessalian forest, and anxiously inquire of her the issue of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> necromancer, by a tedious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of charms and incantations, conjures up the ghost of a soldier who had been lately slain. The phantom, after a long preamble, denounces a prediction much of the same kind with that which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel received from Samuel at Endor; and though we have elsewhere shown, that nothing but the spirit of God could have foreseen the inevitable destruction of Saul, his sons, and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> (see Magic), it was very easy for any man of tolerable sagacity to foresee the defeat of Pompey's raw and undisciplined troops by the hardy veterans of the victorious Caesar. It would be endless to enumerate all the fallacious evocations of ghosts, and the ambiguous responses returned by those pretended spirits, of which we have accounts from the poets and historians of the celebrated nations of antiquity. We shall therefore proceed to mention a few which occur in the fabulous history of more modern nations, and then leave the subject to the meditation of our readers. In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>'s Northern Antiquities, we have the following account of a necromantic exploit, between which, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the ancient heroes into hell, it is impossible not to remark a striking similitude. "Odin the sovereign of man arises. He saddles his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> Sleipner; he mounts, and is conveyed to the subterraneous abode of Hel. The dog which guards the gates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> meets him. His breath and his jaws are stained with blood. He opens his voracious mouth to bite, and barks a long time at the father of magic. Odin pursues his way; and the infernal cavern resounds and trembles under his horse's hoofs. At length he reaches the deep abode of death, and stops near the eastern gate, where stands the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the prophetess. He sings with a voice adapted to call up the dead; he looks towards the world; he engraves Runic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> on her tomb; he utters mysterious words; and he demands an answer, until the prophetess is constrained to arise and thus utter the words of the dead.—'Who is this unknown that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to disturb my repose, and drag me from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, in which I have been dead so long, all covered with snow, and moistened with the rains?' &c. The Gaelic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> pretended to be masters of the same secret. This is evident from the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, not uncommon among the Scotch Highlanders so lately as in the beginning of the 18th century. By a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> excellently versed in the antiquities of that people, and a steady friend to the writer of this article, we have been informed, that not many years ago some of the Highlanders relied implicitly upon certain oracular responses, called in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> taghairm. This word seems to be compounded of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-TA">ta</a>, which in some parts of the Highlands is still used to denote a spirit or ghost, and ghaim, which signifies calling upon or invoking. Taghairm, therefore, in its original import, is necromancy in the most proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of that word. There were different kinds of taghairm, of which one was very lately practised in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>. The diviner covered himself with a cow's hide, and repaired at night to some deep-founding cave, whither the person who consulted lar. Hence it may be inferred that the original import of ob was round or globular: but b and p being labials, are often changed into each other; and therefore, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> ob is derived the Greek οβ, oculus, oculatus, oculus, and the Latin ops, a name under which the earth was worshipped. Upis was a name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>: the father of one of the Dianas was likewise Upis; but this Upis was undoubtedly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between upis and opis is nothing; hence we are led to believe, that as they are all derived from ob, this word was employed by the early idolaters of Egypt to denote the first and greatest of Pagan gods, the sun. If so, those wretches who pretended to be ministers of obis, were exactly the same kind of impostors with the Pythoneses of the Greeks. Necromancers followed soon after without any attendants. At the mouth of the cave he propounded aloud the questions of which he wanted solutions; and the man within pronounced the responses in a tone of voice similar to that with which the OBS, or pretended demons of antiquity, gave from beneath the ground their oracular answers. That in the latter days of *taghairm*, the Gaelic diviners pretended to evoke ghosts, and from them to extort solutions of difficulties proposed, we have no positive evidence; but that such was the original pretence there can be little doubt, when we reflect either upon the place where this species of divination was practised, or upon the import of the word by which it was denominated. As we have been led to mention *taghairm*, we shall beg leave to make a few observations on another species of it, called *taghairm an uighe*, or "taghairm by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>." This too was last practised in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Skye, by a man of the name of M'Cuidhean, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had long been famous for the art. He lived near a beautiful cascade on a small river; and when consulted on any matter of consequence, he covered his whole body with a cow's hide, that necessary implement of Highland divination, and placed himself between the water of the cascade and the rock over which it flowed. Then another man with a heavy pole gave repeated strokes to the water, and the diviner behind it crying out now and then in Gaelic, "Is this a flock of arm?"
