This operation was continued till M'Cuidhean was perceived to be frantic or furious, when he was considered as in a condition to answer the most important questions. He was frequently consulted about futurity; and though he could not, in the proper sense of the word, be called a necromancer, his responses were listened to as proceeding from something more than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a>. A degree of frenzy, either real or affected, seems to have accompanied the predictions of certain kinds of diviners in all ages; and we cannot help remarking the similarity between the madness of M'Cuidhean and that of the Sibyl in the fifth book of the *Æneid*; though we cannot suppose the one to have been borrowed from the other. *At, Phabi nondum patientes, immanis in antro Bacchatur vates, magnum si pectore puffit Executif Deum: tanto magis ille fatigat Oe rabidum, fera corda domans, singulique premendo.* Struggling in vain, impatient of her load, And lab'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> underneath the vind'rous god; The more she strove to shake him from her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, With more and far superior force he press'd. **DRYDEN.** That all these pretences, whether ancient or modern, to the power of divination by means of familiar spirits, or by the art of necromancy, were groundless as well as impious, it would be affronting the understandings of our readers to offer any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Under the article MAGIC we have said enough on the subject, and perhaps more than enough, to those who know that demons, if they have any existence, and the departed spirits of good and bad men, are all under the control of Him who governs the intellectual as well as material world by fixed and equal laws.—These details of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, however, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be useless, if, by showing how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and wretched a creature man becomes when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECROPOLIS">Necropolis</a> left to his own inventions, they shall make any one grateful for the benefits of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the blessings of revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

NECTANEBUS

Pages 381-381
or **NECTANABIS**, a king of Egypt, who defended his country against the Persians. His grandson of the same name made an alliance with Agesilaus king of Sparta, and with his assistance he quelled a rebellion of his subjects. Some time after he was joined by the Sidonians, Phoenicians, and inhabitants of Cyprus, who had revolted from the king of Persia. This powerful confederacy was soon attacked by Darius the king of Persia, who marched at the head of his troops. Nectanebus, to defend his frontiers against so dangerous an enemy, levied 20,000 mercenary soldiers in Greece, the same number in Libya, and 60,000 were furnished in Egypt. This numerous body was not equal to the Persian forces, and Nectanebus, defeated in battle, gave up all hopes of resistance, and fled into Ethiopia, where he found a safe asylum. His kingdom of Egypt became from that time tributary to the king of Persia.

NECTAR

Pages 381-381

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, the drink of the fabulous deities of the heathens; in contradistinction from their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> food, which was called *ambrosia*.

NECTARINE

Pages 381-381

a fruit differing in nothing from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> peach, of which it is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, but in having a smoother rind and a firmer pulp. See **PERSICA**.

NECTARIUM

Pages 381-382

from *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a>*, the fabled "drink of the gods;" defined by Linnaeus to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the corolla, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appendage to the petals, appropriated for containing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> under a fluid form, that oozes from the plant, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of bees and other insects. Notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, which seems to consider the nectarium as necessary a part of the corolla as the petals, it is certain that all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are not provided with this appendage, neither indeed is it essential to fructification. There is, besides, a manifest impropriety in terming the nectarium a part of the corolla. Linnaeus might, with equal propriety, have termed it a part or appendage of the itamina, calyx, or pointal, as the appearance in question is confined to no particular part of the flower, but is as various in point of situation as of form. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> *nectarium* is exceedingly vague; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any determinate meaning can be affixed to it, is expressive of all the singularities which are observed in the different parts of flowers. The tube, or lower part of flowers with one petal, Linnaeus considers as a true nectarium, because it is generally found to contain the sweet liquor formerly mentioned. This liquor Pontedera compares to that called *amnio* in pregnant animals, which enters the fertile or impregnated seeds; but that this is not at Nectarium least its sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, is evident from this circumstance, that the honey or liquor in question is to be found in flowers where there are either no seeds, or those which, from the want of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs, cannot be impregnated. Thus the male flowers of nettle and willow, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side laurel and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bryony, the male and female flowers of clutia, kiggelaria, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, all abound with the honey or nectar alluded to. Vaillant was of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the nectarium was an essential part of the corolla; for which reason he distinguished the singular appearances in fennel flower and columbine by the name of petals; the coloured leaves which are now termed the petals he denominates the flower cup. That the nectarium, however, is frequently distinct from the petals, is evident both from the well known examples <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, as likewise from the flowers of monkshood, hellebore, ilapyrum, fennel flower of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, barrenwort, gras of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, chocolate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, cherleria, and sauvagea. These general observations being premised, we proceed to take a nearer and more particular view of the principal diversities, both in form and situation, of this striking appendage to the flower. 1. In many flowers the nectarium is shaped like a spur or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; and that either in flowers of one petal, as valerian, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> milfoil (uricularia), butterwort, and calves-foot; or in such as have more than one, as larkspur, violet, fumitory, balsam, and orchis. 2. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, the nectarium is properly a part of the corolla, as lying within the substance of the petals: ranunculus, lily, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> imperial, water <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, mouse tail, ananas or pine apple, dog's-tooth violet, pipe-reed buth, valliflora, hermannia, uvaria, and swertia. 3. The nectarium is frequently placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> or row within the petals, though entirely unconnected with their substance. In this situation it often resembles a cup, as in narcissus. A nectarium of this kind is said by Linnaeus to crown the corolla. The following are examples: daffodil, fea daffodil, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPION">campion</a>, viscid cam- pion, fennel-wort, flabella, cynanchum, nepenthes, cherleria, balsam-tree, African spirea, witch-hazel, olax, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>-flower. 4. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>-cress, buckler, mustard, Barbadoes cherry, and monotropa, the nectarium is situated upon or makes part of the calyx. 5. The nectarium in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> flower-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> is seated upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTHER">anther</a> or tops of the stamens; whence the name adenandra, or glandular anthera, which has been given to this genus of plants. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> it is placed upon the filaments; bean-caper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, fraxinella, marvel of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-flower, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-wort, rocella, and com melina. 6. In hyacinth, flowering-rush, stock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> flower, and rocket, the nectarium is placed upon the seed-bud. 7. In honey-flower, orpine, buckwheat, col linonia, lathrea, navelwort, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, clutia, kiggelaria, sea-side laurel, and African spirea, it is attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> receptacle. Lastly, In ginger, nettle, dyer's weed, heart-seed, coffea, turmeric, grewia, bastard-orpine, vanellae, threew-tree, and willow, the nectarium is of a very singular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, and cannot properly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under any of the foregoing heads. In discriminating the genera, the nectarium often furnishes an essential character. Plants which have the nectarium distinct from the petals, that is, not lodged within their substance, are affirmed by Linnaeus to be generally poisonous. The following are adduced as examples: monkshood, hel lebore, cumbine, fennel-flower, gras of Parnassus, barren-root, oleander, marvel of Peru, bean-caper, succulent fennel-wort, fraxinella, and honey-flower.

NECTROPOLIS

Pages 381-381

a suburb of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It signifies "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">City</a> of the Dead;" wherein there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, gardens, and superb mausoleums. Here Cleopatra is said to have applied the apic to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, to prevent being led in triumph by Augustus, who endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her.

NECTROSIS

Pages 381-381

*visceris*, in Medicine, a complete mortification of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; called also *fideratio* and *sphacelar*.

NECUA

Pages 382-382

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mullein. The Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> both used the stalks of a peculiar kind of mullein, called thyallis by Nicander. For the making of wicks of lamps we have a kind of mullein called lychnites, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-wick mullein, from the nymphs of Dioscorides; but it is not certain that ours is the same plant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used the stalks of many different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> for the wicks of their candles and lamps. The rush, stripped of its bark, was as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> with them as with us for this purpose; and they also used the nettle, this mullein, and many other plants, whose stalks were composed of tough filaments, for the same purpose; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them out like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and when dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> them in melted resin, and other such inflammable substances. When thus prepared, they are readily inflammable, like our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a>; and this mullein, having stalks more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and more firm than all the others, was used to make those lights with which they set fire to the funeral pile, for consuming the ashes of their dead friends.

NECYDALIS

Pages 382-382

a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEEDHAM

Pages 382-385

John Tuberville, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> the 10th of September in the year 1713. His parents were descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble families. His father, who had once possessed a considerable patrimony at Hilston, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Monmouth, was of the younger and Catholic branch of the Needham family: the head of the elder and Protestant branch was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kilmory, created vicount in the year 1625. The father of Mr Needham died young, and left but a small fortune to his four children. His eldest son, who is the subject of this article, prosecuted his studies under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> clergy of the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>, where he took orders, taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> for several years, gave eminent proofs of sagacity and genius, and surpassed all the other professors of that seminary in the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In 1740, he was engaged by his superiors in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the English mission, and was intrusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the school erected at Twyford, near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the Roman Catholic youth. In 1744, he was appointed professor of philosophy in the English college at Lilbon, where, on account of his bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he remained only 15 months. After his return, he passed several years at London and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, which were principally employed in microscopical observations, and in other branches of experimental philosophy. The results of these observations and experiments were published in the Philosophical Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of London in 1749, and in a volume in 1750 at Paris in 1750; and an account of them was also given by M. de Buffon, in the first volumes of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. There was an intimate connexion between this illustrious French naturalist and Mr Needham: they made their experiments and observations together; Needham together; though the results and systems which they deduced from the same objects and operations were totally different. Mr Needham was admitted to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the Royal Society of London in the year 1747, and in the Antiquarian Society some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after. From the year 1751 to 1767 he was chiefly employed in finishing the education of several English and Irish noblemen, by attending them as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in their travels through France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and other countries. He then retired from this wandering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the English seminary at Paris, and in 1768 was chosen by the Royal Academy of Sciences in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> a corresponding member. When the regency of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in order to the revival of philosophy and literature in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, formed the project of an Imperial academy, which was preceded by the erection of a small literary society to prepare the way for its execution, Mr Needham was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Cobenzel and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> Neny, and was appointed successively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of both these foundations. He held this place, together with some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferments in the Low Countries, until his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1781. "His piety, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and purity of manners (we follow the expressions of the abbé Mann) were eminent: his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the doctrines and duties of Christianity was inviolable. His zealous opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> infidels was indefatigable, and even passionate. His probity was untainted. He was incapable of every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of duplicity; his beneficence was universal, and his unsuspicious candour rendered him often a dupe to perfidy." These and other good qualities the panegyrist attributes to his deceased friend; and the learned authors of the Monthly Review, to whom Mr Needham was known, admit the justness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. He was undoubtedly (say they), both an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and a worthy citizen; but though his death be a real loss to the literary world, yet he died seasonably for himself; for had he lived to see <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> II. and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, making free with the paint, patches, and trinkets of the mother <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, confiscating her lands, abolishing her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, suppressing her holidays, introducing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> into her worship, erecting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> conductors to disperse the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of the Vatican, and achieving many other things in this style of improvement, it would have vexed full force his feeling heart. For this honest man was narrow even to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and bigotry in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> system; and we never knew a man in whom there was such an unaccountable mixture of implicit <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and philosophical curiosity as in Mr Needham. He was a keen and judicious observer of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, had a peculiar dexterity in confirming his observations by experiments, and he was always occupied (sometimes indeed with too much fancy and precipitation) in generalizing facts, and reducing them to his system. "His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> (says Abbé Mann) was neither remarkable for fecundity nor method: his writings are rather the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of a subject expressed with energy, and thrown upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in a hurry, than finished treaties." His works are well known both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and in France. Needham, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, 73 miles from London, stands on the Orwell, 9 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Huntingdonshire. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>**, a very common little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> utensil made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, pointed at one end, and pierced at the other, used in sewing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">Needles</a> make a very considerable article in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, though there is scarce any commodity cheaper, the consumption of them being almost incredible.—The sizes are from No. 1, the largest, to No. 25, the smallest. In the manufacture of needles, German and Hungarian steel is of most repute. In the making of them, the first thing is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the steel through a coal fire, and under a hammer, to bring it out of its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> into a cylindrical one. This done, it is drawn through a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hole of a wire-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and returned into the fire, and drawn through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> hole of the iron smaller than the first; and thus successively from hole to hole, till it has acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fineness required for that species of needles; observing every time it is to be drawn, that it be greased over with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, to render it more manageable. The steel thus reduced to a fine wire, is cut in pieces of the length of the needles intended. These pieces are flattened at one end on the anvil, in order to form the head and eye: they are then put into the fire to soften them farther; and thence taken out and pierced at each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of the flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> on the anvil, by force of a puncher of well-tempered steel, and laid on a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> to bring out, with another puncher, the little piece of steel remaining in the eye. The corners are then filed off the square of the heads, and a little cavity filed on each side of the flat of the head; this done, the point is formed with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and the whole filed over: they are then laid to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow iron, crooked at one end, in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> fire; and when taken out thence, are thrown into a bath of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to harden. On this operation a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> depends; too much heat burns them, and too little leaves them soft; the medium is learned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. When they are thus hardened, they are laid in an iron shovel, on a fire more or less brisk in proportion to the thickness of the needles; taking care to move them from time to time. This serves to temper them, and take off their brittleness; great care here too must be taken of the degree of heat. They are then straightened one after another with the hammer, the coldness of the water used in hardening them, having twisted the greatest part of them. The next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is the polishing them. To do this, they take 12,000 or 15,000 needles, and range them in little heaps against each other on a piece of new buckram sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERY">emery</a> dust. The needles thus disposed, emery-dust is thrown over them, which is again sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of olives; at last the whole is made up into a roll, well bound at both ends. This roll is then laid on a polishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and over it a thick plank loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which two men <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> backwards and forwards a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> and a half, or two days, successively; by which means the roll thus continually agitated by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the plank over it, the needles within it being rubbed against each other with oil and emery, are infinitely polished. After polishing, they are taken out, and the filth washed off them with hot water and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>: they are then wiped in hot bran, a little moistened, placed with the needles in a round box, suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, which is kept stirring till the bran and needles be dry. The needles thus wiped in two or three different brans, are taken out and put in wooden vessels, to have the good separated from those whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or eyes have been broken either in polishing or wiping; the points are then all turned the same way, and smoothed with an emery <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> turned with a wheel. This operation finishes them, and there remains nothing but to make them into packets of 250 each. Needles were first made in England by a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in 1543, but the art was lost at his death; it was, however, recovered by Christopher Greening in 1560, who was settled with his three children, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, John, and Thomas, by Mr Damar, ancestor of the present Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, at Long Crendon in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>, where the manufactory has been carried on from that time to this present day. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING_NEEDLE"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">Dipping</a>-Needle, or Inclinatory Needle, a magnetic needle, so hung, as that, instead of playing horizontally, and pointing out <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south, one end dips, or inclines to the horizon, and the other points to a certain degree of elevation above it. The dipping-needle was invented in the year 1576, by one Robert Norman, a compass-maker at Wapping. The occasion of the discovery, according to his own account, was, that it being his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to finish and hang the needles of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> before he touched them, he always found, that immediately after the touch, the north-point would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> or incline downward, under the horizon; infomuch that, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the needle again, he was always forced to put a piece of wax on the south end as a counterpoise. The facility of this effect led him at length to observe the precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the dip, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> which the needle would make with the horizon; and this at London he found to be 71° 50′. In 1723, Mr Graham made a great many observations on the dipping needle, and found the angle to be between 74° and 75° degrees. Mr Nairne, in 1772, found it to be somewhat above 75°. It is not certain whether the dip varies, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> direction, in the same place. The trifling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Mr Norman and Mr Nairne would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to imagine that the dip was unalterable; but Mr Graham, who was a very accurate observer, makes the difference more considerable. It is certain, however, from a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments and observations, that the dip is variable in different latitudes, and that it increases in going northwards. It appears from a table of observations made with the marine dipping-needle in a voyage towards the north pole in 1733, that in lat. 60° 18′, the dip was 75°; and in lat. 70° 45′, it was 79° 52′; in lat. 80° 12′, it was 81° 52′; and in lat. 80° 27′, it was 82° 21′. Several authors have endeavoured to apply this discovery of the dip to the finding of the latitude; and Mr Bond attempted to apply it to the finding of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> also; but for want of observations and experiments he could not make any progress. The affair was farther prosecuted by Mr Whitton, who published a treatise on the longitude, and for some time imagined it was possible to find it exactly by means of the dip of the needle; yet he at last despaired of it, for the following reasons; 1. The weakness of the magnetic power. 2. The concussion of the ship, which he found it exceedingly difficult to avoid so much as was necessary for the accuracy of the experiments. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objection was an irregularity in the motions of all magnetic needles, both horizontal and dipping, by which they, within the compass of about a degree, vary uncertainly backward and forward; even sometimes in a few hours time, without any evident cause. For a particular account of these variations, both of the horizontal and dipping needle, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">Variation</a>. Mr Nairne made a dipping needle in 1772 for the Board of Longitude, which was used in the voyage towards the north pole. This is represented at fig. 2. The needle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a> is 12 inches long, and its axis, the ends BB of which are made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, alloyed with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, rests on friction <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> CCCC, of four inches diameter, each end on two friction wheels; which wheels are balanced with great care. The ends of the axis of the friction wheels are likewise of gold alloyed with copper, and moved in small holes made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> metal; and opposite to the ends of the axes of the needle and the friction wheels, are flat agates, set in DDDD, finely polished. The magnetic needle vibrates within a circle of bell metal, EEEE, divided into degrees and half-degrees; and a line, passing through the middle of the needle to the ends, points to the divisions. The needle of this instrument was balanced before it was made magnetic; but by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, the ends of which are FFFFF, (contrived by the reverend Mr Mitchell) fixed on the axis of the needle, on the arms of which are cut very fine screws to receive small buttons, that may be screwed nearer or farther from the axis, the needles may be adjusted both ways to a great nicety, after being made magnetic, by reversing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and changing the sides of the needle. GG are two levels, by which the line of 0 degrees of the instrument is set horizontal, by means of the four adjusting screws LLLLL; H is the perpendicular axis, by which the instrument may be turned, that the divided <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the circle may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> the east or west; to this axis may be fixed an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> I, which points to an opposite line on the horizontal plate K when the instrument is turned half round; MMMM are screws which hold the glass cover to keep the needle from being disturbed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. When this needle is constructed for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it is suspended by an universal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> on a triangular stand, and adjusted vertically by a plumb line and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> above the divided circle; and the dovetail work at the upper 90°; and the divisions on the circle are adjusted so as to be perpendicular to the horizon by the same plumb line, and an adjoining screw; and when it is adjusted, a pointer annexed to a screw, which serves to move the divided circle, is fixed at the lowest 90°. Whenever the instrument is used to find the dip, it must be so placed that the needle may vibrate exactly in the magnetic meridian. Magnetic Needle, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, a needle touched with a lodestone, and sustained on a pivot or centre; on which playing at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, it directs itself to certain points in or under the horizon; whence the magnetic needle is of two kinds, viz. horizontal or inclinatory. See the article Magnet. Horizontal needles are those equally balanced on each side of the pivot that sustains them, and which, playing horizontally with their two extremes, point out the north and south points of the horizon. For their application and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, see the article Compass. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the horizontal needle, a piece of pure steel is provided; of a length not exceeding five inches. Needles, inches, lest its weight should impede its volubility; very thin, to take its verticity the better; and not pierced with any holes, or the like, for ornament sake, which prevent the equable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the magnetic virtue. A perforation is then made, in the middle of its length, and a brads <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> or head foldered on, whose inner cavity is conical, so as to play freely on a style or pivot headed with a fine steel point. The north point of the needle in our hemisphere is made a little <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the southern; the touch always destroying the balance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> well adjusted before, and rendering the north end heavier than the south, and thus occasioning the needle to dip. The method of giving the needle its verticity or directive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> has been shown already under the article Magnet; but if, after touching, the needle be out of its equilibrium, something must be filed off from the heavier side, till it balance evenly. Needles in sea compasses are usually made of a rhomboidal or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form; we have given their structure already under the article Compass. The needle is not found to point precisely to the north, except in very few places; but deviates from it more or less in different places, and that too at different times; which deviation is called its declination or variation from the meridian. See the article Variation. Surgeons Needles are generally made crooked, and their points triangular; however they are of different forms and sizes, and bear different names, according to the purposes they are used for. The largest are needles for amputation; the next, needles for wounds; the finest, needles for sutures. They have others, very short and flat, for tendons; others, still shorter, and the eye placed in the middle, for tying together of vessels, &c. Needles for couching cataracts are of various kinds; all of which have a small, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and sharp point or tongue, and some with a fulcus at the point. Surgeons have sometimes used two needles in this operation; one with a sharp point for perforating the coats of the eye, and another with a more obtuse point for depressing or couching the opaque crystalline <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENS">lens</a>; but care should be taken in the use of any of these, that they be first well polished with cloth or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, before they are applied to the eye. Mr Warner observes, that the blade of the couching needle should be at least a third part larger than those generally used upon this occasion, as great advantages <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found in the depressing of the cataract, by the increased breadth of the blade of that instrument. The handle, also, if made somewhat shorter than usual, will enable the operator to perform with greater readiness, than he can do with a larger handled instrument. It is to be observed, that needles of silver pierce more easily in stitching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> after an amputation, than those made of steel. Needle Fish. See Syngnathus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. Needles, sharp pointed rocks north of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight. They are situated at the western extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which is an acute point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, from which they have been disjoined by the washing of the sea. There were of these lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rocks formerly three, but about 14 years ago the tallest of them, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>'s Wife, which rose 120 feet above low water mark, and in its shape resembling a needle, being undermined by the constant efforts of the waves, was thrown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and totally disappeared.

NEEDS

Pages 385-385
or St Neots, five miles from Huntingdon, 58 miles from London, so called from the monument of a saint of that name in it, who was burnt by the Danes, is a large well built town, having a handsome strong church, with a very fine steeple, and a stone bridge over the Ouse. NEEDWOOD forest, in Staffordshire, between the Trent, Dove, and Blythe, and near Uttoxeter, is said to exceed all the forests in England in the excellency of its soil and the fineness of its turf.

NEFASTI DIES

Pages 385-385

in Roman antiquity, an appellation given to those days wherein it was not allowed to administer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hold courts. They were so called because, non fari licet, the praetor was not allowed to pronounce the three solemn words or formulas of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, do, dico, addico, I give, I appoint, I adjudge. These days were distinguished in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> N. for nefasius; or N. P. Nefasius Primo, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> was only nefasius in the forenoon, or first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>. The days of a mixed kind were called intercisi.

NEGAPATAN

Pages 385-385

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Coromandel. It was first a colony of the Portuguese, but was taken from them by the Dutch, and now forms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the British territory. It is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 79. 10. N. Lat. 11. 15.

NEGATION

Pages 385-385

in Logic, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the mind affirming one thing to be different from another; as that the foul is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. See Logic.

NEGATIVE

Pages 385-386

in general, something that implies a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a>: thus we say, negative quantities, negative powers, negative signs, &c. Negative Sign. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the negative sign, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, is attended with several consequences that at first sight are admitted with difficulty, and has sometimes given occasion to notions that seem to have no real foundation. This sign implies, that the real value of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> represented by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to which it is prefixed is to be subtracted; and it serves, with the positive sign, to keep in view what elements <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> parts enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of quantities, and in Negative what manner, whether as increments or decrements, (that is, whether by addition or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUBTRACTION">subtraction</a>), which is of the greatest use in this art. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, it serves to express a quantity of an opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to the positive, as a line in a contrary position; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> with an opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; or a centrifugal force in opposition to gravity; and thus often saves the trouble of distinguishing and demonstrating separately, the various <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of proportions, and preserves their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> in view. But as the proportions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> depend on their magnitude only, without regard to their position, and motions and forces are said to be equal, or unequal, in any given ratio, without regard to their directions; and, in general, the proportion of quantity relates to their magnitude only, without determining whether they are to be considered as increments or decrements; so there is no ground to imagine any other proportion of $-b$ and $+a$ (or of $-1$ and $1$) than that of the real magnitudes of the quantities represented by $b$ and $a$, whether these quantities are, in any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, to be added or subtracted. It is the same thing to subtract the decrement, as to add an equal increment, or to subtract $-b$ from $a-b$, as to add $+b$ to it; and because multiplying a quantity by a negative <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> implies only a repeated subtraction of it, the multiplying $-b$ by $-n$, is subtracting $-b$ as often as there are units in $n$; and is therefore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to adding $+b$ so many times, or the same as adding $+nb$. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we infer from this, that $i$ is to $-n$ as $-b$ to $nb$, according to the rule, that unit is to one of the factors as the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> is to the product, there is no ground to imagine, that there is any mystery in this, or any other meaning than that the real magnitudes represented by $i$, $n$, $b$, and $nb$ are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a>. For that rule relates only to the magnitude of the factors and product, without determining whether any factor, or the product, is to be added or subtracted. But this likewise must be determined in algebraic computations; and this is the proper use of the rules concerning the signs, without which the operation could not proceed. Because a quantity to be subtracted is never produced in composition by any repeated addition of a positive, or repeated subtraction of a negative, a negative <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> number is never produced by composition from the root. Hence $\sqrt{-1}$, or the square root of a negative, implies an imaginary quantity; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, is a mark or character of the impossible cases of a problem, unless it is compensated by another imaginary symbol or supposition, when the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> may have a real signification. Thus $i+\sqrt{-1}$, and $i-\sqrt{-1}$, taken separately, are imaginary, but their sum is $2$; as the conditions that separately would render the solution of a problem impossible, in some cases destroy each other's effect when conjoined. In the pursuit of general conclusions, and of simple forms representing them, expressions of this kind must sometimes arise where the imaginary symbol is compensated in a manner that is not always so obvious. By proper substitutions, however, the expression may be transformed into another, wherein each particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> may have a real signification as well as the whole expression. The theorems that are sometimes briefly discovered by the use of this symbol, may be demonstrated without it by the inverse operation, or some other way; and though such symbols are of some use in the computations by the method of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a>, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> cannot be said to depend upon arts of this kind. See Algebra and Fluxions. NEGATIVE <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>. See the article Electricity, paffion. See also Positive Electricity. NEGINOTH. This term is read before some of the Psalms, as Psalm lxvii. It signifies string instruments of music, to be played on by the fingers, or women musicians; and the titles of these psalms where this word is found, may be thus translated, A psalm of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of music, who presides over the string instruments.

NEGOMBO

Pages 386-386

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, on the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Ceylon. It has a fort built by the Portuguese, which was taken from them by the Dutch in 1640. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8°. 25'. N. Lat. 17°. 0'.

NEGRO

Pages 386-390

Homo peli nigra, a name given to a variety of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, who are entirely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and are found in the torrid zone, especially in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> which lies within the tropics. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a> we meet with many various shades; but they likewise differ far from other men in all the features of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Round <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> cheek-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, a forehead somewhat elevated, a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, flat nose, thick lips, small ears, ugliness, and irregularity of shape, characterize their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance. The negro women have the loins greatly depressed, and very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> buttocks, which gives the back the shape of a saddle. Vices the most notorious seem to be the portion of this unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; idleness, treachery, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, cruelty, impudence, cheating, lying, profanity, debauchery, naughtiness, and intemperance, are said to have extinguished the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and to have silenced the reproaches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. They are strangers to every sentiment of compassion, and are an awful example of the corruption of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> when left to himself. The origin of the negroes, and the cause of their remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> from the rest of the human species, has much perplexed the naturalists. Mr Boyle has observed, that it cannot be produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>: for though the heat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> may darken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the skin, yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> does not show that it is sufficient to produce a new blackness like that of the negroes. In Africa itself, many nations of Ethiopia are not black; nor were there any blacks originally in the West Indies. In many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the African region inhabited by the blacks, the people are but tawny. He adds, that there are negroes in Africa beyond the southern tropic; and that a river sometimes parts nations, one of which is black, and the other only tawny. Dr Barriere alleges that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALL">gall</a> of negroes is black, and being mixed with their blood is deposited between the skin and scarf-skin. However Dr Mitchel of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, in the Philosophical Transactions, No. 476, has endeavoured by many learned arguments to prove, that the influence of the sun in hot countries, and the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of their inhabitants, are the remote causes of the colour of the negroes, Indians, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and such philosophers as he, whose genius and imagination are too lively to submit to a dry and painful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of facts, have contended that no physical cause is sufficient to change the colour, and what we call the regular features of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> men, to the dark hue and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> of the woolly-headed negro. Their arguments have been examined with much acuteness and ingenuity by Dr Stanhope Smith of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, Dr Hunter, and Professor Zimmerman, who have made it in a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> probable, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the sun is the original and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cause of the black colour, as well as distorted features of the negro. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">AMERICA</a>, No 48—51, and COMPLEXION. True negroes are found in no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe where the heat of the climate is not very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. They exist nowhere but in the torrid zone, and only in three regions situated in that zone, viz. in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and on the western shores of Africa, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, and the Papous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> what is called New Guinea. In all these regions the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is scorching, and the heat excessive. The inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> are whitest; and as we advance southwards towards the line, and those countries on which the sun's rays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> more perpendicularly, the complexion gradually assumes a darker <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. And the same men, whose colour has been rendered black by the powerful action of the sun, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they remove to the north, gradually become whiter (at least their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a>), and lose their burnt colour. Whites when transported into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> regions of the torrid zone, are the first subject to fever; the skin of the face, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and feet, becomes burnt, hardens and falls off in scales. Hitherto the colour of negroes appears to be only local, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRINSIC">extrinsic</a>, and accidental, and their short frizzled and sparse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is to be accounted for in the very same manner. Climate possesses great and evident influences on the hair, not only of man, but of all other animals. If in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> these transmutations are acknowledged to be consistent with identity of kind, they ought not in the other to be esteemed criterions of different species. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> has adapted the pliancy of her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to the situations in which she may require it to be placed. The beaver and sheep removed to the warm latitudes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, the one its fur, and the other its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, for a coarse hair that preserves the animal in a more moderate temperature. The coarse and black <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> of the bear is converted, in the arctic regions, into the finest and whitest fur. The colour of the hair is likewise changed by climate. The bear is white under the arctic circle; and, in high northern latitudes, foxes, hares, and rabbits, are found white. Similar effects of climate are discernible on mankind. The hair of the Danes is generally <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; of the English, fair or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; and of the French, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> black. The hair of all people of colour is black, and that of the African negroes is likewise sparse and curled in a manner peculiar to themselves; but this peculiarity is analogous to the effect which a warm climate has on almost every other animal. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">Cold</a>, by obstructing the perspiration, tends to throw out the perspirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> accumulated at the skin in an additional coat of hair. A warm climate, by opening the pores, evaporates this matter before it can be concreted into the substance of hair; and the laxness and aperture of the pores render the hair liable to be easily eradicated by innumerable incidents. Its curl may result in part from the nature of the secretion by which it is nourished, and in part from external heat. That it depends in some degree on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the secretion is rendered highly probable from its appearance on the chin and other parts of the human body. Climate is as much distinguished by the nature and proportion of the secretions as by the degree of heat. (See PHYSIOLOGY, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 6.) Whatever be the nutriment of the hair, it is evidently combined in the torrid zone of Africa with some fluid of a highly volatile or ardent quality, which produces the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> smell of many African nations. Saline secretions tend to curl and to burn the hair. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of any volatile spirit would render its surface dry and disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>; whilst the centre continuing distended by the vital <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, these opposite dilatations and contractions would necessarily produce a curve, and make the hair grow involved. External and violent heat parching the extremities of the hair, tends likewise to involve it. A hair held near the fire instantly coils itself up. Africa is the hottest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the globe; and the influence of its heat, either external or internal, or both, in giving the peculiar form to the hair of the natives, appears, not only from its sparrows and its curl, but from its colour. It is not of a shining, but of an adult black; and its extremities tend to brown, as if it had been scorched by the fire. The peculiarities of the negro features and form may likewise be accounted for from the excessive heat of the climate and the state of African <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Being savages, they have no arts to protect them from the rays of a burning sun. The heat and ferocity of the sky preserving the lives of the children without much care of the parents, they seem of course to be, in the interior parts of the country, negligent of their offspring. Able themselves to endure the extremes of that ardent climate, they injure their children to it from their most tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. They suffer them to roll in the dust and sand beneath the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> rays of a vertical sun. The mother, if she be engaged, lays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the infant on the first spot she finds, and is seldom at the pains to seek the miserable shelter of a barren shrub, which is all that the interior country affords. When we reflect on the influence of a glare of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> upon the eye, and on the distortions of countenance produced by our efforts to repel or prevent it, we need not wonder, that the plaintive features of a negro infant should, by constant exposure, acquire that permanent irregularity which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> their characteristic ugliness. But besides the climate, food and clothing and modes of life have prodigious effects on the human form and features. This is apparent even in polished <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and labouring part of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> are much more coarse in their features, and ill formed in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, than persons of better fortune and more liberal means of subsistence. What an immense difference exists in Scotland, for instance, between the chiefs and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> of the Highland clans? If they had been separately found in different countries, they would have been ranged by some philosophers under different species. A similar distinction takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and peasantry of France, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and of Germany. That food and clothing, and the different modes of life, have as great an influence upon the shapes and features of the Africans as upon the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, is evident. evident from the different appearances of the negroes in the southern republics of America according to the stations in which they are employed. "The field slaves (says Dr Smith) are badly fed, clothed, and lodged. They live in small huts on the plantations, where they labour, remote from the society and example of their superiors. Living by themselves, they retain many of the customs and manners of their African <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> servants, on the other hand, who are kept near the persons, or employed in the families of their masters, are treated with great lenity; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is light; they are fed and clothed like their superiors; they see their manners, adopt their habits, and infensibly receive the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of elegance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The field slaves are, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, slow in changing the aspect and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of Africa. The domestic servants have advanced far before them in acquiring the agreeable and regular features, and the expressive countenance of civil society. The former are frequently ill-shaped. They preserve, in a great degree, the African lips, nose, and hair. Their genius is dull, and their countenance sleepy and stupid. The latter are straight and well proportioned; their hair extended to three, four, and sometimes even to six or eight inches; the size and shape of the mouth handsome, their features regular, their capacity good, and their look animated." Upon the whole, we hope that the reader, who shall candidly weigh in his own mind what we have said at present and under the article Complexion, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> agree with us, that the black colour in the torrid zone, the sparse crisp hair of the negroes, and the peculiarities of their features and form, proceed from causes altogether extrinsic; that they depend on local temperature and the state of society; and that they are as accidental as the various shades of colour which characterize the different nations of Europe. If the whites be considered as the stock whence all others have sprung, it is easy to conceive how they have degenerated into negroes. Some have conjectured that the complete change may have taken place at the end of three centuries, whilst others have thought that it could not be effected in less than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. Such conjectures can be formed from no certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATA">data</a>; and a much greater length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is undoubtedly necessary before negroes, when transplanted into our temperate countries, can entirely lose their black colour. By crossing the breed with whites, every taint of the negro colour may be expelled, we believe, from the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> (A). But the most serious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> brought against the poor negroes is, that of the vice said to be natural to them. If they be indeed such as their enemies represent them, treacherous, cruel, revengeful, and intemperate, by a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of nature, they must be a different race from the whites; for though all these vices abound in Europe, it is evident that they proceed not from nature, but from wrong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, which gives to the youthful mind such deep impressions as no future exertions can completely eradicate. Let us inquire coolly if the vices of the negroes may not have a similar origin. In every part of Africa with which the nations of Europe have any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> prevails of the worst kind. Three-fourths of the people are slaves to the rest, and the children are born to no other inheritance. "Most parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> differ in their governments; some are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> monarchies, whilst others draw near to an aristocracy. In both the authority of the chief or chiefs is unlimited, extending to life, and it is exercised as often as criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> require, unless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is commuted into slavery; in which case the offender is sold, and if the shipping will not buy the criminal, he is immediately put to death. Fathers of free condition have power to sell their children, but this power is very seldom enforced." In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, however, a father will sell a son or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, or perhaps both, for a piece of cloth, a collar or girdle of coral or beads, Univer. and often for a bottle of wine or brandy. A husband may have as many wives as he pleases, and repudiate or even sell them, though with child, at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The wives and concubines, though it be a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crime for the former to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, have a way to rid themselves of their husbands, if they have let their affections upon a new gallant, by accusing them of some crime for which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> is death. In a word, the bulk of the people in every state of Africa are born slaves to great men, reared as such, held as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and as property sold (see Slavery.) There are indeed many circumstances by which a free man may become a slave: such as being in debt, and not able to pay; and in some of such cases, if the debt be large, not only the debtor, but his family likewise, become the slaves of his creditor, and may be sold. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">Adultery</a> is commonly punished in the same manner, both the offending parties being sold, and the purchase-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid to the injured husband. Obi, or pretended <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a> (in which all the negroes firmly believe, see Witchcraft), is another, and a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> offence, for which slavery is adjudged the lawful punishment; and it extends to all the family of the offender. There are various other crimes which subject the offender and his (A) 1. A white man with a negro woman, or a negro man with a white woman, produce a mulatto, half white and half black, or of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>-blackish colour, with black, short, frizzled hair. 2. A white man with a mulatto woman, or a negro with a mulatto woman, produce a quadroon, three fourths white and one fourth black, or three fourths black and one fourth white, or of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> yellow than the former. In America, they give the name of cabres to those who are descended from a black man and a mulatto woman, or a mulatto man and a black woman, who are three fourths black and one fourth white, and who are not so black as a negro, but blacker than a mulatto. 3. A white man with a quadroon woman, or a negro with a quadroon woman, produce a metizo, seventh eighths white and one eighth black, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> eighths black and one eighth white. 4. A white man with a metizo woman, or a negro with a metizo woman, produce, the one almost a perfect white, the other almost a perfect black, called a quinteroon. This is the last gradation, there being no visible difference between the fair quinteroons and the whites: and the children of a white and quinteroon consider themselves as free from all taint of the negro race. his children to be sold; and it is more than probable, that if there were no buyers, the poor wretches would be murdered without mercy. In such a state of society, what dispositions can be looked for in the people, but cruelty, treachery, and revenge? Even in the civilized nations of Europe, blest with the lights of law, science, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, some of the lower orders of the community consider it as a very trivial crime to defraud their superiors; whilst almost all look up to them with stupid malevolence or rancorous envy. That a depraved people, when they get power into their hands, are revengeful and cruel, the present age affords a dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> in the conduct of the demagogues of a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and it is wonderful that the negroes of Africa, unacquainted with moral principles, blinded by the cruelest and most abhorred superstitions, and whose customs tend to eradicate from the mind all natural affection, should sometimes display to their lordly masters of European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> the same spirit that has been so generally displayed by the lower orders of Frenchmen to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, and the family of their murdered sovereign! When we consider that the majority of the negroes groan under the cruelest slavery, both in their own country and in every other where they are to be found in considerable numbers, it can excite no surprise that they are in general treacherous, cruel, and vindictive. Such are the caprices of their tyrants at home, that they could not preserve their own lives or the lives of their families for any length of time, but by a perpetual vigilance, which must necessarily degenerate, first into cunning, and afterwards into treachery; and it is not conceivable that habits formed in Africa should be instantly thrown off in the West Indies, where they are the property of men whom some of them must consider as a different race of beings. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, that the ill qualities of the negroes have been greatly exaggerated. Mr Edwards, in his valuable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the West Indies, affirms us that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANDINGO">Mandingo</a> negroes display such gentleness of disposition and demeanour, as would seem the result of early education and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, were it not that, generally speaking, they are more prone to theft than any of the African tribes. It has been supposed that this propensity, among other vices, is natural to a state of slavery, which degrades and corrupts the human mind in a deplorable manner; but why the Mandingoes should have become more vicious in this respect than the rest of the natives of Africa in the same condition of life, is a question he cannot answer. "The circumstances which (according to the same author) distinguish the Koromantyn or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> Coast negroes from all others, are firmness both of body and mind; a ferociousness of disposition; but withal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, courage, and a stubbornness, or what an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman would have deemed an elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, which prompts them to enterprises of difficulty and danger, and enables them to meet death, in its most horrid shape, with fortitude or indifference. They sometimes take to labour with great promptitude and alacrity, and have constitutions well adapted for it; for many of them have undoubtedly been slaves in Africa. But as the Gold Coast is inhabited by various tribes, which are engaged in perpetual warfare and hostility with each other, there cannot be a doubt that many of the captives taken in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and sold in the European settlements, were of free condition in their native country, and perhaps the owners of slaves themselves. It is not wonderful that such men should endeavour, even by means the most desperate, to regain the freedom of which they have been deprived; nor do I conceive that any further circumstances are necessary to prompt them to action, than that of being sold into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> in a distant country. One cannot surely but lament (says our author) that a people thus naturally intrepid, should be sunk into so deplorable a state of barbarity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; and that their spirits should ever be broken down by the yoke of slavery. Whatever may be alleged concerning their ferociousness and implacability in their present notions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and wrong, I am persuaded that they possess qualities which are capable of, and well deserve, cultivation and improvement. "Very different from the Koromantyns are the negroes imported from the Bight of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENIN">Benin</a>, and known in the West Indies by the name of Eboes. So great is their constitutional timidity and despondency of mind, as to occasion them very frequently to seek, in a voluntary death, a refuge from their own melancholy reflections. They require therefore the gentlest and mildest treatment to reconcile them to their situation; but if their confidence be once obtained, they manifest as great fidelity, affection, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, as can reasonably be expected from men in a state of slavery. The females of this nation are better labourers than the men, probably from having been more hardly treated in Africa. "The natives of Whidah, who, in the West Indies, are generally called Papaws, are unquestionably the most docile and best disposed slaves that are imported from any part of Africa. Without the fierce and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> manners of the Koromantyn negroes, they are also happily exempt from the timid and desponding temper of the Eboes.
