The cheerful acquiescence with which these people apply to the labours of the field, and their constitutional aptitude for such employment, arise, without doubt, from the great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> paid to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> in their native country. Bofman speaks with rapture of the improved state of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages, and the industry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and obliging manners of the natives. He observes, however, that they are much greater thieves than those of the Gold Coast, and very unlike them in another respect, namely, in the dread of pain, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of death. They are, says he, so very apprehensive of death, that they are unwilling to hear it mentioned, for fear that alone should hasten their end; and no man <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to speak of death in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, or any great man, under the penalty of suffering it himself, as a punishment for his presumption. He relates, further, that they are addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> beyond any people of Africa. All these propensities are observable in the character of the Papaws in a state of slavery in the West Indies. That punishment which excites the Koromantyn to rebel, and drives the Ebo negro to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>, is received by the Papaws as the chastisement of legal authority, to which it is their duty to submit patiently. The case seems to be, that the generality of these people are in a state of absolute slavery in Africa, and, having been habituated to a life of labour, they submit to a change of situation with little reluctance." Having recited such observations as occurred to him on contemplating the various tribes of negroes from each other, Mr Edwards thus estimates their general character, influenced as they are by circumstances which soon efface the native and original impressions which distinguish one nation from another when newly imported into the West Indies. " notwithstanding what has been related of the firmness and courage of the natives of the Gold Coast, it is certain that the negroes in general in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> (such of them at least as have been any length of time in a state of servitude) are of a distrustful and cowardly disposition. So degrading is the nature of slavery, that fortitude of mind is lost as free agency is retrained. To the same cause probably must be imputed their propensity to conceal or violate the truth; which is so general, that the vice of falsehood is one of the most prominent features in their character. If a negro is asked even an indifferent question by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he seldom gives an immediate reply; but, affecting not to understand what is said, compels a repetition of the question, that he may have time to consider, not what is the true answer, but what is the most politic one for him to give. The propensity observable in many of them to the vice of theft has already been noticed; and I am afraid (says our author), that evil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> makes it almost general. It is no easy matter, I confess, to discriminate those circumstances which are the result of proximate causes, from those which are the effects of national customs and early habits in savage life; but I am afraid that cowardice and dissimulation have been the properties of slavery in all ages, and will continue to be so to the end of the world. It is a situation that necessarily suppresses many of the best affections of the human heart.—If it calls forth any latent virtues, they are those of sympathy and compassion towards persons in the same condition of life; and accordingly we find that the negroes in general are strongly attached to their countrymen, but above all, to such of their companions as came in the same ship with them from Africa. This is a striking circumstance: the term "familiar" is understood among them as signifying a relationship of the most endearing nature; perhaps as recalling the time when the sufferers were cut off together from their common country and kindred, and awakening <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> sympathy from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of mutual affliction. But their benevolence, with a very few exceptions, extends no further. The softer virtues are seldom found in the bosom of the enslaved African. Give him sufficient authority, and he becomes the most remorseless of tyrants. Of all the degrees of wretchedness endured by the sons of men, the greatest, assuredly, is the misery which is felt by those who are unhappily doomed to be the slaves of slaves; a most unnatural relation, which sometimes takes place in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> plantations. The same observation may be made concerning their conduct towards the animal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. Their treatment of cattle under their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> is brutal beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. Even the useful and social qualities of the dog secure to him no kind usage from an African master. One of the most pleasing traits in their character is the respect and attention which they pay to their aged countrymen. The whole body of negroes on a plantation must be reduced to a deplorable state of wretchedness, if, at any time, they suffer their aged companions to want the common necessaries of life, or Negroland—many of its comforts, as far as they can procure them. They seem to be actuated on these occasions by a kind of involuntary impulse, operating as a primitive law of nature, which scorns to wait the cold dictates of reason: among them, it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of a common duty, which courts no observation, and looks for no applause." As the colour, and features, and moral qualities of the negroes may be thus easily accounted for by the influence of climate and the modes of savage life, so there is good reason to believe that their intellectual endowments are equal to those of the whites who have been found in the same circumstances. Of those imitative arts in which perfection can be attained only in an improved state of society, it is natural to suppose that they have but little knowledge; but the fabric and colours of the Guinea cloths are a proof of their native ingenuity. In the West Indies many of them are expert carpenters, some watchmakers, and one or two have successfully practised physic; whilst others have figured both in Latin and in English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, so that we cannot doubt but that "God, who made the world, hath made of one blood all nations of men," and animated them with minds equally rational.

NEGROLAND

Pages 390-391
or NIGERIA, a country of Africa, lying next to Guinea towards the north, and extending from 18° of west to 23° of east longitude, and from 9° to 20° of north latitude. On the north it is bounded by Zaara or the Desert; on the east, by countries unknown; on the south, by Guinea; and on the west, by the Atlantic ocean; and is watered by the great river Niger or Senegal, which runs through it from east to west. The Europeans have settlements on the coasts of this country, especially near the mouths of the Niger and Gambia, which last is supposed to be a branch of the former. A great many nations inhabit the banks of the rivers; some Pagans, some Mohammedans, of different languages, and independent of one another. The country is fruitful, especially along the rivers; abounding in rice, Guinea grain, and Indian corn, where it is cultivated; and with cocoa nuts, plantains, pulse, palm trees, and tropical fruits; nor is it destitute of cattle, and a variety of other animals, particularly such as abound in Guinea. See GUINEA. Negroland is fertilized by the overflowing of its rivers the Senegal and Gambia, as Egypt is by the Nile. It hath not yet been ascertained whether the Gambia is a branch of the Senegal or not. As far as the Europeans have penetrated up the country, they appear to be distant; and the Mandingo negroes report that the Gambia has a different origin. The entrance into the Niger, or Senegal river, is narrow and somewhat difficult, by reason of its immovable bar, and sandy shoals, as well as the several islands at the mouth of it, and the several canals and marshes that clog it: but after sailing up eight or ten leagues, it is found broad and deep, and fit to carry large vessels; and, excepting about five or six leagues on each side above the mouth, which is sandy and barren ground, the banks are covered with stately trees and villages, and the country in general is fertile and well watered; for, like the Nile, this river overflows its banks for many leagues, and enriches the land to a great degree, Negroland gree, though, for want of skill, the inhabitants do not reap the advantages which they might obtain from its fertility. The people on both sides of the river live as near to it as they can, and feed great herds of cattle, sowing large and small millet, the former of which is called by us Turkey wheat, in great quantities, and with great increase. If the river fails of overflowing at its usual season, a great scarcity ensues in the adjacent country; and, even when it overflows regularly, it breeds such vast flights of grasshoppers and insects, as quite darken the air, and frequently devour the whole produce of the soil: in which case the people kill those insects and eat them; which they do either by pounding in leather bags, and then boiling them in milk, or, which is reckoned the more delicious method, by frying or broiling them over a light blaze in a fryingpan full of holes. Thus the legs and wings of the insects are burnt off, and the rest of the body is sufficiently roasted to be eaten as a dainty, which they look upon to be very wholesome and nourishing. To the east, north-east, and south-east of the island of Senegal, the country, as far as it is known, is overrun with woods and marshes: the Senegal, Gambia, and Sherbro, which are looked upon by some as branches of one immense river, passing through it in their way to the Atlantic ocean. During the rainy months, which begin in July, and continue to October, they lay the whole country under water; and indeed the sudden rise of these rivers is incredible to such as are not acquainted with the violent rains that fall between the tropics. At Galam, 950 miles from the mouth of the Senegal, the waters rise 150 feet perpendicular from the bed of the river. At the island of Senegal, the river rises gradually, during the rainy season, above 20 feet perpendicular over part of that flat coast; which of itself so refreshes the water, that ships lying at anchor, at the distance of three leagues from its mouth, generally make use of it, and fill their water there for their voyage home. When the rains are at an end, which soon happens in October, the intense heat of the sun usually dries up those stagnating waters which lie on the higher parts, and the remainder from lakes and marshes, in which are found all sorts of dead animals. At last, those two are quite dried up; and then the effluvia that arise are almost quite insupportable. At this season the winds blow so hot from the land, that they may be compared to the heat proceeding from the mouth of an oven, and they bring with them an intolerable smell. The wolves, tigers, lions, and other wild beasts, then resort to the river, steeping their body under water, and only their snouts above it for the sake of breathing. The birds soar to an immense height in the air, and fly a vast way over the sea, where they continue till the wind changes, and comes from the west.

NEGROPONT

Pages 391-391

anciently Euboea, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, stretching along the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Achaia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVADIA">Livadia</a>, from which it is separated by a narrow channel called the Euripus. This strait is so narrow, that the island is joined to the continent by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> thrown over it; and here, it is thought, there was formerly an isthmus. The irregularity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> in the Euripus hath from the remotest antiquity been Nehemiah very remarkable, and this irregularity is found to be connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. From the three last days of the old moon to the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the new moon, and from the 14th to the 20th day inclusive, they are regular; but on the other days they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, flowing 12, 13, or 14 times in the space of 24 hours, and ebbing as often. The island is 90 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in the widest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; and produces corn, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fruit, and cattle, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance. The only <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the island worth notice is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, which is also called Negropont; and which is walled, and contains about 15,000 inhabitants; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> are said to be much more numerous than the Turks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> bawhaw, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, who is also governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the island, and the adjacent continent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, resides here: and the harbour, which is very safe and spacious, is seldom without a fleet of galleys, ready to be put to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> against the pirates and the Maltese. A part of the bridge between the city and the coast of Greece, consists of a draw bridge no longer than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> to let a galley <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through.

NEHEMIAH

Pages 391-393
or NEEMIAS, son of Hachaliah, was born at Babylon during the captivity, (Neh. i. 1, 2, &c.) He was, according to some, of the race of the priests, but, according to others, of the tribe of Judah and the royal family. Those who maintain the first opinion, support it by a passage in Ezra, (x. 10,) where he is called a priest; but those who believe that he was of the race of the kings of Judah, say, 1st, That Nehemiah having governed the republic of the Jews for a considerable time, there is great probability he was of that tribe of which the kings always were. 2ndly, Nehemiah mentions his brethren Hanani, and some other Jews, who coming to Babylon during the captivity, acquainted him with the sad condition of their country. 3rdly, The office of cupbearer to the king of Persia, to which Nehemiah was promoted, is a further proof that he was of an illustrious family. 4thly, He excuses himself from entering into the inner part of the temple, probably because he was only a laic, (Neh. vi. 11.) "Should such a man as I flee? And who is there that, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life?" The Scripture (Ezra ii. 63. Nehem. vii. 65.) calls him neumtir/batha, that is to say, "cup bearer;" for he had this employment at the court of Artaxerxes Longimanus. He had an exceeding great tenderness for the country of his fathers, though he had never seen it; and one day, as some Jews newly come from Jerusalem acquainted him with the miserable estate of that city, that its walls were beat down, its gates burnt, and the Jews were become a reproach among all nations; he was sensibly affected with this relation; he faltered, prayed, and humbled himself before the Lord, that he would be favourable to the design he had then conceived of asking the king's permission to rebuild Jerusalem. The course of his attendance at court being come, he presented the cup to the king according to custom; but with a countenance sad and dejected; which the king observing, entertained some suspicion, as if he might have had some bad design; but Nehemiah (ii.) discovering the occasion of his disquiet, Artaxerxes gave him leave to go to Jerusalem, and repair its walls and gates; but, however, upon this condition, that he should Nehemiah should return to court at a time appointed. Letters were made out, directed to the governors beyond the Euphrates, with orders to furnish Nehemiah with timbers necessary for covering the towers and gates of the city, and the house designed for Nehemiah himself, who was now appointed governor of Judea, in the year of the world 3359. Nehemiah being arrived at Jerusalem with the king's commission, went round the city; and having viewed the condition of the walls, assembled the chief of the people, produced his commission, and exhorted them to undertake the reparation of the gates and walls of the city. He found every person ready to obey him; whereupon he immediately began the work. The enemies of the Jews observing their works in such forwardness, made use of all the means in their power to deter Nehemiah from this undertaking, and made several attempts to surprise him; but finding that their designs were discovered, and that the Jews kept upon their guard, they had recourse to craft and stratagem, endeavouring to draw him into an ambuscade in the fields, where they pretended they would finish the dispute at an amicable conference: but Nehemiah gave them to understand, that the work he had begun required his personal attendance; and therefore he could not come to them. He sent the same answer to four several messengers that they sent one after another on the same subject, (Id. iv. and vi.) Sanballat, the chief of the enemies of the Jews, together with his associates, wrote word, that a report was spread that the Jews were building the walls of Jerusalem only with a design to make it a place of strength, to support them in an intended revolt; so that it was said also that Nehemiah had harboured false prophets to favour his designs, and to encourage the people to choose him king; and to stop the course of these rumours, he advised him to come to him, that they might confer together, and take such resolutions as should be found convenient. Nehemiah gave himself no trouble on this account, but returned for answer, that all those accusations were false and made at random. About the same time he discovered, that a false prophet, called Shemaiah, had been corrupted by his enemies, and that some of the chief of the city were secretly in confederacy with them. Yet all this did not discourage him; he went on with his work, and happily completed it in two and fifty days after it had been begun. Then he made a dedication of the walls, of the towers, and of the gates of Jerusalem, with the solemnity and magnificence that such a work required. He separated the priests, the Levites, and the princes of the people, into two companies, one of which walked to the south and the other to the north, on the top of the walls. These two companies were to meet at the temple. The procession was accompanied with music both vocal and instrumental; and when they were all come to the temple, they there read the law, offered sacrifices, and made great rejoicings. And as the feast of tabernacles happened at the same time, it was celebrated with great solemnity, (Id. viii.) Nehemiah observing that the compass of the city was too large for its inhabitants, he ordered that the chief of the nation should fix their dwelling in the city; and caused them to draw lots, by which a tenth part of the whole people of Judah were to dwell at Jerusalem, (Id. xi.) Then he applied himself to the reformation of such abuses as had crept into the administration of the public affairs. He curbed the inhumanity of the great ones, who held in a state of slavery the sons and daughters of those who were poor or unfortunate, keeping their lands in possession, which these poor people had been obliged either to mortgage or to sell to the rich. Another abuse there was, which Ezra had vainly attempted to redress, that they had contracted marriages with strange and idolatrous women. Nehemiah undertook to dissolve these marriages, succeeded in it, and sent away all such women as had been taken against the express command of the law, (Id. ix.) Having likewise observed, that the priests and Levites were obliged to take refuge wherever they could, and so the ministry of the temple was not attended or performed with that decency it ought, because they did not receive the revenues that the law had appointed for their subsistence; he obliged the people punctually to pay the ministers of the Lord what was due to them, and enjoined the priests and Levites duly to attend on their respective duties, and to discharge their functions, (Id. xiii. 10, 11, &c.) He enforced the observation of the Sabbath, which had been much neglected at Jerusalem, and would not permit strangers to come in to buy and sell, but kept the gates of the city shut all that day. And, to perpetuate as much as was possible these good regulations which he had newly established, he engaged the chief men of the nation solemnly to renew the covenant with the Lord. This ceremony was performed in the temple, and an instrument was drawn up, which was signed by the principal men, both priests and people (Id. ix. x.), in the year of the world 3551. We read in the books of Maccabees, (2 Macc. i. 19, 20, 21, &c.), that Nehemiah sent to search for the holy fire, which before the captivity of Babylon the priests had hid in a dry and deep pit; but not finding any fire there, but instead thereof a thick and muddy water, he sprinkled this upon the altar; whereupon the wood which had been sprinkled with this water took fire presently as soon as the sun began to appear. Which miracle coming to the knowledge of the king of Persia, he caused the place to be encompassed with walls where the fire had been hid, and granted great favours and privileges to the priests. It is recorded in the same books, (2 Macc. ii. 13, 14.) That Nehemiah erected a library, wherein he placed whatever he could find, either of the books of the prophets, of David, or of such princes as had made presents to the temple. Lastly, He returned to Babylon (Id. v. 14. and xii. 6.) according to the promise he had made to King Artaxerxes, about the thirty-second year of this prince, in the year 3563. From thence he returned again to Jerusalem, where he died in peace, about the year 3580, having governed the people of Judah for about thirty years. The book which in the English Bible, as also in the Hebrew, has the name of Nehemiah, in the Latin Bible is called the book of Esdras; and it must be confessed, that though this author speaks in the first person, and though at first reading one would think that he had writ it day by day as the transactions occurred, yet there are some things in this book which could not have been written by Nehemiah himself; for example, memorials are quoted wherein were registered the names of... of the priests in the time of Jonathan the son of Elia- shib, and even to the times of the high priest Jaddus, who met Alexander the Great. These therefore must have been added afterwards. It may well be questioned, whether this Nehemiah be the same that is mentioned in Ezra, (ii. 2. and Neh. vii. 7.) as one that returned from the Babylo- nian captivity under Zerubbabel; since from the first year of Cyrus to the twentieth of Artaxerxes Longi- manus, there are no less than ninety-two years inter- vening; so that Nehemiah must at this time have been a very old man, upon the lowest computation an hun- dred, consequently utterly incapable of being the king's cup-bearer, of taking a journey from Shushan to Jeru- salem, and of behaving there with all the courage and activity that is recorded of him. Upon this presump- tion, therefore, we may conclude that this was a differ- ent person, though of the same name, and that Tir- shatha (the other name by which he is called, Ezra ii. 63. and Neh. vii. 65.) denotes the title of his office, and both in the Persian and Chaldean tongues was the general name given to the king's deputies and gover- nors.

NEHOW

Pages 393-393

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook in his last voyage to the Pacific ocean: these islands are eleven in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and are situated from 18° 44' to 22° 15' N. Lat. and from 154° 56' to 165° 24' W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>.

NEIGHBOUR

Pages 393-393

1. One who dwells <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is seated near to another (2 Kings iv. 3.) 2. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to whom we have an opportunity of doing good (Matt. xxii. 39.) 3. A fellow labourer of one and the same people (Acts vii. 27.) 4. A friend (<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> xvi. 21.) At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of our Saviour, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a> had retrained the word neighbour to signify those of their own na- tion only, or their own friends; being of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that to hate their enemy was not forbidden by their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. But our Saviour informed them, that the whole world were their neighbours; that they ought not to do to another what they would not have done to themselves; and that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> ought to be extended even to their enemies, (Matt. v. 43. Luke x. 29. &c.)

NELSON

Pages 393-396

The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> Viscount, one of the most celebrated naval commanders, was the son of the reverend Edmund Nelson, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNHAM">Burnham</a> Thorpe, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, where his father was rector, in the year 1758. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the school of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Walsham; but we are unacquainted with the particulars relative to his childhood, and whether the progress he made in his studies was in any respect ex- traordinary. It is certain, however, that he discovered a strong predilection for the naval profession at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and having quitted school at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twelve years, went on board the Raisonable of 64 guns, commanded by his mother's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Maurice Suckling. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April 1773, a voyage of discovery to the north pole was undertaken by the honourable Constantine John Phipps, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Mulgrave, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an application by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> to Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>; and although the instructions which were issued, prohibited all boys from being received on board, yet the enterprising spirit of Horatio Nelson earnestly solicited to be appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCKSWAIN">cockswain</a> to Captain Lutwidge, rather than submit to be left behind; and his unsubdued spirit so forcibly struck the captain, that his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> was complied with. When the ship returned to England in the month of October 1773, Mr Nelson having received information that a squadron was fitting out for the East Indies, em- ployed all his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to be appointed to one of the ships. It was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he was placed in the Seahorse of 20 guns, commanded by the celebrated Captain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">Farmer</a>, and stationed in the fore-top to keep watch, but soon after removed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-deck. He obtained the professional order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> on the 8th of April, 1777, and received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of the Lowestoffe of 32 guns, Captain William Locker, in which ship he arrived at Jamaica; but feeling that his glowing mind was cir- cumfused in so small a frigate, he requested the com- mand of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHOONER">schooner</a>, which acted as tender to the Lowestoffe, thus availing himself of the opportunity of becoming an experienced pilot for every intricate pas- sage through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, situated on the northern side of Hispaniola. When Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Parker arrived at Jamaica in the year 1778, Lieutenant Nelson was nominated by that gallant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> to be the third of his own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> ship, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> he soon became the first. In this ship his services terminated in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a lieutenant. On the 11th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, 1779, he obtained the rank of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-captain; and during the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years he had been in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he not only became an able officer by his constant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his duty, and his keen observation, but he also laid the foundation of be- ing a pilot of distinguished eminence. The first ship to which he was appointed after being made a post <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">tain</a>, was the Hinchinbrooke. On the arrival of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> d'Estrigny at Hispaniola, as an attack upon Jamaica was immediately apprehended, Captain Nelson was intrusted with the command of the batteries of Port Royal, with the concurring approbation of the British admiral and general. In the month of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1780, it was re- solved on to reduce Fort Juan, on the river St John, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, when Captain Nelson was made choice of to command the naval department, and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> was committed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Polson. In accomplishing the object of this arduous and interesting undertaking, Nelson's usual intrepidity was again ex- hibited. Having quitted the ship under his command, he superintended the transporting of the troops in boats, 300 miles up a river, which none but Spaniards had ever navigated since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the buccaneers. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and vigorous exertions were represented by Major Polson to General Dalling in their true colours, nor was his gallantry passed over by that officer in silence. After storming an out-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> belonging to the enemy, he constructed batteries, and fought the Spaniards; and it is to his conduct in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Fort Juan that the success of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> has been justly and chiefly ascribed. He was next appointed to the Janes, at that time stationed at Jamaica; on his arrival at which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> every medical assistance was given him which his situation required; but as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on the decline, he deemed it expedient to return to England in his majesty's ship Lion, the honourable William Cornwallis commander, to whose unremitting care and attention he owed the preservation of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He obtained the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a> in the month of August, 1781, which put his delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> to the severest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, as he was stationed during the whole of the ensuing winter in the North seas. He sailed from Quebec in the month of October, 1782, with a convoy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, where he had an opportunity of joining the fleet under Sir Samuel Hood; and in the month following he sailed with him to the West Indies, where he was honourably employed until the termination of hostilities. He soon after received orders to repair to England, being directed to attend in his way, his royal highness <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> William Henry on his visit to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAVANNAH">Havannah</a>. When he reached England, the Albemarle was paid off at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> on the 31st <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, 1783. During the autumn of that year he paid a visit to France, where he continued till the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the ensuing year, when he received the command of the Boreas frigate of 28 guns, and his destination was the Leeward islands, where he continued until June 1787, and was then ordered to repair to England. In the month of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> the same year he was married to the amiable and accomplished widow of Dr Neubitz, of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a>. When the Boreas frigate was paid off at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> on the 30th November, 1787, he retired to the parsonage-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Burnham Thorpe, which had been conferred upon him by his father for a place of residence, there to enjoy the consolations which result from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> felicity. He again came forward on the 30th of January 1793, to shine forth more conspicuous as a naval officer than he had ever done before, at which time he received the command of the Agamemnon of 64 guns, being soon placed under the orders of that truly great and illustrious character, Lord Hood, who at that period was destined to command in the Mediterranean. The unlimited confidence reposed in him by this noble and gallant admiral, is an incontrovertible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation in which his courage and naval abilities were held. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> his superior designed to attack batteries, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cut ships out of the harbours in which they were moored; if troops were to be landed in perilous situations, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> difficulty to be explored, the great Nelson took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> on every such occasion, seconded by the brave officers and crew belonging to the Agamemnon. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOULON">Toulon</a>, Batia, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALVI">Calvi</a>, witnessed his gallant and intrepid deportment, of which Lord Hood did not fail to make honourable mention. At the siege of Calvi Captain Nelson lost the sight of his right eye, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of the enemy having struck that of which he had the command, and driven some particles of sand against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> with irresistible impetuosity. When Lord Hood left his station in the Mediterranean in the month of October, 1794, the command devolved on Admiral Hotham, who honoured our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> with an equal share of his confidence and esteem. On the 13th and 14th of March, and 13th of July 1795, he again rendered himself conspicuous in the actions which then took place with the French fleet; and soon after he was chosen by Admiral Hotham to cooperate with General De Vins, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, in which service he continued so long as Hotham retained the command, who was superceded by Sir John Jervis. This officer so much applauded the conduct of Captain Nelson, that he received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of wearing a pendant of distinction; and in the month of May he was removed from the Agamemnon to the Captain of 74 guns. On the 11th of August he had a captain appointed under him. From April to October 1795, Commodore Nelson was continually employed in the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and arduous service, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, the taking of Porto Ferrajo, with the island of Caprea, and finally in the evacuation of Batia. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1796 he hoisted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> pendant on board La Minerve frigate, and was dispatched with that ship, and La Blanche, to Porto Ferrajo, to bring the naval stores left there to Gibraltar, which the fleet was in much want of. While on this service in the night of the 17th December, he fell in with two Spanish frigates, one of which he immediately attacked, and ordered the Blanche to bear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to engage the other. About half past ten the commodore brought his ship to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which continued without interruption till half past one, when the Spanish frigate of 40 guns, 28 of which were 18 pounders, struck to La Minerve. After various other active and important services during the three preceding months, Sir Horatio Nelson, in April 1797, hoisted his flag on board the Captain of 74 guns as rear-admiral of the blue, and in the end of May he shifted his flag from the Captain to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, when he was appointed to the command of the inner squadron at the blockade of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>. While on this service he exhibited another remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his undaunted personal courage. In the attack on the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-boats in July, he was boarded in his barge, which had only the usual complement of 10 men, and the cookswain. The commander of the Spanish gun-boats, in a barge with 30 men and officers, made a desperate attack on the admiral and his brave companions. The conflict remained long doubtful, but after 18 of the Spaniards were killed, and almost the whole of the remainder wounded, the rear-admiral and his brave crew succeeded in carrying this superior force. On the 15th of July the same year, Admiral Nelson was detached with a small squadron to attack the town of Santa Cruz in the island of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>. A thousand men, including <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>, were landed in the course of a dark night, made themselves masters of the town, and retained possession of it for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hours; but finding it impossible to storm the citadel, they prepared for their retreat, which the Spaniards allowed them to make unmolested, agreeable to the stipulations which had been entered into. In this unfortunate attack the brave Nelson lost his arm by a cannon-shot. But a more splendid <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of the life of our hero is now opening. On the 13th of April 1798 he was detached tached from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> St Vincent's fleet, in pursuit of the French to the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, with 12 sail of the line and one 50 gun ship, while the enemy's fleet consisted of 13 sail of the line and four frigates, protected by the batteries on the shore, and several gun-boats. This memorable action commenced at sunset, and terminated gloriously for the honour of our hero and that of the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. Nine sail of the line fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the conqueror, two were burnt, and two effected their escape. The brave Nelson was wounded in the action, believing himself to have been shot through the head; but after his wound was examined by the surgeon, it was happily found not to be mortal, a circumstance which diffused the most lively satisfaction through the whole fleet. To the honour of this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> it ought to be mentioned, that even under the conviction of approaching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, he prepared for the interesting change with calmness and fortitude, desired his chaplain to recommend him to Lady Nelson, appointed the brave Hardy to the rank of post-captain and to the command of a ship, and took an affectionate leave of Captain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>. The French admiral's ship, L'Orient, was blown up during the action. From the mainmast of this ship Captain Hallowell ordered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> to be constructed, which was presented to Admiral Nelson, and gratefully accepted by the hero, as a token of affectionate regard. For some months he had it placed upright in his cabin; but in consequence of the entreaties of an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, the admiral was at length prevailed on to allow it to be removed. Our readers will not be surprised that Lord Nelson should now be regarded as the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the empire, and the support of her national <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. It is to his gallantry and naval skill that we are indebted for the victory of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, and the annihilation of that formidable northern confederacy which menaced the prosperity, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the very existence of the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. One of the most important services which Lord Nelson performed, was the pursuit of the combined fleets of France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to the West Indies. This fleet had sailed from Cadiz on the 10th of April, and it was at first conjectured that Egypt was the place of their destination. In consequence of this conjecture, Lord Nelson sailed in pursuit of the enemy for the coast of Egypt; and, having missed his object, after reconnoitring that coast, he passed the straits of Gibraltar, and anchored in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAGOS">Lagos</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> on the 10th of May; soon after which he sailed for the West Indies with ten ships of the line; arrived off Barbadoes on the 4th of June; and having touched at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOBAGO">Tobago</a>, Trinidad, and Grenada, at the latter of which places he was informed that the combined fleet had been seen on the 6th off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICA">Dominica</a>; he reached Antigua on the 12th, where he received information that the enemy had been seen on the 8th standing to the northward. Lord Nelson, without the loss of a moment, continued the pursuit of the enemy on their return to Europe, where they arrived about the end of July; and after taking in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> at Gibraltar, and reconnoitring the harbour of Cadiz; he returned to England, where he arrived in the Victory, on the 18th of August, after having been engaged for nearly four months in one of the most arduous, and, at the same time, one of the most important and beneficial, although, in its immediate object, unfruitful enterprises, for which his life was distinguished. His lordship had now been absent from England more than two years, on the Mediterranean station. The concluding scene of this extraordinary man's naval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, kindles emotions of admiration and regret; and at once excites both transport and extreme of sorrow. Perhaps no action, in point of splendour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, can equal that which deprived his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of one of the greatest heroes it ever produced. Britons appear to be sensible of its vast importance; yet it is not improbable that posterity will consider it as still more splendid, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and admiration not being damped by the poignant recollection that they personally <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the man by whose loss it was accomplished. When Lord Nelson perceived that, in consequence of his manoeuvres, he had reduced the enemy to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of engaging him, he exclaimed in the presence of Captain Hardy and the other officers who surrounded him on the quarter deck; "Now they cannot escape us; I think we shall at least make sure of twenty of them.—I shall probably lose a leg, but that will be purchasing a victory cheaply." But alas! amidst the inexplicable satisfaction and delight, which a victory so splendid could not fail to inspire, he has left us to lament that it was purchased by the loss of a life so incomparably valuable. His lordship's flag ship fell on board the Redoubtable, by which means he was exposed to the fire of the musketry from the tops; and the insignia of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, it is supposed, flung him out to the aims of the enemy, which in the issue were too fatally successful. His secretary was cut in two by his side with a chain shot, and soon after a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> grazed his lordship's shoulder, entered his left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and passed through his lungs. He lived about three hours after this tragic event, during which he remained perfectly recollected, and he displayed the same heroic magnanimity in the arms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which had so eminently distinguished him through the whole of his career. His last words to Captain Hardy were, "I know I am dying, I could have wished to survive to breathe my last upon British ground, but the will of God be done!" In a few moments he expired. His last signal ought not, and will not be forgotten, which was by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELEGRAPH">telegraph</a>,— "That England expected every man would do his duty." He spoke in raptures concerning the event of the day only a short time before his dissolution, and sent word to Admiral Collingwood, desiring that he would make his affectionate farewell to all his brother seamen throughout the fleet. In this manner died, in the 47th year of his age, the greatest commander that perhaps ever adorned the British navy, leaving behind him a name dear to Great Britain, and an example of heroism which will inspire his companions in arms to emulate his virtues, that they too may live in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of a grateful posterity. His singular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of attack on this memorable occasion was communicated by his lordship to all his captains, who unanimously gave it as their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it could not possibly fail of success, being concerted with such consummate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; and they even pledged their lives for the favourable result of it. His titles were, Viscount Nelson, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Bronte.—The united <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> voted him a pension of 3000l. a year, to continue during his own life and his two next heirs; the East East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> made him a present of 15,000l.; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signor gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> aigrette worth 4000l.; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Russia gave him a diamond box worth 2500l.; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> made him presents to the amount of 3000l. together with the dukedom of Bronté, and an estate of 3000l. per annum. Thus all Europe conspired to testify the estimation in which they held this distinguished hero; and the numerous monuments which have been, and still are erecting to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> throughout the British empire, will continue lasting evidences of the esteem in which he was held by his grateful country. Parliament also voted a sum for the purchase of an estate for his heirs, and his majesty conferred the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl on his immediate successor. Nor were his talents wholly confined to the knowledge of naval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a>, for it is known that as a senator he was highly respectable, although he enjoyed few opportunities of coming forward in that capacity. When he did, his speeches were heard by their lordships with respect, and the most profound attention. The few specimens we have of his abilities as a politician, afford no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> proof that if he had devoted as much of his time to those studies as he did to his peculiar profession, he would have made a distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>.

NEMEA

Pages 396-396

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, situated between Cleone and Philus in Argolis; whether town, district, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other thing, uncertain; there a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> stood in which the Argives celebrated the Nemean games, and there happened all the fabulous circumstances of the Nemean lion. The district Nemea is called Bembinadia, (Pliny); a village, Bembina, standing near Nemea, (Strabo). Stephanus places Nemea in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>; though not in Elis, but on its borders; Pliny, erroneously, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. In the adjoining mountain is still shown the den of the lion, distant 15 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Nemea, (Pausanias); in which stands a considerable temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Nemeus and Cleoneus, from the vicinity of these two places. This place gave name to the Nemean games, celebrated every third year.

NEMEAN GAMES

Pages 396-396

so called from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEMEA">Nemea</a>, a village between the cities of Cleone and Philus, where they were celebrated every third year. The exercises were chariot-races, and all the parts of the Pentathlum. These games were instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Opheltes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Archemorus the son of Euphantes and Creusa, who was nursed by Hypsipyle; who leaving him in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> while she went to show the besiegers of Thebes a fountain, at her return found him dead, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> twined about his neck: whence the fountain, before called Langia, was named Archemorus; and the captains, to comfort Hypsipyle, instituted these games. Others ascribe their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, after his victory over the Nemean lion. Others allow, that they were instituted first in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Archemorus; but interrupted, and revived again by Hercules. The victors were crowned with parsley, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> used at funerals, and supposed to have sprung from Archemorus's blood. The Argives presided at these games.

NEMEAUSIS

Pages 396-396
or Nemausum, in Ancient Geography, the capital of the Aremicii in Gallia Narbonensis; a colony, (Coin), with the surname Angyloa, (Inscription). In it stands a Roman amphitheatre, which is still almost entire. Now Nîmes in Languedoc. NEMEA (Strabo, Livy); a river of Achaia, running between Sicyon and Corinth, the common boundary of both territories, and falling into the Corinthian bay.

NEMESIANUS

Pages 396-396

Aurelius Olympius, a Latin poet who was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, and flourished about the year 281, under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARUS">Carus</a>, and his sons Carinus and Numerian: the last of which emperors was so fond of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, that he contended the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with Nemesianus, who had written a poem upon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs. We have still remaining a poem of our author called Cynegeticon, and four eclogues: they were published by Paulus Manutius in 1538; by Barthelet in 1613; at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1653; with the notes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> Vitius. Giraldi hath preserved a fragment of Nemesianus, which was communicated to him by Sanazarus, to whom we are obliged for our poet's works; for having found them written in Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, he procured them to be put into the Roman, and then sent them to Paulus Manutius. Although this poem hath acquired some reputation, it is greatly inferior to those of Oppian and Grattan upon the same subject; yet Nemesianus's style is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> enough, and has some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of elegance. The world was so much possessed with an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his poem in the eighth century, that it was read among the classics in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, as appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the celebrated Hincmar bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, to his nephew Hincmar of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAON">Laon</a>.

NEMESIS

Pages 396-396

in Pagan worship, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Neceftity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, of Oceanus and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOX">Nox</a>, had the care of revenging the crimes which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> left unpunished. She was also called Adraftea, because Adraustus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> first raised an altar to her; and Rhamnusia, from her having a magnificent temple at Rhamnus in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. She had likewise a temple at Rome in the Capitol. She is represented with a stern countenance, holding a whip in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scales in the other.

NEMESIUS

Pages 396-397

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> who embraced Christianity, and was made bishop of Emesa in Phoenicia, where he had his birth; he flourished in the beginning of the fifth century. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of his extant, entitled De Natura Hominis, in which he refutes the fatality of the Stoics and the errors of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANICHEES">Manichees</a>, the Apollinarists, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a>; but he espouses the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Origin concerning the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRE_EXISTENCE">pre-existence</a> of souls. (A.) This treatise was translated by Valla, and printed in 1535. Another version was afterwards made of it by Ellebedius, and printed in 1665; it is also inserted in the Bibliotheca Patrum, in Greek and Latin. Lastly, Another edition was published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1671, folio, with a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, wherein the editor endeavours to prove, from a passage in this book, that (A) It is much more probable that he and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> both brought their opinion with them from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, than that either of them borrowed it from the other. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. Chap. IV. the circulation of the blood was known to Nemesius; which, however, was since shown to be a mistake by Dr Freind, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Physic.

NEMINE CONTRADICENTE

Pages 397-397

"none contradicting it;" a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> when anything is carried without opposition.

NEMOURS

Pages 397-397

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, in the Gâtinois, formerly with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is seated on the river Loing, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 45' N. Lat. 48° 15'.

NENAGH

Pages 397-397

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> and fair town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIPPERARY">Tipperary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, 75 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It is situated on a branch of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a> which runs into Lough-Derg. Here stand the ruins of an old castle called Nenagh-round. Also those of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> founded in the year 1200, for canons following the rule of St Augustin. It was dedicated to St John the Baptist, and was usually called Teachon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St John's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the reign of Henry III, a friary for conventual Franciscans was also founded here, and esteemed the richest foundation of that order in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Here is a barrack for two troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. This town was burnt on St Stephen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> 1348, by the Irish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> held here are four.

NENIA

Pages 397-397
or Nenia, in the ancient poetry, a kind of funeral song sung to the music of flutes at the obsequies of the dead. Authors represent them as forry compositions, sung by hired women mourners called Prafice. The first rise of these Nenia is ascribed to the physicians. In the heathen antiquity, the goddess of tears and funerals was called Nenia; whom some suppose to have given that name to the funeral song, and others to have taken her name from it.

NEOCESARIA

Pages 397-397

(Pliny), a town of Pontus on the south <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the left side of the Lycus. About the year 342, when Leontius and Sallustius were consuls, it was entirely ruined by a dreadful earthquake, no edifice having withstood the violence of the shock, except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and the bishop's habitation, who was saved, with the clergy and some other pious persons, while the rest of the inhabitants were buried in its ruins.

NEOMAGUS

Pages 397-397

(<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); a town of Gallia Narbonensis, on the confines of the Tricassini. Now Nyons in Dauphine.

NEOMENIA

Pages 397-397
or Noumenia, a festival of the ancient Greeks, at the beginning of every lunar month, which, as the name imports, was observed upon the day of the new moon, in honour of all the gods, but especially Apollo, who was called Neomenios, because the sun is the fountain of light; and whatever distinction of times and seasons may be taken from other planets, Neophyte yet they are all owing to him as the original of those borrowed rays by which they shine. The games and public entertainments at these festivals were made by the rich, to whose tables the poor flocked in great numbers. The Athenians at these times offered solemn prayers and sacrifices for the prosperity of their country during the ensuing month. See Games. The Jews had also their neomenia, or feast of the new moon, on which peculiar sacrifices were appointed: and on this day they had a sort of family entertainment and rejoicing. The most celebrated neomenia of all others was that at the beginning of the civil year, or first day of the month Tisri, on which no fervile labour was performed: they then offered particular burnt sacrifices, and sounded the trumpets of the temple. The modern Jews keep the neomenia only as a feast of devotion, which any one may observe or not as he pleases.

NEOPHYTES

Pages 397-397

"new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>;" a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> to those heathens who had newly embraced the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; such persons being considered as regenerated, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> born anew by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> neophyte has been also used for new priests, or those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> admitted into orders, and sometimes for the novices in monasteries. It is still applied to the converts made by the missionaries among the infidels.

NEPAL

Pages 397-397

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATNA">Patna</a>, at the distance of about 12 days journey. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are both narrow and dangerous, but in the plains they are allowed to be good. Some parts of it are obnoxious to a putrid fever, of which those who are seized with it die in a few days; but the people in the plains are not obnoxious to it. The plain is about 200 miles in circumference, and the only entrance to it is by the mountains. It contains three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities; Cat'hmandu, having about 18,000 houses; Lelit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PATTAN">Pattan</a> contains 24,000; and B'hatgan 12,000 families. Besides these there are many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are Timi and Cipoli. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the inhabitants, like that of most other countries in a state little removed from barbarism, abounds with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of absurd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and ceremonies, which it would be superfluous to enumerate; but many of them adopt that of the Brahmins, the moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which, in many respects, must be allowed to be excellent. The temple of Baghero in the city of Lelit Pattan, is said to be superior to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, on account of the immense quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and jewels which it contains; and the waters of a river about three miles from Cat'hmandu are considered as holy, to which people of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> are conveyed in the prospect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This kingdom is believed to be of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, as its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and independence have been preserved from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial; yet the dissensions of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> completely ruined it not many years ago, who could not agree about the choice of a proper successor on the death of their sovereign.

NEPENTHES

Pages 397-397

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking among those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPETA

Pages 397-398

Catmint, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nep, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPHELIUM

Pages 398-398

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocota clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPHEW

Pages 398-398

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> relative to uncle and aunt, signifying a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sister's son; who, according to the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is in the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a>, but according to the canon in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>.

NEPHRITIC

Pages 398-398

something that relates to the kidneys. See Kidney. Nephritic Wood, (Lignum nephriticum), a wood of a very dense and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> texture, and of a fine grain, brought to us from New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in small blocks, in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, and covered with its bark. This wood is said to be a good diuretic; and we are told it is used among the Indians in all diseases of the kidneys and bladder, and in suppression of urine, from whatever cause. It is also recommended in fevers, and in obstructions of the visera. The way of taking it among the Indians is only an infusion in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. These uses are not however properly ascertained. See Guilandina, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Nephritic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>. See Jade, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

NEPHRITICS

Pages 398-398

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines proper for diseases of the kidneys. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPOS

Pages 398-398

Cornelius, a celebrated Latin biographer, who flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Julius Caesar, and lived, according to St Jerome, to the fifth year of Augustus. He was an Italian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> Cattalus, and born at Hosflia, a small town in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, in Cisalpine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>. Antonius, however, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it that he was born in the Gauls; and in that they may both be in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, provided that under the name of Gau is comprehended Gallia Cisalpina, which is in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEANDER">Leander</a> Alberti thinks Nepos's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was Verona; and he is sure that he was either born in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> neighbourhood. For the rest, Cicero and Atticus were friends of our author; who wrote the lives of the Greek historians, as he himself attests in that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a>, speaking of Philistus. What he says, also, in the lives of Cato and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, proves that he had also written the lives of the Latin captains and historians. He wrote some other excellent works which are lost. All that we have left of his at present is, "The Lives of the illustrious Greek and Roman Captains;" which were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time ascribed to Æmilius Probus, who published them, as it is said, under his own name, to insinuate himself thereby into the favour of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius; but, in the course of time, the fraud has been discovered, although several learned persons have confounded the two authors. This piece has been translated into French by the Sieur de Claveret, with a dedication to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Longueville, in 1663; and again by M. le Gras, then of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of the Oratory at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1729, 12mo. We have an excellent translation of it into English, by several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, which has gone through several editions.

NEPTUNE

Pages 398-400

in Pagan worship, the god of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Vesta <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ops, and the Neptune, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Pluto. He assisted Jupiter in his expeditions; on which that god, when he arrived at the supreme power, assigned him the sea and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> for his empire. He was, however, expelled from heaven with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> for conspiring against Jupiter, when they were both employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAOMEDON">Laomedon</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; but that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> disliking Neptune without a reward, he sent a sea monster to lay waste the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on which he was obliged to expose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Hesione. He is said to have been the first inventor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> and chariot <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACING">racing</a>; on which account <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> king of Pontus threw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> drawn by four horses into the sea in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of this god; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> instituted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> at his festival, during which all other horses left working, and the mules were adorned with wreaths of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. In a contest with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> he produced a horse by striking the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>; and on another occasion, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of skill with Minerva and Vulcan, produced a bull, whence that animal was sacrificed to him.
