His favourite wife was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AMPHITRITE">Amphitrite</a>, whom he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> courted in vain, till sending a dolphin to intercede for him, he met with success; on which he rewarded the dolphin by placing him among the stars. He had also two other wives, one of whom was called Salacia from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the other Venilia from the ebbing and flowing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. He had likewise many concubines, by whom he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of children. He is represented with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, with a garment of an azure or sea green; holding his trident in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and seated in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> shell drawn by sea horses; attended by the sea gods Paleoemon, Glauceus, and Phorcys, and the sea goddesses Thetis, Melita, and Panopaea, and a long train of tritons and sea nymphs. This deity was known in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> by the name of Canobus or Canopus, and was worshipped as the numen aquarum or spirit of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of certain vases or pitchers, with which the Egyptians filtrated the water of their sacred river, in order to purify and render it fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. From the mouth of each of these vases, which were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, arose the head and sometimes the head and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or woman. Such are the emblems which still remain of the Egyptian Neptune or Canobus; and it was by this emblem that the tutelar god of Egypt vanquished the god of Chaldea in the ridiculous manner mentioned by Ruthenus in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*. * Lib. 25. "The Chaldeans (says he) who adored the fire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 26. carried their god into various countries that he might try his strength in contests with other gods. He vanquished, as we may easily conceive, the images made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, braids, and wood, &c. by reducing them to ashes; and thus the worship of fire was everywhere established. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Canobus, unwilling, as became him, to admit the superiority of strange gods, contrived to make his god vanquish the god of Chaldea in a pitched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The vases which were worshipped as the emblems of Canobus being used for filtering the waters of the Nile, were of course perforated on all sides with very small holes. This faithful priest having stopped all the holes in one of these..." these with wax, and painted the vase of different colours for a reason which the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit to be a good one, filled it up with water, and fitted to its mouth the head of an idol. This emblem of Canobus was then placed in a small fire brought by the Chaldeans as the emblem of their god; and thus the gods of Egypt and Chaldea were forced into battle. The contest, however, was of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> melting the wax made way for the water to run out, which quickly extinguished the fire; and thus Canobus vanquished the god of the Chaldeans." Ridiculous as this story is, it is perfectly suitable to the genius of Paganism, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> artifices of the Pagan priesthood; but we suspect that the historian laboured under one mistake, and substituted the Chaldeans instead of the Persians. See Polytheism. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a>, in the Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, sea nymphs, daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a> and Doris.—The Nereids were esteemed very handsome; inasmuch that Cassiope, the wife of Cepheus king of Ethiopia, having triumphed over all the beauties of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and daring to vie with the Nereids, they were so enraged that they sent a prodigious sea monster into the country; and, to appease them, she was commanded by the oracle to expose her daughter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a>, bound to a rock, to be devoured by the monster. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments, the Nereids are represented riding upon sea horses; sometimes with an entire <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form, and at other times with the tail of a fish. Nereis, a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Nereus, in fabulous history, a marine deity, was son of Oceanus and Thetis. He settled in the Aegean sea, was considered as a prophet, and had the power of assuming what form he pleased. He married his sister Doris, by whom he had 50 daughters called the Nereids, who constantly attended on Neptune, and when he went abroad surrounded his chariot. Neri, Anthony, a learned writer who published a curious book printed at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> 1612, in 4to, with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> Dell' Arte Verraria Libri VII.; or the Art of Glassmaking. Nerium, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 30th order, Contortae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">Dyeing</a> Index. Nero, Claudius Domitius Caesar, a celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Domitius Ahenobarbus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRIPPINA">Agrippina</a> the daughter of Germanicus. He was adopted by the emperor Claudius, A.D. 50, and four years after he succeeded to him on the throne. In the beginning of his reign he showed several marks of the greatest kindness and condescension, affability, complaisance, and popularity. The object of his administration seemed to be the good of his people; and when he was desired to sign his name to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of malefactors that were to be executed, he exclaimed, "Would to heaven I could not write!" He hated flattery; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had liberally commended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, he desired them to keep their praises till he deserved them. These promising virtues soon, however, proved to be <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>: Nero soon displayed the real propensities of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He delivered himself from the sway of his mother, and at last ordered her to be murdered. This unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of barbarity might astonish some, but Nero had his devoted adherents; and when he declared that he had taken away his mother's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself from ruin, the senate applauded his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and the people signified their approbation. Many of his courtiers shared her unhappy fate; and Nero sacrificed to his fury or caprice all such as obstructed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or diverted his inclination. In the night he generally went from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> to visit the meanest taverns, and all the scenes of debauchery which Rome contained. In this nocturnal riot he was fond of insulting the people in the streets; and his attempts to offer violence to the wife of a Roman senator nearly cost him his life. He also turned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, and openly appeared on the Roman stage in the meanest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. In his attempts to excel in music, and to conquer the disadvantages of a hoarse disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, he moderated his meals, and often passed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> without eating. The Olympian games attracted his notice: he went into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and presented himself a candidate for the public honour. He was defeated in wrestling; but the flattery of the spectators adjudged him the victory, and he returned to Rome with all the splendour and pomp of an eastern conqueror, drawn in the chariot of Augustus, and attended by a band of musicians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>, and stage dancers from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the empire. These private and public amusements of the emperor were indeed innocent; his character only was injured, and not the lives of the people. His conduct, however, soon became more abominable: he disguised himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a woman, and was publicly married to one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>. This violence to nature and decency was soon exchanged for another: Nero refused his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and celebrated his nuptials with one of his meanest catamites: and it was on this occasion that one of the Romans observed that the world would have been happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Nero's father had had such a wife. But his cruelty was now displayed in a still higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, for he sacrificed to his wantonness his wife <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVIA">Octavia</a> Poppea, and the celebrated writers, Seneca, Lucan, Petronius, &c. Nor did the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> escape his barbarity. He had heard of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of Troy; and as he wished to renew that dismal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, he caused Rome to be set on fire in different places. The conflagration became soon universal, and during <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> successive days the fire <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. All was desolation: nothing was heard but the lamentations of mothers whose children had perished in the flames, the groans of the dying, and the continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of palaces and buildings. Nero was the only one who enjoyed the general consternation. He placed himself on the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower, and he sang on his lyre the destruction of Troy, a dreadful scene which his barbarity had realized before his eyes. He attempted to avert the public odium from his head by a pretended commiseration of the miseries of his subjects. He began to repair the streets and the public buildings at his own expense. He built himself a celebrated palace, which he called his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It was liberally adorned with gold, with precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and with every thing rare and exquisite. It contained spacious fields, artificial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, woods, gardens, orchards, and whatever exhibited a beautiful scene. The entrance of this edifice could admit a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> of the emperor 120 feet high; the galleries were each a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> long, and the whole was covered with gold. gold. The roofs of the dining halls represented the firmament, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> as well as in figure; and continually turned round night and day, showering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> all sorts of perfumes and sweet waters. When this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> edifice, which, according to Pliny, extended all round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, was finished, Nero said, that now he could lodge like a man. His profusion was not less remarkable in all his other actions. When he went a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, his nets were of gold and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. He never appeared twice in the same garment; and when he took a voyage, there were thousands of servants to take care of his wardrobe. This continuation of debauchery and extravagance at last roused the people. Many conspiracies were formed against him; but they were generally discovered, and such as were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> suffered the severest punishments. The most dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against Nero's life was that of Piso, from which he was saved by the confession of a slave. The conspiracy of Galba proved more successful, who, when he was informed that his plot was known to Nero, declared himself emperor. The unpopularity of Nero favoured his cause; he was acknowledged by all the Roman empire, and the senate condemned the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> to be dragged naked through the streets of Rome, and whipped to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and afterwards to be thrown down from the Tarpeian rock like the meanest malefactor. This, however, was not executed; for Nero prevented it by a voluntary death. He killed himself, A.D. 68, in the 32nd year of his age, after a reign of 13 years and eight months. Rome was filled with acclamations on the occasion; and the citizens, more strongly to indicate their joy, wore caps, such as were generally used by slaves who had received their freedom. Their vengeance was not only exercised against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the deceased monster, but many of his friends were the object of the public resentment; and many were crucified to pieces in such a violent manner, that one of the senators, amid the universal joy, said that he was afraid they should soon have cause to wish for Nero. The tyrant, as he expired, requested that his head might not be cut off from his body, and exposed to the insolence of the populace, but that the whole might be burned on the funeral pile. His request was granted by one of Galba's freedmen, and his obsequies were performed with the usual ceremonies. Though his death seemed to be the source of general gladness, yet many of his favourites lamented his fall, and were grieved to see that their pleasures and amusements were stopped by the death of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of debauchery and extravagance. Even the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a> sent ambassadors to Rome, to console with the Romans, and to beg that they would honour and revere the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Nero. His statues were also crowned with garlands of flowers; and many imagined that he was not dead, but that he would soon make his appearance and take vengeance on his enemies. It will be sufficient to observe, in finishing the character of this tyrannical monster, that the name of Nero is even now used emphatically to express a barbarous and unfeeling oppressor. Pliny calls him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy and fury of mankind; and so indeed he has been called by all writers, who exhibit Nero as a pattern of the most execrable barbarity and unpardonable wantonness. The same Pliny furnishes us with this singular anecdote of him: "Nero had ordered himself to be painted under the figure of a colossus, upon cloth or canvas, 120 feet in height." He adds, "that this preposterous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, when it was finished, met with its fate from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which consumed it, and involved likewise the most beautiful part of the gardens where it was placed in the conflagration."

NERVA

Pages 400-400

COCEIUS, a Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> after Domitian, who was the last of the 12 Caesars. He was a native of Narnia in Umbria; his family however was originally of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius says he was born on the 19th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, in the 18th year of Tiberius's reign, and of the Christian era the 32d. Nero in the 12th year of his reign made him praetor, and erected a statue for him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> on account of his poems (for he was one of the best poets of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>), some of which were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to him. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> in 71 with Vespasian, and in 90 with Domitian. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> authors uniformly celebrate him as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of a most mild and humane temper, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> moderation and generosity, who looked on his office as emperor, not as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was for his own advantage, but for that of his people; and whilst he reigned, which was however but for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his subjects his only end and pursuit. He narrowly escaped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> under Domitian; was naturally of a weak and timorous disposition; and, as some say, addicted to excessive drinking. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> unanimously chose him emperor; and they had no cause to repent of their choice, for he was constantly attentive to what could make them happy; he was generous, merciful, and disinterested. An instance of his great lenity appears in his pardoning Calpurnius Crassus who conspired against him. In short, he omitted nothing that might contribute to the restoring of the empire to its former lustre: recalling those who had been banished for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and redressing all grievances that came to his knowledge. He however found his strength failing, and that it would be impossible for him to finish his designs, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he adopted Trajan. After his death, which happened in the year 98, he was ranked among the gods. He was the first Roman emperor of foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>.

NERVES

Pages 400-400

in Anatomy, certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> glistering cords, proceeding from the brain and spinal marrow, and dividing into very small branches, which are sent off throughout all parts of the body; and which are found to be the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. NERVOUS FLUID. See ANATOMY Index.

NESSUS

Pages 400-400

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a celebrated Centaur, son of Ixion and a Cloud. He offered violence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEJANIRA">Dejanira</a>, whom <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> had entrusted to his care, with orders to carry her across the river Evenus. Hercules <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the distress of his wife from the opposite shore of the river, and immediately he let fly one of his poisoned arrows, which struck the Centaur to the heart. Nessus, as he expired, gave the tunic he then wore to Dejanira, afflicting her that from the poisoned blood which had flowed from his wounds, it had received the power of calling a husband away from unlawful loves. Dejanira received it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and this mournful present caused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hercules.—A river which separates Thrace from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>. It is also called Neftis, Neftos, and Neftus.

NESTOR

Pages 400-401

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a son of Neleus and Chloris, nephew to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELIAS">Pelias</a> and grandson to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. He had eleven brothers, who were all killed with his father by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. His tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> detained him at home, and was the cause of his preservation. The conqueror spared his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and placed him upon the throne of Pylos. He married Eurydice the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Clymenus; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, Anaxibia the daughter of Atreus. He soon distinguished himself in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; and was present at the nuptials of Perithous, when a bloody engagement took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the Lapithae and Centaurs. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pylos and Messenia he led his subjects to the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, where he distinguished himself among the rest of the Grecian chiefs, by eloquence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> displays his character as the most perfect of all his heroes; and Agamemnon exclaims, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had 20 generals like Nestor, he should soon see the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> reduced to ashes. After the Trojan war Nestor retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, where he enjoyed in the bosom of his family the peace and tranquility which were due to his wisdom and to his age. The manner and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> are unknown: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are all agreed that he lived three generations of men; which length of time is supposed to be 300 years, though more probably only 90 years, allowing 30 years for each <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. From that circumstance, therefore, it was usual among the Greeks and the Latins, when they wished a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and happy life to their friends, to wish them to see the years of Nestor. He had many children; two daughters, Pheidice and Polycaete; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sons, Perseus, Stratocles, Aretus, Echephron, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISISTRATUS">Pisistratus</a>, Antilochus, and Thryamedes. Nestor was one of the Argonauts, according to Valerius Flaccus, v. 380, &c.—A poet of Lyconia in the age of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus. He was father to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>, who under the emperor Alexander wrote some fabulous stories—One of the body guards of Alexander. Nestor, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> name is not known, was a native of Ruffia, and the earliest historian of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. He was born in 1056 at Bielozero; and in the 10th year of his age he assumed the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> in the convent of Petcheriski at Kiof, and took the name of Nestor. He there made a considerable proficiency in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; but seems to have formed his style and manner rather from the Byzantine historians, Cedrenus, Zonaras, and Syncellus, than from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> classics. The time of Nestor’s death is not ascertained; but he is supposed to have lived to an advanced age, and to have died about the year 1115. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, to which he has prefixed an introduction, which after a short sketch of the early state of the world, taken from the Byzantine writers, contains a geographical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Ruffia and the adjacent regions; an account of the Slavonian nations, their manners, their emigrations from the banks of the Danube, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>, and settlement in the several countries wherein their descendants are now established. He then enters upon a chronological <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of the Ruffian annals, from the year 858 to about 1113. His style is simple and unadorned, such as suits a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> recorder of facts; but his chronological exactness, though it renders his narrative dry and tedious, contributes to ascertain the era and authenticity of the events which he relates. It is remarkable (says Mr Coxe, from whom we have taken this narrative), that an author of such importance, whose name frequently occurs in the early Ruffian books, should have remained in obscurity above 600 years; and been scarcely known to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> countrymen, the origin and actions of whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> he records with such circumstantial exactness. A copy of his Chronicle was given in 1668 by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Radzivil to the library of Konigburg, where it lay unnoticed, till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great, in his passage through that town, ordered a transcript of it to be sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>. But it still was not known as the performance of Nestor; for when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a> in 1732 published the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a German translation, he mentioned it as the work of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> Theodosius of Kiof; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> which arose from the following circumstance: The ingenious editor not being at that time sufficiently acquainted with the Slavonian tongue, employed an interpreter, who, by mistaking a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, supposed it to have been written by a person whose name was Theodosius. This ridiculous blunder was soon circulated, and copied by many foreign writers, even long after it had been candidly acknowledged and corrected by Muller.

NESTORIANS

Pages 401-402

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, still said to be subsisting in some parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; whose distinguishing tenet is, that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> is not the mother of God. They take their name from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NESTORIUS">Nestorius</a> bishop of Constantinople, whose doctrines were spread with much zeal through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> promoters of the Nestorian cause was Barhumas, created bishop of Nisibis, A.D. 435. Such was his zeal and success, that the Nestorians, who still remain in Chaldea, Persia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and the adjacent countries, consider him alone as their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> and founder. By him Phrozes the Persian monarch was persuaded to expel those Christians who adopted the opinions of the Greeks, and to admit the Nestorians in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, putting them in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seat of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> authority in Persia, the see of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of the Nestorians has always filled even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.—Barhumas also erected a school at Nisibis, from which proceeded those Nestorian doctors who in the fifth and sixth centuries spread abroad their tenets through Egypt, Syria, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. He differed considerably from Nestorius, holding that there are two persons in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, as well as that the Virgin was not his mother, as God, but only as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The abettors of this doctrine refuse the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> Nestorians; alleging that it had been handed down from the earliest times of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the tenth century, the Nestorians in Chaldea, whence they are sometimes called Chaldeans, extended their spiritual conquests beyond Mount Imaus, and introduced the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> into Tartary properly so called, and especially into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Karii, bordering on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of China. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of that country, whom the Nestorians converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, assumed, according to the vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, the name of John after his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, to which he added... Nestorians added the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTER">Presbyter</a>, from a principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>; whence it is said his successors were each of them called Presbyter John until the time of Gengis Khan. But Molheim observes, that the famous Presbyter John did not begin to reign in that part of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> before the conclusion of the 11th century. The Nestorians formed so considerable a body of Christians, that the missionaries of Rome were industrious in their endeavours to reduce them under the papal yoke. Innocent IV., in 1246, and Nicolas IV., in 1278, used their utmost efforts for this purpose, but without success. Till the time of Pope Julius III., the Nestorians acknowledged but one patriarch, who resided first at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, and afterwards at Mosul; but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> arising among them, in 1551 the patriarchate became divided, at least for a time, and a new patriarch was consecrated by that pope, whose successors fixed their residence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> in the mountainous part of Persia, where they still continue, distinguished by the name of Simeon; and so far down as the last century, these patriarchs persevered in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the church of Rome, but seem at present to have withdrawn themselves from it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Nestorian pontiffs, who form the opposite party, and look with a hostile eye on this little patriarch, have since the year 1559 been distinguished by the general denomination of Elias, and re- side constantly in the city of Mosul. Their spiritual dominion is very extensive, takes in a great part of A- sia, and comprehends also within its circuit the Arabian Nestorians, and also the Christians of St Thomas, who dwell along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar. It is observed, to the lasting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Nestorians, that all the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> established in the East, they have been the most careful and successful in avoiding a mul- titude of superstitious opinions and practices that have infected the Greek and Latin churches. About the middle of the 17th century, the Roman missionaries gained over to their communion a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Ne- storians, whom they formed into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> church; the patriarchs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of which reside in the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMIDA">Amida</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIARBEKIR">Diarbekir</a>, and all assume the deno- mination of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>. Nevertheless the Nestorians in ge- neral persevere to our own times in their refusal to en- ter into the communion of the Roman church, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaties and alluring offers that have been made by the pope's legate to conquer their inflexible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>.

NESTORIUS

Pages 402-403

from whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Nestorian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> derive their name, was born in Germanica a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Antioch, where he was likewise baptized; and soon after his bap- tism he withdrew himself to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in the suburbs of that city. Upon his being admitted to the order of priesthood, he quickly acquired so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by the eloquence of his preaching, and the regularity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, that by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius he was deemed a fit person to fill the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> see in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and was accordingly consecrated bishop of Con- stantinople in the year 429. In one of his first sermons after his promotion, he publicly declared his intention to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon here- ties; and with that intolerant spirit which has so often disgraced the preachers of the mild <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, he called upon the emperor to free the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from heretics, promising to give him heaven as a reward for his zeal. To this spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> he added one, that, though carnal, he possibly judged of equal force:—"Join with me (said he) in war against them, and I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> assist you against the Persians." Although the wiser and better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his audience were amazed to see a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, before he had tasted (as the historian expresses himself) the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of his city, declare that he would per- secute all who were not of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAJORI">majori</a>- ty of the people approved of this discourse, and encour- aged him to execute his purpose. Accordingly, five days after his consecration, he attempted to demolish the church in which the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> secretly held their as- semblies; and he succeeded so far in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, that these people, growing desperate, set it on fire them- selves, and consumed with it some of the neighbouring houses. This fire excited great commotion in the city, and Nestorius was ever afterwards called an in- cendiary. From the Arians he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> against the Novatians, but was stopped in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> by the in- terposition of the emperor. He then let loose his fury upon those Christians of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Lydia, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, who celebrated the feast of Easter upon the 14th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; and for this unimportant deviation from the Ca- tholic practice, many of these people were murdered by his agents both at Miletum and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>.—One can- not be sorry that such a relentless persecutor should him- self be afterwards condemned as a heretic, for holding an opinion which no man who speaks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thinks with philosophical accuracy will now venture to controvert. This obnoxious tenet which produced a schism in the church, and was condemned by a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, was nothing more than that "the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> cannot with propriety be called the mother of God." The people being accustomed to hear this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, were much inflamed against their bishop, imagining that he had re- vived the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of Paulus Samotrenus and Photinus, who taught that Jesus Christ was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> man. The monks declared openly against him, and, with some of the most considerable men in Constantinople, separated themselves from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. Several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> wrote to him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> persuasions to acknowledge that Mary was the mother of God; and when he would not com- ply, they procured his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> in the council of Ephesus, which deprived him of his see. He then re- tired to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monastery at Antioch, whence he was taken four years afterwards by the emperor's order, and banished in 435 to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARSUS">Tarsus</a>. That city being taken and destroyed by the barbarians, he was removed to Panopolis, a city of Thebais; where he was not suffer- ed to remain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, but was compelled to go from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, till, being in one of his journeys mortally bruised by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> relieved him from the fury of his persecutors. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we examine such of his writings as remain, we shall find that he was very unjustly condemned. It ap- pears that he rejected the errors of Ebion, Paulus Sa- motrenus, and Photinus; that he maintained in express terms, that the divine Word was united to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in Jesus Christ in the most strict and intimate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> possible; that these two natures, in this state of union, make but one Christ and one person; that the properties of the Divine and human natures may both be attributed to this person; and that Jesus Christ may be said to have been born of a virgin, to have suffered and died; but he never would admit that God could be said to have been born, to have suffered, or to have died.—When we consider that every person partakes of the substance of his mother, and that it is this which constitutes the parental and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> relation between them, it is indeed surprising that the expression "Mother of God" should ever have been admitted into the Christian church, or that any man who understands the meaning of the words should condemn Nestorius for not having used them.

NESTUS

Pages 403-403
or Nessus, a river which separates Thrace from Macedonia. It falls into the Aegean sea near the island Thasos. It is sometimes called Neus and Nessus.

NET

Pages 403-404

a device for catching fish and fowl. See the article FISHERY. The taking fowls by nets is the readiest and most advantageous of all others, where numbers are to be taken. The making the nets is very easy, and what every true sportman ought to be able to do for himself. All the necessary tools are wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, of which there should be several of different sizes, some round and others flat; a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of round pointed and flat scissors; and a wheel to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> off the thread. The pack-thread is to be of different strength and thicknesses, according to the sort of birds to be taken; and the general size of the meshes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not for very small birds, is two inches from point to point. The nets should neither be made too deep nor too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, for they are then difficult to manage; and they must be verged on each side with twisted thread. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the thread is too bright and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and is therefore in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> to be altered. The most usual colour is the ruffet; which is to be obtained by plunging the net, after it is made, into a tanners pit, and letting it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> there till it be sufficiently tinged: this is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the net, since it preserves the thread as well as alters the colour. The green colour is given by chopping some green wheat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> it in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then soaking the net in this green tincture. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour is given in the same manner with the decoction of celandine; which gives a pale straw-colour, which is the colour of stubble in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> nets are to be used on ploughed lands, the green on grassy grounds, and the yellow on stubble lands. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">Day</a>-Net, among fowlers, a net generally used for taking such small birds as play in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> swoop either to prey, gig, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like; as larks, linnets, bunting, &c. The time of the year for using this net is from August to November; and the best time is very early in the morning: and it is to be observed, that the milder the air, and the brighter the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is, the better will be the sport, and of longer continuance. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where this net should be laid, ought to be plain champaign, either on short stubbles, green lays, or flat meadows, near corn fields, and somewhat remote from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages: you must be sure to let your net lie <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the ground, that the birds creep not out and make their escape.—The net is made of a fine pack-thread with a small mesh, not exceeding half an inch <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; it must be three fathoms long, and but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: it must be verged about with a small but strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>; and the two ends extended upon two small long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, suitable to the breadth of the net, with four stakes, tail-rings, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>.—This net is composed of two, which must be exactly alike; and are to be laid opposite to one another, so even and close, that when they are drawn and pulled over, the sides must meet and touch each other. You must stake this net <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with strong stakes, very stiff on their lines, so that you may with a nimble touch <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> them to and fro at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; then fasten your drawing-cord or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-lines (of which there must be a dozen at least, and each two yards long) to the upper end of the foremost staves: and so extend them of such a straitness, that with a little strength they may rise up in the nets and cast them over. Your nets being thus laid, place your gigs, or playing-wantons, about 20 or 30 paces beyond, and as much on this side your nets: the gigs must be fastened to the tops of long poles, and turned into the wind, so as they may play to make a noise therein. These gigs are a sort of toys made of long goose-feathers, like shuttle-cocks, and with little small tunnels of wood running in broad and flat swan-quills, made round like a small hoop; and so, with longer strings fastened to a pole, will, with any small wind or air, move after such a manner, that birds will come in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flocks to play about them. When you have placed your gigs, then place your stake; which is a small stake of wood, to prick down into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, having in it a mortice-hole, in which a small and slender piece of wood, about two feet long, is fastened, so as it may move up and down at pleasure: and fasten to this longer stick a small line, which, running through a hole in the stick above-mentioned, and so coming up to the place where you are to fit, you may, by drawing the line up and down with your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand, raise up the longer stick as you see occasion. Fasten a live lark, or such like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, to this longer stick, which, with the line making it to flit up and down by your pulling, will entice the birds to come to your net. There is another stake, or enticement, to draw on these birds, called a looking-glass; which is a round stake of wood, as big as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s arm, made very sharp at the end, to thrust it into the ground: they make it very hollow in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, above five fingers deep; into which hollow they place a three-square piece of wood about a foot long, and each two inches broad, lying upon the top of the stake, and going with a foot into the hollows: which foot must have a great knob at the top, and another at the bottom, with a deep flenderness between; to which flenderness you are to fasten a small pack-thread, which, running through a hole in the side of the stake, must come up to the place where you fit. The three-square piece of wood which lies on the top of the stake, must be of such a polite and evenness, and the foot of the socket so smooth and round, that it may whirl and turn round upon the least touch; winding the pack-thread so many times about it, which being suddenly drawn, and as suddenly let go, will keep the engine in a constant rotatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>: then fasten with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a> on the uppermost flat squares of the three-square piece, about 20 small pieces of looking-glass, and paint all the square wood between them of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and lively <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; which, in the continual motion, will give such a reflection, that the birds will play about to admiration until they are taken. Both this and the other stake are to be placed in the middle between the two nets, about two or three feet distance from each other; so that, in the falling of the nets, the cords may not touch or annoy them: neither must they stand one before or after another; the glass being kept in a continual motion, and the bird very often fluttering. Having placed your nets in this manner, as also your gigs and stakes, go to the further end of your long drawing lines and stake lines; and, having placed yourself, lay the main drawing line across your thigh, and, with your left, pull the stake line to throw the birds; and when you perceive them to play near and about your nets and stakes, then pull the net over with both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, with a quick but not too hasty motion; for otherwise your sport will be spoiled. See Plate CCCLXIX. where A shows the bodies of the main net, and how they ought to be laid. B, the tail lines, or the hinder lines, staked to the ground. C, the fore lines staked also to the ground. D, the bird stake. E, the looking-glass stake. G, the line which draws the bird stake. H, the line that draws the glass stake. I, the drawing, double lines of the nets, which pulls them over. K, the stakes which stake down the four nether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the nets and the two tail lines. L, the stakes that stake down the fore lines. M, the single line, with the wooden <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> to pull the net over with. N, the stake that stakes down the single line, and where the man should fit; and O, the gig. Net, Neat, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, something pure, and unadulterated with any foreign mixture. Thus, wines are said to be net when not falsified or balderdashied; and coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, &c. are net when the filth and ordure are separated from them. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> is said to be net when it has no flaws or flaws; a crystal, when transparent throughout. Net is also used for what remains after the tare has been taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of any merchandise, i.e. when it is weighed clear of all package. See Tare. Thus we say, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a> weighs 450 pounds; the tare is 50 pounds, and there remain net 400 pounds. Net Produce, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express what any commodity has yielded, all tare and charges deducted. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the Italian words netto proceduto, for net produce.

NETHERLANDS

Pages 404-405

anciently called Belgia, but since denominated Low Countries <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Netherlands, from their low situation, are situated between 2° and 7° of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 50° and 53° 30' of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude; and are bounded by the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the north, Germany on the east, by Lorraine and France on the south, and by another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of France and the British seas on the west; extending near 300 miles in length from north to south, and 200 miles in breadth from east to west. They consist of 17 provinces; 10 of which are called the Austrian and French Netherlands, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> the United Provinces. The greatest part of the Netherlands was conquered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and that part which lies towards <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in their subjection till the decline of that empire; after which the Franks became masters of it; and, under the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, it was part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a> or Austra. Towards the end of the 15th century Maximilian of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, son of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand III. acquired, by marrying the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, the duchies of Brabant, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIMBURG">Limburg</a>, and Luxemburg; the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, Burgundy, Hainault, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>; and the lordship of Friesland. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Austria, son to Maximilian and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, married Jane the daughter of Ferdinand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Arragon and of Isabella <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Castile; by which means their son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> inherited not only almost all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> countries then lately discovered in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, but also those noble provinces of the Netherlands, and was chosen emperor under the name of Charles V. Towards the latter end of the 1527, he added to his dominions the temporalities of the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> on both sides of the Yssel; and Henry of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, being distressed through <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the duke of Guelderland, and tired with the continued rebellion of his own subjects, surrendered to the emperor the temporalities of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, which was confirmed by the pope, and the states of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In 1536, Charles V. bought of Charles of Egmond the reverence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Guelderland and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> should die without issue. The same year the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a> took the oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, and submitted to Charles V. and in 1543 he put a garrison into the city of Cambrai, and built a citadel there. Having thus united the 17 provinces, as it were in one body, he ordered that they should continue for ever under the same prince, without being ever separated or dismembered; for which purpose he published in November 1549, with the consent and at the request of the states of all the provinces, a perpetual and irrevocable edict or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by which it was enacted, that in order to keep all those provinces together under one and the same prince, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of representation, with regard to the succession of a prince or princes, should take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for ever, both in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and collateral line, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> laws of some provinces to the contrary. Charles had even a mind to incorporate these provinces with the Germanic body, and to make of them a circle of the empire, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the circle of Burgundy, in order thereby to engage the princes of the empire to concern themselves for the preferment of those provinces. But the Netherlands, always jealous of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, did not seem to like that incorporation; and when they were demanded to pay their share towards the expenses of the empire, they refused it: whereupon the princes of Germany refused, in their turn, to take any part in the wars in Flanders, and looked upon those provinces as by no means belonging to the Germanic body. Philip of Austria and his son Charles, who were born in the Netherlands, had for these provinces that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> affection which men <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to have for their native country; and, knowing how jealous the inhabitants were of their liberty, and of the privileges granted to them by their former princes, they took great care to preserve them, and suffered willingly that the states, who were the guardians of the people's liberty and privileges, should in a manner share the supreme authority with them. Philip II., son to the emperor Charles V., had not the same affection for the Netherlands, nor those generous sentiments which his father had endeavoured to inspire him with. Being born in Spain of a Portuguese woman, he had no regard but for his native country; and, when he removed out of the Netherlands, he left them to the weak <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a woman, to the proud and haughty spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Grenville, and to the wild ambition of some lords of these provinces, who availing themselves of the imprudent conduct and continual blunders of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Spain, found their private <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the disturbances they could not fail to produce. Philip II., also, instead of the mild and moderate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> which his predecessors had successfully employed on many occasions, as best suiting the genius and temper of the people, had recourse to the most violent and cruel proceedings; which, far from curing the evil, served only to exasperate it more and render it incurable. The Spaniards, whom he sent thither, being born and educated in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> monarchy, jealous of the liberties and envious of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the people, broke through all their privileges, and used them almost after the same manner as they had done the inhabitants of their new and ill-gotten dominions in America. This treatment occasioned a general insurrection. The counts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOORN">Hoorn</a>, Egmont, and the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, appeared at the head of it, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>'s reformation gaining ground about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the Netherlands, his disciples joined the malecontents; whereupon King Philip introduced a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> in order to suppress them, and many thousands were put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, besides those that perished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; for these persecutions and encroachments had occasioned a civil war, in which several battles were fought. The counts Hoorn and Egmont were taken and beheaded; but the prince of Orange, retiring into Holland, with the assistance of England and France, preferred Holland and some of the adjacent provinces, which entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> for their mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> at Utrecht in 1579; and they have ever since been styled the United Provinces; but the other provinces were reduced to the obedience of Spain by the duke of Alva and other Spanish generals. However, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> privileges were in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> restored; every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was allowed its great council or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, whose concurrence was required to the making of laws, and raising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for the government, though these assemblies were too often obliged to follow the dictates of the court. The emperor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> II. endeavoured to deprive them even of the form of their free <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and he might very probably have succeeded, had he not attempted at the same time a reformation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The Austrian Netherlands are wholly Catholic, and so bigotted to the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, that though they had tamely submitted to many encroachments of the archducal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on their civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, no sooner did the monarch encroach upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the holy mother church than they resisted his authority, and claimed all their ancient privileges <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>. The same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and worship made them very lately contribute to expel from their territories the French whom they had invited to relieve them from the Austrian yoke. Thus her religious bigotry for once saved a free people from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod of despotism on the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the cruelties of frantic democrats on the other. The provinces under the government of France were, till the late revolution, under the same severe arbitrary dominion as the other subjects of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and they now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> the same miseries with the rest of the republic. The Spaniards continued possessed of almost eight of these provinces, until the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, general of the allies, gained the memorable victory of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAMILLIES">Ramillies</a>. After which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and great part of these provinces, acknowledged Charles VI. (afterwards emperor) their sovereign; and his daughter, the late empress queen, remained possessed of them till the war that followed the death of her father, when the French made an entire conquest of them, except part of the province of Luxemburg; but they were restored by the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle in 1748, and the French retained only Artois, the Cambresis, part of Flanders, part of Hainault, and part of Luxemburg, of which they have had the dominion now upwards of eighty years. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally fruitful, but differs in the several parts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> also differs in the several provinces; in those towards the south it does not differ much from that of England, though the seasons are more regular. In the northern provinces the winter is generally very sharp, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> sultry hot; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and excessive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> seldom continue above five or six weeks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is reckoned very wholesome, but is subject to thick fogs in winter, through the moistness of the country, which would be very noxious, were it not for the dry easterly winds, which, blowing off a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> continent for two or three months in the year, clear the air, and occasion very sharp frosts in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> and February; during which, the ports, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> shut up. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country is low and flat; for, except some small hills and a few rising grounds in Utrecht and Guelderland, and in the parts lying towards Germany, there is no hill to be seen in the whole 17 provinces. This is the reason why they have been called the Low Countries. French Flanders abounds in grain, vegetables, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and cattle, but is in want of wood. For the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the events which took place in the Netherlands during the French revolution, by which they were united to France, see FRANCE. For the Dutch Netherlands, see UNITED Provinces.

NETHINIMS

Pages 405-405

among the Jews, the poverty of the Gibonites, who were condemned by Joshua to be hewers of wood and drawers of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God.

NETOPION

Pages 405-405

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to a very fragrant and costly ointment, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the finest spicry ingredients. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, in his Treatise of the Diseases of Women, frequently prescribes the netopion in diseases of the uterus; and in other places he speaks of its being poured into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> as a remedy for deafness; these compositions, by their attenuating qualities, dividing the viscid and thick humours. The word netopion is also sometimes used to express the unguentum Ægyptiacum, and sometimes simply for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of almonds.

NETSE

Pages 393-393

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> in Germany, and the residence of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, who has a magnifi- cent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> here. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very wholesome, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are cheap; the inhabitants carry on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in wine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> suffered greatly by an inundation and fire in 1729. It was taken by the Prussians in 1741, who augmented the fortifications af- ter the peace in 1742, and built a citadel to which they gave the name of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is seated on a river of the same name, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 35. N. Lat. 50. 32.

NETTINGS

Pages 405-406

in a ship, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> made of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> seized together with rope yarn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twine, and fixed fixed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> and in the tops; they are sometimes stretched upon the ledges from the waft trees to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> trees, from the top of the forecastle to the poop, and sometimes are laid in the waft of a ship to serve instead of gratings. NETTLE. See URTICA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-Nettle. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> Index, and Animal-Flower. NETTLE-Tree. See Celtis, Botany Index.

NETTUNO

Pages 406-406

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma. It is but thinly peopled, though seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. The inhabitants are almost all hunters. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 57' N. Lat. 41° 30'.

NEUCHATTEL

Pages 407-408

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ruins near it, which show its former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and there are two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> churches, besides a castle where the governor resides. The town contains about 3000 inhabitants. It is situated partly on a small plain, between Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURA">Jura</a> and the lake of Neuchatel, which is 17 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; the side of the harbour is the usual walk of the inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of it too is built upon the side of the mountain; whence some of its streets are very steep. In this small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> several public works have lately been executed, which Mr Coxe thinks are far beyond the revenues, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even the wants, of such a little state. Among these he inflates a superb causeway and a town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> "built (says he) of such <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> materials, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was intended to survive to the most distant posterity, and to rival the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the much-famed Roman capitol." At the beginning of the 18th century, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> was very little followed in this town, owing to an absurd <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which prevailed among the inhabitants of its being disgraceful; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> is now extinguished, and the town in a much more flourishing situation than before. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> article of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> is wine, which is much esteemed; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of printed linens and cottons have been established with considerable success. The flourishing state of Neuchatel is principally owing to the benefactions of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Pury, late banker of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>. He was born at Neuchatel in 1700; but having received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> there, he quitted it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> poverty, and repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, where he served his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a>, but in what line is not mentioned. From Geneva he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he acted as clerk to a dealer in precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and acquired great reputation by estimating the value of diamonds at sight. After a long residence in England he went to Lisbon, where he carried on a very extensive commerce: and having been appointed court-banker, his fortune rapidly increased. His generosity, however, kept pace with his wealth; and he not only remitted large sums to Neuchatel while living, but left his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> his heir when he died.
