His contributions in all are estimated by Mr Coxe at 200,000l.; a considerable part of which has been employed in constructing the public works already mentioned. Neuchatel has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>: the first is composed of 40 persons, with two matters of the keys; the little council consists of 24 members, comprehending the mayor, who is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. These two councils assemble regularly every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> likewise assemble every month, to consult on affairs belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and to fill up the places of ministers that die. They choose a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> every year, who is president of the general assemblies, which are called clôtures; and sometimes he is confirmed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. E. Long. 7° 10' N. Lat. 47° 5'. Neuchatel, a sovereign county of Switzerland, bounded on the west by the Franche Comté, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the bishopric of Bâle, and on the east and south by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Vaud. (a) We have given this detail in Mr Coxe's own words, as it appears to us to deserve <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on account of the greatness of the project, which would have excited admiration had it been attempted by one enlightened by science and liberal arts, much more when it comes through the humble medium of a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>. It was never executed, as we are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> informed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who left St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a> about the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1793; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> remains, and is still shown. The same gentleman (we quote his own words) adds, "that every mechanic thinks it practicable; and that the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> is, that the empress would have built it, had she not found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for all her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in carrying on her warlike and diplomatic transactions with other courts." Neuchattel south by the cantons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> and Friburg. This principality of Neuchattel and Vallengin extend from the lake of Neuchattel to the borders of Franche Compte, being in length about 12 leagues, and fix in breadth. The plain with the lower part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> is occupied by the district of Neuchattel, but Vallengin is totally enclosed by Jura. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">Parallel</a> chains of these mountains run from east to west, forming several valleys in the most elevated parts. The lower grounds of this chain consist of arable lands and vineyards; the higher of large tracts of forest, which in many parts have been cleared and converted into pasture grounds, interspersed with fields of barley and oats. The inhabitants are numerous, and remarkable for their genius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> industry. It contains three cities, one town, 95 villages, and about 300 houses dispersed in the mountains. The inhabitants are all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, except two Roman catholic villages; and in 1529 they entered into a strict <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the cantons of Berne, Friburg, Soleure, and Lucern. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is healthy and temperate, but the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> not everywhere equally fertile; however, there are large vineyards, which produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine, which last is excellent. The pastures on the mountains feed a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle; there are plenty of deer in the forests; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abound with fish. The mildness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and agreeable situation of the inhabitants in general in these districts, is evident from the great increase of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in the space of 32 years. In 1752 they contained only 28,017 subjects and 4318 aliens; but in 1784 the number was augmented to 31,576 subjects and 9704 aliens; being an increase of near a fourth part in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The facility with which the burghership of Neuchattel is acquired, may also be accounted one of the means of augmenting its population; for between the years 1760 and 1770, the magistrates admitted 41 persons to this privilege; from 1770 to 1780, 46; from 1780 to 1785, 51; in all 138; many of whom had children before they purchased their burghership, and 38 of them were foreigners, either German, French, or Dutch. This country has experienced similar changes with the rest of Switzerland during the usurpation of the French.

NEUFCHATEAU

Pages 408-408

a commercial town of France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOSGES">Vosges</a>; formerly having an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of the nuns of St Clair, a commandery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of monks and nuns. It is seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which produces corn, wine, and all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, on the river Mouzon. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 45'. N. Lat. 48° 20'.

NEURADA

Pages 408-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 13th order, Succulente. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEUROPTERA

Pages 408-408

the name of one of the orders into which the class of insects is divided according to the Linnaean classification. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEUS MONS

Pages 393-393

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, at the foot of which stood <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITHACA">Ithaca</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of that name, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>.)

NEUTER

Pages 408-410

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, denotes a sort of gender of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>, which are neither masculine nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a>. See Gender. The Latins have three kinds of genders, masculine, feminine, and neuter. In English, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> tongues, there is no such thing as neuter nouns. See Noun. Verbs Neuter, by some grammarians called intransitive verbs, are those which govern nothing, and that are neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>. See Verb. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> expressed by the verb has no object to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon, but the verb alone supplies the whole idea of the action; the verb is said to be neuter: as, I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, thou yawns, he sneezes, we walk, ye run, they stand still. Some divide verbs neuter into, 1. Such as do not signify any action, but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; as albet, "it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>;" Neutral Salts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a situation, as sedet, "he sits;" or have some relation to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; as adele, "he is present;" or to some other state or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a>, as regnat, "he rules," &c. And, 2. Those that do signify actions, though those such as do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into any subject different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>; as to dine, to sup, to play, &c. But this latter kind sometimes cease to be neuter, and commence active; especially in Greek and Latin, when a subject is given them; as, vivere vitam, ambulare viam, pugnare pugnam. Thus the old French poets say, Soupirer son tourment; the English, to sigh his woer, &c. But this is observed only to obtain where something particular is to be expressed, not contained in the verb: as, vivere vitam beatam, to live a happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; pugnare bonam pugnam, to fight a good fight, &c. According to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> de Dangeau, verbs neuter may be divided into active and passive; the first, those that form their tenses in English, by the auxiliary verb to have; in French, by avoir. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, those that form them in English with the verb to be; in French être.—Thus, to sleep, to yawn, dormir, and eternuer, are neuters active.—To come, and to arrive, are neuters passive. Neutral Salts, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, compounded of an acid with any other substance capable of uniting with it and destroying its acidity, as sulphuric acid and soda, or Glauber's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, muriatic acid and soda, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salt. Neutrality, the state of a person or thing that is neuter, or that takes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with neither side. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_ABBEY">New <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, situated near Kilcullen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. It was founded by Rowland Eustace, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in this county; the tower is still standing, and some part of the abbey; the ruins of the rest have contributed to build several dwellings near it. In the inside Rowland Eustace and his lady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> buried; their figures, clothed in armour, are to be seen there. Near this is a handsome seat of the Carter family, on the opposite side of the river Liffey. Newark upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, in the county of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, is a great thoroughfare in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, 124 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It has bridges over the Trent, which forms an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> here, by dividing itself into two streams two miles above the town, which meet again two miles below it. A magnificent castle was built here in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Stephen, which held out stoutly in the barons wars for King John, who died here, October 19, 1216; and it also stood out for King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., to the last; but after he had put himself into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Scots <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> then before it, the governor by his order surrendered it, after which it was demolished.—It was situated near the river; the walls of the towers are very thick, and of a very great height; and were there no historical testimony, these remains are sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that it was formerly of great importance. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> before these ruins is a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a> green, and near it a manufactory of facking. The town being subject to inundations from the river Trent, and often from that circumstance made impassable, a turnpike road, at the instigation of a publican, was made about twenty years ago, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to be passed with safety in the greatest floods, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of brick being made in several places to carry off the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, constructed by Mr Smeaton, at the expense of £2,000. Near the town there is a bridge constructed for the same purpose, made mostly upon dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> arches. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which is reckoned one of the finest in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, was built by Henry VI. and has a lofty spire. Newborough, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWBURGH">Newburgh</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLESEY">Anglesey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, distant from London 254 miles, though but a small town, situated over against <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERNARVON">Caernarvon</a> in North Wales, about 17 miles southwest from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUMARIS">Beaumaris</a>, is governed by a mayor, two bailiffs, and a recorder. Its Welsh name is Rhôsffir, or Rhosfaer. Newburg, the name of several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Germany, two of which are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towns of duchies of the same name; one in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and the other in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWBURY">Newbury</a>, a town in the county of Berks in England, 16 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, and 56 from London, arose on the decay of Spinham-Land. Notwithstanding its name signifies New-Borough, it is as old almost as the Conquest. It made so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cloth formerly, that in the reign of Henry VIII. here flourished John Wincomb, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Jack of Newbury, one of the greatest clothiers that ever was in England, who kept 100 looms in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and in the expedition to Flodden Field against the Scots, marched with 100 of his own men, all armed and clothed at his own expense; and he built all the west part of the church. Also Mr Kenric, the son of a clothier here, though afterwards a merchant in London, left £4000 to the town, as well as £3000 to Reading, to encourage the woollen manufactory. It makes a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of shalloons and druggets, but not near so much broad cloth now as formerly; yet it is a flourishing town, with spacious streets, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> market place, in which is the guild-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. In the neighbourhood, on the banks of the Kennet, there is a stratum of petrified wood dug out for firing, where they frequently find trunks of large oaks yet undecayed, with petrified hazel nuts, fir cones, &c. with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and horns of stags, antelopes, &c. tusks of boars, and heads of beavers. The river Kennet, which abounds with excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, eels, and cray-fish, runs through the town; and here is plenty of all other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. It was made a corporation by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and is governed by a mayor, high <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, aldermen, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>-under-Line, a town in England, in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, on a branch of the Trent, is 15 miles north of Stafford, 33 south south-east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRINGTON">Warrington</a>, and 149 from London: had a castle, now in ruins; and is so called from an older castle, which formerly stood two miles off, at Chesterfield-under-Line. It was incorporated by King Henry I. and again by Queen Elizabeth and King Charles II., and is governed by a mayor, two justices, two bailiffs, and 24 common <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. The clothing trade flourishes here; but its chief manufactory is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, here being an incorporated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of felt-makers. A great quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> is made near this place. Newcastle on Tyne, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the county of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> in England, 15 miles north of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, 94 north of York, 63 south by east of Berwick, 60 east of Carlisle, and 271 from London, stands at the end of the Piets wall, on the north side of the Tyne, Newcastle over which it has a stately bridge into the bishopric of Durham, in which its suburb called Gatefide is situated; for the liberties of Newcastle extend no farther than the great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> gate upon the bridge which has the arms of the bishop of Durham carved on the east side and those of Newcastle on the west side. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. s. 27. N. Lat. 55. 3. It is admitted to have been a Roman station, though no evidence at present appears, except at Pandon-gate, whose superstructure is of different workmanship and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> from any others of the town, the arches being circular. The Carpenter's tower is also of Roman origin. In the Saxons' <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was called Moncalf, from the monks here, who all fled when it was depopulated by the Danes; and afterwards Newcastle, from a castle built here by William the Conqueror's son, Robert, in 1080, to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> against the Scots, whose kings had this town before the Norman conquest, and sometimes resided here. Several monasteries and houses were built here soon after the castle; and it was greatly enlarged and enriched by a good trade to the coasts of Germany, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of its coal to other parts of England; for which, and for other merchandise, it is become the great emporium of the north of England, it being the neatest and largest town in those parts, next to York. In the reign of Edward I. it was burnt by the Scots; but a very rich burglar who was taken prisoner, soon ransomed himself for a good sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and began the first fortifications of the place, which he extended from Sand-gate to Pampeldon, and thence to the Austin friars gate; which the townsmen finished, and encompassed with stout walls, which extended two miles, wherein are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> gates and many turrets, with several cafemats <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. To which two other gates were added in more modern times, viz. Bridge-gate and Sand-gate: the wall between them was afterwards removed to open the quay. Edward III. granted the corporation the duties and customs of the town for seven years, to enable them to complete the fortification. It is a borough at least as ancient as King Richard II. who granted that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> should be carried before the mayor; and King Henry VI. made it a town and county corporate of itself, independent of Northumberland. Henry VII. built a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> here for the Franciscans. Besides which, it had several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> foundations, several of which structures have been converted to companies halls and private residences. In the reign of Henry VIII. this place is said to have exceeded in the strength and magnificence of its works all the cities of England, and most places in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The town is governed by a mayor, 12 aldermen, a recorder, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, town clerk, a clerk of the chambers, two coroners, eight chamberlains, a sword-bearer, a water <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, and seven sergeants at mace. Its situation, especially the most bulky part of it towards the river, is very uneven, it being built on the declivity of a steep hill, and the houses very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. The castle overlooks the whole town. That part built by Robert was of great strength, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and surrounded by two walls; the square was 62 feet by 54, and the walls 13 feet thick, within which was a chapel. The outward fortifications are now defaced, and their site crowded with buildings. The tower remains entire, and situated on a lofty eminence, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> entrance is to the south. This castle belongs to the county, and makes no part of the liberties.—It is Newcastle now the county prison, and in the great hall the judges hold the assizes. Here Baliol king of Scotland did homage to King Edward I. in 1292; as did Edward Baliol in 1334 to King Edward III. Here is a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> and a customhouse; and a very fine quay. There is a handsome mansion house for the mayor, who is allowed 1000l. a-year, for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, besides a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COACH">coach</a> and barge. The old bridge was carried away in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and the present was erected about 1775, of nine noble elliptic arches. With the old bridge 22 houses were thrown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and six lives lost. It was originally built of wood; but having been destroyed by fire in 1248, was rebuilt of stone, and consisted of 12 arches, three of which on the north side were closed up, and served for cellars: this was again rebuilt about 1450, and was crowded with wooden buildings; but near the middle was a tower with an iron gate, used as a town prison. A strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> crossed the bridge, which was used as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>. On the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> was a statue of King Charles II. The water which destroyed this bridge, on November 11, 1771, was upwards of 12 feet above high water mark in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>.—On removing the foundations of the piers of the old bridge to erect the present, by observations made, and medals found, part of it is supposed to have existed from the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It is computed that above 6000 keelmen are employed here, who have formed themselves into a friendly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; and, by their own contributions, built a noble <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> containing 50 chambers, for such of their fraternity as are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, disabled, or past their labour; and it is supported by the contribution of those that are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The town is extremely populous; and, notwithstanding the multitude of those employed in and about the coal pits, with which the town is in a manner surrounded, has abundance of poor; but it has also many wealthy inhabitants, and it is said they pay above 4000l. a-year to their relief. It is observed, that this town has the greatest public revenue in its own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> as a corporation, of any town in England, it being computed at no less than 8000l. a-year. In 1774, the receipts of the corporation were 20,360l. gs. 8d.; and their disbursements about 19,445l. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants is about 36,891, exclusive of a number of seamen who cannot be accurately estimated. Here are four churches or chapels. That of St Nicholas is the mother church, a curious fabric, built <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>-wise by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> king of Scots, 240 feet long, 75 broad, and proportionably high, with a tower steeple 194 feet in height, of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; also St Andrew's, St John's, and All Saints, lately rebuilt on the site of the old structure, of a circular form. Here are also several meeting houses, and four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> for 300 children; a fine hall for the surgeons, and a large prison called Newgate; also a hospital for lunatics, another for the lying-in of married women, as well as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> raised for the relief of those who are delivered at their own houses. Here is a well endowed and large infirmary, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> room that attracts <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, containing every useful apartment, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>-room 93 feet by 40: The front is ornamented with six Ionic pillars, &c. In another part of the town is a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. Here is a very neat set of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. A free grammar school was granted by James I. from an old foundation

NEVA

Pages 406-407

a river at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>, in Russia. The views upon the banks exhibit the grandest and most lovely scenes. The river is in most places broader than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is deep, rapid, and transparent as crystal, and its banks are lined on each side with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> range of handsome buildings. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side the fortresses, the academy of sciences and that of art are the most striking objects; on the opposite side are the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, the mansions of many Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, and the English line, so called because (a few houses excepted) the whole row is occupied by the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of these buildings, on the south side, is the quay, which stretches for three miles, except where it is interrupted by the admiralty; and the Neva, during the whole of that space, has been lately embanked at the expense of the emperors, by a wall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, and pavement of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>; a most elegant and durable monument of imperial munificence. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the opposite sides of the river by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of pontoons, which when anything is apprehended from the force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> rushing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the stream, can be, and is generally indeed, removed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> depth of the river, it appears, prevents the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> bridge; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it could be built, there is no reason to suppose it could possibly resist the force of those vast shoals of ice which in the beginning of winter come down this rapid river. An attempt, however, has been made to remedy this inconvenience; and a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> has actually projected the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of throwing a wooden bridge of one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> across it, which in its narrowest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is 980 feet in breadth. As we think this is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of very considerable importance, as well as of curiosity, we shall give the following copious account of the plan and its author, in Mr Cox's own words; who tells us that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> had then executed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> 98 feet in length, which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> and examined with considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. "The bridge is upon the same principle with that of Shaffhausen, excepting that the mechanism is more complicated, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. I shall attempt to describe it by supposing it finished, as that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> convey the best idea of the plan. The bridge is roofed at the top, and covered at the sides; it is formed by four frames of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, two on each side, composed of various beams <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trusses, which support the whole machine. The road is not, as is usual, carried over the top of the arch, but is suspended in the middle. "The following proportions I noted down with the greatest exactness at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when they were explained to me by the artist: Length of the abutment on the north end, 658 feet. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">Span</a> of the arch, 980 feet. Length of the abutment on the south end, 658 feet. Length of the whole structure, including the abutments, 2296 feet. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the road upon its first ascent makes an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of five degrees with the ordinary surface of the river. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> level of the river to the top of the bridge in the centre, 168 feet. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">Ditto</a> to the bottom of the bridge in the centre, 126 feet. Height of the bridge from the bottom to the top in the centre, 42 feet. Height from the bottom of the bridge in the centre to the road, 7 feet. Height from the bottom of ditto to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, 84 feet. Height from the water to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the arch, 56 feet. So that there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of 35 feet between the road at the spring of the arch and the road at the centre; in other words, an ascent of 35 feet in half 980, or in the space of 490 feet, which is little more than eight tenths of an inch to a foot. The bridge is broadest towards the sides, and diminishes towards the centre. In the broadest part it is 168 feet. In the centre or narrowest part, 42 feet. The breadth of the road is 28 feet. "The artist informed me, that to complete the bridge would require 49,650 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> nails, 12,908 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trees, 5500 beams to strengthen them; and that it would cost 300,000 rubles or £6,000l. He speaks of this bold project with the usual warmth of genius; and is perfectly convinced that it would be practicable. I must own that I am of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, though I hazard it with great diffidence. What a noble effect would be produced by a bridge striking across the Neva, with an arch 980 feet wide, and towering 168 feet from the surface of the water! The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of such a bridge seems almost chimerical; and yet upon inspection of the model we become reconciled to the idea. But whether the execution of this stupendous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> may be deemed possible or not, the model itself is worthy of attention, and reflects the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> on the inventive faculties of that unimproved genius. It is so compactly constructed, and of such uniform solidity, that it has supported 3540 pood, or 127,440 pounds, without having in the least swerved from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, which I am told is far more, in proportion to its size, than the bridge if completed would have occasion to sustain from the pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> added to its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. "The person who projected this plan is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Russian peasant. This extraordinary genius was apprentice to a shopkeeper at Nizhni Novgorod: opposite to his dwelling was a wooden clock, which excited his curiosity. By repeated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> he comprehended the internal structure, and without any assistance formed one exactly similar in its proportion and materials. His success in this first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> urged him to undertake the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of metal clocks and watches." watches. The empress, hearing of these wonderful exertions of his native genius, took him under her protection, and sent him to England; from whence, on account of the difficulties attending his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, he soon returned to Russia. I saw a repeating watch of his workmanship at the Academy of Sciences: it is about the bigness of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; in the inside is represented the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of our Saviour, with the stone at the entrance, and the sentinels upon duty: suddenly the stone is removed, the sentinels <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> appear, the women enter the sepulchre, and the same chant is heard which is performed on Easter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>. These are trifling, although curious performances; but the very planning of the bridge was a most sublime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>. This person, whose name is Kulibin, bears the appearance of a Russian peasant: he has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, and wears the common dress of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He receives a pension from the empress, and is encouraged to follow the bent of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> genius.

NEVEL

Pages 407-407
or NEBEL, in the Jewish antiquities, a kind of musical instrument. See NABLUM.

NEVERS

Pages 407-407

a town of France, in the department of Nièvre, and situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 14' N. Lat. 46° 59', on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, which here receives the rivulet Nièvre, from which this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> derives its name. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, supposed to be Caesar's Noviodunum in Æduis, where he erected magazines for his armies. Francis I. made it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> and peerage in 1521, in favour of Francis of Céves, to whom it came by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. It devolved afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, and then to the Palatine family, who in 1651 sold it to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarine. The cardinal obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and peer for his nephew <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Mancini, in whose family it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the late revolution. The town is fortified with walls, defended with many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers and deep ditches, and is the seat of a bishopric, suffragan of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENS">Sens</a>, as likewise of a bailiwick and chamber of accounts. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> on the Loire, with 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, a draw-bridge on each side, and towers to defend them. This town is famous for its manufacture of glass and earthenware, and is said to contain about 8000 inhabitants. In the centre of Nevers, on the summit of a hill, is built the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dukes. It appears to have been constructed in the fifteenth century, and exhibits a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and delicacy of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The apartments are hung with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> of 200 years old, which have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> and rude magnificence.

NEVIS

Pages 408-408

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Montferrat, and separated from St Christopher's by a narrow channel. It makes a beautiful appearance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, being a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> conical mountain covered with fine trees, of an easy ascent on every side, and entirely cultivated. The circumference is about 21 miles, with a considerable tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground all around. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is reckoned to be warmer than Barbadoes, but it is more temperate towards the summit. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fine in the lower part, but grows coarser as we ascend. The productions are nearly the same with those of St Christopher's. There are three pretty good <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bays, with small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in their vicinity; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Town, Moreton <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>. This pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was settled under the auspices of Sir Thomas Warner from St Christopher's. His successor, Governor Lake, was considered as the Solon of this little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in which he disposed of every thing with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, as procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation with the French as well as English. In the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> they met with some disturbance from the French; but by being covered by an English squadron, the enemy were obliged to desist from their intended invasion, after a smart engagement in sight of the island. Sir William Stapleton sometimes resided here, and Sir Nathaniel Johnston constantly, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the inhabitants of Nevis were computed at 32,000. In the war immediately after the revolution, they exerted themselves gallantly, and had two regiments of 300 men each. In that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> they behaved equally well, though they were less fortunate; for the French landing with a superior force, and having inveigled most of their slaves, they were forced to capitulate. About 4000 of these slaves the French carried away and sold to the Spaniards, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, after making due inquiry into the losses they had sustained, voted them about a third part of the sum which they had suffered. These losses by war, an epidemic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and repeated hurricanes, exceedingly diminished the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the people. They are now thought not to exceed 2000 or 3000 whites, and 6000 blacks. There is here a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> governor, with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, which is composed of three members from each of the five parishes into which the island is divided. The commodities are cotton and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; and about 20 sail of ships are annually employed in this trade.

NEW STYLE

Pages 415-415

first used in England in 1753, was introduced into the western world by Pope Gregory XIII. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, No. 24.

NEWCASTLE

Pages 410-413

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, which returns two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and holds two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, 9th of May and 8th of October. NEWCASTLE is also the name of a handsome town- in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a> and province of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a>, 114 miles from Dublin. Here was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> possessed by the knights <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPLARS">templars</a>. It is said, they used some barbarous customs which greatly disgusted the Irish, who, watching a favorable opportunity, attacked a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the knights riding out together and put them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is still remembered where their remains were interred. This order was suppressed in the famous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, 22d of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1312. Newcastle consists of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> and fairs are held; on the northern side stands a market house, with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> room; on the south side is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which is the neatest in the county; it was finished in 1777 at the sole expense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Courtenay. It stands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the walls and fortifications of the knights templars, of which one of the castles is fitted up for Lord Courtenay's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. Newcastle, a small town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, 35 miles below <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, on the west <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> river. It was first settled by the Swedes about the year 1627, and called <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>. It was afterwards taken by the Dutch, and called New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. When it fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, it was called by its present name. It contains about 60 houses, which have the aspect of decay, and was formerly the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. This is the first town that was settled on Delaware river. Newcastle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of. See Cavendish. New England. See England, New. New Forest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> in England, is a tract of at least 40 miles in compass, which had many populous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, and 36 mother churches, till it was destroyed and turned into a forest by William the Conqueror. There are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> walks in it; and to every one a keeper, under a lord warden, besides two rangers, and a bow-bearer. As this large tract lay many ages open and exposed to invasions from foreigners, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. built some castles in it; and it has now several pretty towns and villages. It is situated in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Hampshire which is bounded on the east by Southampton river, and on the south by the British Channel. It possesses advantages of situation, with respect to the convenience of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> carriage and nearness to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCK">dock</a> yards, superior to every other forest, having in its neighbourhood several ports and places of shelter for shipping <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, among which Lymington is at the distance of only two miles, Bexley about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, and Redbridge three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four miles from the forest; and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, the most considerable dock yard in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, is only about 30 miles from the nearest of those places. This is the only forest belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of which the origin is known. Doomsday-book contains the most distinct account of its afforestation by William the Conqueror: the contents of every field, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, or estate afforested, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, carucates, or virgates, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> was then computed, together with the names of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> and villages, and of the former proprietors (which are for the most part Saxon), the rent or yearly value of each possession, and the tax which had been paid for it to the crown during the reign of Edward the Confessor, before the inhabitants were expelled, and that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> laid waste, are all to be found in that most curious and venerable record, New Forest. Wishing to discover the original extent of the forest, we extracted, for our own information, all that relates to it in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> survey. The extract is far too voluminous for insertion. The names of many of the places having been changed since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it is difficult to ascertain with precision what were then the limits of the forest. The oldest perambulation we have met with is among the Pleas of the Forest, in the eighth year of King Edward I., preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">Chapter</a>-house at Westminster. The boundaries there described include all the country from Southampton river on the east to the Avon on the west, following the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> as far as the southern boundary between those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and extending northwards as far as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Chafehead, or North Charford, on the west, and to Wade and Oarebrugg, or Owerbridge, on the east; and the greatest part, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the whole, of that extensive district, is mentioned in Doomsday book to be the forest belonging to the crown. Another perambulation was however made in the 29th of the same king, which leaves out a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the country contained within the former. This perambulation, which is preserved in the tower of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, confines the forest to limits which, as far as we can trace them, appear to have been followed in the 22nd year of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., when the forest was again perambulated. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">Charta</a> de Foresta, all lands not belonging to the crown which had been afforested by Henry II., Richard I., or King John, were to be disafforested; but as no provision was made for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the more ancient afforestations, it is easy to account for the great diminution of this forest in the reign of Edward I., who was not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> likely to submit to any encroachment on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>. The perambulation of the 22nd of Charles II. is the last which we find on record: it contains the present legal bounds of the forest, and was given to the surveyors as their guide, in taking the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which they have made lately by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. From that plan, with the approbation of the lords commissioners of his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, an engraving was made. According to the last-mentioned perambulation and the plan, the forest extends from Godshill on the north-west to the sea on the south-east, about 20 miles; and from Hardley on the east to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RINGWOOD">Ringwood</a> on the west, about 15 miles; and contains within those limits about 92,365 acres statute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. The whole of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, however, is not forest land, or now the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the crown: there are several manors and other considerable freehold estates within the perambulation, belonging to individuals, to the amount of about 24,797 acres; about 625 acres are copyhold or customary lands belonging to his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Lyndhurst; about 1004 acres are lease-hold under the crown, granted for certain terms of years, and forming part of the demised land revenue, under the management of the surveyor-general of crown lands; about 901 acres are purprelures or encroachments on the forest; about 1103 acres more are enclosed lands held by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-keepers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOM">groom</a>-keepers, with their respective lodges; and the remainder, being about 63,845 acres, are woods and waste lands of the forest. To perpetuate the spot where William Rufus was killed by the glance of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was erected in 1745. George III. visited <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. See Holland, New. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. See York, New. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>. See Zealand, New. New Years Gifts, presents made on the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the new year. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONIUS">Nonius</a> Marcellus refers the origin of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to Tatusius king of the Sabines, who reigned at Rome conjointly with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, and who having considered as a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a> a present of some branches cut in a wood consecrated to Sirenia, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of strength, which he received on the first day of the new year, authorized this custom afterwards, and gave to these presents the name of frena. However this may be, the Romans on that day celebrated a festival in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a>, and paid their respects at the same time to Juno; but they did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it in idleness, lest they should become indolent during the rest of the year. They sent presents to one another of figs, dates, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, &c. to show their friends that they wished for a happy and agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Clients, that is to say, those who were under the protection of the great, carried presents of this kind to their patrons, adding to them a small piece of silver. Under Augustus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, the knights, and the people, presented such gifts to him, and in his absence deposited them in the capitol. Of the succeeding princes some adopted this custom and others abolished it; but it always <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> among the people. The early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> condemned it, because it appeared to be a relic of Paganism and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; but when it began to have no other object than that of being a mark of veneration and esteem, the church ceased to disapprove of it.

NEWEL

Pages 413-413

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, is the upright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> which a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of winding stairs turn about; this is properly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which bears on the ground, and is formed by the end of the steps of the winding stairs.

NEWFIDLER-SEA

Pages 413-413

a lake in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, 17 miles in length and 6 in breadth.

NEWFOUNDLAND

Pages 413-414

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, lying between 46° 50' and 51° 30' N. Lat. and between 53° 30' and 58° 20' W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The form is that of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> triangle, the base <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> south side being 80 leagues in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; the east side is the longest; and the whole circumference about 150 leagues. It is bounded on the north by the straits of Belleisle, which separate it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABRADOR">Labrador</a>; on the east and south it hath the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, and on the west the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of St Lawrence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is rather severe; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, at least on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, which is all that we know of it, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and barren. A few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> vegetables, with strawberries and raspberries, are all its produce. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> within <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is mountainous, and abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; there are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which are plentifully stored with various sorts of fish, abundance of deep bays, and many good ports. St John's and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a> are the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> settlements, and at each of these there is a fort; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people who remain here in the winter hath been computed at 4000. The French, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, were permitted to fish from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONAVISTA">Bonavista</a> on the east side round the north of the island to Point Rich on the west; and by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, they are allowed the isles of St Pierre and Miquelon, upon which they are to dry their fish, but not to erect fortifications of any kind. The great importance of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> arises from its fishery, which is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> carried on by the inhabitants at the several harbours, which are about 20 in number, who take vast quantities of cod near the coast, which they bring in and cure at their leisure, in order to have it ready for the ships when they arrive. But the great and extensive fishery is on the banks at some distance from the island. The great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> lies 20 leagues from the nearest point of land from the latitude 41° to 49°, stretching 300 miles in length and 75 in breadth.—To the east of this lies the False Bank; the next is styled Vert, or the Green Bank, about 240 miles long, and 120 over; then Banquero, about the same size; the shoals of Sand Island, Whale Bank, and the Bank of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, with several others of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, all abounding with fish. The cod are caught only by a hook; an expert fisher <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> take from 150 to 300 and upwards in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; for the fish never bite in the night: the labour is very great. The season is from May to October, in the height of which there are from 500 to 700 sail upon the banks at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The fish caught in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> months are best; they are cured in very different ways. Some are styled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fish, others mud fish, which are flowed and salted in the hold, and will not keep long; but the best and most valuable are the dried cod. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> taken is prodigious: yet in some seasons and in different places varies considerably, as the fish frequently change their stations. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> ships, as they are called, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> upon the banks, with the help of their boats take and cure their own fish, and as soon as they are full sail for a market. The pack ships proceed directly to the island, where they purchase fish from the inhabitants either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> or bills of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> for cod are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the West Indies. The value of this fishery is computed at some hundred thousand pounds annually; employing, besides several hundred ships, some thousands of seamen, and affording a maintenance to a number of tradesmen of different occupations, by which many large <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the west side of England accumulate much wealth, and at the same time contribute in many respects to the benefit of the public. The great utility of this fishery was very early seen, and very vigorously pursued; for in the beginning of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. we had two hundred and fifty sail employed therein. It is computed, that three quintals of wet fish make one quintal of dried cod. Besides, the Evers of every hundred quintals make a hoghead of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; and exclusive of these there are many lesser advantages that go in diminution of the expense. The fishery, as we have said above, produces differently in different seasons; but it is judged to be a very good one when it produces 300,000 quintals of fish and 3000 barrels of oil, both equally saleable and valuable commodities. As every ship carries twelve, and each of their boats eight men, and as these return home in six months, there cannot be a more noble nursery for seamen. Newfoundland-seamen. The artificers and traders employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, victualling, and repairing these vessels, are very numerous in the respective ports from which they sail. These circumstances justify the particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> paid by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to this branch of the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; in respect to which that they may be well informed, an annual and very distinct account, by which the whole is seen at one view, is delivered by the proper officer to the governor of Newfoundland, that is, to the commodore of his majesty's squadron. Mr Pennant, in the appendix to his Arctic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, gives us, from what appears to be very good authority, the following account of this island. "Within the circuit of 60 miles of the southern part, the country is hilly, but not mountainous. The hills increase in height as they recede from the sea; their course is irregular, not forming a chain of hills, but rising and falling abruptly. The coasts are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the shores most remarkably bold. The same may be said of almost every part of this vast island. The country is much wooded, and the hills (such as have not flat tops to admit the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> to stagnate on them) are clothed with birch, with hazel, spruce, fir, and pine, all small; which is chiefly owing to the inhabitants taking off the bark to cover the fish stages. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> is so indented by the fine and deep bays of Placentia, St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">Conception</a>, and Trinity, that it may be penetrated in all parts, which is done for the sake of fowling, or the procuring of fish for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, ears, &c. The island is on all sides pierced with deep bays, which penetrate it in many places by isthmuses most remarkably narrow.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> on the south-west side, near the sea, are very high, and terminate in lofty headlands; such as Chapeau Rouge, a most remarkably high promontory, Cape St Mary's, and Cape le Hane. Such in general is the formation of the island; on the north-east, most of the hills in the interior part of the country terminate pyramidically, but form no chain. The interior parts of the country consist chiefly of morasses, or dry barren hammocks, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> land, with frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> or ponds, and in some places covered with stunted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spruce. The rivers of Newfoundland are unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, but they are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in floating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the wood with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> floods. Still the rivers and the brooks are excellent guides for the hunters of beavers and other animals, to penetrate up the country, which as yet has never been done deeper than 30 miles. Near the brooks it is that timber is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> met with, but seldom above three or four miles inland, and in valleys; the hills in the northern district being naked and barren. "In some parts of Newfoundland there is timber sufficiently large for the building of merchant ships: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HULK">hulk</a> is made of juniper, and the pine furnishes masts and yards; but as yet none has been found large enough for a mast for a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a>. The fishery is divided into two seasons; that on the shore, or the shore season, commences about the 20th of April, and ends about the 10th of October; the boats fish in from four to 20 fathoms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The most important, the bank fishing season, begins the 10th of May, and continues till the last of September, and is carried on in 30 to 45 fathoms depth of water. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANKING">Banking</a> vessels have sailed from St John's to the bank as early as the 12th of April. At first they use pork or birds for a bait; but as they catch fish, they supply themselves with a Newmarket shell fish called clams, which is found in the belly of the cod. The next bait is the lobster; after that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>, which last till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, when the capelan comes on the coast, and is another bait. In August the squid comes into use, and finally the herring again. The greatest number of cod fish taken by a single fisherman in the season has been 12,000, but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> is 7000. The largest fish which has been taken was four feet three inches long, and weighed 40 pounds. A banking vessel of 12,000 fish ought to be filled in three weeks, and so in proportion; and 80 quintals (112 lb. each) for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> in the same time. "In 1785, 541 English vessels fished on the bank, a number exceeding that of the French. A heap of dried fish, 20 feet long and ten wide, and four deep, contains 300 quintals. Such a heap settles, in the course of 48 hours after it is made, about ¼. An extraordinary splitter will split five quintals of fish in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The average in that time is two. There is no fishing during winter, on account of the inclemency of the season. It is supposed that the fish in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> quit the banks before that time, as in general they are very scarce when the fishing vessels go upon the banks early in the spring. "There are a few small towns on the coasts, which have gardens sown with English <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>; but many of the inhabitants quit the country in winter. "An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> or some sea officer is generally governor of Newfoundland."

NEWMARKET

Pages 414-414

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, 13 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, 13 from St Edmundsbury, and 60 from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is a town with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> street, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, the south side in Cambridgeshire. It is a healthy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> thoroughfare in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from London to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>; but stands mostly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races every year in April and October, here being the finest course in England; on which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> when he comes to the races, which was built by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. The king gives a plate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two every year, besides those given by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; and wagers are laid upon the horses, which are seldom under 500l. and often above 1000l. Here are two coffeehouses, at which, every night and morning during the races, there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, as there is also at the houses of the nobility and gentry. Here are also cock matches. Here is a little chapel, which is a chapel of ease to the mother <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Ditton; and another in the Suffolk side, which is parochial. The town was burnt in 1683, but soon rebuilt.

NEWROSS

Pages 414-414

a borough town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEXFORD">Wexford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, 67 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. This town was formerly walled, and some of the gates still remain. It lies on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>, which is here very deep, and ships of burden can come up to the quay even when the tide is out. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but the customhouse and quay are both small, and sometimes overflown many feet. It is one of the staple ports for exporting <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, yet its trade is but inconsiderable; beef and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> exported. Here is a barrack for a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and a good ferry into the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILKENNY">Kilkenny</a>. Near this town is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> school. It is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> town, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Gore. It was formerly fortified, and adorned with

NEWSPAPERS

Pages 414-415

periodical publications, daily, weekly, &c., for the purpose of communicating to the world every thing of importance, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> literary, &c., which is going on.
